Google SecOps

Feature

Specify whether to reopen closed cases when the grouping is by Source Grouping Identifier

You can now specify whether Google SecOps reopens closed cases when grouping SOAR alerts by Source Grouping Identifier. When the option is enabled and a new alert is received with a source grouping identifier of a case that was previously closed in Google SecOps, then Google SecOps reopens the case. For more information, see Configure alert grouping.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.22

We've released version 6.22 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Transcript separation for chat

You can now configure Google Cloud CCaaS to deliver a separate transcript file for each participant segment in a chat, instead of one combined transcript per session. Under Settings > Chat > Chat Transcript, select Per Segment in Transcript Separation to generate individual transcript files for each agent, virtual agent, or supervisor who joins the chat—helpful for identifying which participant handled each part of a transferred or escalated conversation. Your consumers still receive a single, full-chat transcript regardless of this setting.

For more information, see Chat transcripts and chat history.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Campaign-based scheduled callbacks

Agents can now schedule a callback during an outbound campaign call. The callback belongs to the campaign, not to an individual agent, and the dialer calls the consumer back in the time slot they chose. Administrators set slot length, capacity, booking window, and expiry for each campaign, and supervisors can track upcoming, completed, and expired callbacks from the campaign list.

For more information, see Campaign management.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where direct access point (DAP) greeting messages played twice when a call was deflected to an internal phone number due to queue overcapacity.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata for top-level menu paths and selected menus was incorrectly displayed in English instead of the user's configured language.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed Salesforce lookup was incorrectly treated as having no matches, which resulted in the creation of duplicate records.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound transfer restrictions remained in force even after being hidden in the administrator interface, causing queues to become silently unreachable for transfers.

  • Fixed an issue where hold music continued to play throughout a call recording after a warm transfer was completed.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound virtual agent audio was prematurely truncated during multi-message turns.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Monitoring Queues report didn't accurately count skill-matched agents for skills-based queues, often displaying zero available agents despite their availability.

  • Fixed an issue where calls deflected to an external phone number after entering a queue were incorrectly recorded as abandoned by the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where the credit card tokenizer was missing from the SmartActions menu during outbound callback calls.

  • Fixed an issue where mandatory call dispositions were discarded if an agent's voice connection dropped but their session remained active.

  • Fixed an issue where the text resize menu in the chat widget wasn't scrollable at 400% browser zoom, which prevented users from accessing all available text size options.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly prevented saving automatic call redirection settings when the target was a virtual agent-operated queue.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate call records were created for a single inbound call, causing incorrect wait times to appear in the real-time queue view.

  • Fixed an issue where empty data attributes caused an error in the agent interface during call connections.

  • Fixed an issue where the Transfer Restrictions destination picker provided no feedback when a queue was ineligible, making it indistinguishable from a typo or search error.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls were rejected with a SIP 603 error due to high database latency and connection timeouts.

  • Fixed an issue where the documentation for the Apps API and call session metadata schema didn't define the top-level parentId and finishReason fields.

  • Fixed an issue where certain inbound call failures were incorrectly reported as a busy signal.

  • Fixed an issue where the event processor service crashed during scaling or rebalancing of the system.

  • Fixed an issue where the conversation ID was missing from chat events during active sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where report exports didn't download or remained stuck in a processing state indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where agents could transfer calls to queues that were already closed if their transfer list was loaded while the queue was still open.

  • Fixed an issue where queued chats were assigned to agents after the end-user had become unresponsive without being prompted to check in.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls cold-transferred to an over-capacity queue generated duplicate reporting records and incorrect queue wait times if the callback leg failed.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls deflected to voicemail during after-hours played three separate audio prompts sequentially.

  • Fixed an issue where a single call was simultaneously assigned to two different agents if the pickup coincided with the cascade timer expiry.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls weren't projected to agents in a breakthrough-enabled status if another call was already waiting in their queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a gray empty area appeared below the chat container in the agent adapter when the iframe width was narrower than 449px.

  • Fixed an issue where several Kubernetes and Google Cloud service accounts were granted overly broad permissions, which could have allowed for unauthorized privilege escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's status sequence was recorded in the incorrect order following a brief connection loss during an active chat.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting a contact during a native campaign call didn't automatically open the corresponding record in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where AI-generated Smart Disposition suggestions were inconsistently displayed for outbound calls during the wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings became distorted or garbled when multiple holds were placed during a call.

  • Fixed an issue where audio uploads were accepted based on the file extension rather than the actual file content, which caused call disconnections when incompatible formats were played.

  • Fixed an issue where the call duration timer in the external call adapter didn't match the In-call status timer in the agent desktop for inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue where the sentiment score was incorrectly displayed in the call adapter for calls escalated from a virtual agent, even when the Sentiment Analysis setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate reporting rows were generated for call and wrap-up durations due to concurrent system events.

  • Fixed an issue where agents couldn't sign in or refresh their status if their account was linked to a deleted or unknown status.

  • Fixed an issue where the Manager API documentation for agent activity logs omitted 17 chat routing and activity values, leading to incomplete reporting data for customers.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR custom callback numbers for certain international regions, including Norway and Denmark, were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix.

  • Fixed an issue where metadata for calls deflected between virtual agent assignment and connection wasn't exported to the Cloud Storage bucket.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent to human chat escalations experienced delays of up to 300 seconds during agent assignment.

  • Fixed an issue where the Answer button didn't appear for dial-by-extension calls when other calls were already waiting in an agent's queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a supervisor's name didn't appear in the chat widget when joining a conversation using the monitor then barge workflow.

  • Fixed an issue where ending a chat session in one browser tab didn't automatically close the chat widget in other open tabs.

title: October 22, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 22, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-7).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
573663408 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the ingress gateway to patch security vulnerabilities.
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
568535165 Skip main_task_wait_time and nio_task_wait_time metrics for the first 12 Prometheus scrapes during Message Processor startup warmup.
573602919 Fix generated OpenAPI specs' servers[] to carry the Apigee envgroup hostname instead of the backend target host.
562964081 The sgpUserIntentMatchingMode verdict-log field is now always present, including on dry-run policy records, and shows the mode used for the evaluation, including when sgpUserIntentMatching isn't set (CONSTRAINTS_AND_INTENT, or INTENT_ONLY when no policies match the tool call).
524115876 Fix an intermittent HTTP 400 error in the OASValidation policy's strict parameter validation that rejected valid requests.
572025634 Responses with a compressed text/event-stream body to a proxy with an EventFlow now skip EventFlow processing and pass through intact instead of returning a corrupted body.
549078690 If no SGP policy is attributed for a denial, a customer sees the generic fallback message. This fix short-circuits to show the rationale instead when no matched policy has a configured denial message.
492041991 VerifyAPIKey and VerifyAccessToken now set the apiproduct.operation.llmTokenQuota.* flow variables only from the LLM operation(s) that matched the request; they are no longer set from unmatched LLM operations or for requests that match no LLM operation.
567244615 Semantic Governance now evaluates LLM requests it previously skipped, such as OpenAI requests whose message content is an array of parts, which can produce new denials and judge-model usage. It considers every system message rather than only the last, and a non-streaming OpenAI or an Ollama tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON is now an evaluation error.
567244615 Semantic Governance no longer evaluates a request or response with a field it cannot read when a tool call is involved. It records verdict ERROR naming the field, with status MODEL_ERROR. The inline SemanticGovernance policy instead raises GovernedLLMResponseParseError or GovernedLLMProviderDetectionFailed (HTTP 500), in DRY_RUN too unless continueOnError is true. It also reads every text part of a Gemini system instruction and Gemini tool parameters given as parametersJsonSchema, and no longer loses the rest of a Claude or Gemini request when one field has an unexpected shape.
560272924 Added continuous-scan bidirectional gRPC streaming support for the SanitizeModelResponse policy over Server-Sent Events (SSE) streams, preserving native LLM provider SSE JSON envelopes and event framing.
555332621 Model Armor policies now honor HTTPClient.managementplane.skip.proxy: with it set, Model Armor callouts bypass the forward proxy like other googleapis traffic. Streaming (ContinuousScan) Model Armor traffic uses the forward proxy.
158204922 VerifyJWT now rejects a JWT whose header contains "b64":false, with fault steps.jwt.InvalidToken, as RFC 7797 section 7 requires. Previously, such a token could be accepted if KnownHeaders listed b64, IgnoreCriticalHeaders was true, or the header had no crit.
158204922 GenerateJWS supports RFC 7797 unencoded payloads. GenerateJWS now raises MissingPayload, InvalidPayload or FailedToResolveVariable for payload errors, where it previously raised GenerationFailed. KnownHeaders and CriticalHeaders in the JWS and JWT policies accept names separated by whitespace, such as one per line. A b64 header supplied through AdditionalHeaders is now rejected, with steps.jws.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWS and steps.jwt.InvalidNameForAdditionalHeader for GenerateJWT. A proxy that set b64 through an AdditionalHeaders variable produced an RFC 7797 JWS before this change, and must move to UnencodedPayload, with DetachContent for the detached form.
158204922 VerifyJWS verifies RFC 7797 unencoded-payload JWS (b64:false), attached or detached. b64 in crit no longer needs a KnownHeaders entry. VerifyJWS rejects b64:false unless crit lists b64, with the new fault steps.jws.UnencodedPayloadNotCritical; IgnoreCriticalHeaders does not change that. DecodeJWS reports the raw payload of such a JWS.
559228730 ext_proc: ImmediateResponse now carries any Content-Type (raw body bytes + preserved Content-Type); replies too large to buffer use StreamedImmediateResponse.
544751120 Semantic Governance Policies marked as dry run are now evaluated and logged without blocking the request. Each dry-run policy adds a second judge evaluation per tool-calling response, whose tokens are billed. Dry-run verdicts are written to the semantic-governance-policy log as separate records flagged sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation=true; queries that count verdicts should add sgpDryRunPolicyEvaluation != true to exclude them.
554114419 Fixed: an AssignMessage/HTTPModifier/RaiseFault policy that creates a new request (createNew="true") in an HTTP/2 flow can now set the :path and :authority pseudo-headers instead of failing with an invalid-header error.
567812025 FILESYSTEM persistence mode makes the synchronizer skip Cassandra entirely (no connections, reads, writes, or datastore health probes).
559009293 Fixed elevated OAuth latency and Cassandra read load for AppGroup apps, including access token verification and token and authorization-code generation, by caching AppGroup lookups in the message processor runtime, matching Developer behavior.
568860869 Fixed RegularExpressionProtection patterns of the form "...." whose middle section contains regular expression syntax (for example, ".?Exception in thread." or "(?i).<script.>.*") being matched as literal text instead of as regular expressions. Such patterns now raise steps.regexprotection.ThreatDetected for all matching input.
564945600 Enhance VerifyAPIKey policy to better handle leading spaces.
502231886 Fixed the default source templates for SanitizeUserPrompt and SanitizeModelResponse so a policy that omits the source element extracts content correctly when IgnoreUnresolvedVariables is false.
562964081 Semantic Governance now honors the sgpUserIntentMatching AuthzExtension metadata key (ENABLED or DISABLED) to toggle user-intent matching in policy evaluation; DISABLED evaluates against constraints only.
565004219 Fixed Semantic Governance Policy skipping evaluation for Anthropic requests that send system as a content-block array (the form ADK and LiteLlm emit). Affected agents are now evaluated, which may produce new denials and new judge-model usage on the consumer project.
527517087 SGP policy logs written to your project now identify their originating region. resource.type changes from "global" to "generic_node" and the region appears in resource.labels.location. Anything selecting these entries by resource.type="global" must be updated -- including log-based metrics, sinks, exclusion filters and alerts, which stop matching silently rather than erroring.
575439485 JavaCallout policies that run remotely (per-contract offload) can now pass every value type allowed by the GCP-2025-023 setVariable restriction between policies (collections, maps, arrays, primitive wrappers including Character, Date, BigDecimal, UUID, java.time, atomics, JDK enums, Optional), with their types preserved, instead of failing with steps.remotepolicy.NonSerializableVariable.
575439485 Remotely executed (per-contract offload) JavaCallout policies with continueOnError="true" now continue the flow when the callout faults, instead of returning HTTP 500.
567244901 In enforce mode, Semantic Governance now blocks a tool call when the governance check cannot be completed, instead of letting it through.
573622417 Fixed an issue where istio-ingressgateway forwarded the x-envoy-decorator-operation header to upstream runtime and target backends.
571679067 removes old version of ApigeeTelemetry CRD.
571378258 The Apigee Redis container is now built from the Valkey engine (BSD-3-Clause, Linux Foundation) at version 8.1.10. Wire protocol is unchanged (RESP2) and the redis-server/redis-cli binary names are preserved.

Data Studio

Feature

You can connect Data Studio to a BigQuery Graph or query a graph by using a custom SQL query in the BigQuery connector, which imports graph measures as metrics that you can use in your reports. For more information, see Connect to Google BigQuery.

Firestore

Feature

Data modification language (DML) operations are generally available (GA). Added support for insert and upsert.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Single-user quota limits

Gemini Enterprise administrators can configure single-user quota limits on the Usage & Spending > Usage page in the Google Cloud console to prevent an individual user from using all of an edition's shared subscription quota pool. You can enable a single-user quota limit and set a quota multiplier for each edition and location across the Gemini Enterprise Standard, Gemini Enterprise Plus, and Gemini Enterprise Standard Emerging Market editions.

This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see:

  • Single-user quota limits
  • Configure a single-user quota limit
  • Configure pay-as-you-go usage above quota

Announcement

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon becomes the default model for AlphaEvolve on October 26, 2026

On October 26, 2026, Gemini 4 Argon will replace Gemini 3.8 Flash as the default model for new AlphaEvolve experiments. AlphaEvolve uses the default model when you don't specify a model in the models field of generationSettings.

From that date, new experiments that use the default model are billed at Gemini 4 Argon token prices instead of Gemini 3.8 Flash token prices. To keep using Gemini 3.8 Flash, specify gemini-3.8-flash in the models field.

Experiments created before October 26, 2026 keep the model recorded in their configuration.

For more information, see Default model.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards prerelease notes 6.24

Here are the pre-release notes for updates to the advanced reporting dashboards and other reporting in CCAI Platform. When we release these updates, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Important: The next version of the advanced reporting dashboards could be greater than 6.24.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where call and chat type names were cut off in the Dashboard Reports selector on wide-screen displays.

  • Fixed an issue where the Individual Call History and Individual Chat History reports, run for all agents, left out calls and chats that were never assigned to an agent (for example, abandoned, deflected, or expired calls) when only one agent or no agents had activity in the selected period. The All Call History and All Chat History files are now always included.

  • Fixed an issue where the Interactions Detail by Agent report omitted outbound calls placed without a queue when generated for all agents.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Queue Monitoring and Campaign dashboards incorrectly displayed English queue names for French and Spanish interactions.

  • Fixed an issue where "wrap-up" and "hold" metrics in advanced reporting were displayed with inconsistent and inaccurate French Canadian (fr_CA) translations.

  • Fixed an issue where Spanish chat queues incorrectly displayed English names in Real-time Queue Monitoring and advanced reporting dashboards.

  • Fixed an issue where call disposition fields appeared blank on dashboards when viewing date ranges between 46 and 365 days.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware 1.34.1000-gke.111 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud 1.34.1000-gke.111 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.7-gke.200.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for use with GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.1000-gke.111:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where updating or upgrading a cluster to an advanced cluster failed to join control plane nodes if the cluster's certificate authorities (CAs) were previously rotated. For more information, see Control plane nodes fail to join during an update or upgrade to an advanced cluster after CA rotation.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.34.1000-gke.111 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.34.1000-gke.111 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.7-gke.200.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for installations or upgrades with the GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Feature

The following features were introduced in 1.34.1000-gke.111:

  • Fixed an issue in clusters using bundled BGP load balancing where control plane upgrades or configuration updates could cause up to 20 seconds of API server connection failures while a control plane node restarted. After the fix, failover to a healthy control plane node completes in approximately 4 seconds.
  • Fixed an issue where the NodePool controller prematurely updated Status.ManagedFields on partial reconciliation failures, causing removed taints and labels to remain stranded on affected nodes.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.1000-gke.111:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed BareMetalMachine conditions during maintenance mode transitions.
  • Fixed an issue where updating control plane configurations caused multiple API servers to restart simultaneously, leading to transient control plane unavailability.

This note is missing a fix included in 1.34.1000-gke.111. See entry for October 26, 2026.

Google SecOps

Feature

Bulk case selection

In the enhanced Investigation Management experience, you can select up to 50 cases at a time in the case queue to perform bulk operations:

  • Range selection: Hold Shift while clicking to select a range of cases.
  • Select all: Click the header checkbox to select up to 50 loaded cases; this action automatically scrolls your view back to the top of the list.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.26

We've released version 6.26 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Scheduled callback for IVR overcapacity

Scheduled callback is now available as an overcapacity deflection option for IVR queues. When a queue is over capacity, callers can choose to schedule a callback. Google Cloud CCaaS then hands the call to your configured virtual agent, which books the callback through the Callback call API. Administrators choose the virtual agent, an optional greeting, and the data parameters to pass at the global or queue level. Reporting shows whether each caller submitted a callback or left without one.

Administrators: You can configure scheduled callback for overcapacity deflection globally at Settings > Call > Overcapacity Deflection, or per queue at Settings > Queue > IVR (Interactive Voice Response) > Edit / View > [QUEUE] > Overcapacity Deflection > Configure.

For more information, see Overcapacity deflection per-queue and Callback call API.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Feature

Salesforce: PKCE and refresh token rotation support

You can now connect Google Cloud CCaaS to Salesforce apps that require Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) and refresh token rotation. Salesforce turns both settings on automatically for newly created connected apps and external client apps. Google Cloud CCaaS uses PKCE when authorizing Salesforce administrator and agent connections. It also saves replacement refresh tokens returned by Salesforce, keeping connections working across subsequent token refreshes. Salesforce apps that don't use these settings keep working as before. This update adds no new configuration steps in Google Cloud CCaaS.

For more information, see Salesforce integration guide.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Branded caller ID label was truncated in the Outbound Number selector when the agent application language was set to French Canadian.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound calls experienced significant delays in connecting after being assigned to an agent.

  • Fixed an issue where whisper announcements played more than once and the call panel was slow to load in the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce case creation was delayed until the end of a call for inbound callers without a matching contact record.

  • Fixed an issue where callbacks to Norwegian, Danish, and Swedish landline numbers were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix, causing the calls to fail.

  • Fixed an issue where merged call recordings incorrectly reported only the duration of the first segment in the Calls API.

  • Salesforce account linking now completes only in the browser that started it. An authorization link opened in another browser or an incognito window is refused and can't be reused afterwards, and an administrator's Link New User action must be finished by the same signed-in administrator. Android and iOS agent apps link as before. This behavior is off by default and can be enabled per instance.

  • Fixed an issue that affected call connection stability during active calls for instances using Agent Assist.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent callback calls incorrectly required manual acceptance even when queues were configured for Auto-Answer.

  • Fixed an issue where Telnyx and Twilio virtual agent calls remained stuck in a connected state for an extended period if the carrier didn't send a terminal status callback.

  • Fixed an issue where SMS replies to auto-dismissed chats were incorrectly recorded as an agent timeout instead of an end-user timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where the Unanswered Transferred Call Expiration setting wasn't enforced for calls parked in an overcapacity deflection state.

Cloud DNS

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, CNAME chasing behavior will change so that Cloud DNS follows CNAME chains between public and private zones. If your private zones or response policies have overlapping domain names with public CNAME targets, queries might resolve to unintended internal IP addresses or return resolution errors.

The following table outlines the current and updated behaviors.

Source of CNAME answer Current behavior (until January 5, 2027) New behavior (starting January 5, 2027)
Cloud DNS public zone Subsequent queries search only public DNS zones and internal DNS. Private zones, forwarding zones, and response policies are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order: response policies, private zones, forwarding or peering zones, internal DNS, and public zones.
Cloud DNS private zone Subsequent queries search only authorized private zones. Public DNS zones are ignored. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in authorized private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.
Cloud DNS response policy zone Cloud DNS systems don't perform queries for CNAME answers received from response policy local data rules. Subsequent queries follow the complete VPC name resolution order. If the target isn't found in response policies or private zones, Cloud DNS queries public DNS zones.

Review your CNAME chasing needs before January 5, 2027. Test your DNS query paths using dig or nslookup to identify CNAME chasing scenarios.

  • Look for private-to-public CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from response policies or private zones that don't match any response policy or record in a private zone. Previously, these queries resulted in a NXDOMAIN answer but after January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a record in a public zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses.
  • Look for public-to-private CNAME chasing scenarios: Look for CNAME answers from public zones that don't match any record in a public zone. Previously, these CNAME chasing scenarios would have resulted in a NXDOMAIN response. After January 5, 2027, these scenarios might match a response policy or record in a private zone or continue to be NXDOMAIN responses if the private zone doesn't have the record.
  • For CNAME chasing scenarios under your control: As best practice, configure matching time-to-live (TTL) values for all records in the CNAME chain.

Announcement

Starting January 5, 2027, Cloud DNS will disable full responses to DNS queries of type ANY (QTYPE=ANY) in public authoritative zones. Instead, a single resource record will return for ANY queries, chosen from the existing resource record sets that match the query.

Standard traffic from web browsers, applications, and API traffic query specific record types directly and are therefore unaffected with no action required.

However, certain legacy scripts, automated health checkers, debugging commands (for example, dig example.com ANY), or custom third-party monitoring systems that explicitly query ANY records will receive the first available record instead of a full zone inventory. You must complete the following configuration updates before January 5, 2027:

  • Identify legacy queries: Review internal tools, deployment scripts, or third-party DNS monitoring configurations for commands or API calls that request the ANY record type. Cloud DNS logs in Cloud Logging can be helpful with this.
  • Transition to specific queries: Update the tools to query the specific, individual record types they require (for example, querying for A, AAAA, MX, or TXT records separately).
  • Retrieve full zone records: If you use ANY queries to retrieve all records in a zone, use the Cloud DNS REST API (resourceRecordSets.list), the gcloud CLI (gcloud dns record-sets list), or the Google Cloud Console instead.

Risks associated with not making these changes include the following:

  • False monitoring alarms: Automated uptime or DNS monitoring tools checking ANY responses may misinterpret the new response as a system failure and trigger false alerts.
  • Broken automation pipelines: Internal deployment or CI/CD scripts that rely on parsing a full zone dump with an ANY query will fail to retrieve the expected data payload and may crash.
  • Disrupted IT diagnostics: Network administrators running manual legacy troubleshooting commands will no longer see a quick summary of all domain records, which could delay active network incident diagnostics.

VMware solution on Google Cloud is generally available (GA). VMware solution lets you deploy, configure, and manage VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) on dedicated bare-metal Compute Engine instances within your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) network under a Bring Your Own License (BYOL) model.

Key features include the following:

  • Provision dedicated bare-metal ESXi nodes (z3-highmem-192-highlssd-metal) directly in your project with deletion protection and Local SSD storage for vSAN.
  • Automate node preparation, Secret Manager credential storage, vSwitch and Dynamic NIC networking, Cloud DNS zone and record synchronization, vSAN storage initialization, and VCF installer appliance deployment by using Terraform and the VMware solution toolkit.
  • Distribute nodes across isolated availability domains by using spread placement policies to align with vSAN fault domains for high availability.
  • Connect ESXi nodes and VLAN-tagged Dynamic NICs directly to your VPC subnets without requiring private services access peering.

For more information, see VMware solution on Google Cloud overview and Compare VMware Engine models.

title: October 28, 2026
description:
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

Announcement

The following AlloyDB AI and vector search features and improvements are generally available (GA):

  • The alloydb_scann extension supports four-level tree (4LT) ScaNN vector indexes on PostgreSQL 17 and later, providing support for tables with up to 10 billion vector rows. For more information, see Four-level ScaNN tree indexes.

  • 4LT ScaNN vector indexes support automatic index maintenance. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and Maintain vector indexes automatically.

  • You can enable streaming functionality for ScaNN vector indexes by setting the scann.satisfy_limit parameter to relaxed_order. When enabled, the vector scan continues searching through additional leaf partitions until it finds enough results to satisfy the LIMIT clause of your query, improving recall on filtered searches. Additionally, you can enable this feature for parallel process scans by setting the scann.enable_parallel_satisfy_limit database flag to on. For more information, see ScaNN index reference and Best practices for tuning ScaNN indexes.

  • Vector assist simplifies the deployment and management of your AlloyDB vector workloads by helping you set up production-ready vector search capabilities, including embedding generation, query optimization, and index creation for vector types such as Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW). For more information, see Vector assist overview.

  • For AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances running PostgreSQL 17 and later, the maximum supported value for num_leaves when building ScaNN vector indexes is increased from 30,000,000 to 104,857,600. For more information, see Create a ScaNN index and ScaNN index reference.

  • You can use the external_search_fdw extension to connect to external search clusters and query their data directly from your database using the following search sources:

    • Elasticsearch

    • Solr

    • OpenSearch

  • AlloyDB supports the rum extension for high-performance full-text search operations on PostgreSQL 17 and earlier. The rum extension extends standard GIN indexes by storing positional information directly in the index, letting you perform faster phrase searches and relevance ranking without accessing the table data. For more information, see Create and manage a RUM index.

Fixed

AlloyDB provides more accurate memory usage estimation and prevents out-of-memory (OOM) errors when you build a ScaNN four-level tree index. This feature is in Preview. This update improves the stability of index builds by enforcing memory limits and improving memory estimation under constrained conditions.

Feature

Identity and Access Management (IAM) group authentication is generally available (GA) for new and existing AlloyDB clusters running PostgreSQL 15 and later. With IAM group authentication, you can manage database roles and privileges at the group level across primary instances and read pool instances, including first-time sign-ins directly to read pool instances. You can also preserve individual and IAM group user configurations when you migrate from a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL backup.

For more information, see IAM database authentication overview and Manage IAM authentication.

Security

In response to GCP-2026-071, Google is updating AlloyDB managed components. The fix to the certificate store is shipped in a new maintenance version that AlloyDB applies during scheduled maintenance, so you don't need to manually update AlloyDB managed instances. You can also apply the fix by performing self-service maintenance.

Depending on how you connect to AlloyDB, take the following actions:

  • If you use the AlloyDB Auth Proxy, then upgrade it to v1.17.2 or later. If you run the standalone proxy binary, then also update the host's certificate authority (CA) certificates.

  • If you use the AlloyDB Language Connectors, then update the language runtime and operating system CA certificates (for example, Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 or later).

You can configure Bigtable tables with microsecond timestamp granularity to capture and store high-frequency data. By supporting microsecond precision for cell timestamps, Bigtable helps you prevent data loss from write collisions in workloads with high event rates. Cloud Database Migration Service

Feature

Database Migration Service for homogeneous SQL Server migrations now supports Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations in general availability (GA).

With DAG migrations, you can use gcloud CLI and Database Migration Service API to migrate databases from self-managed SQL Server Enterprise Edition instances directly to Cloud SQL for SQL Server over a private network connection. DAG migrations don't require exporting backup or transaction log files to Cloud Storage, and support post-promotion reverse replication for zero-data-loss failback.

For more information, see About Distributed Availability Group (DAG) migrations and Migrate from self-managed SQL Server using Distributed Availability Groups.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Managed replica indexes for Cloud SQL for MySQL are generally available (GA). This feature lets you automatically retain and restore secondary indexes on read replica instances when Cloud SQL re-creates a replica.

Previously, re-creating a read replica deleted custom secondary indexes because primary backups don't have replica-only index definitions. With managed replica indexes, Cloud SQL tracks secondary index metadata on the primary instance, replicates this metadata to read replicas, and automatically rebuilds secondary indexes after replica re-creation.

Managed replica indexes are supported on instances that are running Cloud SQL for MySQL 8.0 or later, Cloud SQL Enterprise edition or Cloud SQL Enterprise Plus edition, and maintenance version R20260726.00_05 or later.

For more information, see Read replica indexes overview and Create and manage read replica indexes.

CodeMender updates (v0.17.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Support bundle diagnostics: Introduce cm support-bundle to collect environment metadata, configuration policies, health reports, and session logs into a compressed archive for streamlined troubleshooting.
  • Plain output mode: Add the persistent --plain flag (configurable via the CM_PLAIN environment variable or output.plain in config.yaml) to suppress decorative emojis, ANSI escape sequences, and Unicode borders for compatibility with screen readers and CI/CD log pipelines.
  • Dedicated exit codes for setup failures: Assign distinct exit codes (such as code 10 for credential issues) to configuration and authentication failures, preventing CI/CD pipelines from confusing environment setup issues with security findings.
  • Tailored CI/CD credential guidance: Provide environment-specific authentication guidance when running inside automated CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, and Jenkins instead of interactive login prompts.
  • Single-line JSONL statistics: Add the --jsonl flag to cm stats to output single-line JSON records with model and team attribution for seamless integration with Cloud Logging and log aggregation pipelines.
  • Granular sandbox and policy flags: Replace the overloaded --unrestricted flag with orthogonal flags (--sandbox=false) and configurable command policies to decouple container sandboxing from execution safety controls.
  • Sandbox configuration protections: Mount .git/hooks, .git/config, and .codemender read-only within writable execution sandboxes during cm fix and cm verify to prevent modifications to repository security policies.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Added a security warning when commands are executed with both sandbox isolation disabled and interactive approval skipped.
    • Enforced allowedRoots path boundaries across host discovery and remediation file operations to prevent traversal via dangling symlinks.
    • Supplied exact finding line ranges to remediation agents during cm fix to eliminate manual file scanning overhead.
    • Updated cm report import to properly treat findings without location data as file-level findings rather than defaulting to the first line.
    • Ensured cm session cancel routes requests to the session's original region regardless of local environment overrides.
    • Fixed finding status tracking in cm verify so unexploitable verdicts update the local state database rather than leaving findings open.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

title: AI SDK harness layer now supports native subscription authentication
description:
The AI SDK harness layer now supports authenticating harnesses through their native subscriptions, where the underlying harness supports them. The harness layer runs different coding agents through the same HarnessAgent interface, so you can switch agents without changing your application code.

No code changes or new settings are required. The direct authentication mode uses explicit provider environment credentials when they are present, and otherwise a native subscription found on the host. The default auto mode does the same when no AI Gateway credentials are set. The ai-gateway mode never reads native subscriptions.

Native subscription credentials stay on the host. Just like with API keys, credentials are resolved at the host boundary. OAuth access tokens are refreshed there as needed. Where the sandbox supports it, the harness receives placeholder credentials and the real token is injected into outbound requests on the host.

Native subscriptions work across harness adapters wherever the harness itself supports subscription login. These include Claude Code, Cline, Codex, Cursor, fx, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, OpenCode, and Pi.

Read the harness documentation to learn more.

title: How Delphi ships 100 times a day with its Python backend on Vercel
description:
Delphi on Vercel

  • 10 engineers with no dedicated infrastructure role

  • Everyone ships code, including product and design

  • 100+ production deploys a day behind feature flags

Delphi builds digital minds. They capture what someone has written, recorded, and taught, so anyone can tap that expertise on demand. Delphi is “a destination where you can find and interact with interesting minds,” says founding engineer Spencer Schoeben.

Nobody has built a digital mind network before, so Delphi figures out what to build by shipping features and watching how people use them. That only works if the product is fast to change. "If we are going to win, we need to have an excellent developer and agentic experience," Spencer says. "Otherwise, we could not adapt to how fast our user’s demands change."

Delphi's frontend had run on Vercel since day one. "The frontend has always been easy," Spencer says, "but the backend was a nightmare." Six months ago, the team rebuilt its Python backend on Vercel as well. Today the whole team ships to production 100+ times a day.

Building a Python backend that's easy to work on

The backend slowed every change

Delphi's backend previously ran on AWS, with ECS, Docker Desktop, and local databases. In the earliest days, the setup worked because the team was small and much of the context lived in people’s heads. As Delphi grew, that made onboarding slower than the team wanted: getting a new engineer to their first deploy took a full day of environment setup. 

Delphi could have fixed that without leaving AWS. But fixing it properly would have meant designing and owning the infrastructure themselves, and the team didn't want to own infrastructure at all. "That is not our current goal as a company," Spencer says. After moving the backend to Vercel, new engineers could get to production much faster, with the same deploy workflow the rest of the team used every day.

Workflows and Queues made the move possible

When Delphi was founded, Vercel Workflows and Vercel Queues didn't exist. Without them, Spencer says, the move would have been much harder, if possible at all.

Delphi's backend depends on long-running work and queued background jobs. Digital minds need durable agents that generate content ahead of time, plus ingestion that turns a person's books and talks into a knowledge graph.

Workflows handles the long-running work and Queues handle the background jobs. Neither requires setup. A developer writes the workflow or the queue handler as a function in the codebase, and Vercel provisions what's needed to run it on deploy.

100+ deploys a day, straight to production

Moving the backend to Vercel let Delphi stop treating backend changes as heavyweight releases and ship them as everyday product work. The team used to deploy to staging, then production. Now it skips the middle step, shipping 100+ times a day behind feature flags and running A/B tests instead of batching changes into a release.

Vercel Agent's anomaly detection watches production at that pace, flagging when something is misbehaving and why. Before, Spencer says, they often would not have known.

Moving fast has helped clear a backlog of small experiments that never used to make the priority list. Many of those experiments test how to turn a visitor into an owner, someone who arrives to talk to a mind and leaves having started their own.

Shipping isn't limited to engineers, either. Delphi's CPO and its growth teams build and deploy dashboards, prototypes, and experiments themselves, which Spencer says wouldn't have happened on the old setup.

Infrastructure built for agents and engineers

Preview deployments are how agents check their work

Delphi's engineers hand problems to cloud agents, with very little development happening locally. The preview deployment is where they first see what the agent built. Vercel preview deployments give every push its own live URL, so anyone can check the result from a phone or a Slack thread without pulling the branch.

When an agent fails, it's usually because it couldn't get at the information it needed. Vercel exposes the data and controls agents need through the SDK, MCP, and CLI, so an agent can read logs, inspect a deployment, or change an environment variable through whichever it's using. For Delphi, agents are now the main users of those tools, so the platform has to be as easy for them as it is for people.

An internal agent on Sandbox for customer success

Delphi's own agents run on Vercel as well. One of them, an internal agent on Vercel Sandbox, simplifies working with the company's codebase. The customer success team uses Slack to ask it about reported issues, find the problem, and hand an engineer a root cause and a proposed fix.

Edge cases used to fall through the cracks. "Before, we either couldn't get to everything, or we had to spend way more time than we had available," Spencer says. "Now we have an agent they can just ask in Slack."

Vercel Sandbox gives the agent an isolated environment with a file system, where it can check out the codebase, run it, and pull in whatever data a question needs. The agent itself is built with eve, Vercel's agent framework. Delphi's first version ran on a hosted agent platform and could only use the integrations that platform offered. In eve, tools are code Delphi writes, so when a question needs one that doesn't exist, the team adds it.

AI Gateway picks the model for each mind

Delphi's chat traffic runs through AI Gateway. Every digital mind is different, and some come out better on one model than another, so Delphi picks the model for each customer and adjusts as its own evals change. When a new model ships, open-source or otherwise, Delphi can route to it the same day.

Gateway also handles failover. Before, Delphi worked directly with a model provider to line up fallback capacity on other clouds, and it was hard. "With AI Gateway, we always know that we're going to get the fallbacks if they exist," Spencer says.

What's next

Delphi's first chapter was training digital minds and letting people chat with them. Now it is building the interface beyond chat. Spencer describes a search page where you bring a question, get perspectives from several minds at once, and have the page adapt to who you are.

That work runs as long-running agents on Workflows, with AI Gateway supplying whichever model each experiment calls for.

About Delphi: Delphi is a platform that turns a person's knowledge, thinking, and voice into a digital mind others can talk to. Anyone can create their own Delphi to make their expertise discoverable and accessible, part of a network of minds people can seek out, learn from, and converse with.

title: Is Agentic now tailors its audit by site type
description:
Is Agentic reports now let you view your checks through one of four site types: Docs & content, Business, App, or Commerce.

For example, the Commerce view highlights payment and checkout standards like x402, UCP, and ACP, while the App view highlights API discovery, authentication, error handling, and SDK support.

Your score stays the same in every view, and you can change views on an existing report without rescanning. Only the highlighted checks change, so you can focus on what matters for your kind of site while keeping scores comparable across sites.

To set the default view, add a single meta tag to your page's <head>:

Set the value to match your site type:

  • content for Docs & content

  • business for Business

  • app for App

  • store for Commerce

The tag only sets which view readers see first. It doesn't add points or change your score. If no type is declared, Is Agentic infers one and shows which type it chose.

Run a check at is-agentic.com or read the documentation.

title: TypeSafe AI's Jev now available on AI Gateway
description:
Jev from TypeSafe AI is now available on AI Gateway.

Jev is a probabilistic decision model for software: state goes in, typed Choice, Score, and Boolean answers come out.

Regular language models generate text one token at a time, which the application then parses and validates. Jev evaluates all declared questions in parallel and returns typed answers plus probabilities directly. That removes unnecessary text generation and makes it straightforward to automate clear cases while routing uncertain ones to review.

TypeSafe reports Jev was up to 193.6x faster and 444.6x cheaper than LLMs on its workflow evaluations. Example use cases include:

  • Choosing the next tool or subagent in an agent loop

  • Deciding whether to continue, retry, ask the user, or stop

  • Scoring urgency or risk before an action

  • Verifying model outputs and enforcing guardrails.

AI SDK 7 exposes Jev through the experimental evaluate API. Choice selects an option, Score grades an ordered rubric, and Boolean estimates the probability of true. Install the current AI SDK (AI SDK 7.0.105 onwards supports the evaluate API):

Each evaluation specifies:

  • model: the evaluation model to call,

  • state: the shared string, object, or array to evaluate, and

  • questions: a map of named decisions to make about that state.

Call the model with typesafe-ai/jev. This example turns one support case into a queue, priority, and refund-review decision, with uncertain routing sent for manual review:

The result preserves question IDs and Choice keys. TypeSafe reports separate Choice and Score confidence in result.providerMetadata.typesafe.confidence. Calibrate probabilities and confidence against labeled examples from your workflow.

Jev supports Zero Data Retention and No Training, enabled per request in the example. Evaluation calls also appear in logs and custom reporting, count toward budgets, and accept other Gateway provider options in the same providerOptions.gateway object.

Read the documentation on evaluation models on AI Gateway for more details, discover practical use cases for Jev, and browse resources in the knowledge base.

title: Open-weight models take 56% of token volume, Astra doubles Fable 5.1 spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — September 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from June, July, and August.

September 2026 summary

The September index reports on AI Gateway data collected through August 2026.

  • Open-weight models ran the majority of gateway tokens for the first time, up from 7% in December to 56% in August.

  • The average token costs less than half what it did five months ago. Price per token fell 23.2% in August, the third straight monthly drop, and the median team paid 7.6% less.

  • Fable 5, Anthropic's most capable model, lost two-thirds of its share of gateway spend in one month. Opus 5, at half the price, tripled its share. Anthropic kept 64% of all spend.

  • Gemini 3 Flash has lost 95% of its share of gateway tokens since May, and more than three-quarters of the volume it lost went to models from other labs.

Latest Index updates

The monthly report covers data through August. We add notable developments here between editions.

  • September 17: OpenAI launched Astra on September 3, and it took a third of OpenAI's spend within two days and twice Fable 5.1's share of gateway spend. Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend in its first twelve days while Fable 5.1, launched two days earlier at the same price, took 3.7%.

  • September 18: Jev is now the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history. Within its first 24 hours, it was being used by nearly 13% of paid teams, 2x as many as the GPT-5.6 family and over 6x as many as Fable 5.1.

Open-weight models take a majority of token volume for the first time

In August, open-weight models ran 56% of all tokens on AI Gateway, marking the first month they took the majority of volume.

In December 2025, they processed fewer than one in ten tokens, and only eight months later, they ran more token volume than all closed-weight models combined.

Though the frontier kept the majority of spend, open-weight dollar share is accelerating. As open-weight models become more capable, customers are moving more production workloads over to them.

Growth in open-weight model adoption helped push the average price per token across the gateway down 23.2% in August, its third consecutive monthly drop and the steepest since April. Among teams running more than ten million tokens in both months, the median team paid 7.6% less per token, more than double July's 2.9% decline.

Teams can now get more inference from the same budget and reserve frontier models only for the tasks that justify the premium.

Frontier plateaus as Fable spend goes to Opus 5

Production workloads that justify a frontier model don't always need the most expensive one. They need one that’s good enough.

Fable is the most capable model Anthropic sells. Opus is the tier below it and costs roughly half of Fable’s price per token. When the US export control on Fable 5 was lifted and its access restored on July 1, its gateway spend share surged to 13.2%. At the end of that same month, Opus 5 came online.

In August, Fable 5’s share of gateway spend fell to 4.9%, and Opus 5's share rose to 22.5%. Nine in ten of the teams that ran Fable cut their usage, and more of them moved their workloads to Opus 5 than any other model. Fable’s extra capability wasn’t worth double the price.

Teams left Fable, Anthropic's most expensive and capable model, but the lab retained the lion’s share of gateway spend because those workloads stepped down to Opus 5, not a different lab.

Anthropic has taken at least 61 cents of every dollar spent through AI Gateway every month since December, and 64 cents in August. Its models have held the top two spots by spend every month since December, even as the models in those spots changed.

Customer loyalty follows the model profile, not the lab

Lab loyalty doesn’t follow brand, it follows model profile, and consistency wins.

When a new model preserves what users valued in its predecessor, the lab retains its customers. When it doesn’t, those customers fill the need through other providers.

When Claude Opus 5 launched, it gained almost twice what Fable lost, because it handled the same workloads at half the price. And within five days of Z.ai launching GLM-5.3-Flash, it was running three times GLM-5.2's daily volume.

Google struggled to retain customers with its new models. Because the new offerings didn’t provide a relative advantage on capability or price, a majority of Gemini 3 Flash’s workloads moved to OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepSeek.

About half of the volume that left Gemini 3 Flash went to cheaper models, led by GPT-5.6 Luna, which costs less than half as much per token. Most of the other half went to higher-priced models, led by Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5, which cost roughly nine and three times as much as Gemini 3 Flash, respectively.

The flight to better-fit models meant that over the same period, Google’s share of gateway token volume fell from 30% to 5%, with Gemini 3 Flash accounting for 22 of the 25 percentage points lost.

Special report: Astra took a third of OpenAI spend within 48 hours and outpaced Fable 5.1 two to one at launch

GPT-6 Astra launched on the AI Gateway on September 3 at the same price as Fable 5.1 and two and a half times the price of GPT-5.6 Sol. Two days later, it accounted for one in every three dollars spent on OpenAI models through the gateway. Its share of spend has held, hovering between 28% and 39% since.

Within OpenAI’s model lineup, Astra and Sol processed 27% of OpenAI’s tokens but accounted for 71% of its spending from September 4 through 16. Luna and Nano processed more than twice as many tokens for about one-ninth as much spending.

Anthropic launched Fable 5.1 on September 1, two days before Astra. Over each model's first twelve days on the gateway, Astra took 7.7% of all gateway spend, more than twice Fable 5.1's share of 3.7%, and was used by twice as many teams.

OpenAI’s cheaper models carry its volume, while Astra’s early lead over Fable shows it can also attract teams at the highest price point. Together, they let OpenAI compete with other frontier labs for both scale and premium spend.

Stay tuned for more in next month's report.

Also in August’s data

  • Google's Nano Banana took the lead in image spend for the first time, at 50% to GPT Image's 44%, even as GPT Image took back the lead in images generated, 46% to 39%.

  • Google's Veo rose to second in video spend, at 20%, up from 15% in July. Seedance remained in first on both videos generated and video spend.

  • The share of videos generated by xAI’s Grok Imagine has more than halved since June, from 42% to 31% to 19%.

About this report

This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through August 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Token volume includes input, output, reasoning, cached-input, and cache-creation tokens.

  • Spending is estimated using labs’ published list prices; actual bills may differ. Average price per token is estimated spending divided by token volume.

  • Statements about where volume moved compare changes among the same teams. They do not trace individual tokens between models.

  • Open-weight classifications follow the current AI Gateway model list, which is broader than the definition used in earlier reports.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: Reproducing, disclosing, and fixing the libheif vulnerability with Hacktron and the maintainers
description:
In August 2026, Hacktron reported what looked like a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Next.js image optimization. Their investigation found that the vulnerable code was not in Next.js itself, but upstream in libheif, an AVIF image decoder used by Next.js, ImageMagick, WordPress, sharp, and much of the web.

Shortly after Hacktron notified us, we worked with them to reproduce the RCE against a current Next.js build and disclose it to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. We then deployed a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and started working with the maintainers on a fix.

The dependency chain

Next.js image optimization lets applications resize and optimize images through the <Image> component (next/image). For AVIF images, the image-processing dependency chain is as follows:

  • <Image> invokes /_next/image,

  • /_next/image calls sharp

  • sharp calls libvips

  • libvips uses libheif to decode the image

That meant the vulnerable code was not in Next.js, but it was still reachable through Next.js image optimization. A malicious AVIF image sent to the image optimization endpoint would invoke libheif through sharp and libvips.

As such, one obvious mitigation was to disable AVIF optimization in Next.js. Malicious AVIF images would then stop at the image optimization endpoint instead of being passed through sharp and libvips to libheif. The exploit would not propagate upstream.

However, only mitigating Next.js, without an upstream fix, posed a disclosure problem.

Disclosing the vulnerability and coordinating the upstream fix

After we worked with Hacktron to successfully reproduce the issue, we rolled out a platform-wide mitigation on Vercel and reached out to the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif to disclose the vulnerability and begin working on a fix.

Here is the timeline:

  • August 11-12: Hacktron reported the issue to Vercel; Hacktron and Vercel reproduced the RCE with a working proof of concept.

  • August 13: Vercel applied a platform mitigation through its Image Optimization Service.

  • August 19: The Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and began coordination across sharp, libvips, and libheif.

  • August 24: Next.js informed its security partners.

  • August 25: Next.js published a security release that disabled AVIF optimization.

The Vercel security team contacted the maintainers of sharp and libvips by email, and opened coordination with libheif through a GitHub Security Advisory. Hacktron had also submitted vulnerability and exploit details to libheif. On August 19, the Next.js team met with the libvips maintainer and aligned on the path forward across sharp, libvips, and libheif. The libheif maintainer continued remediation through Hacktron’s GitHub Security Advisory.

On August 24, Next.js informed its security partners of the libheif vulnerability and its impact on Next.js (partner notifications are a routine part of Next.js’ security release process).

On August 25, six days after the August 19 meeting, the libheif maintainer released v1.23.2, which remediated the RCE.

Vercel and Next.js mitigations

Securing Vercel and its customers was straightforward: all Next.js image optimization requests on Vercel go through a central Image Optimization Service. Therefore, we disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in that central service. Any incoming AVIF images were not passed to libheif for decoding and RCE was not possible on Vercel.

Protecting self-hosted applications required a Next.js release. On August 25, Next.js published a security release that had originally been planned to address a separate issue. After coordinating an upstream fix, we bundled the AVIF mitigation into that release and shipped it a day earlier than planned. The release disabled AVIF optimization and resizing in Next.js; given that the patched libheif release was still propagating downstream, this was the most timely option. We also published a security advisory to communicate the issue’s severity.

Our commitment to making the web more secure

The volume of OSS vulnerabilities discovered continues to increase, and the numbers are overwhelming:

  • In 2026, the CVE program has published more than 35,000 CVEs.

  • Private vulnerability reports on GitHub grew from 500 per week in January to 3,000 per week in May.

  • GitHub also reported 1,560 reviewed advisories in May 2026, the highest monthly volume in the advisory database’s history.

As LLMs accelerate vulnerability research, we expect to see more upstream vulnerabilities like the libheif RCE surface across the OSS ecosystem. There have been a higher number of Next.js security releases in recent months, and we expect that trend to continue as we mitigate new vulnerabilities that both we and the research community uncover.

We are committed to proactively finding vulnerabilities before attackers, responsibly disclosing everything we find, and collaborating with researchers and maintainers on fixes.

Credit

Thanks to Hacktron for responsibly disclosing the AVIF vulnerability, working with us to reproduce the issue, and coordinating with the upstream maintainers through remediation.

We also want to thank the maintainers of sharp, libvips, and libheif. Their work on the upstream fix made coordinated remediation possible across the image processing dependency chain.

We work with a talented set of researchers to secure Next.js and other open source frameworks through Vercel's Open Source Bug Bounty. Anyone interested in contributing to the security of eligible frameworks is encouraged to participate there.

References

  • Next.js August 2026 security release

  • Upstream libheif advisory

  • Vercel security release changelog

  • Just a rumor of a bug is enough to find a security exploit

title: Jev is the fastest-adopted model in AI Gateway history
description:
Within 24 hours of launching on AI Gateway, Jev from TypeSafe AI reached more than twice as many paid teams as any previous model launch, making it the fastest-adopted model in gateway history.

Jev passed every other comparison model in its first twelve hours and continued to widen its lead for the rest of the day. By hour 24, nearly 13% of paid teams were using it. That's 2x the GPT-5.6 family and more than 6x Fable 5.1's share.

Jev’s launch shows how quickly a specialized model can find a place in production. Its first-day adoption was unmatched among recent launches; the next test is whether that early adoption lasts.

About Jev

Jev was introduced on September 15 as a probabilistic decision model designed to support structured decision-making within software. An application sends it context and a set of questions. Jev evaluates those questions in parallel and returns typed choices, scores, or true-or-false answers, along with probabilities.

Unlike the text produced by a general-purpose language model, Jev’s answers come in a format the code can use directly. Developers can use it to:

  • choose an agent’s next tool or subagent

  • decide whether a workflow should continue, retry, ask the user, or stop

  • score urgency or risk before taking an action

  • verify model outputs, enforce guardrails, or send uncertain cases for human review

In its own workflow evaluations, TypeSafe AI reports that Jev was up to 194 times faster and 445 times cheaper than language models.

See the September AI Gateway Production Index for more model usage data, or try Jev through AI Gateway and build with the AI SDK.

title: Python on Vercel is now generally available
description:
Python is now a first-class language and runtime on Vercel. Build APIs, full-stack applications, and AI agents with native Python SDKs and a shared development and deployment workflow for your Python backend and JavaScript frontend.

Python framework and runtime support

Vercel handles the infrastructure so you can focus on your application:

  • Automatic framework support: FastAPI, Flask, and Django applications are automatically recognized and configured, with framework-specific support for serving static assets through the Vercel CDN.

  • Native Python runtime and tooling: Vercel runs CPython on Linux and supports uv and pyproject.toml for dependency management.

  • Compute for APIs and workers: Scale request-driven applications with Fluid compute and run long-running pull-based workloads with Vercel Daemons.

Native Python SDKs

Within your application, Python SDKs let you build agents, run untrusted code, and orchestrate durable workflows.

  • Sandbox: Give your application or agent an isolated Linux VM on demand.

  • AI SDK for Python (Beta): Generate or stream model responses and call tools. Get started with uv add ai.

  • Workflow SDK for Python (Beta): Persist execution state and retry failed workflow steps.

  • Queues (Beta): Send and receive messages for background work.

  • Connect: Obtain credentials for calling external APIs.

  • Blob: Upload and retrieve files in object storage.

Use the SDKs individually or combine them in the same Python application.

Your frontend and backend, together

For full-stack applications, Vercel Services allows you to deploy your frontend and backends together in one project, with shared previews and atomic deployments and rollbacks. Within that project, you can view logs by service and connect backends privately through service bindings.

For a frontend in frontend/ and a FastAPI app defined in backend/main.py, add this vercel.toml at the repository root.

Requests under /api/ reach matching FastAPI routes with the path unchanged, while other requests reach the frontend. Run both services locally with vercel dev, then deploy them together from the same repository.

Read the Python documentation to get started.

title: Vercel Connect adds Enterprise-Managed Authorization
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) in public beta. Your apps and agents can access supported services on behalf of signed-in users without separate consent prompts for each service.

Here's how access works:

  • Admin-managed access: Administrators can grant or revoke access to supported services through the identity provider.

  • Corporate sign-in: Users sign into your app with their corporate account through a compatible identity provider such as Okta.

  • Scoped tokens: Your app requests the scopes it needs, and Connect handles token exchange, caching, and renewal. Access is limited to approved scopes and the user’s existing service permissions.

If your app uses Vercel Passport, you can request a token for Slack’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server with the signed-in user’s identity:

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 1T9cFkjaRDDmRFQ5bWVmD6

Connect supports Cross-App Access (XAA), including its use for MCP authorization through EMA. Follow the Vercel Connect EMA setup guide to configure your identity provider and services and enable EMA on their Connect connectors.

Enterprise teams can now run Vercel Functions in their own AWS account with Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC). With BYOC, your function code and execution stay inside your security and compliance boundary. Vercel continues to handle deployments, environments, routing, and static assets.

During deployment, you provision functions in your AWS account and Vercel serves everything else. You keep control over function execution with your own IAM permissions, network access, and resource lifecycle policies.

With BYOC, you can:

  • Run Node.js and Python Vercel Functions in your AWS account

  • Meet strict compliance, security, and isolation requirements

  • Connect privately to backends and services in your VPC

  • Use existing AWS commitments

BYOC is available on Enterprise plans. Contact sales or your account team to get started, or learn more in the documentation, and read the complete guide to BYOC.

title: Vercel Drives is now generally available
description:
Vercel Drives is now generally available for Vercel Sandbox on Hobby, Pro, and Enterprise.

A Drive is persistent storage that you mount as a directory in a Vercel Sandbox. Its files remain available after the sandbox stops, so later runs and other sandboxes can access them by mounting the same Drive.

Use Drives to preserve an agent’s workspace or file-based memory across runs, or to make datasets, models, dependencies, and build artifacts available across sandboxes.

You can also fork a Drive into independent writable Drives. Forks inherit the source Drive's data, region, and maximum size, then store their own changes. Parallel workers can start with the same files and make changes without affecting the original or one another.

Learn more in the Drives documentation.

title: Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute
description:
Vercel Connect now supports Secure Compute, allowing connectors to reach providers with IP allowlists, such as Salesforce and Snowflake.

With Secure Compute routing enabled, Connect’s provider requests use the selected network’s dedicated static IP addresses instead of Connect’s shared IPs. Requests to obtain and refresh access tokens follow that route; your app’s direct API routing is unchanged by this setting. Credential management stays the same, so you don’t need to store long-lived provider secrets in your app or build OAuth flows yourself.

To enable Secure Compute routing for a supported connector and all projects that use it:

  • Open your connector’s Settings in the Vercel dashboard.

  • Under Secure Compute Routing, choose an existing network.

  • If your provider uses an IP allowlist, add the selected network’s displayed IP addresses to it in the provider’s settings.

  • Save your changes in Connect.

Requests for initial connector creation and all provider discovery requests bypass the selected network and connect directly to providers. If the selected network is unavailable, routed requests fail instead of falling back to Connect’s shared IPs.

Read the Secure Compute routing documentation for configuration details.

title: Liquid AI's d1-ultra now available on AI Gateway
description:
d1-ultra from Liquid AI is now available on AI Gateway. It is a multimodal decision model for classification, routing, and scoring across text and images, including visual defect inspection and checking damage claims against customer photos.

Rather than generating text, d1-ultra returns structured answers with probabilities. Ask a Boolean question to get the probability of a yes/no answer, use Choice to select among named categories, or use Score to rate an ordered scale. title: Vercel Daemons is now in public beta
description:
Vercel Daemons is now in public beta, allowing you to run long-running processes that pull and execute work from Vercel Queues, databases, or third-party systems without requiring an HTTP server:

  • Consumers using Vercel Queues poll mode, Celery, BullMQ, RabbitMQ, or Kafka.

  • Temporal or Cadence workers that long-poll their task queues.

  • Self-hosted CI runners for GitHub Actions, GitLab, or CircleCI that poll for jobs without requiring inbound connections.

Daemons run containers on Fluid compute and deploy alongside your app in the same project. Vercel builds your image and maintains the instance count you configure in each region, restarting instances that exit or crash.

Get started by packaging your application and dependencies in a Dockerfile or Containerfile, then adding a daemons entry to one configuration file at your project root. This example uses worker/Dockerfile to run one Celery worker in iad1 (Washington, D.C.):

Set any connection details your worker needs in your project's production environment variables, then deploy to production. Vercel starts the configured instances, and their output appears in your project's Logs. CPU and memory metrics are available with Observability Plus.

Learn more in the Vercel Daemons documentation and read the complete guide.
