title: JWT verifiers need an explicit token-purpose policy
description:
JWT verifiers need an explicit token-purpose policy

A JSON Web Token can carry a request, a session, an access grant, a logout event, or a signed claim from an external service. If a verifier accepts all of them through the same key and the same parser, the token's header becomes a hint rather than a security control. RFC 8725 recommends explicit typing for this reason, and RFC 9068 gives OAuth access tokens a concrete type value that resource servers can enforce.

The algorithm field is another decision point. The token header names an algorithm, but the verifier must choose the acceptable key type and algorithm from its own configuration. Trusting a kid to select any key in a shared set, or trusting alg to select a key type without an allowlist, expands the attack surface across every token issuer that shares the parser.

Give each token a purpose

RFC 8725 describes explicit typing as a way to distinguish different kinds of JSON Web Tokens. A token minted as an ID token, a token minted for a public form, and a token minted for an administrative API should not be interchangeable. They may use the same signing library, but they should not share an undefined token type.

RFC 9068 is a useful example. Its JWT access-token profile requires the typ header to identify the token as an access token. A resource server enforcing that profile must reject any other value. The rule is not that every JWT must use one universal string. The rule is that the verifier knows the expected purpose and rejects a token that does not declare it.

Applications can define their own media types when they need them. The value should be documented, registered where appropriate, and checked before claims are consumed. A missing typ field may be tolerated for a legacy token, but that decision needs an explicit compatibility scope. It should not become the default for new issuers.

Validate the algorithm and key together

Use an allowlist of signing algorithms for each issuer and token purpose. Reject none unless the protocol explicitly requires an unsecured token and the verifier has a separate path for it. Compare the key type to the algorithm. A key identifier should select a key from the issuer's trusted set, not from an arbitrary document supplied by the caller.

Do not let a token carry its own JWKS URL or issuer URL when the verifier is supposed to trust a fixed issuer. Resolve metadata through a preconfigured, authenticated discovery process and cache it with an expiry. Validate the issuer, audience, expiration, issued-at time, and any subject constraints after the signature check. The exact claim requirements depend on the profile, so use the profile rather than a generic JWT valid function.

Audience is especially easy to misuse. A token minted for a calendar integration should not be accepted by a billing API merely because the signing key is trusted. Separate audience values, or separate keys, for materially different trust domains. If one issuer serves many applications, make the audience and token type part of the resource server's configuration.

Make errors indistinguishable to clients

Return a small set of public error codes, such as invalid token or insufficient scope. Keep detailed diagnostics in the security log: issuer, key ID, expected type, algorithm, audience check, and verification stage. Do not put the token in the log. A token can contain personal data, a session identifier, or another bearer secret.

Monitor rejected token types across services. A spike may come from a deployment that started issuing the wrong header or from a client replaying a token to the wrong API. Track accepted tokens by issuer, audience, and type, but aggregate the metrics so an operator cannot reconstruct a user's activity from debugging dashboards.

Test with tokens that look valid

Create test cases for a trusted signature with the wrong typ, the wrong audience, an expired time, a key from another issuer, and an algorithm outside the allowlist. Test nested tokens and encrypted tokens separately. If the application supports both JWTs and opaque tokens, test that an opaque token cannot be interpreted as a JWT and that a JWT cannot bypass the opaque-token lookup.

Do not use a token's type as a substitute for authorization. A correctly typed administrative token still needs a scope or role check. A correctly typed user token still needs an object-level authorization decision. The verifier's job is to establish what the token is and whether it was issued for this service. The application still decides what the subject may do.

References

  • IETF, RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices
  • IETF, RFC 9068: JSON Web Token (JWT) Profile for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens
  • IETF, RFC 7519: JSON Web Token (JWT)

title: Rename or Reorder CSV Columns in the Browser: What the Export Actually Contains
description:
The Data Studio in OnePassApps has eleven tool tabs. Nine posts on this site cover ten of them; the Columns tab had never had one, so that is today's post: the one place where you pick a column, rename it, move it left or right, and then check what the exported file actually contains.

I work on OnePassApps.

You can try it at the Data Studio. The written walkthrough is on the OnePassApps guides page.

Before you load anything

The panel is the usual three steps - 01 Source, 02 Options, 03 Result - and the action button on this tab is "Load / refresh columns", not "Parse CSV". The options step is empty until you press it, and the panel tells you so: "Column options appear once the CSV is loaded."

The preview area reads "CSV PREVIEW" with "No data yet", and the stage hint says "Load the columns, then rename or reorder them in Options." The source hint is the Data Studio's usual one: "Drop a data file, or browse CSV, TSV, JSON or YAML · up to 20 MiB · or paste rows in Source".

The four controls that appear

After the load, 02 Options holds four things:

  • Delimiter - the same picker as everywhere else, shipping on "Auto detect · comma", with Comma, Tab, Semicolon and Pipe behind it.
  • Column - a picker whose options are your real header names. On a six-column file it offered id, name, score, active, note, price.
  • Position - two arrow buttons, "Move column left" and "Move column right".
  • Rename column - a text input, prefilled with the selected column's name, with a Rename button beside it.

Renaming a column, and reading the export

Pick name, clear the rename field, type employee_name, press Rename. The result step reports "Column name updated in the active table." The preview header changes with it - the column now reads employee_name with a TEXT badge - and so does the exported file.

The "Download CSV" button on this tab writes a real file. After the rename it was 169 bytes of text/csv;charset=utf-8, and its header row was:

"id","employee_name","score","active","note","price"

Moving a column

With the first column selected, "Move column left" is disabled - there is nothing to its left. "Move column right" moved id one slot along: the preview became name, id, score, active, note, price, and the downloaded file was 160 bytes with the header

"name","id","score","active","note","price"

To move a column a longer way, select it in the picker (the last column, price, is fine) and press "Move column left" as many times as you need. Two clicks on price gave name, id, score, price, active, note, and the file matched:

"name","id","score","price","active","note"

Rename and reorder in the same pass

The two controls are independent, and the export carries both. After renaming the moved column from price to amount, the preview read name, id, score, amount, active, note and the downloaded file was 161 bytes:

"name","id","score","amount","active","note"

What the bytes keep

Every field is quoted, the line endings are CRLF, and the values are untouched: a cell holding 007 was still "007" in the export, so nothing was coerced to a number, and the empty cell was an empty quoted field rather than the em dash the preview shows. The preview's type badges (id NUMBER, score NUMBER, the rest TEXT) are a label for the eye - the export does not convert anything on the strength of them.

The caveat worth knowing

"Reload CSV" re-reads the source you pasted. After I renamed a column and then pressed it, the rename was gone and the header was back to its original name, while the counts were unchanged - "Loaded 3 rows and 6 columns.", "3 rows · 6 columns · no parsing issues", "Delimiter found Comma". The rename lives in the active table inside that tab, not in your file, so export before you reload.

What leaves the tab, and what it costs

Nothing, as usual. The page says "Nothing leaves this tab." and the stage says "Processing stays in this browser.", and the limits box spells it out: "Pasted text supports up to 10,000 lines. Pasted CSV supports up to 8 MiB and 10,000 data rows; CSV files support up to 20 MiB, 100,000 rows, and 2 million cells. JSON supports up to 2 MiB and YAML up to 1 MiB. Your data stays on this device."

The plan block on the same page still reads FREE PROMOTIONAL PERIOD - Standard is free right now, $0 / month, 100,000 credits every 30 days, No end date set, No card required, and No automatic paid subscription.

If you want the same treatment for the other Data Studio tabs, the guides are linked above. I work on OnePassApps - the studios process the file in the tab, not on a server.

title: WordPress Core flaw: interpreting 62.969 blocked attack attempts
description:
Wordfence reported blocking 62.969 attack attempts in 24 hours targeting a WordPress Core vulnerability. This measures attempts Wordfence says it blocked, not successfully compromised websites. The cited data does not establish an exploitation success rate.

The vulnerability affects WordPress Core versions 4.7 through 7.1.3, has a CVSS score of 8,1, and has no CVE identifier. A patch was released on 28 October 2026. TMGS recommends updating affected installations to 7.1.4.

Why the upgrade window matters

During a Core update using a full package, affected versions extract files into a predictable directory under wp-content/upgrade. On many servers, this staging area is accessible through the web. An unauthenticated attacker reaching it at the right moment could interact with the staged WordPress installation and progress to PHP code execution on the server.

Wordfence emphasizes that successful exploitation requires hitting a very narrow window while the full Core update is being extracted. That condition limits what can be inferred from the attempt count. TMGS assesses that the short window does not justify lowering remediation priority when attack attempts have already appeared.

TMGS defensive recommendations

TMGS recommends inventorying WordPress websites, identifying affected versions, and prioritizing updates to 7.1.4. Prepare backups, recovery options, and post-update operational checks.

TMGS also recommends:

  • Verify the running version after updating and record it in the asset inventory.
  • Review suspicious requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade, focusing on activity before, during, and after the upgrade.
  • Correlate requests with error logs and file changes before concluding that a compromise occurred.
  • For outsourced website management, assign clear responsibilities across content administrators, hosting providers, and security teams. Record the final version, upgrade time, and contact responsible for access logs.

Read the full analysis on TMGS: https://tmgs.vn/tin-tuc/wordpress-doc-dung-62-969-luot-tan-cong-bi-chan-i.d487a618-e176-4ef5-b74a-5dd1345f7d37

title: I Built an Editable Timeline for AI Agents: Skills, MCP, and Transactional Video Editing
description:
An AI agent can generate an FFmpeg command. But what happens when the next request is: “Shorten the second shot, move the voiceover and its captions together, and give me a project I can keep editing”?

That is the problem I have been working on in Timeline Studio, an open-source, local-first browser video editor with an Agent Skill and a shared command layer.

  • Source code
  • Try the editor

This post focuses on the editing architecture: how an agent turns a request into an inspectable plan, how that plan changes project state, and where rendering still has explicit limits.

Start with an editable project

A rendered MP4 does not preserve the decisions needed for the next edit: clip identity, source ranges, timing, transforms, and caption/audio relationships.

Timeline Studio uses an editable .timeline project as the source of truth. In the local command workflow, the archive contains project.json and embedded media. Asset import probes necessary metadata, computes SHA-256 integrity information, and embeds the media bytes.

This gives both the user and the agent a concrete state to return to. The user can reopen the project in the editor. The agent can inspect it before making another change.

Separate editorial decisions from state changes

The model can decide that a voiceover should start at three seconds. The application should enforce whether the clip exists, whether the time is valid, and how linked captions follow it.

The architecture looks like this:

User request + media evidence
             |
     Skill: analyze and plan
             |
     Structured edit plan
             |
 CLI / local MCP / browser WebMCP
             |
 Shared command registry and reducers
             |
 Editable project + verified output

The transports have different environments. The CLI operates on local archives. The local STDIO MCP adapter exposes that command runner to an agent. Browser WebMCP, when exposed by the host, operates on the open editor and commits through its normal history.

The important constraint is to reuse editing rules rather than implement a separate editor for each transport.

An edit plan needs preconditions

Here is a simplified plan that moves an existing voiceover to project time 3s:

{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "project": "/projects/input.timeline",
  "baseRevision": 12,
  "dryRun": false,
  "operations": [
    {
      "id": "move-voice-001",
      "type": "timed.move",
      "track": "audio",
      "clipId": "voice-1",
      "start": 3
    }
  ],
  "output": {
    "project": "/projects/output.timeline"
  }
}

The revision and clip ID are illustrative: they must come from inspecting the actual project.

Each field has a job:

  • baseRevision checks the state on which the plan was based.
  • Operation IDs support idempotent handling of retries.
  • clipId identifies an existing project object.
  • type restricts the action to a supported operation.
  • output.project declares a new output artifact.

For this audio move, still-linked captions move by the same delta. That behavior belongs in the editing rules.

Preview a semantic diff before applying

The workflow is:

inspect -> plan -> validate -> diff -> apply -> inspect

The CLI exposes it directly:

npm run agent -- project.inspect /projects/input.timeline

node skills/edit-timeline-studio/scripts/validate_edit_plan.mjs \
  /projects/plan.json

npm run agent -- project.diff /projects/plan.json
npm run agent -- project.run /projects/plan.json

The standalone validator checks transport shape, finite time fields, and duplicate operation IDs. It does not prove that a plan is valid for a particular project.

project.diff is the project-aware dry run. It uses the same command registry and reducers as application, without writing an archive. It checks supported operations and preconditions, then reports project fields, clip additions/removals, changed fields, ordering, and duration changes.

This makes accidental scope expansion visible. A request to move narration should not quietly change the visual sequence duration.

Retries and concurrent edits are normal cases

Three mechanisms matter here.

Idempotency

If an operation completes but its response is lost, retrying the same operation ID should not insert the same clip twice. Previously applied IDs are treated as no-ops.

Revision checks

If the agent inspected revision 12 and the user subsequently edited the project, a stale plan containing new operations must fail with a revision conflict. The agent needs to inspect again and reconsider the plan.

Transactional application

A failed batch should not leave a partially edited output archive. Local CLI and MCP writes also require a new output path and reject overwriting the input or an existing output.

These are familiar application-engineering techniques. They become especially useful when the caller is an agent that may retry or reason from outdated state.

Video editing has more than one clock

A timestamp can refer to source media, a clip-local position, or the final project.

For a constant-speed clip:

sourceTime = sourceIn + (timelineTime - clipStart) * speed

With a speed curve, source-time mapping must accumulate the changing playback speed over time.

An agent identifying an action at source time 8s cannot assume that the cut belongs at project time 8s. Trimming, splitting, keyframes, thumbnails, and effect analysis all depend on maintaining that mapping.

Tracks also have different semantics. Main visuals form a contiguous sequence; narration, captions, and overlays have explicit timing. Whether a duration change shifts other tracks depends on ripple mode, links, and track locks.

These rules need to be explicit application behavior.

Skills and MCP serve different purposes

The Skill describes the workflow: inspect material, plan the edit, choose an execution path, and verify the result.

The MCP adapter exposes concrete tools, including:

timeline_project_inspect
timeline_track_inspect
timeline_clip_inspect
timeline_project_diff
timeline_project_apply
timeline_project_render

The local adapter is a thin transport over the existing command runner. It does not duplicate timeline editing logic.

To install the Skill:

npx skills add MartinDelophy/ai-video-editor \
  --skill edit-timeline-studio

To explore the repository and local MCP server:

git clone https://github.com/MartinDelophy/ai-video-editor.git
cd ai-video-editor
npm install
npm run mcp

Installing the Skill does not install the complete runtime. Local MCP needs the checkout and Node dependencies; media operations need their corresponding tools. The Skill includes a host dependency-check workflow.

An edited project is not yet a verified video

The current local project.render path supports the documented portable Visuals, Voiceover, and Music subset. It uses FFmpeg to produce H.264/AAC MP4 and ffprobe to check dimensions, duration, and audio-track presence.

It rejects unsupported composition features rather than silently dropping visible captions, overlays, transitions, or effects. Richer compositions require the browser renderer.

Verification needs several levels: inspect the project, reopen it and resolve archived media, check the output container, and actually play the important visual and audio boundaries. A valid project structure alone cannot prove that the final mix sounds right.

Where to read the implementation

Useful entry points in the repository:

  • src/lib/projectCommandEngine.js — shared project command engine
  • scripts/timeline-command.mjs — local archive operations and rendering entry point
  • skills/edit-timeline-studio/mcp/server.mjs — STDIO MCP adapter
  • src/hooks/useWebMcpEditor.js — browser editor integration
  • skills/edit-timeline-studio/SKILL.md — agent workflow

The command reference documents the current contract and limits.

The larger lesson for me is that agent reliability depends on the application interface: explicit state, constrained operations, reviewable changes, and verifiable outputs.

If you are building agent tools or working on browser media, I would welcome feedback on the architecture. Real editing failures and reproducible cases are particularly useful. You can explore the source, try the editor, or browse the editing handbook.

Writing disclosure: this article was drafted with AI assistance using the project's source code and documentation.

title: How Does Website Speed Affect Search Engine Crawling and User Experience?
description:
Website speed plays an important role in both search engine optimization (SEO) and user experience. When a website loads quickly, visitors can access information easily, navigate between pages smoothly, and interact with the website without unnecessary delays. On the other hand, slow-loading websites can frustrate visitors, increase bounce rates, and make it harder for search engines to efficiently process website content.

In today's competitive digital environment, website speed is not just a technical requirement; it is an important part of building a successful online presence.

  1. Website Speed and Search Engine Crawling

Search engines use automated bots, such as Googlebot, to discover and crawl website pages. Website performance can influence how efficiently these bots access and process content.

A slow server response, frequent timeouts, or technical errors may make crawling less efficient. Improving server performance and reducing unnecessary loading delays can help search engines access website content more reliably.

  1. Faster Websites Improve User Experience Visitors expect websites to load quickly, especially when browsing through mobile devices. If a page takes too long to display, users may leave before finding the information they need.

A fast website provides:

  • Smooth navigation.
  • Faster access to important information.
  • Better mobile browsing.
  • Improved interaction with website elements.
  • A more comfortable overall experience.
  1. Website Speed and Google Rankings

Google considers page experience signals when evaluating search results. Core Web Vitals are important performance measurements that help website owners understand the experience visitors receive.

The three main Core Web Vitals are:

  • Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): Measures how quickly the main content becomes visible.
  • Interaction to Next Paint (INP): Measures how quickly a page responds to user interactions.
  • Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): Measures unexpected movement of page elements during loading.

Improving these metrics can contribute to a better page experience, although good Core Web Vitals scores do not guarantee higher rankings.

  1. Slow Websites Can Increase Visitor Drop-Off

When users encounter slow-loading pages, they may lose interest and move to another website. This can reduce engagement and potential conversions.

For example, imagine a customer searching for a local digital marketing agency. If one website loads within a few seconds while another takes much longer, the customer may prefer exploring the faster website.

  1. Mobile Website Speed Is Equally Important

A large number of users access websites through smartphones. Websites should therefore be optimized for different screen sizes, network conditions, and mobile devices.

Responsive design, optimized images, lightweight scripts, and
efficient hosting can help improve mobile performance.

  1. How Can Businesses Improve Website Speed?

Businesses can follow several practical steps:

  1. Compress and optimize website images.
  2. Use reliable web hosting.
  3. Enable browser caching.
  4. Minimize unnecessary CSS and JavaScript.
  5. Use a Content Delivery Network (CDN).
  6. Remove unnecessary plugins and scripts.
  7. Optimize website code and database performance.
  8. Regularly monitor Core Web Vitals using Google PageSpeed Insights.
  9. Website Speed and Business Growth

Website speed can influence how customers interact with a business online. A fast and responsive website makes it easier for visitors to explore services, read information, submit enquiries, and complete purchases.

For small businesses, improving website performance can support better customer experiences and help create a more professional online presence.

Conclusion

Website speed affects more than just loading time. It influences how efficiently search engines access website pages and how comfortably visitors interact with online content. Businesses should focus on technical performance, mobile optimization, and Core Web Vitals to create websites that are both search-engine-friendly and user-friendly.

title: NDIS Funding Changes 2026: What Participants Need to Know
description:
The National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) is undergoing significant changes in 2026. These reforms are intended to improve the long-term sustainability of the scheme while changing how certain support budgets are calculated and managed.

For participants, families and carers, understanding these updates is important when preparing for a plan reassessment, reviewing support arrangements or choosing a disability support provider.

One of the most important developments is the funding reset that began on 1 October 2026. However, the changes do not affect every NDIS support category. Essential day-to-day assistance remains protected under the announced funding adjustments.

This guide explains the key NDIS funding changes in 2026, what participants should review and how to maintain continuity of everyday support.

What Are the Major NDIS Changes in 2026?

The Australian Government passed the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment (Securing the NDIS for Future Generations) Act 2026 in August 2026.

The reforms introduce changes to funding, plan reassessments, provider compliance and the way the scheme operates.

One of the most significant changes is the reset of funding allocations for two support categories:

  • Social, Economic and Community Participation.
  • Improved Daily Living Skills.

The announced budget reset includes a 50% reduction in allocations for Social, Economic and Community Participation and a 10% reduction for Improved Daily Living Skills.

These are changes to budget allocations, not an automatic reduction in every participant's actual spending or all their NDIS funding. The impact will depend on individual circumstances and the supports included in a plan.

When Will the NDIS Funding Changes Apply?

The funding changes are being introduced progressively over 12 months.

The new allocations apply:

  • From 1 October 2026 when a new plan is approved or an existing plan is reassessed.
  • From 1 February 2027 when plans are renewed.

Participants do not all experience the changes on the same date. Existing participants can continue using their current plans and supports until their plans are reassessed or renewed.

This makes it important to understand your plan's dates rather than assume that every funding change applies immediately.

Which NDIS Supports May Be Affected?

The funding reset applies to the two identified budget categories.

1. Social, Economic and Community Participation

This category can include eligible supports that help participants access community activities, develop social connections and participate in everyday community life.

Participants who rely on these supports should review their current arrangements and consider how their goals can be achieved within the revised budget.

2. Improved Daily Living Skills

This category can include eligible capacity-building supports that help participants develop skills and greater independence.

Examples may involve therapy and assessment services, depending on the participant's plan and the applicable support rules.

Participants should check how their funded services are classified rather than assuming that every daily living service is affected.

Are Essential Daily Living Supports Still Funded?

Yes. The October 2026 budget reset does not automatically reduce all essential daily living supports.

The Government has identified several day-to-day supports that are not affected by these particular budget reductions, including assistance with:

  • Eating and drinking.
  • Dressing and toileting.
  • Laundry and cleaning.
  • Medication assistance and nursing care.
  • Home and vehicle modifications.
  • Personal mobility equipment.

This distinction is particularly important for participants who depend on regular support to manage everyday activities at home.

Eligible personal care services Melbourne participants use and assistance with daily living NDIS Melbourne services should be considered according to the participant's plan, support needs and applicable funding rules.

What Should NDIS Participants Do Now?

Understanding your funding is the first step. Participants can take practical steps to prepare for changes.

Review Your Current NDIS Plan

Check the funding categories, allocated budgets, plan dates and supports you currently use.

Identify which services fall under Social, Economic and Community Participation or Improved Daily Living Skills.

Discuss Your Support Requirements

Speak with your support coordinator, plan manager or my NDIS contact about any concerns.

If you expect your plan to be reassessed or renewed, discuss how the revised budget allocations may affect your arrangements.

Keep Relevant Documentation

Maintain reports, assessments and records that explain your disability-related support needs.

Documenting how assistance contributes to daily routines, safety and independence can help when discussing your support requirements.

Review Your Service Provider

Choosing reliable ndis providers melbourne participants can communicate with is important during periods of change.

Look for providers that explain services clearly, respect participant choices and understand the importance of consistent support.

Choosing the Right NDIS Support Provider in Melbourne

Funding changes can make it more important to understand how your services are delivered and how they relate to your goals.

When comparing ndis support providers melbourne participants should consider:

  • Whether the provider understands their individual support requirements.
  • Whether services are explained clearly.
  • Whether workers respect privacy, dignity and personal preferences.
  • Whether support encourages independence rather than unnecessary dependence.
  • Whether communication is consistent with participants and their representatives.

How Sahima Care Services Supports Everyday Independence

Depending on individual needs and plan funding, support may include personal care, assistance with daily living, household tasks, transport and community participation.

title: T3 Code: A Free, Open-Source Control Panel for Claude Code, Codex and Other Coding Agents
description:
If you use AI coding agents every day, you have probably hit this wall: three terminals running Claude Code, one running Codex, all poking at the same repo, and no single place to see what each one is doing or what it changed.

T3 Code is an attempt to fix that. It comes from Theo Browne's team (the people behind the T3 Stack and T3 Chat), it is MIT licensed, and it costs nothing. In this post I will cover what it actually is, how to get it running, what you need to watch out for, and how it stacks up against the free and paid alternatives.

TL;DR

  • T3 Code is not a coding agent and has no model of its own. It is a GUI and control layer that drives the agent CLIs you already have installed.
  • It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode and Google Antigravity, using your existing subscriptions.
  • You get a desktop app (macOS, Windows, Linux), a web app, and iOS/Android apps for checking on agents remotely.
  • Each task is a thread that can run on its own Git branch or worktree, with an inline diff and a one-click PR flow.
  • It is very early software (v0.0.x). New threads default to Full access, which means no approval prompts. Change that first.

What T3 Code actually is

The project describes itself as an "agent harness control surface". In plain terms:

 You (desktop / web / phone)
          |
          v
   T3 Code server  <-- owns processes, terminals, Git, project files
          |
   +------+-------+-----------+----------+
   |      |       |           |          |
 Claude  Codex  Cursor CLI  OpenCode   Grok / Antigravity
  Code    CLI

A server process on your machine owns everything that runs: the agent processes, terminals, Git operations and project files. The desktop, web and mobile apps are thin clients that connect to that server. The desktop app bundles its own server, so on a single machine you do not have to think about this split at all.

Because T3 Code drives the official CLIs, it signs in through each CLI's own login. It does not resell API keys or add its own usage quota. Whatever you pay Anthropic, OpenAI or Cursor today is what you keep paying. T3 Code itself is $0.

Why developers are paying attention

One window for many agents. Run Claude Code and Codex side by side, compare their approaches on the same problem, and switch models in the middle of a thread.

Branch per thread. Each thread can work on its own branch or Git worktree. A worktree is a second checkout of the same repo on a different branch, so two agents can edit files at the same time without stepping on each other.

Diff review and PRs in the same place. You see the diff as the agent works, then commit, push and open a pull request from the app. The PR gets a generated title and body.

Remote control. Leave the agents running on your workstation and check on them from your phone or laptop.

An MCP server. Other agents (Claude Code in a terminal, Codex, ChatGPT) can connect to T3 Code over MCP to read threads and start new ones. That makes a "coordinator agent" pattern possible without writing your own plumbing.

Getting started

Step 1: Install and log in to at least one agent CLI

T3 Code cannot do anything without an agent behind it. Set up at least one of these first:

# Claude Code
claude auth login

# Codex
codex login

# Cursor CLI
agent login

# OpenCode
opencode auth login

# Grok Build
grok login

Google Antigravity is the exception: you enable it inside T3 Code's settings and sign in with Google. No CLI needed.

Step 2: Install T3 Code

Pick whichever fits your workflow.

Try it once without installing anything permanent:

npx t3@latest

Install the CLI (server plus local web app):

# macOS / Linux
curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://t3.codes/install.ps1 | iex

Then:

t3                   # start the server and open the local web app
t3 service install   # keep it running in the background
t3 update            # move to a newer release
t3 --help            # full reference

Install the desktop app:

# macOS
brew install --cask t3-code

# Windows
winget install T3Tools.T3Code
# or
scoop install extras/t3code

# Debian / Ubuntu (download the .deb from GitHub Releases first)
sudo apt install ./T3-Code-*.deb

# Arch Linux
yay -S t3code-bin

Step 3: Change the default permission mode

Do this before your first real task. See the next section for why.

Step 4: Open a project and start a thread

Add your repo as a project, start a thread, choose the agent and whether it should run in a new worktree, and give it a task. When it finishes, review the diff and decide whether to open a PR or throw the branch away.

Permission modes: the setting that matters most

Every thread has a permission mode that decides how much the agent can do without asking you:

Mode What it does When to use it
Supervised Asks before commands and file changes. Work outside the workspace is restricted. Important repos, unfamiliar tasks
Auto-accept edits File edits go through, commands still need approval Refactors where you mainly care about shell commands
Auto Routine actions run, risky ones still ask Day-to-day work with providers that support it
Full access No prompts at all for commands or edits Throwaway worktrees and sandboxes only

Two things to know:

  1. Full access is the default for new threads. The agent can run any command and edit any file without asking. For a tool designed to run several agents at once, that is a risky default. Change it in Settings to Supervised or Auto.
  2. Auto mode depends on the provider. Codex hands routine approvals to an AI reviewer and Claude uses its own auto permission mode. Providers without an equivalent, such as OpenCode, fall back to asking every time, like Supervised.

The mode is set per thread, so changing it in one thread does not affect others.

Remote access in practice

The machine running T3 Code does the work. Your phone or laptop is just a remote. That means the host has to stay awake and reachable.

You have three main ways to connect:

LAN or Tailscale (traffic stays on your network):

t3 serve --host <your-lan-or-tailnet-ip>
t3 pair            # prints a QR code and a one-time pairing link

For HTTPS over Tailscale:

t3 serve --tailscale-serve

T3 Connect (no router or VPN setup):

t3 connect

This needs a T3 account and routes the connection through T3's relay. Convenient, but be aware of that trade-off if your company has rules about where code-related traffic goes.

SSH from the desktop app: add an SSH host in Settings, and T3 Code starts a server there and forwards the port for you. Projects, credentials and agent work stay on the remote machine. The remote host must be Linux or an Apple Silicon Mac.

Treat pairing links and codes like passwords. Keep them out of screenshots, logs and bug reports.

Letting other agents drive T3 Code (MCP)

Every T3 Code environment exposes an MCP endpoint at https://<environment-address>/mcp. For example, to connect Claude Code running in a terminal:

claude mcp add --transport http t3 https://<environment-address>/mcp
claude mcp login t3

For Codex:

codex mcp add t3 --url https://<environment-address>/mcp
codex mcp login t3

A new agent gets Read only access by default. You can raise it to Supervised or higher so it can start, message and stop threads. The address must be HTTPS (or localhost on the same machine), and sign-ins expire after 30 days.

What to know before you adopt it

It is early. The README says to expect bugs, and stable releases are still on v0.0.x with nightly builds shipping several times a day. Stick to the stable channel for real work.

Contributions are mostly closed. The team says small fixes may be considered, but big features will not be accepted for now. Feature ideas go to GitHub Discussions. If you need something specific, the MIT license lets you fork.

Docs live in the repo. There is no docs site yet. Everything is under docs/, and it is genuinely useful.

Your existing agent config still applies. Because T3 Code runs the real CLIs, things like your CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, hooks and MCP servers configured for each CLI should keep working.

The PR flow assumes a Git and GitHub-style workflow. If your work is not branch-and-PR shaped, you will get less out of it.

Costs still exist, just not here. Running four agents in parallel burns through your Claude or ChatGPT plan limits four times faster.

How T3 Code compares to other tools

There are two broad groups to compare against: orchestrators (tools like T3 Code that sit on top of agents) and AI editors and first-party agent apps (tools that come with their own model access).

Orchestrators and agent managers

Tool Price License Platforms Agents supported Interface Mobile / remote
T3 Code Free MIT macOS, Windows, Linux, web Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Grok Build, Antigravity Desktop + web GUI Yes: iOS, Android, web
Conductor Free local plan; paid Pro for cloud workspaces Closed source macOS only Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode Native Mac app Cloud workspaces on paid plan
Claude Squad Free AGPL-3.0 macOS, Linux (Windows via WSL) Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Aider, others Terminal UI (tmux) Via SSH
Vibe Kanban Free Apache-2.0 Cross-platform (runs via npx) 10+ including Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot, Amp, Cursor, OpenCode Kanban board in browser Self-host and tunnel

Quick notes on each:

  • Conductor is the closest competitor and the most polished Mac experience. It uses Git worktrees per workspace, like T3 Code. Its free plan covers local workspaces; reviews list Pro at around $50/month for cloud workspaces that keep running when your laptop is closed. If you are not on a Mac, it is not an option.
  • Claude Squad is a lightweight Go binary built on tmux and worktrees. It is great if you live in the terminal and do not want a GUI at all. No phone app.
  • Vibe Kanban frames agent work as kanban tickets, which suits people who like to plan a backlog first. Its original company, bloop, shut down in 2026 and the project continues as a community-maintained open-source tool, which is worth weighing for long-term support.

AI editors and first-party agent apps

Tool Price What you get Difference from T3 Code
Cursor Free Hobby tier; Pro $20/mo, Pro+ $60/mo, Ultra $200/mo, Teams $40/user/mo Full AI code editor with bundled model usage It is an editor with its own billing. T3 Code is a control layer and can even drive the Cursor CLI.
Codex app Included with ChatGPT plans OpenAI's own app for Codex Codex only
Claude Code / Claude desktop Included with Claude plans Anthropic's own agent, with built-in worktree support Claude only

The key difference: Cursor, Codex and Claude Code are where the model access and billing live. T3 Code does not replace them. It sits on top and lets you run several of them from one place.

Which one should you pick?

  • You use more than one agent and want a GUI on any OS: T3 Code.
  • You are on a Mac, want the most polished experience, and are fine with closed source: Conductor.
  • You prefer staying entirely in the terminal: Claude Squad.
  • You want to plan agent work as tickets on a board: Vibe Kanban.
  • You only use one agent and are happy with it: Its own app or CLI is probably enough. Claude Code and Codex both support parallel work on their own.
  • You want an editor with AI built in, not an agent manager: Cursor.

Wrapping up

T3 Code is not trying to be another AI model or another editor. It is a free, open control layer for the agents you already pay for, with worktrees, diffs, PRs and a phone app in one place. It is rough around the edges and changing fast, so treat it as early-adopter software and lock down the permission defaults. But if you already juggle several coding agents, it is one of the more interesting open-source projects to try right now.

Links:

  • GitHub: pingdotgg/t3code

Pricing and feature details were checked in early November 2026. These tools change quickly, so verify on each project's site before making a decision.

title: Announcing the World's Largest Free Font Collection: 500,000+ Typefaces Across 100 Sovereign Script Vaults
description:
Announcing the World's Largest Free Font Collection: 500,000+ Typefaces Across 100 Sovereign Script Vaults

Typography is the foundational voice of human civilization and digital culture. Yet, in modern web development, Linux server infrastructure, and digital publishing, non-Latin, minority, and indigenous writing systems frequently suffer from missing glyphs, font fragmentation, commercial paywalls, and broken links.

To solve this permanently, I architected and curated the Open Typography Foundation — a non-profit, censorship-resistant digital heritage preservation initiative dedicated to curating, indexing, and distributing 100% free and open-source typefaces worldwide.

Today, we officially achieved our grandest historic milestone: 500,337 verified open-source fonts categorized across 100 sovereign script vaults, spanning over 100 writing systems.

🏛️ The Master 500k Archive at a Glance

Metric Details
Total Verified Fonts 500,337 Typefaces (Clean TTF, OTF, WOFF binaries)
Sovereign Script Vaults 100 Dedicated Script Vaults
Global Languages & Scripts 100+ Writing Systems (Major, Regional, Endangered, Classical)
Licensing 100% Free & Permissive (SIL OFL 1.1, Apache 2.0, MIT)
Direct Single Downloads 1-Click .TTF Download on every font card
Master GitHub Hub Open-Typography-Foundation/100-Sovereign-Fonts-Vaults
Permanent Preservation Redundant mirrors on GitHub, GitLab, and the Internet Archive

🌐 The Universal Font Browser: Instant In-Browser Search Engine

Handling over half a million font files in a browser without browser freeze or gigabytes of memory consumption was our primary engineering challenge.

We developed a client-side Two-Tier Micro-Index Engine:

  1. Core Instant Search (1,941 curated families): Loads instantly with 0ms latency.
  2. Deep On-Demand Vault Indexes (382,980+ raw fonts): Broken into 100 ultra-compact JSON indexes (~13 MB total). When a user searches for any rare font, the browser asynchronously scans the indexes with automatic debounce and pulls live download links from redundant raw mirrors.

👉 Launch the Universal Font Browser:

https://mohammadgolamrabbii.github.io/typography/font_browser.html

🇧🇩 Major Script Vault Highlights

1. Bengali Typography Mega Vault (Vault 01)

  • Coverage: Complete collection of verified Bengali typefaces including Kalpurush, SolaimanLipi, Siyam Rupali, Hind Siliguri, Charukola Unicode, BenSen, and Li Ador Noirrit.
  • Specimen Feature: Branded cultural specimens honoring the blood-bought heritage of the Bengali alphabet ("রক্তে কেনা বর্ণমালা আর হৃদয়ে আঁকা বাংলা লিপি — মোহাম্মদ গোলাম রাব্বী").

2. Developer & Coding Monospace Suite (Vault 16)

  • Coverage: Curated programming typefaces with ligature support: Fira Code, Cascadia Code, JetBrains Mono, Hack, Source Code Pro, and Ubuntu Mono.

3. Polyglot & World Heritage Vaults

  • Arabic & Islamic Typography: Complete classical Naskh, Thuluth, Ruq'ah, and modern Kufic scripts (including Amiri, Lateef, Scheherazade).
  • Indic & Devanagari: Hindi, Marathi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, and Gujarati.
  • Cyrillic, Hellenic & CJK: Comprehensive Russian/Slavic typefaces, Greek Hellenic, Japanese Kanji/Kana, Korean Hangul, and Chinese Hanzi.
  • Endangered & Classical Scripts: Brahmi, Cuneiform, Egyptian Hieroglyphs, Phoenician, Runic, Cherokee, Osage, Bamum, and Batak.

💻 1-Click Terminal Fast Installers

For developers, DevOps engineers, and Linux system administrators, you can install fonts directly onto your machine via CLI:

Windows (PowerShell): 

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Open-Typography-Foundation/100-Sovereign-Fonts-Vaults/main/install.ps1 | iex

Linux / macOS: 

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Open-Typography-Foundation/100-Sovereign-Fonts-Vaults/main/install.sh | bash

🤝 Open Source & Preservation

Every font in this archive is preserved under open-source licenses allowing unrestricted commercial and personal usage in print, mobile apps, web design, and digital media.

  • Live Web Studio: https://mohammadgolamrabbii.github.io/typography/font_browser.html
  • Master Repository: https://github.com/Open-Typography-Foundation/100-Sovereign-Fonts-Vaults
  • Internet Archive Hub: https://archive.org/details/open-typography-foundation

Curated with passion by **Mohammad Golamrabbii.

title: Overflowing Septic Tank on a Weekend: A Homeowner's Game Plan
description:
Septic problems have terrible timing. The house is full of guests, the washer has been running all day, and somebody notices the shower is not draining. Then the downstairs toilet bubbles. Then there is a wet, smelly spot spreading across the backyard. It is Saturday evening, and you are wondering what on earth to do.

First, take a breath. A septic overflow is unpleasant, but with a few quick steps you can keep it from getting worse while you get help on the way.

Step One: Stop Sending Water Down the Drains
This is the single most important thing you can do. A septic tank that is overflowing or backing up has nowhere for new water to go. Every flush, every load of dishes, every shower adds to the problem.
Tell everyone in the house to stop using water. Turn off the dishwasher and washing machine if they are running. Do not flush toilets unless you absolutely have to. If there are guests, let them know kindly but clearly. A few hours without a shower is far better than wastewater coming up through a floor drain.

If you have a sump pump or anything else that sends water into the septic line, turn it off too.

Step Two: Keep People and Pets Away

Septic overflow carries bacteria and other germs that can make people sick. Keep children and pets away from wet spots in the yard and any fixtures where sewage has come up. Do not let dogs drink from puddles near the tank or drain field.

If wastewater has come up inside, close off that room if you can. Avoid walking through it and spreading it around the house.

Step Three: Look, but Do Not Open
It helps to notice where the water is showing up. Is it inside the house, around the tank lid, or out over the drain field? That information will help the crew figure out what is happening.
What you should not do is try to open the tank yourself. Concrete lids are heavy, older ones can crack, and the gases inside a septic tank can be dangerous. An open tank is also a serious fall hazard. Leave that part to people with the right equipment.

Step Four: Call for Emergency Help

Some septic problems can wait until a weekday. An active overflow is not one of them. When wastewater is backing up into the house or pooling in the yard, it is time to call.

When you call, have a few details ready. When did you first notice the problem? Which fixtures are affected? Where is the water showing up outside? When was the tank last pumped, if you know? Has anything unusual gone down the drains recently?

What Usually Causes a Weekend Overflow

There are a handful of common reasons. The tank is simply overdue for pumping and the solids have built up to the point where nothing can flow. Heavy water use, such as many guests or several loads of laundry in a row, pushes more water into the system than it can handle in a short time. Heavy rain saturates the drain field, especially in clay soil, so it stops accepting water. A clog forms in the line between the house and the tank, or at the inlet baffle. Or the drain field has been failing slowly and the weekend surge was the last straw.

What the Emergency Crew Will Do

Once the crew arrives, they will usually start by locating and opening the tank. If it is full, pumping it out gives immediate relief and lets them see what is going on inside. They will check the inlet and outlet, the baffles, and the liquid level after pumping to judge whether the problem is the tank, the line, or the drain field.

If a line is blocked, they can clear it. If the tank or drain field needs repair, they will explain the options and what can wait until regular business hours. The goal of an emergency visit is to stop the overflow and make the home usable again.

Cleaning Up Afterward

Once the system is working, clean any affected surfaces inside the house with a disinfectant, wearing gloves. Throw away porous items like rugs that were soaked. Outside, let the wet area dry naturally and keep traffic off it for a few days. Avoid spreading lime or chemicals over the drain field unless a professional recommends it.

Here When the Calendar Is Not Cooperating

CSRA Site Work and Septic is a family owned team based at 720 B North Liberty St. in Waynesboro, with more than 20 years in septic work across Augusta, Evans, Martinez, Hephzibah, Blythe, McBean, Girard, Keysville, and Waynesboro. Our office is open from 7 AM to 10 PM every day, including weekends, and emergency help is available 24/7. You can reach us at (706) 871 3955 or (706) 814 0189.

Keep the Plan Handy

A weekend septic emergency is stressful, but the plan is simple. Stop the water, keep everyone safe, do not open the tank, and get help. Save our number in your phone today so you are not searching for it with a backup underway. If your system overflows on a Saturday night or a holiday, our weekend emergency septic service is ready to answer the call.

title: Zetix for Agencies: Running Client Projects and Approvals in One Workspace
description:
Short answer: An agency can use Zetix AI to run the full client workflow in one workspace: new-business leads, client onboarding, recurring projects, feedback and approvals, client messages and monthly reporting. You describe how your agency works, and Zetix's agent, ZET, sets up the apps you need.

The workflow problem

Agency work moves through the same loop for every client: win the client, onboard them, deliver work every month, collect feedback, get approvals and report results. In many agencies each step lives in a different place: leads in one tool, tasks in another, client feedback in WhatsApp and email, files in shared drives and reports in slides. Account managers spend a large part of their week stitching it together.

The workflow in Zetix

1. New business

Enquiries from your website, referrals and WhatsApp land in Lead Management with an owner and a next step. Proposals are stored in Documents and linked to the lead.

2. Client onboarding

When a deal is won, the client moves into an onboarding stage with a checklist: contract, brand assets, account access, kickoff meeting. Automation creates the tasks and reminds owners.

3. Recurring delivery

Monthly retainers become recurring tasks in Workforce, with owners, due dates and statuses such as In progress, Internal review, With client and Approved.

4. Feedback and approvals

Client messages from WhatsApp and email arrive in a shared Omnichannel Inbox linked to the client record, so feedback isn't lost in someone's personal chat.

5. Reporting

Analytics shows work due and overdue by client and by team member, plus lead and pipeline numbers for new business.

Example prompt for ZET

"We're a 15-person digital marketing agency with about 30 retainer clients. We onboard new clients, run monthly content and ads work, get approvals over WhatsApp and send a monthly report."

ZET might suggest: Lead Management, CRM, Workforce, Omnichannel Inbox, Documents, Scheduling, Automation and Analytics. You can remove any of them before you click Build.

Why one workspace helps agencies

  • One client record shows deals, tasks, files and conversations together.
  • Fewer status meetings, because the board shows what's waiting on whom.
  • Smoother handovers when an account manager is away.
  • Pay for what you use: Zetix pricing depends on how many tools you choose.

FAQ

Can Zetix handle recurring retainer work?

Yes. Recurring tasks can be set up for monthly or weekly deliverables, with owners and due dates.

Can clients' WhatsApp messages be linked to their project?

Yes. The Omnichannel Inbox links conversations, including WhatsApp, to the client record.

Do we need a developer to set it up?

No. You describe your agency to ZET and it configures ready-made apps.

Get started

Describe your agency's workflow to ZET at zetix.ai.

title: How to recover overwritten or deleted files in your app
description:
By Octave · drafted with AI, tested on Hubfly space. Originally published on the Hubfly space blog.

TL;DR

  • What you get: an upload flow where every replaced or deleted file keeps its earlier copy, plus the version ID you need to bring it back.
  • Who it's for: developers whose users upload contracts, invoices, photos or exports into their app.
  • Time needed: about 20 minutes.
  • Cost: old copies are billed like any stored file, about $0.011 per GB a month.

A customer uploads contract.txt for the second time, and the new one is the wrong file. Or a support agent deletes a folder that was still needed. Without versioning, the original is gone, and the support ticket ends with "sorry".

This guide sets up a Hubfly space Storage bucket that keeps every earlier copy, so you can bring it back instead of apologising. You'll enable versioning, upload from the browser through short-lived upload links, and save the version ID each upload returns. That last step is what makes recovery easy.

Try it on Hubfly space → Create a free account, no card needed.

How versioning works, in one paragraph

A bucket stores files by key, such as tenant-001/contract.txt. With versioning off, uploading to the same key replaces the file for good. With versioning Enabled, the old copy stays in the bucket as an older version, and the new one becomes the current version. Deleting a file adds a delete marker instead of erasing the data. Your app only sees the current version, but the older ones are still there to read.

Step 1: Create a bucket and turn on versioning

  1. In the dashboard, click Create Project, pick Storage, choose the region and click Create Project.
  2. Click New bucket, name it (for example customer-uploads) and click Create bucket.
  3. Open the bucket, click Settings, set Object versioning to Enabled, then click Save settings.

Bucket settings: versioning, image cache retention, and the delete rule for buckets.

Do this before the first upload. Versioning only protects files written after it's on.

One-way switch. Once a bucket's versioning is enabled, you can set it to Suspended later but not back to Disabled. Suspended stops keeping new versions; the old ones stay. From a terminal, the same setting is hubfly storage buckets update customer-uploads --versioning enabled.

Step 2: Let the browser upload through a short-lived link

Browsers shouldn't hold storage secrets, and presigned S3 uploads from a browser don't work on Hubfly space (the S3 endpoint rejects the cross-origin check browsers send first). Instead, your server asks for an upload session, and the browser sends the file straight to the link it gets back.

First, create a storage API key: open the project's API access tab and click Create API key. Limit it to the customer-uploads bucket. The key starts with hfs_ and is shown once, so put it straight into your server's secrets as HUBFLY_STORAGE_KEY. It's limited to Storage upload sessions, so it can't manage the project, its keys or its settings.

Then add a small endpoint to your server (Node.js 18+, Express):

import path from "node:path";
app.use(express.json());

const ALLOWED = new Set(["application/pdf", "image/png", "image/jpeg", "text/plain"]);

function cleanName(name) {
  const base = path.basename(String(name || "")).replace(/[^\w.\- ]/g, "_").slice(0, 200);
  if (!base || base === "." || base === "..") throw new Error("bad file name");
  return base;
}

// POST /uploads/start  { fileName, contentType }
app.post("/uploads/start", requireLogin, async (req, res) => {
  if (!ALLOWED.has(req.body.contentType)) return res.status(400).json({ error: "file type not allowed" });
  let name;
  try { name = cleanName(req.body.fileName); } catch { return res.status(400).json({ error: "bad file name" }); }
  const objectKey = `${req.user.tenantId}/${name}`;    // e.g. "tenant-001/contract.txt"
  const r = await fetch(
    `https://api.hubfly.space/api/v1/projects/${process.env.HUBFLY_PROJECT_ID}/storage/objects/upload-session`,
    {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.HUBFLY_STORAGE_KEY}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        bucket: "customer-uploads",
        objectKey,
        contentType: req.body.contentType,
      }),
    }
  );
  if (!r.ok) return res.status(502).json({ error: "upload link failed" });
  const { data } = await r.json();   // { upload_url, object_key, expires_at, content_type }
  res.json({ uploadUrl: data.upload_url, objectKey: data.object_key });
});

The key is built on your server from the logged-in user, and the file name is cleaned first, so one customer can't write into another customer's folder. The content type is checked against a short allowlist, so nobody stores an HTML page in your bucket. The link works for one bucket and one key, and expires after an hour. Upload sessions take no size limit, so cap the file size in your app before you ask for a link.

Step 3: Upload, and keep the version ID

In the browser, send the file to the link. The response tells you which version you just created:

const start = await fetch("/uploads/start", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ fileName: file.name, contentType: file.type }),
}).then(r => r.json());

const put = await fetch(start.uploadUrl, {
  method: "PUT",
  headers: { "Content-Type": file.type },
  body: file,
});
if (!put.ok) throw new Error("upload failed or link expired");
const result = await put.json();
// 201 → { "object_key": "tenant-001/contract.txt", "version_id": "ver_5f96…", "size": 44 }

await fetch("/uploads/finish", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify(result),
});

On the server, save a row per upload, but only for keys inside the user's own folder:

app.post("/uploads/finish", requireLogin, async (req, res) => {
  const { object_key, version_id, size } = req.body;
  if (!String(object_key).startsWith(`${req.user.tenantId}/`) || !String(version_id).startsWith("ver_")) return res.status(403).end();
  await db.fileVersions.insert({ object_key, version_id, size, user_id: req.user.id, event: "upload", at: new Date() });
  res.status(204).end();
});

Asking for the link takes two to three seconds, and the upload itself under a second for small files. When your app deletes a file, record that too. The Storage delete call returns { "delete_marker": true, "version_id": "ver_…" }; that ID is the marker itself, not a copy to restore. The last upload row before it is the version to bring back.

Why save the version ID? The dashboard and the Storage object list show only the current version of each key. Neither has a "show old versions" list. Your own upload history is the simplest index of every version you might need to restore.

You can check any file's current version in the dashboard: open the bucket, switch to Raw, and click the info icon on a file.

Object details for the current version of tenant-001/contract.txt.

The Raw view shows one card per key, the current version only. Files added with the dashboard's Upload button get their own uploads/<id>/ key, so they never replace each other.

Step 4: Restore an earlier version

The dashboard's download button always returns the current version, so restoring goes through the S3 endpoint. Create an S3 access key in the project's Access keys tab (read/write, scoped to customer-uploads) and keep it on your server only.

Hubfly space's S3 endpoint lets an object GET address an older version with versionId. To restore, look up the version ID in your upload history, read that version, and write it back to the same key, which makes it the current version again. Before you do, check that the key starts with the requesting customer's folder, the same way /uploads/finish does.

What it costs

Every version is a stored file, billed at the Hubfly space Storage rate of $0.00001536 per GB-hour:

  • 1 GB for a month: 1 × 0.00001536 × 730 = $0.0112.
  • 10 GB of current files: 10 × 0.00001536 × 730 = $0.11 a month.
  • The same 10 GB where each file was replaced twice (30 GB kept): 30 × 0.00001536 × 730 = $0.34 a month.

Versioning, upload sessions and version IDs are free. Old versions count toward the project's storage quota (100 GB by default), so check Storage used on the project page now and then.

What can go wrong

  1. "I turned it on, but the file from yesterday is gone." Versioning protects only writes made after it was enabled. Turn it on when you create the bucket.
  2. Switching versioning back to Disabled is rejected (the API returns a 400 error). Once enabled, a bucket can only be Suspended. Choose Suspended to stop keeping new versions.
  3. Files re-uploaded with the dashboard's Upload files button don't create versions. Each dashboard upload gets its own uploads/<id>/ key, so nothing is replaced. Versions build up only when your app writes to the same fixed key, as in Step 2.

Limits, honestly

  • No version list in the dashboard or the Storage object list, so you need your own record of version IDs. Restoring goes through the S3 endpoint.
  • No automatic expiry for old versions is documented yet. If files change often, budget for the extra storage.
  • A normal delete only adds a delete marker; every earlier version stays stored and billed. To erase a customer's file for good (for example on a deletion request), delete each version by its version ID from your history.
  • A bucket must be empty, including retained versions, before you can delete it.
  • Files are stored without encryption at rest. Encrypt sensitive documents in your app before upload.
  • Once enabled, versioning can only be suspended, not turned off.

Who this is not for

If you need legal-hold or write-once storage (compliance archives that nobody, not even an admin, can delete), versioning isn't that, and no object lock is documented on Hubfly space. Use a provider with object lock for that case. If your files never change after upload, give each upload a unique key instead and skip versioning.

Read next: How to resize and watermark product photos with just a URL · How to get a managed PostgreSQL database for about $2 a month

Go further on Hubfly space

  • Hand out temporary download links for files in the same bucket.
  • Write S3 keys into your app as secrets with hubfly storage keys create … --to <cell-project>, which stores the secret as a Cell project variable.
  • Read the Storage limits and security notes before you put customer files in production.

Start free, 360 hours included. Create your Hubfly space account →

title: You Have Been Offered Shares Instead of a Pay Rise
description:
Your review went well. Your manager says so, the feedback says so, and then comes the part you were waiting for. There is not much budget for salary increases this year, but they would like to give you a grant of shares instead. A lot of them, they add, and they could be worth far more than a raise one day. You smile and say thank you, and then on the way home you realise you have no idea whether that was a good offer.

It might be. It is worth understanding before you decide how you feel about it.

Start with what you are actually being given. Shares, options and restricted units are different things. With options, you usually have to pay a set price to buy the shares later, sometimes a large sum, and sometimes with a tax bill attached. Ask which kind it is, and ask for the documents rather than a summary.

Then ask how they vest. Most grants are released over several years, often with nothing at all until the first anniversary. If you leave after eighteen months, how much is really yours? And what happens to unvested shares if the company is sold?

Ask what the number means. Ten thousand shares tells you nothing on its own. What percentage of the company is that, and how many shares exist in total? Will more be issued when the company raises money, making yours a smaller slice?

Most important of all, ask how you would ever turn them into money. In a private company there may be no way to sell until a sale or a listing that may never come. Plenty of people have held shares for years that ended up worth nothing.

So value the offer at a discount, perhaps a steep one. A pay rise pays your rent this month and lifts every future raise built on top of it. Shares are a bet. A bet can be worth taking, but it should not quietly replace your salary year after year.

It is perfectly reasonable to ask for some of both. You can say, I appreciate the shares, and I would still like to talk about base pay. Is there anything possible there?

Whatever you decide, decide it with the numbers in front of you, not the story.

– Asael Shinder

title: Tutorial: Connect an AI Support Agent to Order and Refund APIs With Tool Calling
description:
Tutorial: Connect an AI Support Agent to Order and Refund APIs With Tool Calling

Customer support automation becomes much more useful when an AI agent can do more than generate replies. It can check an order's shipping status, retrieve tracking information, verify refund eligibility, and help customers resolve common account issues.

But connecting an AI agent to business APIs introduces an important engineering challenge: how do you ensure that automated replies contain accurate information and that actions such as refunds or account changes follow business rules?

Imagine a customer asking, "Where is my order?"

A chatbot using only a static knowledge base might explain the company's shipping policy but cannot reliably tell the customer whether their specific order has shipped.

Now imagine connecting that chatbot to an order management API. The agent can retrieve the latest order status and generate a response based on actual business data.

This is the foundation of an AI support agent order API tool calling architecture.

Instead of allowing an AI model to guess operational details, developers give it access to controlled tools that retrieve information and perform approved actions.

This tutorial explains how to build that workflow using Python, API endpoints, permission checks, and audit logging. It also explores how Conversational AI Chatbots can handle common Tier 1 support requests without unnecessary human escalation.

1. Prerequisites

Before implementing the integration, you should have:

  • Basic Python knowledge.
  • Familiarity with REST APIs and JSON.
  • Access to an ecommerce order management system or mock order database.
  • A support chatbot or LLM orchestration layer that supports tool calling.
  • A backend environment for executing API requests.

For this example, we'll use FastAPI to build a lightweight support API.

The example will support two operations:

  1. Retrieve a customer's order status.
  2. Submit a refund request for approval.

The refund operation will not automatically transfer money. It will create a controlled approval request.

2. Step One: Define the Tools Available to the AI Agent

Start by deciding which operations the AI agent should perform.

Keep read-only operations separate from actions that modify business data.

For example:

Tool Purpose Permission
get_order_status Retrieve order details Read-only
request_refund Submit a refund request Approval required

The model should not have unrestricted access to your database or payment system.

Instead, it should call predefined backend functions with validated parameters.

A simplified tool definition might look like this:

tools = [
    {
        "name": "get_order_status",
        "description": "Retrieve the current status of an authenticated customer's order.",
        "parameters": {
            "order_id": "string"
        }
    },
    {
        "name": "request_refund",
        "description": "Create a refund request that requires approval.",
        "parameters": {
            "order_id": "string",
            "reason": "string"
        }
    }
]

These definitions tell the AI agent what tools are available. They do not grant permission to execute them.

The backend must independently verify every request.

3. Step Two: Build the Order and Refund API

Install FastAPI and Uvicorn:

pip install fastapi uvicorn

Create a file named main.py:

from fastapi import FastAPI, Header, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from uuid import uuid4

app = FastAPI()

orders = {
    "ORD1001": {
        "customer_id": "CUST01",
        "status": "shipped",
        "tracking": "TRK12345",
        "amount": 1200
    }
}

refund_requests = []
audit_logs = []

class RefundRequest(BaseModel):
    order_id: str
    reason: str

def audit(action, customer, outcome):
    audit_logs.append({
        "id": str(uuid4()),
        "action": action,
        "customer": customer,
        "outcome": outcome,
        "timestamp": datetime.now(
            timezone.utc
        ).isoformat()
    })

@app.get("/orders/{order_id}")
def get_order_status(
    order_id: str,
    x_customer_id: str = Header(...)
):
    order = orders.get(order_id)

    if not order or order["customer_id"] != x_customer_id:
        audit("get_order_status", x_customer_id, "denied")
        raise HTTPException(404, "Order not found")

    audit("get_order_status", x_customer_id, "success")

    return {
        "order_id": order_id,
        "status": order["status"],
        "tracking": order["tracking"]
    }

@app.post("/refunds/request")
def request_refund(
    request: RefundRequest,
    x_customer_id: str = Header(...)
):
    order = orders.get(request.order_id)

    if not order or order["customer_id"] != x_customer_id:
        audit("request_refund", x_customer_id, "denied")
        raise HTTPException(404, "Order not found")

    refund = {
        "request_id": str(uuid4()),
        "order_id": request.order_id,
        "reason": request.reason,
        "status": "pending_approval"
    }

    refund_requests.append(refund)

    audit("request_refund", x_customer_id, "pending_approval")

    return refund

This example provides basic customer ownership checks and records tool execution events.

In production, replace the in-memory dictionaries with a database, use verified authentication rather than trusting a customer ID header, and add idempotency keys to prevent duplicate refund requests.

Start the API:

uvicorn main:app --reload

Your local API will be available at:

http://127.0.0.1:8000

FastAPI also provides interactive API documentation at /docs.

4. Step Three: Connect the Tools to the AI Agent

Once your backend is available, connect the tool definitions to an LLM orchestration layer.

The workflow should look like this:

  1. Customer submits a question.
  2. The AI agent identifies the customer's intent.
  3. The agent selects the appropriate tool.
  4. The orchestration layer validates the requested arguments.
  5. The backend checks authentication and permissions.
  6. The API retrieves information or creates an approval request.
  7. The result returns to the AI agent.
  8. The agent generates a customer-friendly response.

For example:

Customer: Where is order ORD1001?

AI agent: Calls get_order_status.

API response:

{
  "order_id": "ORD1001",
  "status": "shipped",
  "tracking": "TRK12345"
}

AI agent: Your order has been shipped. Your tracking number is TRK12345.

Notice that the model does not invent the order status. It uses the information returned by the API.

For a refund request, the workflow changes.

Customer: I want a refund for order ORD1001.

AI agent: Calls request_refund.

API response: Refund request created with pending_approval status.

AI agent: Your refund request has been submitted for review. We will notify you when it has been approved.

This separation prevents the AI agent from claiming that a refund has been completed when it has only been requested.

5. Step Four: Add Permissions and Audit Logging

Two additional controls are essential before deploying the integration.

Permission rules

  • Allow verified customers to retrieve only their own order information.
  • Require refund eligibility checks before creating requests.
  • Require human approval for sensitive or high-value refunds.
  • Restrict account changes to authenticated workflows.
  • Never allow the model to bypass backend authorization.

Audit logging

Record every tool call, including:

  • Tool name.
  • Customer or authenticated actor ID.
  • Request identifier.
  • Execution timestamp.
  • Authorization result.
  • Operation status.
  • Approval outcome.

Avoid storing passwords, access tokens, or unnecessary sensitive customer information.

For state-changing operations, also implement idempotency keys so retries cannot accidentally create duplicate refunds or account changes.

6. Step Five: Test the Integration and Handle Failure Cases

Before deploying the agent, test normal requests and unexpected scenarios.

You can test the order endpoint with:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/orders/ORD1001 \
  -H "X-Customer-ID: CUST01"

Expected result:

{
  "order_id": "ORD1001",
  "status": "shipped",
  "tracking": "TRK12345"
}

Test a refund request:

curl -X POST \
  http://127.0.0.1:8000/refunds/request \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Customer-ID: CUST01" \
  -d '{
    "order_id": "ORD1001",
    "reason": "Customer requested refund"
  }'

The expected response should contain:

{
  "order_id": "ORD1001",
  "reason": "Customer requested refund",
  "status": "pending_approval"
}

Important Failure Scenarios

Invalid customer access: A customer attempts to retrieve another customer's order. The API should reject the request.

API timeout: The order service becomes temporarily unavailable. The agent should communicate that it cannot verify the latest status instead of guessing.

Duplicate refund request: A customer repeats the same request or the orchestration layer retries after a timeout. Use an idempotency key and persistent operation state to prevent duplicate requests.

Missing tracking information: The order exists, but tracking information has not been generated. The agent should communicate that the shipment details are not yet available.

Approval rejection: A refund request is rejected. The agent must communicate the actual decision rather than suggesting the refund was completed.

These scenarios should be included in automated integration tests before production deployment.

7. Which AI Support Platforms Can Handle Tier 1 Customer Service Without Escalation?

Developers do not always need to build every component from scratch. Several customer support platforms offer AI agents, API integrations, workflow automation, and configurable actions.

The right platform depends on the existing support stack and the types of requests you want to automate.

Gorgias AI Agent

Gorgias is particularly relevant to ecommerce businesses using Shopify.

Its AI Agent supports post-purchase conversations, including order tracking, returns, cancellations, and order changes. Configurable actions can update Shopify orders and shipping information under defined conditions.

It also supports customer confirmation and action conditions. However, certain operations involving fulfillment integrations or complex order changes may still require human intervention.

Documentation: Gorgias AI Agent.

Intercom Fin

Intercom Fin supports customer service automation through knowledge, workflows, procedures, and integrations.

Its developer platform allows Fin to be used as a tool within an existing agent architecture. Developers can also configure escalation workflows and procedures for specific support requests.

This makes it relevant to SaaS teams handling common questions about account access, product usage, and customer onboarding, provided the required authentication and account integrations are configured.

Documentation: Fin AI Agent.

Zendesk AI Agents

Zendesk provides AI agent capabilities that developers can extend through custom CRMs, business systems, and third-party APIs.

Its developer documentation covers workflow automation, webhooks, conversation management, and custom escalation logic.

This can be useful for SaaS and ecommerce support teams that already use Zendesk and need to connect AI workflows to existing business applications.

Documentation: Zendesk AI Agents Developer Docs.

Platform Comparison

Platform Relevant Tier 1 use cases Integration approach
Gorgias AI Agent Shipping, returns, order changes Shopify and connected app actions
Intercom Fin Common support questions, workflows, account-related procedures Workflows, procedures, APIs
Zendesk AI Agents Order inquiries, account support, ticket automation Custom APIs, webhooks, integrations
