I ran every code block below against the real archive files, and every output is pasted from those runs.

Why nothing warns you

A random split assumes the rows are independent. Copies break that assumption silently. Nothing throws, the shapes are right, the class counts look fine, and the score goes up. A higher score looks like a better model, so nobody goes looking for the cause.

Comparing every test row with every training row would find them, but that is n * m comparisons of long vectors. A hash set does it in one pass over each split. Give each row a fingerprint, put the training fingerprints in a set, and look up each test row.

Two passes, one lookup per test row.

Two details decide whether this is useful. Leave the label out of the hash, because a copy with a different label is still a copy, and it is one of the more interesting things you can find. And keep the row indices rather than a count, because every later step needs them.

Run it on a .ts file

UCR and UEA ship in the .ts format. audit_ts.py reads it with only the standard library. A row's identity is its text with the label cut off, so this is the whole idea:

audit_ts.py

def read_ts(path):
    keys, labels = [], []
    in_data = False
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for raw in f:
            line = raw.strip()
            if not line or line.startswith(b"#"):
                continue
            if in_data:
                body, _, label = line.rpartition(b":")
                keys.append(hashlib.md5(body).digest())
                labels.append(label.decode())
            elif line.lower().startswith(b"@data"):
                in_data = True
    if not keys:
        sys.exit(f"{path}: no @data rows found")
    return keys, labels

MD5 is fine here. Nobody is attacking this hash, and all it has to do is tell rows apart. Download the archive zip, then run it on a train and test pair:

git clone https://github.com/mahmadmanzoor/archive-audit
python archive-audit/audit_ts.py PowerCons_TRAIN.ts PowerCons_TEST.ts

n_train: 180
n_test: 180
duplicate_rows: 130
test_rows_with_train_twin: 67
test_twin_pct: 37.22
twin_rows_with_conflicting_label: 0
groups_with_conflicting_labels: 0

test_rows_with_train_twin is the number that matters. duplicate_rows counts across both splits: 360 rows in total, 230 distinct, so 130 are repeats. The two conflict lines count copies whose labels disagree, and here there are none.

It stays fast on bigger data. Crop has 24,000 rows, and the same command finished in 0.06 seconds and reported 2,753 of 16,800 test rows, or 16.39%. Add --json to get the row numbers.

17 of 128 UCR datasets and 3 of 30 UEA datasets leak on their default split. Eight of the UCR ones leak at least 1%.

The same check for arrays and dataframes

Your benchmark probably is not in .ts files. Once the data is numeric you can hash the values instead of the text, which also means 1.0 and 1.00 finally match.

fingerprint.py

import hashlib
import numpy as np

def fingerprints(X, decimals=6):
    """One hash per row, after rounding away float noise."""
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float64)
    X = np.round(X, decimals) + 0.0  # + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
    return [hashlib.blake2b(row.tobytes(), digest_size=16).hexdigest()
            for row in X]

def leak_report(X_train, X_test, decimals=6):
    train = set(fingerprints(X_train, decimals))
    test = fingerprints(X_test, decimals)
    twins = [i for i, h in enumerate(test) if h in train]
    pct = round(100 * len(twins) / len(test), 2)
    return {"test_rows": len(test), "twins": len(twins),
            "pct": pct, "indices": twins}

row.tobytes() does not care about shape, so this works on a batch of images as well as on a table. If you want to follow along with the archive files, this loader turns them into arrays:

load.py

import numpy as np

def load_ts(path):
    X, y = [], []
    in_data = False
    for line in open(path):
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        if in_data:
            body, label = line.rsplit(":", 1)
            X.append([float(v) for v in body.split(",") if v != "?"])
            y.append(label)
        elif line.lower().startswith("@data"):
            in_data = True
    return np.array(X), np.array(y)

The decimals argument needs checking, because rounding is a trade-off. Too strict and float noise hides real copies. Too loose and different rows collapse into one. So run it at several values and see if the count holds:

X_train, y_train = load_ts("PowerCons_TRAIN.ts")
X_test, y_test = load_ts("PowerCons_TEST.ts")
for d in (2, 3, 4, 6, 10):
    print(d, leak_report(X_train, X_test, decimals=d)["twins"])

noisy = X_test + 1e-9
strict = leak_report(X_train, noisy, decimals=12)["twins"]
rounded = leak_report(X_train, noisy, decimals=6)["twins"]
narrow = leak_report(X_train, X_test.astype(np.float32))["twins"]
print("noise, decimals=12:", strict)
print("noise, decimals=6: ", rounded)
print("float32:           ", narrow)

2 67
3 67
4 67
6 67
10 67
noise, decimals=12: 0
noise, decimals=6:  67
float32:            67

The count is flat from 2 to 10 decimals, so these are real copies and not an artefact of rounding. The noise lines show why exact bytes are not enough: add 1e-9 to every value and a strict match finds nothing at all, while decimals=6 still finds all 67. If your own count climbs as you lower decimals, you are starting to merge rows that are merely similar.

Exact matching also misses a copy that has been rescaled. If your pipeline normalises each row, hash after normalising:

def znorm(X):
    X = np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float64)
    std = X.std(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    std[std == 0] = 1
    return (X - X.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)) / std

scaled = X_test * 2
raw = leak_report(X_train, scaled)
normed = leak_report(znorm(X_train), znorm(scaled), decimals=3)
print("raw:         ", raw["twins"])
print("z-normalised:", normed["twins"])

raw:          0
z-normalised: 67

With a dataframe, pandas has the hash built in. Drop the label column first:

import pandas as pd
from pandas.util import hash_pandas_object

columns = [f"x{i}" for i in range(X_train.shape[1])]
train_df = pd.DataFrame(X_train, columns=columns).assign(label=y_train)
test_df = pd.DataFrame(X_test, columns=columns).assign(label=y_test)

features = [c for c in train_df.columns if c != "label"]
def row_hashes(df):
    return hash_pandas_object(df[features].round(6), index=False)

is_copy = row_hashes(test_df).isin(set(row_hashes(train_df)))
print(is_copy.sum(), f"{is_copy.mean():.2%}")

67 37.22%

Those are the same 67 rows the array version found.

Measure what the copies do to your score

A leak rate tells you copies exist. It does not tell you what they cost. For that, split your accuracy into twin rows and the rest:

from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

X_train, y_train = load_ts("PowerCons_TRAIN.ts")
X_test, y_test = load_ts("PowerCons_TEST.ts")

report = leak_report(X_train, X_test)
is_twin = np.zeros(len(X_test), dtype=bool)
is_twin[report["indices"]] = True

model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=1).fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = model.predict(X_test)
correct = pred == y_test
print(f"all rows:  {correct.mean():.2%} ({len(correct)})")
print(f"twin rows: {correct[is_twin].mean():.2%} ({is_twin.sum()})")
print(f"the rest:  {correct[~is_twin].mean():.2%} ({(~is_twin).sum()})")

all rows:  97.78% (180)
twin rows: 100.00% (67)
the rest:  96.46% (113)

This is raw values on the one default split, so treat it as a demonstration. The twin rows are a free 100%, and removing them takes the score down by over a point. Worms on the same setup goes from 45.45% to 37.31%.

For a fairer estimate the paper averages 30 resamples with and without twins:

  • 1-NN on z-normalised values: PowerCons 91.67% to 86.63%, Worms 47.75% to 35.52%, Crop 71.06% to 65.47%.
  • MiniRocket (2,000 kernels): PowerCons 95.52% to 92.83%, Worms 70.48% to 66.48%, Crop 69.99% to 65.44%.

So this is not only a nearest-neighbour effect. A model that trains on a row and is tested on that same row benefits whatever its design. On the published fold-0 predictions, the mean over 17 classifiers on Crop goes from 74.7% to 69.8%.

Warning: Do not try to find twins with kneighbors and distance == 0. On PowerCons, sklearn reported a non-zero nearest distance for 24 of the 67 rows I had confirmed identical, as high as 1.58e-06. Compare fingerprints instead.

Check both directions

Everything above asks how much of the test set is in train. InsectEPGSmallTrain shows why that is not enough:

X_a, _ = load_ts("InsectEPGSmallTrain_TRAIN.ts")
X_b, _ = load_ts("InsectEPGSmallTrain_TEST.ts")

in_train = leak_report(X_a, X_b)["twins"]
in_test = leak_report(X_b, X_a)["twins"]
print(in_train, "of", len(X_b), "test rows are in train")
print(in_test, "of", len(X_a), "train rows are in test")

15 of 249 test rows are in train
15 of 17 train rows are in test

Reported the usual way, this dataset leaks 6% and you move on. Flip the arguments and 15 of its 17 training rows are in the test set. Freezer's SmallTrain variant has 26 of 28, while MixedShapes' is clean. A dataset that exists to test learning from a few examples should not test on nearly all of those examples.

Same copies, very different headline.

Read the copies before you call it a bug

Not every copy is a mistake. ElectricDevices has 208 test rows with a training twin, 2.7% of its test set. But 54 of its twin groups carry conflicting labels, and 101 test rows have no training twin with their own label. Over 30 resamples, removing the twins there raises 1-NN accuracy slightly, from 69.39% to 69.65%, because twin rows only score 61.5%. So copies do not always help.

The reason shows up when you count distinct values in each twin row:

def median_distinct(X_tr, X_te):
    rows = X_te[leak_report(X_tr, X_te)["indices"]]
    counts = [len(set(row)) for row in rows]
    return int(np.median(counts)), rows.shape[1]

X_e, _ = load_ts("ElectricDevices_TRAIN.ts")
X_f, _ = load_ts("ElectricDevices_TEST.ts")
print("ElectricDevices:", median_distinct(X_e, X_f))
print("PowerCons:      ", median_distinct(X_train, X_test))

ElectricDevices: (2, 96)
PowerCons:       (77, 144)

Each result is the median number of distinct values and the row length. ElectricDevices twins are mostly on/off patterns, so two different appliances can produce the same row by coincidence. PowerCons twins are far richer, which makes a chance match much less believable. A copy can also be legitimate in the sense that real deployments see it too. So I would report the score both ways, and I would not quietly delete rows.

Do not loosen the match

The tempting upgrade is near-duplicate detection, because exact matching obviously misses some copies. Here is what a strict-looking correlation threshold does on OliveOil:

X_o, _ = load_ts("OliveOil_TRAIN.ts")
X_q, _ = load_ts("OliveOil_TEST.ts")

best_r = (znorm(X_q) @ znorm(X_o).T / X_o.shape[1]).max(axis=1)
share = (best_r >= 0.9999).mean()
print("best r >= 0.9999:", f"{share:.0%}", "of test rows")
print("lowest best r:   ", round(float(best_r.min()), 6))
print("exact twins:     ", leak_report(X_o, X_q)["twins"])

best r >= 0.9999: 100% of test rows
lowest best r:    0.999963
exact twins:      0

Every test row correlates above 0.9999 with something in train, and none of them is a copy. These are smooth spectra, and smooth spectra correlate. The paper sees the same thing on Wine (92.6%) and Meat (83.3%). A near-match is fine as a lead to go and look at, but I only count exact matches as leakage, and I accept that the result is a lower bound.

Fix the split

If you control the split, make the fingerprint the group, so all copies of a row land on the same side:

from sklearn.model_selection import (GroupShuffleSplit,
                                     StratifiedGroupKFold)

X = np.vstack([X_train, X_test])
y = np.concatenate([y_train, y_test])
groups = np.array(fingerprints(X))

def show(tr, te):
    twins = leak_report(X[tr], X[te])["twins"]
    print(len(tr), "train,", len(te), "test,", twins, "twins")

splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, test_size=0.5, random_state=0)
show(*next(splitter.split(X, y, groups=groups)))

folds = StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=2, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
show(*next(folds.split(X, y, groups=groups)))

180 train, 180 test, 0 twins
181 train, 179 test, 0 twins

GroupShuffleSplit does not balance classes, so use StratifiedGroupKFold when that matters. Both keep repeated rows together instead of deleting them.

Random resampling does not wash this out. It makes copies on both sides the normal case.

If the split is fixed, because it is the official one, keep it and report a second number without the twins. You do not need to retrain anything. Drop the rows from your existing predictions. For UCR and UEA the indices are already in the release folder:

import json

path = "release/clean_default_test_ucr.json"
entry = json.load(open(path))["PowerCons"]
drop = entry["test_rows_to_drop"]
keep = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(entry["n_test"]), drop)

before = (pred == y_test).mean()
after = (pred[keep] == y_test[keep]).mean()
print(f"{before:.2%} -> {after:.2%}")

97.78% -> 96.46%

Make it fail in CI

A check you ran once protects one version of the data. Put it next to the code that builds the split, so a new data drop cannot bring copies back unnoticed:

check_split.py

def assert_no_copies(X_train, X_test, max_pct=0.0, decimals=6):
    report = leak_report(X_train, X_test, decimals)
    if report["pct"] > max_pct:
        raise AssertionError(
            f"{report['twins']} of {report['test_rows']} test rows "
            f"are in train ({report['pct']}%): {report['indices'][:5]}"
        )

assert_no_copies(X_train, X_test, max_pct=40.0)  # passes
assert_no_copies(X_train, X_test)                # fails

AssertionError: 67 of 180 test rows are in train (37.22%): [6, 8, 9, 14, 15]

max_pct is there for data like ElectricDevices, where you have read the copies, decided they are fine and want to catch only an increase.

What this does not catch

  • Anything inexact. Shifted windows, augmented rows and resampled versions all hash differently. Every count here is a lower bound.
  • Shared sources. Two recordings of one patient are not copies but they still leak. For that you need a subject or source column to group on, and a hash cannot replace it.
  • Whether a ranking is wrong. More copies do not automatically mean a broken leaderboard, and in the archives the ranking barely moved.

On that last point, among the 15 classifiers I could rescore, 0 of 105 pairwise outcomes changed on twin-free fold 0. That is a weak test, since only 16 datasets have twin test rows, and the newest classifiers publish no per-row predictions, so I could not rescore them. I would still trust the broad order of the field. I would trust one score on one of these datasets a lot less. The paper is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. I could not find an earlier report of these copies, though that does not prove there is none, and the claim is about what the scores measure, not about the people who built the archives.

If you only take one thing from this, take fingerprint.py and run it on whatever you are benchmarking next. The row indices for both archives and the audit script are in the repo.

Originally published on my site. More posts and projects at mahmadmanzoor.com.

title: Zoom system design interview
description:
Zoom system design interview

A Zoom system design interview looks simple until the discussion moves past "use WebRTC and an SFU." That is usually where weaker answers stall. Interviewers want to see whether you can turn a familiar product into a concrete video-conferencing system architecture with measurable constraints, failure handling, and clear trade-offs.

This matters because group video exposes several hard problems at once: low-latency real-time media, bursty traffic, unreliable networks, and room-level fan-out that can overload a design long before average traffic looks dangerous. A basic whiteboard sketch is not enough once the conversation reaches scaling and production readiness.

This newsletter covers three things:

  1. How to frame requirements with capacity and latency targets.
  2. Why an SFU is the default, and where it still breaks.
  3. How to discuss routing, shared state, failures, and metrics like an experienced engineer.

What the system must optimize for

For interview purposes, define the problem before drawing components. A Zoom-like system supports interactive group meetings in which users create rooms, join from desktop or mobile, publish audio and video, share screens, exchange chat messages, and optionally trigger recording. Those are functional requirements, but they do not tell you which architecture to choose.

The stronger signal is converting fuzzy goals into explicit targets. In a Zoom system design interview, interactive conversation usually needs sub-300 ms end-to-end latency, with audio often requiring tighter bounds to prevent people from talking over one another. You also need high availability, regional placement close to users, and adaptation when network quality changes during a call.

Capacity assumptions matter early. A set of one-to-one calls, a ten-person team meeting, and a 200-person all-hands meeting create very different traffic patterns. In practice, candidates should state room-size bands, expected concurrent rooms, and the traffic mix, such as camera video, screen sharing, and audio-only listeners.

Note: Interviewers usually care less about exact numbers than about whether the numbers are internally consistent and drive your design.

A useful split is between the control plane and the media plane. The control plane handles auth, room membership, mute state, chat, and signaling. The media plane carries real-time audio and video packets, where latency and packet loss matter most. This signaling-vs.-media-plane split is one of the clearest ways to explain the gap between the control plane and the data plane in conferencing systems.

To make that split concrete, the architecture diagram should come early.


Separate control from media from the start.

The takeaway is simple: start with SLOs, room assumptions, and traffic classes before naming technologies. That is the foundation for clarifying the functional and nonfunctional requirements that Zoom interview questions usually test. The next question is which media topology actually fits those constraints.

Why an SFU wins for most meeting workloads

A serious answer compares an SFU, an MCU, and mesh in production terms. Mesh means that every participant sends media directly to every other participant. That works for very small calls, but uplink and downlink usage grow badly as participants increase, so client bandwidth and device CPU quickly become the limiting factors.

An #key# MCU: A multipoint control unit that receives streams, decodes and mixes or composites them, and then sends back processed outputs. #key# It reduces endpoint complexity because clients receive fewer streams. The trade-off is server-side transcoding cost, higher CPU usage, and extra latency from decode, mix, and re-encode steps.

An #key# SFU: A selective forwarding unit that routes media streams between participants without decoding the media payload. #key# It is usually the default for interactive meetings. Clients still encode their own tracks, but the server forwards selected streams to subscribers with much lower compute cost than an MCU requires.

That does not mean that an SFU is cheap. Fan-out shifts the bottleneck from media processing to outbound bandwidth, packet routing, pacing, and per-subscriber congestion control. If each publisher offers simulcast layers, the server must track subscriptions and forward the right layer to each receiver efficiently.

A concrete example helps here. In a 12-person team meeting, an SFU is usually the obvious choice because each user may watch a grid of several live cameras plus a screen share, and latency matters more than perfect visual composition. In contrast, an MCU can still make sense for a recording pipeline that needs a single mixed output or for a PSTN bridge in which the endpoint cannot handle multiple live video subscriptions. This is also where meeting-recording-vs.-live-streaming trade-offs arise naturally in a system design answer.

The trade-off summary is worth stating explicitly before going deeper.

Comparison of Mesh, SFU, and MCU Topologies

Dimension Mesh SFU MCU
Latency Lowest added latency 100-200 ms added 200-400 ms added
Client Bandwidth Upload/Download (N-1) Upload 1, Download up to (N-1) Upload 1, Download 1
Server CPU Almost none Low to moderate Very high
Server Bandwidth ~0 Egress scales O(N²), Ingress O(N) Egress scales O(N)
Scalability ~4-6 participants Dozens to thousands 20-50 participants
Quality Control Full client-side control Client-side layout, encryption Server-decided layout
Best-Fit Use Case Small/secure group calls Large interactive meetings Recording, low-power clients

Practical tip: Use an SFU as the default answer, then mention an MCU as a targeted addition for recording pipelines, PSTN bridges, or very weak clients.

The main takeaway is that an SFU wins because it preserves low latency while scaling better than mesh or an MCU for meetings. After that, you need to explain how signaling and media actually move through the system and how to choose among an SFU, an MCU, and a mesh topology based on workload.

How the media and signaling planes work

Once a user joins a meeting, the path should be explained step by step. The client authenticates, fetches room metadata, opens signaling over WebSocket, and negotiates media transport using WebRTC. During setup, the client gathers network candidates through STUN and TURN, then completes ICE and DTLS-SRTP to establish secure media.

A quick sequence helps keep this answer precise:

  1. Auth and room lookup: Validate identity, authorization, and room policy.
  2. Signaling setup: Exchange offers, answers, ICE candidates, and control events.
  3. Media publish and subscribe: Send tracks to a regional SFU and receive selected remote tracks.

The signaling path carries metadata, not the media itself. It tracks membership, mute state, active-speaker hints, screen-sharing state, and subscription changes. After setup, audio and video packets bypass signaling and flow directly between the client and the SFU over SRTP, which keeps the control plane lightweight and recoverable. In practice, this is the core of real-time media routing in a Zoom-like system.

Quality adaptation depends on layered encoding. #key# Simulcast: A technique in which the sender encodes the same video at multiple resolutions or bit rates so that receivers can subscribe to different versions. #key# A related option is #key# SVC: Scalable video coding, in which a stream is encoded into dependent layers that can be selectively forwarded. #key# Both approaches let the SFU serve different receivers without server transcoding. This is the practical heart of adaptive bit rate and simulcast in video meetings.

A simple failure case makes this more concrete. If a user is on unstable Wi-Fi and the downlink drops, the SFU can switch that subscriber from a higher simulcast layer to a lower one instead of forcing a full renegotiation. If that is still not enough, the system may pause remote video tiles and preserve audio first, because degraded video is usually more acceptable than broken conversation. That is effectively how to handle packet loss and jitter in Zoom-style system discussions, even if you keep the explanation concise.

A sequence view makes this easier to discuss in an interview.


Signal first, then forward media directly.

The takeaway is that a Zoom-like design depends on a clean split: signaling manages session state, while the SFU forwards real-time media. That baseline sets up the next question: where the system actually breaks under load.

Where scaling fails under room fan-out

Many candidates say "the SFU scales horizontally" and stop there. That misses the main cost driver. In practice, load is driven less by participant count than by total active subscriptions: publishers times consumers times subscribed layers.

A 100-person room illustrates the problem. If each person publishes audio and some publish video, the system can create thousands of forwarding relationships. Even if each individual stream is modest, aggregate outbound bit rate, packet pacing, congestion feedback, and routing overhead can saturate the host.

Think in operational metrics, not just room size. Useful capacity signals include maximum outbound bit rate per server, consumers added per second, #key# jitter: Variation in packet-arrival timing that degrades smooth playback. #key# packet loss at P95 and P99, RTP router CPU, and NIC queue pressure. Autoscaling on participant count alone can hide hot rooms that dominate fan-out. This is why load estimation for video-conferencing infrastructure should focus on subscriptions and layers, not just head count.

Watch out: A room with 50 active videos can be far more expensive than several hundred mostly muted listeners. Capacity models should reflect subscription behavior, not just head count.

Mitigations are usually pragmatic rather than theoretical:

  1. Room caps per node: Limit how many large rooms or subscriptions a single host carries.
  2. Subscription pruning: Pause unseen video, prioritize active speakers, and lower layers for background tiles.
  3. Cascaded SFUs: Distribute fan-out across nodes or regions instead of concentrating all subscribers on one box.

A common failure pattern is a company all-hands meeting with one presenter and dozens of visible participants. Average regional load may still look healthy, but one SFU host can hit outbound bandwidth or packet-pacing limits because that single room dominates subscriptions. The fix is usually not "scale everything," but to shard that room more carefully, reduce unnecessary video subscriptions, or cascade forwarding across multiple routers. That is the practical answer to "how many participants can a Zoom-like system support?" It depends more on subscription behavior than on a single room-size number.

A diagram helps make the bottleneck visible.


Fan-out, not joins, usually defines the limit.

The main point is that SFU scaling fails at outbound fan-out and routing overhead, not only at raw participant totals. Once you recognize that, the next production concern is what happens when nodes or regions fail.

How to survive node and region failures

A single healthy SFU node is not enough for a production answer. Rooms need affinity so that participants in the same meeting land on the right media router, but that mapping cannot live only in process memory. Most designs keep room-to-router metadata in a fast shared store such as Redis so that signaling services can resolve where a participant should publish or subscribe.

Sticky routing helps during normal operation. A user who reconnects after a temporary disconnect should be routed back to the same room context when possible, which reduces renegotiation and state churn. However, shared state also needs versioning because stale affinity can send users to dead processes or duplicate routers after partial failures.

Failure handling is where distributed-systems depth shows up. If an SFU process crashes, signaling should detect the loss, remap the room or affected tracks, and rebuild subscriptions from preserved metadata. If a host dies entirely, clients may need an ICE restart and track republish, but user identity and room membership should survive through the control plane. This is central to building fault tolerance in live video-call systems.

Note: #key# ICE restart: A recovery step in which endpoints gather new transport candidates and renegotiate connectivity without creating a brand-new meeting identity. #key# This is common after media-path failure.

Regional failure adds another layer. You may keep control-plane identity global while placing media regionally. That allows a user to remain in the same logical room even if media must be redirected to another region with degraded quality or a temporary reconnection delay.

Consistency trade-offs should be named explicitly. A strongly consistent room mapping simplifies correctness but can slow failover. Eventual consistency can restore service faster, but without versioned updates and idempotent rebuild logic, you can expose duplicate subscriptions, dropped tracks, or split-brain routing.

One realistic failure mode is stale room affinity after a partial outage. A signaling service may still think room R belongs to process A, while health checks have already moved new publishers to process B. If rebuild logic is sloppy, some clients reconnect to the old route, others reconnect to the new one, and you get missing tracks or duplicate subscriptions until the control plane converges.

A failure matrix keeps this grounded.

Failure Modes and Management Strategies

Failure Mode Symptoms/Examples Detection Signals Recovery Mechanisms Trade-offs
Worker Crash Worker process stops, no heartbeats from worker Missing heartbeats, error logs, OS-level monitoring Restart process, job re-assignment, checkpointing Fast detection risks false positives, more frequent checkpoints add overhead
Host Failure Multiple services unreachable, host unresponsive Failing health checks, loss of OS metrics Shift workload, distributed storage, fault domain isolation Redundancy incurs cost, live migration adds overhead
Signaling Disconnect Commands not received, jobs hang Discrepancies in heartbeats vs control messages Use heartbeat channel, retry signals, fallback to defaults Complex mechanisms increase network use, timeout risks, coupling adds architectural complexity
Redis Inconsistency Replica lag, torn writes, stale cache entries Replication lag metrics, keyspace events Promote replicas, cross-shard consistency patterns Strong consistency reduces speed, eventually consistent architecture risks stale data
TURN Exhaustion Failed peer connections, high latency in relays TURN server metrics, connection failure logs Scale infrastructure, rate-limit requests, use TURN server pools Expensive bandwidth, increased cost for availability, fallbacks affect user experience
Regional Outage Unreachable services, error reports from affected region Global monitoring, provider status updates, missing heartbeats Multi-region architecture, disaster recovery plans, DNS failover Active-active complex and costly, active-passive slower with data loss risk equivalent to replication lag

Watch out: TURN exhaustion is easy to overlook. When direct connectivity drops and relay usage spikes, a healthy SFU fleet can still look broken to users.

The takeaway is that production readiness depends on shared state, routing discipline, and controlled recovery paths. After that, the final step in an interview answer is proving the design with metrics.

What to measure and how to answer

A good design answer ends with observability, because that is how you validate the architecture instead of asserting that it works. On the client side, track RTT, estimated one-way delay, packet loss, jitter, frame rate, decode failures, join time, and reconnect rate. On the server side, monitor SFU CPU, router event-loop lag, memory, packet-queue depth, NIC saturation, and subscription churn.

Room-level quality metrics matter more than host averages. A single overloaded room can hide within a healthy regional aggregate. Many teams use percentile views at P95 and P99 for join latency, audio loss, freeze rate, and reconnect success because tails determine whether meetings feel reliable.

Practical tip: Organize metrics by user session, room, router, host, and region. That makes it much easier to answer whether the issue is local congestion, bad routing, or a broader infrastructure problem.

In an interview, the closing pattern can be compact:

  1. State that the default architecture is WebRTC clients publishing to regional SFUs, with the control plane managing auth, signaling, room state, and subscriptions.
  2. Mention that MCU-style processing may still appear in side pipelines for recording, PSTN interop, or special endpoints.
  3. Call out the real scaling pressure: fan-out across consumers and layers, not simply participant count.
  4. End with the production gap: multi-node routing, shared-state consistency, and failure recovery.

If you want more practice with this style of reasoning, developers often find useful detail in resources such as Educative's system design interview courses, Educative's WebRTC-focused content, and the MDN WebRTC guides. They are most useful once you already have a rough architecture in mind and want to pressure-test the weak spots.

The takeaway is that observability closes the loop between architecture and user experience. In a Zoom system design interview, that is often what separates a component list from a convincing explanation of trade-offs in a video-conferencing system design.

Closing

A strong Zoom system design interview answer is not about naming an SFU and moving on. It is about framing the workload, identifying fan-out as the main scaling cost, and showing how routing and shared state behave during failure. In practice, these same principles also appear outside interviews: large classrooms, internal all-hands meetings, telehealth sessions, and support calls all run into the same latency, routing, and recovery trade-offs at different scales.

If you keep the control plane and the media plane separate, define measurable SLOs early, and discuss recovery paths clearly, your answer will sound like production reasoning rather than whiteboard pattern matching. That is usually what interviewers are testing for when they ask you to design a video-conferencing system architecture under interview pressure.

title: 17 Products Launched on LaunchNests This Week - Here Are 4 Worth Checking Out
description:
Every week, new products ship across developer tools, AI, infrastructure, and productivity. Some solve very specific problems, while others are worth watching because of the space they're building in.

This week, 17 products were launched on LaunchNests. Here are four that caught my attention.

1. Prisma Postgres — Managed PostgreSQL for Modern Apps

If you're building with TypeScript, working on an AI application, or deploying a backend, your database infrastructure matters.

Prisma Postgres offers managed PostgreSQL for TypeScript applications and AI agents, with built-in connection pooling and a free plan.

It's worth checking out if you're looking for a managed database option for your next project.

2. SiftingIO Market Data API — Financial Data for Developers

Building anything around financial markets often means finding reliable ways to access market data.

SiftingIO Market Data API provides real-time and historical market data through an API for developers.

For anyone building financial dashboards, data-driven applications, or market analysis tools, APIs like this can be useful building blocks.

3. TriRank — AI Visibility for Search Console

Search visibility is changing as people increasingly discover information through AI-powered search experiences.

TriRank focuses on AI visibility for Google Search Console users.

It's an interesting area to follow for developers, founders, and teams thinking about how their products get discovered online.

4. TermiGram — SSH and SFTP Inside Telegram

Sometimes, a useful product is one that brings an existing workflow into a tool you already use.

TermiGram brings SSH terminal access and SFTP file management into Telegram.

If you're curious about alternative ways to access remote servers and manage files, this is one to explore.

More launches to discover

These are just four highlights from this week's 17 launches. The wider batch includes products across AI video generation, productivity, and other developer and consumer tools.

You can explore this week's launches on LaunchNests and discover something that fits your workflow—or a product that inspires your next build.

Building something yourself?

If you've recently shipped a product, tool, or side project, consider submitting it to LaunchNests. It's a place to discover new products and help builders get their work in front of more people.

What caught your attention this week? Share a product you think more developers should know about in the comments.

title: Vitest vs Jest vs node:test in 2026: Benchmarked on a Real TypeScript Project
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

I ran the same TypeScript test suite under Vitest 5.1, Jest 30.5 and Node's built-in node:test, and timed cold runs, warm runs, single files, watch mode and coverage. The suite is 39 test files and 183 tests against a small NestJS-style orders service, an HTTP API and an MCP server. The result surprised me: with default settings, Jest with @swc/jest was the fastest full run, and Vitest was the slowest of the three. Change one isolation setting and the order flips. Below are the numbers, the setup for each runner, and the TypeScript and ESM problems I hit along the way.

What I tested

Everything ran on November 3, 2026 on one Linux VM with 8 vCPUs (Intel Xeon) and 16 GB of RAM, on Node.js 24.22.1:

  • Vitest 5.1.0 (Vite 8.3.5), @vitest/coverage-v8 5.1.0
  • Jest 30.5.2 with @swc/jest 0.2.39 and @swc/core 1.16.21, and separately with ts-jest 29.4.15
  • node:test from Node 24.22.1, using Node's built-in type stripping (no loader)
  • TypeScript 6.0.3 for type checks. ts-jest 29.4.15 declares typescript >=4.3 <7, so it doesn't support TypeScript 7.0.2, the current latest on npm.

The code under test is real, not generated: money math with cent allocation, slugs, cursor pagination, an LRU cache, a token-bucket rate limiter, retry with backoff, a CSV parser, an event bus, Zod order schemas, a pricing service, an orders service with status transitions, a node:http JSON API, and the MCP server from my MCP testing guide. That's 387 lines of source and 501 lines of tests. The HTTP and MCP tests start real servers on random ports and call them with fetch and the official MCP SDK client.

To keep the suite identical, every test file imports describe, it and hooks from #t, a one-line shim that each runner maps to its own API, and asserts with node:assert/strict. Fakes are hand-written, so no runner-specific mocking runs inside the benchmark. I compare the mocking APIs separately below.

How I measured: a script ran each configuration 10 times in shuffled order. "Cold" means I deleted the runner's caches first (jest --clearCache, and node_modules/.vite plus node_modules/.vitest-cache for Vitest). "Warm" is the next run with caches in place. Times are whole-process wall clock, and I report the median. Every run had to exit 0 with all 183 tests passing.

One honest caveat: this VM is shared, and other jobs were running (load average between 3 and 13 on 8 cores). Absolute times are noisy, so read the ranking more than the decimals. I ran the main configurations in two separate batches, and Vitest, Jest and node:test each landed within about 0.1 s of their first-batch medians.

Results: the full suite

39 files, 183 tests, median of 10 runs:

Runner and config Cold Warm
Vitest 5.1, defaults (forks pool, isolated) 1.59 s 1.51 s
Vitest, --pool=threads 1.55 s 1.42 s
Vitest, --pool=vmThreads 0.91 s 0.91 s
Vitest, --no-isolate 0.75 s 0.68 s
Vitest, --fsModuleCache 1.63 s 1.52 s
Jest 30.5 + @swc/jest (CommonJS output) 0.99 s 0.81 s
Jest + @swc/jest, native ESM (--experimental-vm-modules) 1.19 s 1.01 s
Jest + ts-jest (type-checks every file) 4.30 s 3.13 s
Jest + ts-jest, isolatedModules: true 1.44 s 1.14 s
node --test (process per file) 1.23 s 1.24 s
node --test --test-isolation=none 0.52 s 0.51 s

The threads, vmThreads and --test-isolation=none rows come from the second batch. In that batch, the Vitest default, Jest + @swc/jest and node --test rows measured 1.52/1.40 s, 0.95/0.80 s and 1.14/1.23 s.

What the numbers say:

  • Isolation is most of the cost. Vitest's default forks pool starts a fresh child process for each test file, and its own summary told me so: "39 workers spawned, ~81ms startup each". node --test also runs each file in its own process. Jest isolates each file in a separate vm context but reuses its 7 worker processes. Turn isolation off and Vitest (0.68 s) and node:test (0.51 s) both beat Jest.
  • vmThreads is the middle ground for Vitest. It kept per-file isolation and cut the run from 1.51 s to 0.91 s. The catch is that it runs each file in a vm sandbox, like Jest does. Vitest's docs warn that this leaks memory on large suites (workers restart when they pass vmMemoryLimit) and that objects from Node APIs such as fetch's response.json() and structuredClone() have a different prototype. That's the same realm problem I hit with Jest below, and this suite only passed under vmThreads because I had already fixed those tests.
  • ts-jest with type checking costs about 2.3 seconds here. It was 3.13 s warm against 0.81 s for @swc/jest. With isolatedModules: true it skips the type checker and drops to 1.14 s. Running tsc --noEmit on the whole project separately took about 1.5 s (median of 5), so a separate type-check step is cheaper than type-checking inside Jest.
  • Caches barely mattered at this size. Cold and warm runs differ by 0.1 to 0.2 s for Vitest and Jest with SWC. Vitest 5 made fsModuleCache stable, but on a project this small it made no measurable difference. node --test has no transform cache at all, because type stripping is cheap.

Results at 4x the size

To see how the gap scales, I copied the test tree three more times: 156 files and 732 tests, same source. Median of 7 runs:

Runner and config Cold Warm
Vitest, defaults 5.15 s 5.03 s
Vitest, --pool=vmThreads 2.29 s 1.99 s
Vitest, --no-isolate 1.32 s 1.08 s
Jest + @swc/jest 1.75 s 1.52 s
node --test 4.32 s 4.26 s
node --test --test-isolation=none 1.08 s 1.10 s

The per-file process cost grows with the file count. Isolated Vitest went from 1.5 s to 5.0 s, while Jest went from 0.8 s to 1.5 s. Without isolation, Vitest and node:test stay around one second. On a busy machine, process startup is exactly the thing that gets slower, so your numbers on a quiet laptop may be closer together, but the direction should hold.

One file, the inner loop

Running only test/orders/service.create.test.ts (4 tests), warm, median of 7:

Runner Time
node --test 0.18 s
Jest + @swc/jest 0.39 s
Vitest 0.40 s
Jest + ts-jest 1.40 s

Node has nothing to boot except itself. Vitest and Jest each spend about 0.2 s more starting their runner.

Watch mode

I started each runner in watch mode, waited for the first run, then edited a source file and timed the rerun (median of 5). money.ts is imported by 3 test files. events.ts is imported by the shared test fixtures, so 18 files depend on it.

Watch command Edit money.ts Edit events.ts
vitest --watch 0.23 s, 3 files 0.97 s, 18 files
jest --watch (needs git) 0.25 s, 3 files 0.52 s, 18 files
jest --watchAll 0.66 s, all 39 files 0.61 s, all 39 files
node --test --watch 0.31 s, 3 files 0.94 s, 18 files

All three rerun only the affected test files. Vitest follows the module graph, and node:test did the same in my test. Jest's --watch uses git to find changed files, and outside a git repo it refuses to start ("--watch is not supported without git/hg, please use --watchAll"). Vitest's interactive watch UI is the nicest of the three (filter by name, rerun failed tests, the optional browser UI), but on raw rerun speed they're close.

Coverage

Full suite with coverage on, median of 5 runs after one warm-up:

Runner Time Lines reported
Vitest, @vitest/coverage-v8 1.99 s 97.38%
Jest + @swc/jest, default (Babel/Istanbul) 0.99 s 97.81%
Jest + @swc/jest, --coverageProvider=v8 1.66 s 98.44%
node --test --experimental-test-coverage 1.36 s 100% lines, 95.79% branches

Coverage added about 0.5 s to Vitest and less to Jest with Istanbul. The percentages aren't comparable between tools, because each counts lines, statements and branches differently. Node said 100% of lines while the others found a few uncovered lines in the same code. Pick one tool for your coverage threshold and stay with it. Node's coverage is still behind the --experimental-test-coverage flag on Node 24.

Setup for each runner

Vitest 

// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    include: ["test/**/*.test.ts"],
    coverage: { provider: "v8", include: ["src/**"] },
    // isolate: false,   // 0.68 s instead of 1.51 s, if your tests don't leak state
    // pool: "vmThreads", // keeps isolation, 0.91 s here
  },
});

That's all it needed. ESM, TypeScript, .ts extensions in imports, top-level await and import.meta all worked without extra config. The exception is decorators: a class with a legacy decorator and a constructor parameter property failed with "SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token" under my bare config, even with experimentalDecorators in tsconfig.json. Adding unplugin-swc 2.0.0 to the plugins, with experimentalDecorators and emitDecoratorMetadata in tsconfig, fixed it. If you're on NestJS 12, the Vitest config that nest new generates already handles this. I covered that in my NestJS 12 migration guide.

Jest with @swc/jest 

// jest.config.cjs
/** @type {import('jest').Config} */
module.exports = {
  testEnvironment: "node",
  testMatch: ["<rootDir>/test/**/*.test.ts"],
  transform: { "^.+\\.ts$": ["@swc/jest"] },
};

This works if SWC compiles your ESM TypeScript to CommonJS, which is what happens when you don't list .ts in extensionsToTreatAsEsm. It broke in three places:

  1. Top-level await and import.meta. My MCP server file had an if (import.meta.url === ...) block with a top-level await to start the server when run directly. As CommonJS, Jest failed to parse it: "await is only valid in async functions and the top level bodies of modules". I moved the entry point to its own main.ts, which is cleaner anyway, and used the same code for all three runners.
  2. Realm mismatches with node:assert. Jest runs each file in a vm context with its own Object.prototype. Objects created by Node's globals, like Response.json() from fetch or structuredClone(), come from the outer realm. assert.deepStrictEqual checks prototypes, so it failed with "Compared values have no visual difference". Jest's own expect().toEqual() and toStrictEqual() passed on the same objects. Vitest's default pool and node:test didn't have the problem. I changed those tests to JSON.parse(await r.text()) for all runners.
  3. jest.mock hoisting. With @swc/jest 0.2.39, a jest.mock() call wasn't hoisted when jest was imported from @jest/globals. The real module ran, and my "must not send email" guard threw. Using the global jest object fixed it, and so did ts-jest, which hoisted the same file correctly.

For native ESM, add extensionsToTreatAsEsm: [".ts"], tell SWC to keep ES modules, and start Node with --experimental-vm-modules. On Node 24.22, Jest 30.5 still printed "VM Modules is an experimental feature" for every worker. In this mode, module mocks use jest.unstable_mockModule() followed by a dynamic import().

// jest.esm.config.cjs, run with NODE_OPTIONS=--experimental-vm-modules
module.exports = {
  testEnvironment: "node",
  testMatch: ["<rootDir>/test/**/*.test.ts"],
  extensionsToTreatAsEsm: [".ts"],
  transform: { "^.+\\.ts$": ["@swc/jest", { module: { type: "es6" } }] },
};

Jest with ts-jest

ts-jest uses the TypeScript compiler, so it type-checks your tests, which explains the 3.1 s run. It also brings tsconfig friction. My project tsconfig uses "module": "nodenext" and verbatimModuleSyntax in a "type": "module" package, and ts-jest's CommonJS mode failed every file with TS1295: "ECMAScript imports and exports cannot be written in a CommonJS file under 'verbatimModuleSyntax'". I needed a separate tsconfig.jest.json with "module": "commonjs", verbatimModuleSyntax: false, and a paths entry for the #t import (Node-style imports aren't resolved with node10 resolution). You also can't move to TypeScript 7 with ts-jest yet, because of the <7 peer range.

node:test 

{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "node --test \"test/**/*.test.ts\"",
    "test:watch": "node --test --watch \"test/**/*.test.ts\"",
    "test:cov": "node --test --experimental-test-coverage --test-coverage-include=\"src/**\" \"test/**/*.test.ts\""
  }
}

No dependencies and no config. Node 24 strips types by default, and the test runner finds .ts files from the glob. The price is that your TypeScript has to be erasable: Node removes types but doesn't compile anything. I checked each case on Node 24.22.1:

Syntax node file.ts --experimental-transform-types
enum Status { ... } ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX works
constructor(private readonly repo: Repo) ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX works
@Injectable() decorator ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX SyntaxError

So a NestJS codebase full of decorators and parameter properties can't run under plain node --test. My orders service is written NestJS-style, with constructor injection, but it assigns dependencies to private fields by hand instead of using parameter properties. That makes it erasable, and "erasableSyntaxOnly": true in tsconfig keeps it that way. You also need .ts extensions in relative imports (allowImportingTsExtensions plus noEmit for tsc) and import type for type-only imports (verbatimModuleSyntax).

Mocking APIs compared

The same two jobs in each runner: replace an ES module that sends email, and fake a 60-second timer. All three files below passed.

// Vitest: vi.mock is hoisted above the imports
import { vi, it, expect } from "vitest";
import { sendReceipt } from "./receipts.ts";
import { sendEmail } from "./mailer.ts";
vi.mock("./mailer.ts", () => ({ sendEmail: vi.fn(async () => ({ id: "msg_1" })) }));

it("mocks an ES module", async () => {
  expect(await sendReceipt("a@b.co", 7)).toBe("msg_1");
  expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith("a@b.co", "Receipt for order #7");
});
// timers: vi.useFakeTimers(); vi.advanceTimersByTime(60_000);

// Jest (CommonJS output): use the global jest object so jest.mock gets hoisted
import { sendReceipt } from "./receipts.ts";
import { sendEmail } from "./mailer.ts";
jest.mock("./mailer.ts", () => ({ sendEmail: jest.fn(async () => ({ id: "msg_1" })) }));
// timers: jest.useFakeTimers(); jest.advanceTimersByTime(60_000);

// node:test: needs --experimental-test-module-mocks, then a dynamic import
import { mock, it } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
const sendEmail = mock.fn(async (_to: string, _subject: string) => ({ id: "msg_1" }));
mock.module("./mailer.ts", { exports: { sendEmail } });
const { sendReceipt } = await import("./receipts.ts");

it("mocks an ES module", async () => {
  assert.equal(await sendReceipt("a@b.co", 7), "msg_1");
  assert.deepEqual(sendEmail.mock.calls[0].arguments, ["a@b.co", "Receipt for order #7"]);
});
// timers: mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout"] }); mock.timers.tick(60_000);

Vitest has the smoothest module mocking for ESM. Jest's is fine in CommonJS but needs unstable_mockModule and dynamic imports in ESM. Node's mock.module() works, but it's experimental: without the flag, mock.module is not a function. Node 24 also prints a deprecation warning if you use the older namedExports option instead of exports. Node's mock.fn(), mock.method() and mock.timers need no flag and covered everything else I needed. For most service code, constructor injection with hand-written fakes, like this suite uses, avoids module mocking altogether.

Which test runner should you use?

Pick Vitest for a new TypeScript or ESM project, a Vite or React frontend, or a NestJS 12 app. It needed the least configuration, handled ESM and top-level await without flags, and has the best mocking and watch experience. Its default per-file process isolation is the slowest option at scale, so try pool: "vmThreads" or isolate: false once your suite is stable. Those settings made it the fastest or close to it in my runs.

Keep Jest if you have a large, working Jest suite, especially CommonJS. With @swc/jest it was the fastest default configuration here, and moving to Vitest is mostly an API rename (jest.fn to vi.fn) that buys you little speed unless you also change isolation. Swap ts-jest for @swc/jest and run tsc --noEmit separately: that alone took this suite from 3.13 s to 0.81 s.

Pick node:test for libraries, CLIs and backend code written in erasable TypeScript, where zero dependencies matters. It had the fastest single-file runs (0.18 s) and the fastest full run without isolation (0.51 s). You give up a rich expect, snapshot ergonomics and stable module mocking, and decorator-heavy code won't run. If you're comparing runtimes too, I measured Bun against Node separately, and I covered what changes in TypeScript 7 for build tooling.

FAQ

Is Vitest faster than Jest?

Not with default settings in my test. On a 39-file TypeScript suite, Jest 30.5 with @swc/jest took 0.81 s warm and Vitest 5.1 took 1.51 s, because Vitest's default forks pool starts a process per test file. With isolate: false Vitest took 0.68 s, and with pool: vmThreads 0.91 s. At 156 files the default gap grew to 1.52 s for Jest against 5.03 s for Vitest.

Can node:test run TypeScript without a loader?

Yes, on Node 24 type stripping is on by default and node --test picks up .ts files from a glob. It only removes types, so enums, constructor parameter properties and decorators fail with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX. You also need .ts extensions in relative imports and import type for type-only imports.

Should I use ts-jest or @swc/jest?

Use @swc/jest and run tsc --noEmit as a separate step. In my runs ts-jest took 3.13 s warm because it type-checks every file, against 0.81 s for @swc/jest, while tsc on the whole project took about 1.5 s. ts-jest 29.4.15 also declares typescript below 7, so it doesn't support TypeScript 7 yet.

Does Jest support ESM in 2026?

Yes, but still behind Node's --experimental-vm-modules flag. Jest 30.5 on Node 24.22 ran my suite as native ESM in 1.01 s warm, but printed an experimental warning for every worker, and module mocks need jest.unstable_mockModule plus a dynamic import. Compiling to CommonJS with @swc/jest avoids the flag but breaks top-level await and import.meta.

Which test runner has the fastest watch mode?

They were close. After editing a file imported by 3 test files, Vitest reran in 0.23 s, jest --watch in 0.25 s and node --test --watch in 0.31 s, and all three reran only the affected files. jest --watch needs a git repository; jest --watchAll reruns every file.

Node.js and Express are widely used to build the backend layer that connects your mobile or web application with databases, authentication, APIs and business logic.

For example, in an e-commerce app:

Flutter App → Express API → Node.js Backend → Database

A request like POST /api/orders can validate the user, check product availability, create the order and return the result to the app.

The important part isn’t just creating API endpoints. Good backend engineering means keeping business logic organized, validating data, handling errors, securing endpoints and designing the API so the application can scale.

That’s how I approach Node.js/Express projects: the backend should be reliable, maintainable and easy for the frontend to work with.

If you’re building a mobile or web application, don’t treat the backend as an afterthought. Build the foundation properly from the start.

title: How to Design a Guided Camera Flow People Actually Follow
description:
Here is the brief. A person is standing in a car park. They are holding a phone in one hand and car keys in the other. It is bright, they are in a hurry, and they are not a photographer.

You need eight specific photos from them, from specific angles, consistent enough that all eight look like they belong to the same set.

Most capture flows fail at this, and they fail in the same few ways. These are the lessons that came out of building one.

## Nobody reads the instructions

The instinct is to explain. "Stand about three metres from the front left corner of the vehicle, with the car filling roughly 80 percent of the frame."

Nobody reads that. Not because users are careless, but because they are standing outside holding things, and reading is a task you just added on top of the task they came to do.

Replace the sentence with a picture. A faint outline on the camera view showing where the car should sit does the entire job with no reading at all. People align things to shapes automatically. They do not parse spatial instructions.

If you have text at all, it should be three words. "Front left corner."

Show the target, not the error

Telling someone they got it wrong after the fact is the worst possible moment. They have already moved, already tapped, already mentally finished that step.

Put the guidance before the shutter. An outline they are aligning to, that changes colour when they are close enough, is a conversation that happens while they can still act on it. The user fixes the problem without ever being told there was one.

This is the single biggest difference between a flow people finish and a flow people abandon.

## Validate immediately, but never block

Check the photo the instant it is taken. Too dark, too blurry, object not found, obviously the wrong angle. Those checks are cheap and they catch most real problems.

But do not trap people. If someone has tried twice and it is still not passing, let them through. Mark the photo as needing review and move on.

A flow that refuses to advance is a flow that gets closed. You will lose the other six photos as well as the one you were arguing about, and you will never get that person back to the car park.

Accept and flag beats reject and insist, every time.

## Progress is the motivator, not quality

A counter showing "3 of 8" does more for completion than any amount of feedback about image quality.

People finish things that look finishable. A visible end point turns an open-ended chore into a short list, and short lists get completed. Quality nagging does the opposite, because every correction makes the end feel further away.

Show progress prominently. Show quality feedback quietly.

## Assume the worst conditions, because they are the normal ones

Direct sunlight means they cannot see your subtle grey overlay. Use high contrast.

One hand is busy. Keep everything reachable with a thumb, and never put a critical control at the top of the screen.

Signal is bad. Car parks are famously bad for this, and often half underground. Capture locally, queue the upload, and let them walk away. If your flow requires a successful upload before the next photo, you have built something that fails outdoors, which is the only place it will ever be used.

And assume they will be interrupted. Save state after every single photo so that a phone call does not cost them the whole session.

## The thing that is actually hard

None of the above is technically difficult. The hard part is accepting that the person using your flow does not care about it and never will.

They are not evaluating your interface. They want to put the keys down and go back inside. Every decision gets easier once you design for that person instead of the attentive user in your head.

We wrote up what good capture actually looks like from the photography side, which is the other half of this problem.

title: Building a code editor inside itself, with AI agents writing every line
description:
I'm Pavel, a developer in Prague. Around October 28, 2026 I launched Edit (https://rustedit.dev), an agentic code editor written in Rust. It is free for now. This post is about how it was made, because the process is the unusual part: AI agents wrote all of the code, and Edit was built in Edit.

What Edit is

Edit has two faces. One is a GPU-drawn desktop app. The other is a Rust terminal UI that runs in any terminal, with window docking and syntax highlighting. Both share the same idea: the editor and the coding agent should live in one place, and working with the agent should feel like using an IDE, not reading a log.

The AI Assistant does not ship its own model wrapper. It runs the command-line coding agents developers already use: Claude Code, Cursor Agent and Codex. Edit's job is to make working with them pleasant.

The bootstrap problem

A tool that is built in itself has an obvious chicken-and-egg problem. Early on, the editor has to be just good enough to host the agent that will improve it. From that point, every rough edge I hit while directing agents became the next task. If something annoyed me while working, I was the first user to feel it, and it went straight back into the backlog.

My role changed from writing code to deciding what to build, describing it clearly, reviewing what the agents produced, and testing it by using it. The agents wrote the Rust. They also built the website.

Lesson one: agent output should be something you act on

Coding agents reply in Markdown. In a plain terminal that means reading around raw asterisks and hash signs. One of the first things the agents built was rendering: in Edit's terminal, agent replies arrive formatted, with headings, lists, tables and code blocks.

Formatting was only half of it. Agents often end a reply with numbered options: "Should I do 1, 2 or 3?" In Edit those options become rows you can pick, either with a click or by pressing 1 to 9. That sounds small, but when you spend the whole day steering agents, it removes a lot of typing.

You can also select and copy any line of a reply. When the agent produces a command or a path, you grab it directly instead of fighting the terminal's own selection.

Lesson two: settings matter when agents do the work

When agents write everything, how they are allowed to work matters as much as what they write. The composer has a model menu grouped by model, with the effort level and a Fast toggle inside, so switching between a careful run and a quick one is one choice instead of a long list.

Agent Settings collects the controls I kept needing:

  • Skills: the instructions agents can use for particular kinds of tasks.
  • Autopick Skills: more on this below.
  • Run Commands Without Asking: for when you trust the task and want fewer interruptions.
  • Use MCP Servers: whether the agent can reach your MCP tools.
  • Sandbox: limiting what the agent can touch.

Being able to change these quickly made it practical to let agents take on bigger pieces of the editor while keeping risky work contained.

Lesson three: skills only help if the right ones are used

Skills are useful, but there is a catch. Once you have more than a handful installed, you stop remembering which one fits the task in front of you. The agent may not pick it up either.

So I came up with Autopick Skills. When it is on, Edit automatically picks the right skills for the task, so each prompt goes to the agent with the skills that fit it. I invented it for Edit, and as far as I know no other agentic system has it. In practice it meant the agents building Edit got the relevant guidance without me attaching it by hand every time.

What working this way felt like

A few honest observations:

  • Review is the real work. Agents produce code fast. Deciding whether it is right, and whether it is what you meant, is where my time went.
  • Dogfooding is relentless. Since I used Edit to build Edit all day, every bug was personal. That pushed quality up faster than any checklist.
  • Clear descriptions beat clever prompts. The better I described the behavior I wanted, the less back-and-forth followed.
  • The tool shapes the process. Features like pickable options and skill autopicking came from friction I felt while directing agents, not from a roadmap.

Try it

Edit runs as a GPU app or in any terminal, works with Claude Code, Cursor Agent and Codex, and is free for now. If you try it, I'd especially like to hear how Autopick Skills works for your setup and what feels missing in the terminal UI.

https://rustedit.dev

title: 1,000 users, 1 API call: the fan-out pattern that saved my rate limit
description:
If every visitor's browser polls your API, your usage grows with your audience. Mine doesn't: whether one person or a thousand open the app, the upstream API gets a single call.

The app is this live airspace visualizer, a 3D globe that shows live air traffic, with new aircraft positions every 15 seconds. If you wonder how the aircraft keep flying smoothly between updates, I explained it in this other article.

The data comes from a third-party API with a rate limit per account, not per user. If each browser called it directly, a hundred open tabs would mean a hundred calls every 15 seconds, and I'd hit the limit long before the app got any traffic. Besides, the API key can't live in the frontend.

One poller, many clients

The solution is a small proxy between the browsers and the API. It has a single poller that asks the API for new data every 15 seconds and sends the result to every connected browser over Server-Sent Events (SSE). The number of users only changes how many connections the proxy keeps open, not how many requests reach the API.

Each browser opens a connection to /api/states. The proxy sets the SSE headers, keeps the response open and hands it to the poller. When the browser closes the connection, the poller forgets about it.

  app.get('/api/states', (req, res) => {
    res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/event-stream')
    res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'no-cache')
    res.flushHeaders()

    const client_id = poller.register(res)
    // The browser closed the tab or lost the connection
    req.on('close', () => poller.unregister(client_id))
  })

On every tick, the poller makes one request and writes the result to every connection it has. An SSE message is just text, so writing to an open response is enough. If the request fails, the clients get an error event instead and the poller tries again on the next tick. There's also a lock so two requests don't overlap when the API is slow, and a timeout so one that never answers can't hold that lock forever.

  private broadcast(event: string, data: unknown) {
    // An SSE message: event name, data and a blank line
    for (const res of this.clients.values()) {
      res.write(`event: ${event}\ndata: ${JSON.stringify(data)}\n\n`)
    }
  }

  private async dispatcher() {
    // The previous request is still running: skip this tick
    if (this.is_fetching) return
    this.is_fetching = true
    try {
      // One request, no matter how many clients there are
      const data = await this.get_data_with_timeout()
      this.latest_data = data
      this.latest_data_at = Date.now()
      this.broadcast('success', data)
    } catch (error) {
      this.broadcast('error', { message: this.error_message(error) })
    } finally {
      this.is_fetching = false
    }
  }

The poller only runs while someone is watching. The first client to connect starts it. Since the latest result is cached, anyone who connects later gets it straight away instead of waiting up to 15 seconds for the next tick. If the cache is more than a minute old, it's thrown away rather than served stale.

  register(res: express.Response) {
    const client_id = randomUUID()
    this.clients.set(client_id, res)

    // Older than a minute (or nothing yet): discard it
    const age = Date.now() - (this.latest_data_at ?? 0)
    if (age > MAX_DATA_AGE_MS) this.latest_data = null
    // The new client doesn't wait for the next tick
    if (this.latest_data !== null) this.write_sse(res, 'success', this.latest_data)

    // First client: start polling
    if (this.interval_id === null) {
      void this.dispatcher()
      this.interval_id = setInterval(() => void this.dispatcher(), this.time_ms)
    }
    return client_id
  }

When the last client disconnects, the interval is cleared and the proxy stops calling the API until someone comes back.

  unregister(client_id: string) {
    this.clients.delete(client_id)
    // Last one out turns off the lights
    if (this.clients.size === 0 && this.interval_id !== null) {
      clearInterval(this.interval_id)
      this.interval_id = null
    }
  }

Why SSE and not WebSockets

WebSockets would work too, but they solve a problem I don't have. Here the data only goes one way, from the server to the browser, and that's exactly what SSE is for. It works over plain HTTP, so it goes through proxies and load balancers without extra setup, and the browser reconnects on its own if the connection drops. On the client it's just a few lines:

  const event_source = new EventSource(api_url('states'))
  event_source.addEventListener('success', (event) => {
    layer.update_aircrafts(JSON.parse(event.data))
  })

With WebSockets I'd have to handle the protocol upgrade, the reconnection and a message format myself, for a channel where the browser never sends anything.

Disconnecting when no one is watching

There's one case left. If someone opens the app and leaves it in a background tab, the SSE connection stays open. If they're the only user, the poller keeps calling the API every 15 seconds for nobody.

To avoid it, the frontend listens to the visibilitychange event. When the tab is hidden it starts a one-minute timer, and when the timer runs out the stream is paused. If the user comes back before that, the timer is cancelled and nothing happens.

  const INACTIVE_DISCONNECT_MS = 60_000

  const handle_visibility_change = () => {

const handle_visibility_change = () => {
  clearTimeout(timeout)
  if (document.hidden) {
    // Hidden tab: pause the stream after a minute
    timeout = setTimeout(() => set_stream_paused(true), INACTIVE_DISCONNECT_MS)
  } else {
    set_stream_paused(false)
  }
}
document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', handle_visibility_change)


typescript

Pausing the stream closes the EventSource. To the proxy that's just another client leaving, so if it was the last one, polling stops. When the user comes back, a new connection opens and gets the cached data if it's still fresh, or starts the poller again if it isn't. I also add a "Paused" prefix to the page title, so the tab bar shows why the data isn't moving.

useEffect(() => {
  if (stream_paused) return
  const event_source = new EventSource(api_url('states'))
  // ...
  // Closing it unregisters this client in the proxy
  return () => event_source.close()
}, [stream_paused])

Conclusion

This pattern works for any project that needs regular updates from an API you don't control: prices, weather, scores, the status of a deploy. If the data is the same for everyone, there's no reason for each user to ask for it. One poller, a cache and a list of open connections are enough, and the cost stays the same with one user or a thousand.

It has its limits: it only works when everyone sees the same data, and the connections live in the memory of one process, so if you run several instances, each one has its own poller. For a project like this one, it's a good trade-off.

You can see it live at airspace.juanesroig.com. The code is on GitHub: the frontend in airspace-visualization and the proxy in opensky-proxy.
