title: I built a Windows SQL client where an LLM drafts the query and you stay in control
description:
Disclosure: I work at Mirinai and built this app. This post was drafted with the help of AI and reviewed by me.

Letting an LLM near a database worries me in two ways: what leaves my machine, and what happens if the generated SQL is wrong. I built Chat DB Manager, a Windows desktop database client, around those two questions.

You ask a question in plain language and the app fills the editor with SQL for the connected DBMS. Nothing runs until you read it and press Run.

What goes to the LLM

  • Default mode (SQL Helper) sends the schema in a compact notation (tables, columns, types, keys, comments, indexes), not table rows. Conversation history, files you attach, and the DB error text on auto-repair are also sent. Asking for an execution plan explanation sends the SQL and the plan. Sample values of code-like columns are sent only if you turn that on (off by default).
  • Agent mode runs read queries itself and reads the rows, so it needs explicit consent per recipient company. Switching provider resets it to SQL Helper.
  • With a local model behind an OpenAI-compatible URL (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM), LLM requests go only to that URL.
  • No telemetry. The app only contacts your LLM provider and our server for update checks.

What happens before SQL runs

  • Risk is decided by the app parsing the SQL, not by the model's label. A script is judged by its worst statement, so SELECT 1; DROP TABLE t is not a SELECT.
  • Read-only connections refuse anything but SELECT.
  • Writes run in an open transaction. You see the affected row count and commit or roll back. No answer in 2 minutes means rollback.
  • DDL and UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE need an extra confirmation, plus a checkbox on connections tagged prod.
  • Agent reads run in a read-only transaction and are rolled back (SQL Server and SAP HANA get rollback only).

Read-only is an app-level guard. It cannot catch SELECT some_writing_function(), so please use a read-only DB account for production.

Supported

  • DBMS: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite, MS SQL Server, Oracle, SAP HANA
  • LLMs: Anthropic Claude, OpenAI, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, Azure)

Limits

  • Windows x64 only (Electron). No macOS or Linux build. I tested it on Windows 11 Home 26H2.
  • The installer (~143 MB) is not code-signed, so SmartScreen will likely warn you. It installs per user without admin rights, and the SHA-256 is on the download page.
  • No account or sign-up. Bring your own LLM API key or a local endpoint.
  • Free for now. The source code is not public.

If you have no test database, a single SQLite file is enough to try the main flow.

Feedback I would like

  • Which databases would you want next?
  • Is the line between "schema only" and "schema plus rows with consent" in the right place?
  • What other guard would you need before letting a tool like this near a production database?

Download and details: https://www.mirinai.com/chatdbmanager/
Contact: mirinai.help@mirinai.com

title: Testing a Japanese Name Generator Without Mistaking Suggestions for Verified Names
description:
Wery AI's brand team wrote this article with AI support.

A Japanese name suggestion can be useful for a fictional character and still be a poor application fixture. A developer may accidentally treat a pleasant explanation as a verified reading, strip meaningful text while cleaning a field, or assume every name fits the same family-name structure. Before putting generated suggestions into a demo, separate two questions: does the application handle the text correctly, and has a suitable reviewer checked the name itself?

Define what your application actually needs

Start with the display contract. Does the interface show a full written name, a reading, a romanized form, or a short explanatory note? Keep these as separate fields in your own fixture. A single display string is convenient for a mockup, but it can hide assumptions that later become difficult to change. For example, a search input and a printed character card may need different information.

The Wery AI page describes suggestions with kanji, kana, romaji, meaning notes, and reasons for fit. Those are useful categories for a manual review sheet. If you copy a candidate into a local fixture, label the source and the review status yourself. Do not build an integration around an undocumented object shape that merely looks plausible.

Write down what the fixture is for as well. Testing a fictional cast list is different from validating a real person's name. This workflow is for handling text in a prototype.

Keep the source text and your comparison form separate

A common mistake is to clean a string once and overwrite the original. That makes it difficult to explain why a saved display value differs from the text a reviewer approved. Keep the original value available, and derive a comparison key only for the operation that needs one. A normalization choice is a technical decision, not a linguistic judgment.

Unicode's normalization specification explains the normalization forms. For a small illustrative test, JavaScript can compare a composed kana character with a base character followed by a combining mark. The example below tests equivalence after NFC normalization.

const composed = 'が';
const decomposed = 'が';
const equalAfterNfc =
  composed.normalize('NFC') === decomposed.normalize('NFC');
console.assert(equalAfterNfc);
console.assert(composed !== decomposed);

Use a narrowly named helper if you adopt this idea. A function called normalizeEverything invites unrelated transformations. A comparison function should make clear whether it changes case, whitespace, punctuation, or Unicode representation. Review those decisions against your product's purpose instead of stacking them together because a test passes.

Build fixtures around behaviors, not invented naming rules

Create a small table of cases before adding a large cast of generated candidates. Include a reading that uses combining marks, an intentionally blank optional note, a long explanation, and text containing punctuation that your renderer must display safely. Mark each fixture as synthetic. These cases can reveal layout and storage defects without claiming that the sample text is a recommended name.

Case What to check What it does not establish
Equivalent Unicode sequences Your chosen comparison behavior A correct name reading
Missing optional explanation The empty-state presentation That an omitted field is always optional
Long meaning note Wrapping and reading order The truth of the explanation
Punctuation in a note Safe text rendering Permission to render arbitrary HTML

For a manual candidate, record the written form, reading, romanization, explanation, and the person who reviewed it. A blank reviewer field should remain visible as a missing prerequisite. Do not replace it with an automated confidence label that no one has defined.

Review the actual component, not just the string

Put the fixture into the component at the width people will use. Check whether kana wraps awkwardly, whether a meaning note pushes the action button out of view, and whether a screen reader encounters the label before the value. A string can survive a round trip through storage while the interface still makes it hard to understand.

A short review sequence is enough to start:

  1. Paste the original candidate into the local fixture without silently rewriting it.
  2. Verify that saving and loading retain the intended display value.
  3. Exercise the exact search or comparison operation your app supports.
  4. Review the narrow layout with a long note and a missing optional value.
  5. Ask a suitable language reviewer to check the candidate before public use.

Keep a failed technical check separate from a failed content review. If the renderer truncates a reading, repair the renderer. If the reading is unverified, keep the content status unverified. Combining the two into one green check makes both problems harder to see.

Leave a useful handoff for the next reviewer

A compact handoff can contain the fixture's purpose, its source, the transformations applied for comparison, and the unresolved questions. It should also say which parts were only tested locally. Do not describe a pasted candidate as a live API integration, and do not call a normalization assertion a test of the generator's cultural accuracy.

The next step is to choose one component and one synthetic fixture that stresses its display behavior. Once that works, bring in a manually reviewed candidate. Keeping technical correctness and name review separate lets the prototype move forward without turning an unverified suggestion into a product rule.

title: Cloud vs On-Premises Infrastructure
description:
Modern businesses require reliable IT infrastructure to manage applications, store information, and provide support for staff. But what will you choose, cloud infrastructure or on-premises infrastructure?

Cloud infrastructure provides flexibility and scalability plus you are able to take advantage of managed technology. On the other hand, on-premises provides you with full control over hardware, predictable scalability, and you are managing the technology.

It really depends on your workload, needs, security requirements, and cost.

What is Cloud Infrastructure?

Cloud infrastructure enables you to utilise computing resources such as servers, storage, databases, and networking from third party cloud providers.

Rather than buying your own hardware, you can lease what you need. Some popular options are Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud.

Advantages of Cloud Infrastructure

  • Scalability – Easily increase or decrease resources to meet demand.
  • Lower up front cost – You will not have to buy expensive hardware.
  • Remote access – Employees will have access to applications.
  • Faster – New environments and applications can be deployed quickly.
  • Managed – You can take advantage of managed databases, monitoring, backups, etc.

Cloud infrastructure can be useful for businesses with changing workloads, expanding digital platforms, and remote teams.

What is On-premises IT Infrastructure?

  • On-premises infrastructure is where you will purchase, install, and manage computing resources.
  • You will be managing your own servers, storage, networking hardware, security, and updates.

Advantages of On-premises Infrastructure

  • More control – You are managing your own hardware.
  • Management – You have full control over where your information is stored.
  • Predictable costs – Once you have bought your hardware, there will be less costs depending on how much you use each month.
  • Low latency – Systems on the same network will have low latency.
  • Customisable – You can set the infrastructure to suit your needs. This option may be suitable if you have steady workloads, specialised hardware, strict data handling, or have invested in infrastructure.

What Workloads Benefit Most from Cloud Infrastructure?

There are some workloads that will greatly benefit from using cloud infrastructure.

Websites/E-commerce

Websites and e-commerce sites can suffer from unpredictable traffic. Cloud infrastructure means you can easily scale resources when running promotions, seasonal sales, or high traffic periods.

Development

Development teams often require temporary environments to develop, test, and deploy software. With cloud infrastructure these can easily be created and removed.

Data Analysis

If you have large amounts of data to analyse, you can utilise cloud based analysis tools. This means you are not having to invest in extra computing hardware. You can also reduce unnecessary data transfer by keeping your analysis tools close to your data.

Backup

Cloud storage can assist with backup and disaster recovery. This means you can keep copies of your important business information in different locations.

Unpredictable resource demand

If you have applications that require unpredictable resources, cloud infrastructure can help you scale your resources. This will save you having to buy hardware for occasional peak times.

What Workloads Benefit Most from On-premises Infrastructure?

Despite the move towards cloud infrastructure, on-premises infrastructure can still be useful.

Predictable resource demand

If you have systems that are always running with predictable resource demand, you may want to invest in dedicated hardware. This will save you having to pay for unused cloud infrastructure flexibility.

Strict data handling

Some businesses will have strict data handling requirements due to contractual, regulatory, or internal policies. Depending on your requirements, you may want to utilise dedicated on-premises infrastructure.

Low latency

If you have manufacturing systems, industrial machinery, or applications that are talking to local hardware you may require very fast local network responses. On-premises or edge computing can help with this.

Legacy applications

Some legacy applications will require specific hardware, or operating systems. This may mean that you will have to heavily redevelop them to use them in the cloud.

Specialised hardware

If you have specialised computing hardware or bespoke infrastructure then on-premises infrastructure may be more suitable.

Why Hybrid Infrastructure is Becoming Important

  • Sometimes you may not want to choose just one option.

  • Hybrid infrastructure enables you to use a mix of both cloud and on-premises infrastructure to ensure your workloads are in the best environment.

For example:

  • Main business applications can be hosted on cloud infrastructure.
  • Sensitive databases can be kept on a secure on-premises infrastructure.
  • Development can be completed on temporary cloud resources.
  • Backups can be done via cloud storage.

This gives you flexibility, whilst still keeping control over your workloads.

Hybrid infrastructure will need to be properly integrated. You will need to have centralised identity, monitoring, network access, and backup.

Things to Consider

Before choosing your infrastructure, you should consider:

Total Cost

Infrastructure costs can be more than just servers or monthly costs. You will need to consider electricity, cooling, maintenance, licences, staff, storage, network usage, and data transfer costs.

Security

You need to know what security requirements you will have. What access control, encryption, and regulatory requirements you have.

Scalability

If you expect to grow quickly or have unpredictable workloads then cloud infrastructure can help you scale. If you have predictable workloads then on-premises can be more cost effective.

Current Infrastructure

You should consider your current hardware, application requirements, and migration needs.

Technical Skills

Cloud infrastructure requires you to have knowledge of cloud architecture, identity, networking, and optimising costs. On-premises will require you to have hardware, networking, and virtualisation skills.

Common Mistakes

When choosing between cloud and on-premises infrastructure, you should not make your decision purely based on industry trends.

Common mistakes include:

  • Moving everything to the cloud.
  • Not considering data transfer/storage costs.
  • Underestimating hardware maintenance and replacement costs.
  • Ignoring licence requirements.
  • Assuming cloud infrastructure will be more secure.
  • Keeping identities and monitoring separate.

By analysing your workloads you can avoid unnecessary costs of migrating.

Final Thoughts

Both cloud and on-premises infrastructure play an important role in modern IT. Cloud infrastructure provides scalability, flexibility, and faster deployment. On-premises infrastructure provides you with full control over your hardware, predictable scalability, and the ability to customise.

Many organisations choose hybrid infrastructure.

The best option is to analyse each of your workloads, understand your technical requirements, calculate the total cost, and choose the infrastructure that will provide the most value in the long term.

title: Webhooks or polling for inbound mail, and when to use both
description:
Webhooks feel modern and polling feels dated, but the right answer depends on what happens when a delivery is missed — and every webhook system misses deliveries eventually.

Webhooks give latency, not guarantees

A webhook is an HTTP request to your endpoint, retried a few times with backoff. If your service is down for longer than the retry window, or returns 500 consistently, the event is dropped unless the sender keeps a replayable log. Latency is excellent, guarantees are not.

Polling gives completeness, not speed

Polling an endpoint for messages since a cursor is boring and reliable: you control the pace, you can replay, and an outage costs you delay instead of data. The cost is a constant trickle of requests and a latency floor equal to the poll interval.

The combination that works

Webhook for latency, poll as reconciliation. On each webhook, enqueue the message id; run a periodic poll that asks for anything newer than the last processed id and fills the gaps. The poll makes the system correct, the webhook makes it fast.

One detail that makes reconciliation cheap

Make the cursor the message id, not a timestamp. Timestamps collide at second granularity and drift between clocks, so a poll built on them either re-fetches or skips messages. A monotonic id gives you exact resume semantics.

Volanea delivers inbound mail by webhook and also exposes a cursor-based read endpoint, so reconciliation is a loop instead of a guess.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them

ACH Return Codes Explained: R01–R85 and How to Handle Them

When an ACH transaction fails, the originating bank receives a return code. Understanding what each code means—and how to respond—is critical for any developer building payout systems, payroll integrations, or marketplace payment flows.

Unlike credit card declines, which happen in milliseconds, ACH returns arrive 1–5 business days after the transaction posts. By then, your system may have already marked the payout as complete. A well-designed integration catches these codes, logs them, and decides whether to retry, escalate, or route to an alternate payment rail.

The Most Common ACH Return Codes

The National Automated Clearing House Association (Nacha) maintains the official R-code set. Here are the ones you'll encounter most often:

Code Meaning Cause Retry?
R01 Insufficient funds Account balance too low Yes (after funds available)
R03 No account / unable to locate Account closed or number wrong No
R04 Invalid account number Malformed or fake account No
R05 Account closed by institution Bank closed the account No
R07 Authorization revoked Receiver revoked permission No
R10 Customer advises not authorized Receiver claims they didn't authorize No
R29 Corporate customer advises not authorized Business receiver disputes No
R31 Permissible return by receiver Receiver requested return (soft return) Maybe
R51 Receiver does not participate in ACH Rare; account not ACH-eligible No
R82 Non-transaction account Savings account, not checking No

Return codes R01–R85 cover everything from technical failures (R02: route not found) to fraud disputes (R10, R29) to settlement issues (R82: wrong account type).

Handling R01: Insufficient Funds

R01 is the most common return and the most likely to succeed on retry.

async function handleAchReturn(returnCode, payoutId, recipientAccount) {
  if (returnCode === 'R01') {
    // Insufficient funds — likely temporary
    const payout = await db.getPayoutById(payoutId);

    // Schedule retry in 3 business days
    await db.updatePayout(payoutId, {
      status: 'pending_retry',
      nextRetryDate: addBusinessDays(new Date(), 3),
      returnCode: 'R01',
      attemptCount: payout.attemptCount + 1
    });

    // Log for monitoring
    logger.info(`R01 return for payout ${payoutId}; retry scheduled`);

    // Optionally notify recipient
    await notificationService.sendEmail(payout.recipientEmail, 
      'Your payout is pending. We'll retry in 3 business days.');

    return { action: 'retry_scheduled' };
  }
}

Retry R01 up to 3 times, spaced 3–5 business days apart. After that, escalate to manual review.

Handling R03, R04, R05: Account Issues

These codes indicate the account itself is invalid or closed. Do not retry.

if (['R03', 'R04', 'R05'].includes(returnCode)) {
  // Account is bad; need new banking details
  await db.updatePayout(payoutId, {
    status: 'failed_account_invalid',
    returnCode: returnCode
  });

  // Notify recipient to update account
  await notificationService.sendSMS(payout.recipientPhone,
    `Your payout failed (${returnCode}). Please update your bank details.`);

  // Flag for manual review if high-value payout
  if (payout.amount > 10000) {
    await escalationQueue.add({
      payoutId,
      reason: 'Account invalid; manual review needed'
    });
  }

  return { action: 'failed_account_invalid', requiresManualReview: true };
}

Handling R10, R29: Unauthorized Claims

R10 (customer disputes authorization) and R29 (corporate customer disputes) are fraud-adjacent. The receiver is claiming they never approved the payout.

if (['R10', 'R29'].includes(returnCode)) {
  // Potential fraud or permission issue
  await db.updatePayout(payoutId, {
    status: 'disputed',
    returnCode: returnCode,
    flaggedForFraudReview: true
  });

  // Notify compliance team
  await complianceQueue.add({

---

*Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The [ACH Return Codes API](https://rapidapi.com/payoutrail-ach-return-codes/api/ach-return-codes-api?utm_source=nichestream&utm_medium=devto&utm_campaign=payoutrail-ach-returns) returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.*

title: Where agent inboxes store mail is a product decision
description:
An agent inbox holds customer conversations, which means it holds personal data, which means somebody will eventually ask which country it lives in and how long it stays.

Residency is per tenant, not per product

Two customers can have incompatible requirements: one wants everything in the EU, another has no constraint but a strict retention limit. A single global bucket satisfies neither. The storage location has to be a property of the tenant, decided at creation and recorded somewhere an auditor can read.

Retention needs a clock per mailbox

Deleting on a schedule means knowing what the schedule is for each mailbox, not for the product. Store the retention policy with the mailbox and run deletion from that, so changing the global default does not silently rewrite history for existing customers.

Backups are part of the answer

A deletion that leaves the data in a nightly backup has not deleted anything. Either expire backups on the same schedule or document the gap plainly, because the first audit question after 'do you delete it' is 'including backups'.

The detail that avoids a scramble

Attachments are the part everyone forgets. If the body is in the region and the attachments are in a shared global bucket, residency is not satisfied and the answer to the questionnaire is wrong.

Volanea attaches storage and retention settings to each inbox, so residency follows the tenant instead of the deployment.

title: Reading DSN bounces correctly
description:
A bounce is not a sentence, it is a structured report: a delivery status notification with a status code, a reporting MTA, and the original headers attached. Parsing the human text is the reason bounce handling is unreliable.

The fields that matter

message/delivery-status carries per-recipient blocks with Action (failed, delayed, delivered, relayed), Status (the three-digit enhanced code) and Diagnostic-Code. A 5.1.1 means unknown recipient; a 4.2.2 means mailbox full; a 5.7.1 usually means the receiver blocked you. Those three lead to completely different actions.

The original message id is in there

The third part of a DSN is the original message headers. That is how you correlate a bounce with the send that caused it — not by matching the recipient address, which may appear in several campaigns. Without the correlation, a bounce cannot update the right record.

Delayed is not failed

Action: delayed arrives hours before a failure and after the message eventually succeeds. Treating it as a bounce suppresses valid addresses and makes the dashboard look worse than reality. Store it as a state, not as a failure.

One detail that prevents a support loop

Keep the Diagnostic-Code verbatim. When a customer forwards a bounce, the remote server's sentence is the only thing that distinguishes a full mailbox from a blocklist, and your own classification will not carry that nuance.

Volanea parses DSNs into action and status per recipient and keeps the raw diagnostic next to the original send.

title: NestJS Explained: Node Backends With Structure Built In
description:
Node.js makes it easy to start a server and hard to keep one organised. A few routes become a few dozen, shared logic drifts into copy pasted handlers, and six months later nobody is sure where a feature lives. NestJS is a framework that gives a Node backend a deliberate shape from the first file, borrowing ideas from Angular and from enterprise frameworks in other languages.

The shape has three parts, and each has one job. Controllers receive HTTP requests and return responses, and they should do nothing else. Services hold the business logic, such as talking to a database or applying a rule. Modules group controllers and services that belong together, so a feature can be understood and tested as one unit. When you want to find where something happens, you already know which kind of file to open.

Here is the smallest complete example: a controller that answers a GET request by asking a service for a greeting.

import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AppService } from './app.service';

@Controller()
export class AppController {
  constructor(private readonly appService: AppService) {}

  @Get()
  getHello(): string {
    return this.appService.getHello();
  }
}

import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class AppService {
  getHello(): string {
    return 'Hello World!';
  }
}

The decorators do the wiring. @Controller marks the class as a request handler, @get marks the method as the answer to a GET request, and @Injectable marks the service as something NestJS can create and hand to whoever needs it. The controller never builds the service itself; NestJS injects it through the constructor, which is the dependency injection pattern. That one habit is what makes NestJS code testable: in a test, you can hand the controller a fake service and check its behaviour without starting a server or touching a database.

NestJS also standardises the pieces every real backend needs. Guards handle authentication, pipes validate incoming data, interceptors transform responses, and exception filters turn errors into consistent responses. Because these are framework concepts rather than one off middleware, a new developer joining the project meets the same patterns in every module.

TypeScript is not optional decoration here. Types on controllers and services catch mismatched shapes at build time, and the decorators only make sense with the type metadata TypeScript provides. If you dislike TypeScript, NestJS will feel like friction from day one.

The honest trade

NestJS trades freedom for consistency. You write more files and more boilerplate than you would with a minimal framework like Express, and the decorator heavy style can feel like magic until you learn what each piece does. For a small API with three endpoints, that structure is overhead. For a backend that will grow to dozens of endpoints, several developers, and years of maintenance, the structure is exactly what keeps the project readable. The wrong time to adopt NestJS is a weekend prototype; the right time is the moment a prototype starts turning into a product.

Structure you can grow into

Start with one module, one controller, and one service, exactly like the example above, and add a second module only when a second feature arrives. If the shape still feels helpful at five modules, it will still feel helpful at fifty.

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/nestjs-explained-node-backends-with.html

title: DupeLens after v1.0.0: what changed, and what’s next
description:
I joined the DEV community three years ago, but this is only my second post here. My first one introduced a small Java project I’d just released: DupeLens, a command-line tool for finding duplicate files.

That post didn’t get any responses. I’m sharing an update now because the project has continued to grow, with improvements from me and contributions from others.

DupeLens is a read-only Java CLI that finds files with identical contents and can create an offline HTML report. It shows you what it found without deleting or moving anything.

Since my first post, the project has grown in a few useful ways:

A simpler start: You can run it from source with Java 17 or newer. Maven is optional.

Safer scans: DupeLens groups files by size before hashing candidates with SHA-256. It skips symbolic links and reports unreadable files as warnings.

A portable report: The generated HTML works offline in a browser, with no server or external scripts.

More careful reporting: Results are sorted by redundant bytes, and the tool avoids overwriting an existing report.

Broader checks: The project now includes integration checks and GitHub Actions coverage across Java 17 and 21 on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

A quick example:

java -jar target/dupelens.jar ./your-folder --html report.html

Or run it directly from source:

java src/main/java/dev/dupelens/Main.java ./your-folder --html report.html

This is still a small tool, and there are limits: a scan isn’t an atomic snapshot, and DupeLens doesn’t compare file bytes after matching SHA-256 hashes. It’s designed to help you inspect duplicates while keeping control of your files.

Thanks to everyone who has contributed feedback, code, or time to the project. Open-source work gets better when people take a look and help shape what comes next.

The README lists exclusion patterns, machine-readable output, and scan cancellation as possible next steps. If one of those would be useful to you—or if you spot something I could improve—please open an issue or pull request.

Repository: https://github.com/illusionoftalha/dupelens

If you try DupeLens, I’d love to hear what worked, what didn’t, and what you’d like to see next.

title: The desktop app you scrape updated overnight: a version watch that re-checks what you depend on, once per change
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the tool described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code. Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

Relaymote (MIT, Node.js) is a phone remote for Claude Desktop's Code-tab sessions. Desktop has no API for that, so Relaymote reads two things it does not own: the Code tab's sidebar (through the debugger port) and the session transcripts on disk. Both can change shape whenever Desktop or the Claude Code it bundles updates, and nobody sends you a changelog for the parts you scrape.

This post is about the small module that turns "it silently broke after an update" into one message on the day of the update: lib/claude-version-watch.js.

The failure that started it

One Desktop update (2.42304.2 to 3.1623.0) moved screen-reader-only status text inside each sidebar row's button. Relaymote read the row's text as the session title, so titles came out as " Awaiting input". 404 of 473 session titles were polluted before anyone noticed. Nothing crashed. Nothing logged an error. The data was just wrong.

The lesson is not "write a better selector". Selectors for someone else's UI will keep breaking. The lesson is: notice the update, run a live check of every surface you depend on, and say the result once.

Step 1: know the installed versions without asking the app

Both versions are visible on disk. Desktop installs into app-<version> folders and Claude Code into version-named folders, so the newest folder name is the installed version:

const cmpVer = (a, b) => {
  const x = String(a).split('.').map(Number), y = String(b).split('.').map(Number);
  for (let i = 0; i < Math.max(x.length, y.length); i++) {
    const d = (x[i] || 0) - (y[i] || 0); if (d) return d;
  }
  return 0;
};
const newest = (names) => names.filter(n => /^\d+(\.\d+)+$/.test(n)).sort(cmpVer).pop() || null;

Two details matter. Compare versions numerically, part by part: as strings, "3.999" sorts after "3.1623". And filter to names that look like versions, so a stray folder never becomes "the version".

Step 2: the live check names problems in plain sentences

check() does not compare against a stored snapshot of the UI. It asks questions whose answers must hold whatever the layout is:

  • Can we reach Desktop's debugger at all?
  • Did the sidebar read return any sessions? Zero rows means the session list moved.
  • Does any title match the known pollution pattern (/\s(Awaiting input|Unread response|Started (from|by) .*)$/)?
  • With 20 or more rows, does at least one show a status? If none do, the status labels changed.
  • Does the newest transcript parse, and does it contain record types we have never seen?

Each failure is pushed as a sentence someone can act on ("the Code tab sidebar read 0 sessions — Desktop changed its session list"), not as a stack trace.

Step 3: separate problems from notes

New transcript record types are common: Claude Code adds them regularly (api-request, cost-state and several others appeared between Claude Code 2.1.300 and 2.1.304). Relaymote skips unknown types safely, so a new type is a note, not a problem:

if (t.unknown.length)
  notes.push('new transcript record types (skipped safely): ' +
    t.unknown.map(([k, n]) => `${k}×${n}`).join(', '));

If every new record type raised an alarm, the alarm would be ignored by the second week. Keep "needs a fix" and "worth knowing" in different lists, and only the first makes the result not OK.

To find the types cheaply, it reads only the last 2 MB of the most recently modified transcript and drops the first (probably cut) line. That is enough to see what the current version writes.

Step 4: run on change, not on a schedule

The watch ticks every few minutes, but almost every tick is a no-op:

const was = load();
if (!was) { save({ ...now, at: new Date().toISOString(), checked: null }); return { first: true, now }; }
if (was.desktop === now.desktop && was.code === now.code && !was.pending) return null;
  • First sight only records. On a fresh install there is no "before", so there is nothing to report.
  • Same versions, nothing pending: return. The expensive live check runs only when a version actually changed.
  • One alert per change. After the check, the new versions are saved with the result, so the next tick is quiet again.

Step 5: don't blame the update for a restart

An update usually restarts Desktop, and for a minute the debugger is simply not up yet. Reporting "cannot reach Desktop" at that moment would be a false alarm on every single update. So if the only problem is the unreachable debugger, the change is parked as pending and retried, up to six ticks:

if (!r.ok && r.problems.every(p => /debugger link down/.test(p)) && (was.pendingTries || 0) < 6) {
  save({ ...was, pending: now, pendingTries: (was.pendingTries || 0) + 1 });
  return { waiting: true };
}

After six tries it reports anyway, because a debugger that never comes back is a real problem.

What the message looks like

One push notification, titled with what changed (Claude updated: Desktop <old> → <new>, Claude Code <old> → <new>, only the parts that changed) and a body that is either "everything it reads from Claude works" plus the notes, or the list of problems. The same line goes to the log. That is the whole output: no dashboard, nothing to open.

Takeaways

  • If you scrape or parse an app you don't own, its updates are your incidents. Detect them from the install on disk.
  • Check invariants ("some row has a status"), not a frozen copy of the UI.
  • Split problems from notes, or the alert becomes noise.
  • Run the expensive check once per version change, and record the result so it doesn't repeat.
  • Give a restart time to finish before calling it a failure, with a hard limit on how long you wait.

The code is in lib/claude-version-watch.js in the Relaymote repo, with its test in test/claude-version-watch.js. Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

title: The Role of UI/UX Design in Improving Digital Payment Experiences
description:
Digital payments have become an essential part of everyday life. From shopping online and paying bills to transferring money and purchasing services, people increasingly rely on digital payment platforms to complete financial transactions quickly and conveniently. Mobile wallets, banking applications, payment gateways, and contactless payment solutions have transformed how businesses and customers exchange money.

However, providing digital payment functionality is no longer enough to attract and retain customers. Users expect payment platforms to be fast, secure, simple, and reliable. Even a small usability issue, such as a confusing checkout process or unclear transaction status, can frustrate customers and cause them to abandon a payment.

This is where User Interface (UI) and User Experience (UX) design become important. Effective UI/UX design helps businesses create digital payment experiences that reduce friction, improve accessibility, build customer confidence, and encourage repeat usage.

In this article, we will explore the role of UI/UX design in improving digital payment experiences and discuss the essential design practices businesses should consider when developing modern payment solutions.

Simplifying the Payment Process

One of the biggest goals of UI/UX design is to make digital payments as simple as possible. Customers want to complete transactions without navigating complicated menus, filling out unnecessary forms, or following multiple steps.

A complicated payment process can discourage users and increase checkout abandonment. Designers should focus on creating straightforward payment journeys that allow customers to complete transactions with minimal effort.

  • Some effective practices include:
  • Reducing unnecessary form fields.
  • Using clear and recognizable payment buttons.
  • Organizing payment information logically.
  • Providing simple navigation between checkout steps.
  • Offering guest checkout options where appropriate.
  • Supporting autofill for frequently used information.

For example, an e-commerce checkout page should allow customers to review their orders, select a payment method, and confirm their purchases without unnecessary interruptions.

A simplified payment experience saves time and makes customers more comfortable using the platform.
Building Trust Through Secure UI/UX Design

Security is one of the most important considerations in digital payment applications. Customers share sensitive information, including card details, personal information, and banking credentials. Therefore, they need confidence that their information is handled securely.

Although technical security measures protect financial data behind the scenes, UI/UX design helps communicate those protections to users.

Designers can improve perceived security through features such as:

  • Biometric authentication.
  • Multi-factor authentication.
  • Clear security notifications.
  • Secure password recovery processes.
  • Recognizable payment method icons.
  • Transaction confirmation screens.
  • Transparent privacy information.

For example, a payment application can display a clear verification screen before processing a sensitive transaction. It can also explain why additional authentication is required.

Security features should be easy to understand and should not create unnecessary friction. The objective is to balance user convenience with appropriate protection.

Creating a Mobile-Friendly Payment Experience

Mobile devices have become a major channel for digital transactions. Customers frequently use smartphones to pay bills, purchase products, transfer money, and manage their finances.

As a result, digital payment platforms must provide seamless experiences across different screen sizes and devices. Responsive design ensures that payment interfaces adjust to different screen dimensions while maintaining usability and visual consistency.

Important mobile UI/UX practices include:

  • Touch-friendly buttons: Payment buttons and interactive elements should be large enough to select comfortably.
  • Readable typography: Text should remain clear and readable without requiring users to zoom in.
  • Simple layouts: Avoid unnecessary visual elements that distract users from completing payments.
  • Easy navigation: Place important actions where users can access them conveniently.
  • Optimized forms: Reduce typing by supporting autofill, input formatting, and appropriate mobile keyboards.

A mobile payment interface should feel natural rather than like a smaller version of a desktop website. According to Stripe's mobile checkout guidance, reducing unnecessary typing and optimizing touch interactions can make payment experiences more efficient.

Improving Payment Speed and Efficiency

Speed is another important factor influencing digital payment experiences. Customers expect transactions to happen quickly, and unnecessary delays can create frustration.

UI/UX design can improve perceived speed by making interactions more efficient and communicating what is happening during payment processing.

For example, when a user clicks the payment button, the interface should immediately provide visual feedback instead of leaving the user wondering whether the action was registered.

Designers can improve payment efficiency through:

  • Streamlined checkout flows.
  • Clear progress indicators.
  • Optimized form layouts.
  • Convenient saved payment methods.
  • Digital wallet integrations.
  • Responsive interface interactions.
  • Reduced unnecessary page redirects.

Loading indicators are particularly important when a transaction requires additional processing time. They reassure users that the system is working and help prevent repeated payment attempts.

A well-optimized payment experience reduces uncertainty and makes transactions feel smoother.

Providing Clear Transaction Feedback

Customers should always understand what happens after they initiate a payment. Without proper feedback, users may become uncertain about whether their transaction was successful.

For example, imagine someone transferring money through a mobile banking application. After confirming the transfer, the application displays no notification or transaction status. The user may worry that the payment failed and attempt the transaction again.

This situation can create unnecessary confusion and potentially lead to duplicate payments.

Effective UI/UX design prevents these problems by providing immediate and understandable feedback.

  • Useful transaction feedback features include:
  • Payment success notifications.
  • Transaction processing indicators.
  • Clear failure messages.
  • Digital receipts.
  • Transaction reference numbers.
  • Real-time payment status updates.

Error messages should also explain the problem and provide practical solutions.

Instead of displaying a generic message such as "Payment Failed," the application should explain whether the issue relates to an incorrect card number, insufficient funds, or a temporary processing problem when that information is available.

Clear feedback makes customers feel informed and in control of their transactions.

Reducing Payment Errors Through Better UX

Payment errors can negatively affect customer satisfaction and trust. Incorrect information, accidental clicks, expired cards, and unclear instructions can interrupt transactions.

Good UX design helps prevent many common errors before they happen.

Some useful error-prevention techniques include:

  • Real-time form validation.
  • Automatic formatting of card numbers.
  • Clear input field labels.
  • Confirmation steps for important transactions.
  • Helpful error messages.
  • Appropriate input restrictions.
  • Easy options to review and edit payment information.

For example, when a customer enters an incorrectly formatted card number, the application can immediately highlight the field and explain how to correct it.

Similarly, before sending money, a payment application should display the recipient's information and transaction amount for review.

Preventing mistakes is generally more effective than simply explaining them after they occur.

Personalizing the Digital Payment Experience

Personalization can make digital payment platforms more convenient and relevant to individual customers.

By offering personalized features, businesses can help users complete frequent transactions faster and manage their payment activities more efficiently.

Examples of useful personalization features include:

  • Saved payment methods.
  • Frequently used recipient lists.
  • Customized payment dashboards.
  • Transaction history and spending summaries.
  • Personalized notifications.
  • Preferred language and currency settings.

For instance, a digital wallet can allow users to save their preferred payment method and select it automatically during future transactions.

However, personalization should always respect user privacy. Customers should understand how their information is used and have control over their preferences.

When implemented responsibly, personalization makes digital payment experiences more convenient and user-friendly.

How Much Does Digital Payment App UI/UX Design Cost?

The cost of designing a digital payment application depends on its functionality, complexity, security requirements, platform compatibility, and design scope.

A basic payment application with simple transaction features will generally require less design work than a comprehensive digital wallet or financial management platform.

Several factors can influence the overall design budget:

  • User research and competitor analysis.
  • Wireframing and interactive prototyping.
  • UI design and design system development.
  • Payment gateway integration requirements.
  • Authentication and security workflows.
  • Responsive design for multiple devices.
  • Accessibility considerations.
  • Usability testing and design revisions.

Businesses should consider these factors before starting a digital payment project to establish realistic budgets and development priorities.

If you are planning a fintech product, this guide to fintech app design cost provides additional insights into the factors that influence design investment.

Working with experienced design professionals can also help businesses identify usability challenges early and develop more effective digital payment experiences. A professional global ux agency can help businesses create user-centered digital products that combine functionality, usability, and visual consistency.

Conclusion

UI/UX design plays a significant role in improving digital payment experiences. As customers increasingly depend on digital transactions, businesses must provide payment platforms that are simple, secure, accessible, and convenient.

From simplifying checkout processes and improving mobile usability to providing clear transaction feedback and preventing payment errors, thoughtful design influences every stage of the customer journey.

Businesses should also prioritize accessibility, consistent interfaces, flexible payment options, and continuous usability testing to meet changing customer expectations.

Ultimately, successful digital payment platforms are not defined only by how quickly they process transactions. They are also defined by how easily and confidently customers can use them. Investing in effective UI/UX design helps businesses create smoother payment experiences, strengthen customer relationships, and build long-term digital trust.

title: Making My Portfolio Less Boring: 4 Small Redesigns That Made a Big Difference
description:
When I first launched my portfolio, it worked, but it felt empty. Some pages had big text and lots of blank space. Some sections said "Coming soon". Two pages almost looked the same.

I didn't rebuild anything. I made four small changes, and the site felt much more finished. Here they are, with examples you can copy.

1. Replace "Coming soon" with real work

My Projects page ended with two cards that said "Coming soon" and "A new piece is finding its final frame." They looked unfinished, and they told visitors there was nothing there.

I deleted them and used real things I had already built instead:

  • A side project (a Python script that publishes a blog post every day with GitHub Actions)
  • My articles on dev.to

Placeholder cards don't help anyone. If you have nothing new to show, remove the section. If you have something real, even a small project or an article, show that.

<a
  href="https://github.com/your-username/your-repo"
  target="_blank"
  rel="noopener noreferrer"
  className="flex flex-col gap-3 rounded-2xl border border-[var(--border)] bg-[var(--surface)] p-5 transition-colors hover:border-[var(--accent)]"
>
  <span className="text-xs uppercase tracking-wider text-[var(--text-muted)]">Project</span>
  <h3 className="text-lg font-semibold">Daily blog automation</h3>
  <p className="text-sm leading-6 text-[var(--text-muted)]">
    A Python script that writes and publishes a blog post every day.
  </p>
  <span className="mt-auto text-sm font-semibold text-[var(--accent)]">View on GitHub →</span>
</a>

2. Use the empty space next to a big heading

My Contact page had a huge heading on one side and nothing on the other. A visitor had to scroll to find out how to reach me.

I moved the contact options next to the heading as three clickable cards: Email, WhatsApp and LinkedIn. Under the heading, I added small chips for what I can help with.

<div className="grid gap-8 lg:grid-cols-2 lg:items-center">
  <div>
    <h1>Let's make something good.</h1>
    <p>Have a project in mind? I'd love to hear what you're thinking.</p>
  </div>
  <div className="flex flex-col gap-3">
    {/* three contact cards here */}
  </div>
</div>

The same idea worked on my Skills page: the empty right side now shows four small cards that link to the skill details below.

3. Turn a row of small links into cards

My "Find me online" section was a row of tiny text chips. They were easy to miss, and a visitor couldn't tell what each link was.

I changed them into larger cards with an icon, a name and one short line, such as "Articles on web development and automation". Now each link explains itself before anyone clicks it.

Keep each card focused on one job: an icon, a title, one line of description and one clear action.

4. Check your contrast

My "Let's Work Together" banner had white text on a light lavender background. On my laptop it looked fine, but it was hard to read on a phone, and the button text was also light.

The fix was simple:

  • Use a deeper purple for the banner background
  • Use white text on it
  • Make the button text the same deep purple on a white button

If you can barely read something when you squint, a visitor with a small screen and bright sunlight will not read it at all.

A bonus: make every page do a different job

My Home and About pages used the same hero, the same photo and the same story. I changed them:

  • Home: a short hero, a few skills and clear buttons
  • About: the full story, what I'm currently learning, and my profiles

When two pages say the same thing, a visitor sees no reason to open the second one. It can also confuse search engines.

My rules for every change

  1. Use only real content. No invented numbers, clients or promises.
  2. One change at a time. Then I look at the page on a phone-sized window and a laptop.
  3. Remove before adding. Often the best fix was to delete something.
  4. Check on a real phone. Some problems only show up there.

Wrapping up

None of these changes needed a new framework or a big rewrite. They only needed me to look at my own site the way a visitor does.

You can see the result here: ritika-rajput-portfolio.vercel.app. I also share videos on RitikaMoments.

What is one thing on your portfolio that you know looks unfinished?

title: Your SMTP connection pool is probably leaking
description:
A worker opens a connection, sends, and forgets to close it. Nothing breaks for a week, then the provider starts refusing new connections and every send fails at once.

Connections are the scarce resource

Providers cap concurrent connections per account and per IP, often at a low number. A pool that grows because closed connections are not returned will hit that cap, and the failure mode is total rather than gradual: once the cap is reached, every new send blocks.

Where the leak comes from

An exception between MAIL FROM and QUIT skips the close. A timeout on DATA leaves the socket open until the OS reaps it. A retry path that creates a fresh connection without releasing the failed one doubles the count. None of these show up in a happy-path test.

The fix

Wrap the whole conversation in a context manager that guarantees QUIT, and on any exception close the socket rather than returning it to the pool — a connection in an unknown protocol state is worse than no connection. Then export the pool size as a metric and alert when it approaches the provider's cap.

One detail worth copying

Reuse connections for multiple messages to the same domain, but reset state with RSET between recipients. Reconnecting for every message is slow and looks like abuse to the receiver; not resetting leaks the previous envelope into the next send.

Volanea manages the SMTP session per domain and exposes connection and deferral counters next to the send log.

title: Greylisting is a 4xx you should not panic about
description:
A first-time sender gets a temporary rejection from a server it has never talked to before, and the message is delayed by minutes. That is greylisting, and it is the single most misdiagnosed response in transactional email.

What the server is doing

It records the triplet of sender IP, envelope sender and recipient, answers with a 4xx at RCPT or DATA, and waits. A real mail server retries after a delay; a spam bot usually does not. When the retry arrives after the configured window, typically a few minutes, the triplet is on the allow list and the message goes through.

Why the first message to a domain is special

Greylisting hits new triplets, so your very first message to a new recipient domain is the one that gets delayed. The second is fine. That means a signup confirmation to a never-contacted domain can arrive minutes late through no fault of yours, and the fix is to retry rather than to re-send a new message with a new id — the new id is a new triplet, and it gets greylisted again.

What to do

Treat 4xx as retryable with an interval longer than the typical greylist window, keep the same message id and the same envelope sender, and cap total attempts. Do not reset the message, do not switch provider mid-flight, and do not mark the address as invalid.

The detail that matters

Log the triplet and the retry timing. When a customer says their verification email took eight minutes, 'greylisted at the recipient, delivered on attempt two' is a complete and correct answer.

Volanea retries with a stable message id and surfaces the remote 4xx text, so a greylisting delay is visible instead of mysterious.

title: Your Canvas Is Freezing the Page. OffscreenCanvas Fixes That.
description:
You open the profiler, record a session, and the flame chart looks great. 60 frames a second, steady, no dropped frames. You ship it.

Then someone clicks a button while the animation is running, and for half a second, nothing happens. Not a dropped frame — the whole page. The click just sits there, queued, waiting for a thread that's busy painting pixels nobody asked it to interrupt.

Here's the part that doesn't show up in a frame-rate graph: your canvas animation was never competing with itself. It was competing with every click handler, every layout pass, every bit of input handling on the page — because by default, all of that runs on exactly one thread, and canvas drawing calls are first-class citizens on it.

The fix everyone reaches for first

The instinct is to blame the math. Heavy canvas work — thousands of particles, a live chart redrawing every tick, a game loop doing collision checks — looks like a computation problem, so people reach for a Web Worker to do the computation off-thread.

// main.js
const worker = new Worker("particles-worker.js");
worker.postMessage({ type: "tick" });
worker.onmessage = (e) => {
  const positions = e.data.positions;
  // ...now draw them, back on the main thread
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
  for (const p of positions) ctx.fillRect(p.x, p.y, 2, 2);
};

This genuinely helps — the position math moves off the main thread. But watch what's still happening in that onmessage handler: clearRect, fillRect, every actual drawing call, is still running on the main thread, because that's the only thread with access to the <canvas> element's rendering context. You moved the arithmetic. You didn't move the part that was actually fighting your clicks for time.

The part that's easy to miss: drawing itself blocks the page

A <canvas> element's 2D or WebGL context has always been tied to the DOM, and anything tied to the DOM only exists on the main thread. That's not a performance detail, it's a structural one: a worker has no document, so it has never been able to hold a canvas context at all — until there was a way to give it one that isn't attached to the page.

That's what OffscreenCanvas is. Not a faster canvas. A canvas whose rendering context can live somewhere other than the main thread, so the fastest possible canvas is one where the drawing calls stop queuing up behind your click listeners in the first place.

The fix: move the context itself into the worker 

<canvas id="scene" width="600" height="400"></canvas>

// main.js
const canvas = document.getElementById("scene");
const offscreen = canvas.transferControlToOffscreen();
const worker = new Worker("render-worker.js");
worker.postMessage({ canvas: offscreen }, [offscreen]);

// the main thread still owns input — forward what the worker needs
canvas.addEventListener("pointermove", (e) => {
  worker.postMessage({ type: "pointer", x: e.offsetX, y: e.offsetY });
});

// render-worker.js
let ctx;
let pointer = { x: 0, y: 0 };

self.onmessage = (e) => {
  if (e.data.canvas) {
    ctx = e.data.canvas.getContext("2d");
    requestAnimationFrame(loop);
  }
  if (e.data.type === "pointer") pointer = e.data;
};

function loop() {
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, ctx.canvas.width, ctx.canvas.height);
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.arc(pointer.x, pointer.y, 20, 0, Math.PI * 2);
  ctx.fill();
  requestAnimationFrame(loop);
}

transferControlToOffscreen() detaches the canvas element from its own rendering context and hands you an OffscreenCanvas you can transfer to a worker like any other transferable object. Inside the worker, getContext("2d") gives back something that draws almost exactly like the context you're used to — same fillRect, same beginPath, same drawImage — except every one of those calls now runs on a thread that has nothing else to do but draw.

The one thing that doesn't come along for free is input. A worker has no DOM, so it can't attach its own pointermove or click listeners to anything. The main thread stays the one place that owns events, and your job is to forward the few fields the worker actually needs — as shown above, just x and y, not the whole event object, which isn't transferable anyway.

Why the page stays responsive now

Open two tabs in your head. In the first, with everything on the main thread, a click has to wait in the same queue as every pending fillRect call — if the canvas is mid-frame, the click waits for the frame to finish. In the second, with OffscreenCanvas, the canvas's frame is happening on a different thread entirely. The main thread's event queue is short again, because the one thing that used to dominate it moved out.

This is the distinction worth sitting with: OffscreenCanvas doesn't make your particle system compute faster, and it doesn't raise your frame rate. It makes the main thread's queue shorter by taking an entire category of work out of it. A canvas that was drawing 10,000 particles at 60fps before will still be drawing 10,000 particles at roughly 60fps after — the difference is that a click, a keypress, or a scroll now gets handled in the same frame instead of after it.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

When the main thread was fine all along

Not every canvas needs this. A sparkline that redraws once when new data arrives, a static chart, an icon you draw once on mount — none of that is holding the main thread hostage, because none of it is running every frame. The tell isn't "I use canvas," it's "my canvas work and my users' clicks are both trying to happen right now, repeatedly, for as long as the page is open." Games, live data visualizations, drawing tools, anything with a requestAnimationFrame loop that runs indefinitely — that's the category where this earns its complexity.

It's also not free complexity. You lose direct DOM access inside the worker, so anything that reads layout, measures text against real fonts in edge cases, or needs synchronous access to other page state has to be designed around message passing from the start, not bolted on later.

Is this safe to ship today?

Yes. Chrome has supported OffscreenCanvas since 2018, Firefox enabled it for workers a few years after that, and Safari was the last to land it, in Safari 16.4 in March 2023. All three major engines have carried it for a while now, so there's no meaningful fallback story you need to write — check "OffscreenCanvas" in window if you want a belt-and-suspenders guard, but you're unlikely to need it.

The next time a profiler shows you a perfectly smooth 60fps canvas sitting on top of a page that still stutters when someone clicks, you'll know the frame rate was never the number that mattered.

What's the heaviest thing you're currently drawing to a <canvas> on the main thread? I'm curious how many of you are one transferControlToOffscreen() call away from fixing a bug you've been blaming on something else.
