title: Building rutis: Replaceable Plugins Across Languages and Machines
description:
By Eric Cheng · Arcships · First published in Chinese on October 23, 2026

TL;DR: rutis is a Rust-based plugin runtime for agents and other long-running software. Plugins provide named services, so a caller can keep using calendar while its implementation changes language or moves to another machine. rutis tracks dependencies, cleanup, and the restart of affected plugins so those changes can happen without restarting the host.

Agents can write integration code quickly. The harder question is how to try that code, replace it, and roll back failures while the system keeps running. This post explains rutis's lifecycle model, how it crosses process and machine boundaries, and where the design is headed.

1. When changing code is no longer expensive

In the past, we designed software on the assumption that changes were costly. We tried to settle requirements first, stabilize interfaces, lock down dependencies, and then change as little as possible.

When changes become cheap, that assumption no longer holds. For software that can iterate on itself, the everyday activity is not simply running. It is trying things out:

  • Today it needs to connect to an internal calendar system, so it writes a first version and tries it.
  • Tomorrow it finds a better interface for that system and swaps in a new version.
  • The next day it needs a model on a GPU machine, so it moves part of its capability there.
  • Later, a heavily used component needs to be faster and more reliable, so it is rewritten in another language.

Each change is small. But a running system may go through dozens of these small changes in a week.

The hard part shifts from how to write it to how to keep replacing it. When a component is replaced, are old connections, timers, and listeners left behind? Do the components that depend on it break? Can a bad replacement be rolled back? If a service moves to another machine or is rewritten in another language, must all of its callers change too?

These questions determine whether software can really grow.

2. Wait for others to adapt, or connect to them ourselves?

Today, the usual way for software to gain a new capability is to wait for someone else to make it available.

The maintainers of an environment provide an API, an SDK, an open platform, or, more recently, an MCP server. Software calls what they provide. This is a good approach, but it assumes that what software can do depends on what someone outside it has prepared. The connection sits outside the software. It belongs to the environment, not to the software.

Once software can write its own code, that assumption becomes unnecessary. It can reverse the direction of the work:

It can spend its own effort connecting to and adapting to other systems.

Whatever it needs to reach, it can write a plugin to connect to it—in the language that fits best, perhaps with an agent writing the plugin. It can try, revise, and replace that plugin. The connection becomes part of the software, with its own lifecycle. It can be observed and cleanly removed.

Eventually, software could even replace an external interface or system. That may sound like a slogan, but in rutis it follows from a simple mechanism:

A consumer depends on a service's name, not on its implementation.

Suppose a scheduling feature depends on a service named calendar.

  1. At first, a plugin provides calendar by wrapping the company's existing calendar system.
  2. After real use, the team understands which methods calendar needs and what they should return.
  3. Later, the provider is replaced with an in-house implementation that still exposes the name calendar.

The scheduling feature does not change a line of code across those three stages, and the host program does not restart. Adapting to a system and replacing it are two stages of the same process. There is no separate migration project between them.

Both approaches can coexist. An MCP client can be an ordinary plugin in rutis. But the environment should not determine the limits of what software can do.

3. The foundation: replace one piece while the system keeps running

For software to iterate this way, it first needs to be split into pieces that can be replaced individually at runtime. Those pieces are plugins.

Plugin systems are not new. But replacing plugins frequently while a system is running demands stronger guarantees. The rutis core focuses on a few of them, each stated as a promise and backed by tests:

  • A plugin does not start before its dependencies are ready. It declares the services it needs and runs only when all of them are available.
  • Everything it registers is cleaned up exactly once when it stops. Services, listeners, background tasks, and child plugins are released in the reverse order of registration—no more and no less.
  • A failed startup rolls back. Anything already registered is withdrawn, leaving no half-finished state.
  • Replacing one piece restarts only the parts that use it. When a service provider changes, its dependent plugins stop and wait for the new provider to become ready. Unrelated parts keep running.

With those guarantees, replacing a component once and replacing it a thousand times should be equally safe. Software can iterate in smaller steps: replace one part instead of releasing the whole system, test it in a real running environment, and switch back if it does not work.

The term hot update can mean different things. Some systems replace machine code in place. rutis replaces running components. This approach is in the same tradition as Erlang/OTP and Java's OSGi. Rust's ownership model gives clean unloading a firmer foundation: in a garbage-collected environment, one stray reference can keep an old module alive indefinitely.

But plugins are only the foundation. What rutis really aims to do is let this kind of iteration spread outward.

4. Let iteration cross processes, languages, and devices

If iteration can happen only within one process and one language, the environments software can reach remain limited to that ecosystem. To use Python's model ecosystem, it has to be brought in. To use a device on another machine, someone has to build a separate remote-call layer. Every boundary forces the system to solve startup, dependencies, and cleanup again.

rutis makes those boundaries invisible to a plugin: a plugin does not need to know which process provides a service, which language implements it, or which machine runs it. It knows the service by name. rutis handles where the service comes from, what happens when the connection drops, and how dependents follow a replacement.

The following three examples cross three different kinds of boundary.

Example 1: an agent whose shell runs on another machine

Imagine an agent built with rutis. Its model calls, conversations, and decisions happen locally, but it needs to execute commands somewhere else—perhaps in an isolated sandbox or on a GPU machine with CUDA installed.

The shell can be a plugin running in a Python runtime on that machine:

import asyncio
from rutis import define_plugin


class Shell:
    async def run(self, command):
        proc = await asyncio.create_subprocess_shell(
            command, stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE, stderr=asyncio.subprocess.STDOUT
        )
        out, _ = await proc.communicate()
        return out.decode()


def apply(ctx, config):
    ctx.provide("shell", Shell())


plugin = define_plugin(apply, provides={"shell": Shell})

That machine runs a listening Python runtime with shell_tool installed. The rutis host where the agent lives decides how to configure the plugin and when it starts and stops:

{
  "id": "agent",
  "rows": [
    { "id": "sandbox", "name": "rutis-host/dial",
      "config": { "address": "wss://sandbox.example.com:7443/rutis" } },
    { "id": "shell", "name": "sandbox:shell_tool" }
  ]
}

This is an architecture example, not a complete deployment recipe. The remote runtime also needs TLS and a shared token; the node connection guide covers those steps.

The agent's side depends only on the name shell. As a result:

  • Moving to another execution environment requires changing one address in the configuration.
  • If the remote machine disconnects, the parts that depend on shell stop and wait instead of crashing. They load again when the connection returns.
  • The execution environment can evolve too. The shell plugin may begin in Python and later be replaced with a Go version without changing the agent's code.

The agent's "hand" has reached another machine, yet it uses that hand much as it would a local one.

Example 2: a server with components spread across processes and machines

Consider a more familiar case: a backend service.

Its main logic is written in Rust, but different supporting components belong in different places:

Server's main logic (Rust)
  ├─ Database client                 Same process
  ├─ Third-party API integration     Python process, using the official SDK
  ├─ Inference service               Runtime on a GPU machine
  └─ Adapter for a legacy system     To be replaced with an in-house implementation later

Each component is a plugin that provides a named service. The main logic uses those services by name. Where they run and which language implements them live in configuration, not in the callers' code.

This has several consequences:

  • Failures have boundaries. If the Python process crashes, the services it provided are withdrawn and their dependents stop and wait. Other parts of the same host keep running. rutis can also restart a failed runtime according to a backoff policy.
  • A configuration change does not leave the service half-broken. Reloading configuration at runtime is all-or-nothing. If the new configuration is invalid, the old one keeps running unchanged.
  • Adapt first, replace later happens here. A plugin initially wraps the legacy system. Once the service contract has settled under real traffic, it is replaced with an in-house implementation. The main logic does not need to know this happened.

Example 3: multiple rutis hosts sharing capabilities

The final boundary is the device. Each rutis host can be a node in a network.

Office node ── exports calendar ──▶ Cloud node running the agent ◀── exports device ── Home node
            ◀── shared services · remote plugins · forwarded events ──▶

Nodes are joined by an encrypted connection. Over that connection, they can:

  • Share services: export a local service to another node or import a remote service as a local one.
  • Run plugins on another node: a plugin uses that machine's services while its configuration and lifecycle are controlled from here.
  • Forward events: an event on one side can be received on the other.

A dropped connection reconnects automatically. While the other node is offline, the parts that depend on it wait and then resume when it returns.

This is the clearest picture of iteration spreading outward: each node contributes the capabilities of its own environment. The office node can reach internal systems, the home node can reach devices at home, and the cloud node has compute capacity. When one node learns to connect to a system, software across the network gains access to that capability.

Further ahead, phone and desktop apps could join in the same way. An app could expose contacts, location, or notifications as plugins, connect to rutis, and become part of the network. This part is still at the design stage, but the direction is the same.

5. Give the stable parts to Rust and the changing parts to the ecosystems

This works because rutis makes a basic division:

Give what is stable and unlikely to change to the systems layer. Give what changes and needs an ecosystem to other languages.

  • The stable part is the lifecycle: what starts first, what happens when a dependency disappears, how cleanup works, and what cannot be done across a process boundary. rutis implements those rules once, in Rust. Its core depends on tokio and only a handful of other libraries. Each guarantee is recorded and tied to specific tests.
  • The changing part is connection and adaptation. Python has an ecosystem for AI and data processing; Node has npm and existing Cordis plugins; Go has a large set of infrastructure libraries; and another machine has its own processes and devices. On these language-specific sides, there is only a small SDK, not another implementation of the framework.

This division also describes a progression over time. A capability often starts in Python or TypeScript so it can be tried quickly. Real use gradually clarifies its shape. The parts that have stood the test of time can then be rewritten in Rust for reliability and performance. An early design note put it this way:

TypeScript is the lab; Rust takes the graduates.

Which parts deserve to "graduate"? Parts whose meaning has settled; parts that are mechanisms rather than wording; parts that are performance-sensitive or sit on a trust boundary. For an agent, for example, the mechanism for assembling prompts can be made permanent, while the prompt content should remain changeable.

Because consumers depend only on service names, the path from experiment to stable implementation can be taken one step at a time. There is no need to stop one day for a large migration. Each additional runtime connects the software's ability to evolve to another ecosystem.

6. A new container for growth

Placing rutis next to an operating system helps clarify what it is.

Traditional operating system rutis
Assumption The program has already been written and runs inside it The program keeps growing and changing while it runs
What it manages CPU, memory, and processes Connections and capabilities: who provides what, and who depends on whom
Boundary One machine Across processes, languages, and devices
How a program gains a new capability Install software or a driver Write a plugin to connect to something, try it, and replace it
Main concern Isolation and scheduling Whether the whole system remains correct and clean after one piece is replaced

rutis does not replace the operating system; it runs on top of it. An operating system lets programs run. rutis aims to let programs grow. From the perspective of rutis, plugins are like processes, services are like system calls, and language runtimes and remote nodes are like drivers. All of them follow the same lifecycle rules; none receives special treatment.

Closing

For the first time, software has a chance to understand and engage with the world around it on its own. Instead of waiting for someone else to prepare an interface, it can go out, connect, try, improve, and, when needed, replace what is there.

That requires a container that remains reliable through frequent change, one that is not confined to a process, a language, or a device. That is what rutis aims to become.

The rutis lifecycle model comes from Cordis by Shigma. rutis implements it in Rust and carries it across more languages, processes, and machines.

Try it with Node 22+:

npx @arcships/rutis-host new weather --lang node
cd weather && npm install
npx rutis-host dev        # Run the plugin and reload it automatically when files change

Python, Bun, and Go can be starting points as well.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/arcships/rutis
  • Design philosophy: How rutis is designed

English translation prepared with AI assistance. Original article by Eric Cheng.

title: TypeScript `@throws` JSDoc and Error Typing in 2026: Why Exceptions Are Still Untyped and What to Do About It
description:
TypeScript @throws JSDoc and Error Typing in 2026: Why Exceptions Are Still Untyped and What to Do About It

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Developers write try/catch blocks around TypeScript functions without knowing what exceptions those functions throw. The compiler stays silent when a function that throws NetworkError gets called without a handler, and the codebase ships with runtime crashes that static analysis should have caught. This happens because TypeScript treats exceptions as invisible to the type system.

Problem flow showing unhandled exception propagation in TypeScript

Languages with checked exceptions force developers to declare and handle throws behavior at compile time. TypeScript documentation includes a @throws JSDoc tag, but the tag has no enforcement mechanism. Engineers who write @throws {NetworkError} above a function signature get zero compiler feedback when callers ignore that annotation. The gap between documentation and verification creates a dangerous false confidence.

Solution flow showing explicit Result type error handling

Teams that need predictable error handling in TypeScript codebases must build their own type-safe patterns. Result types, discriminated unions, and explicit error boundaries provide the guarantees the language does not. The solutions require more code than a hypothetical throws keyword, but they work today without waiting for a language feature that may never arrive.

Key Takeaways

  • TypeScript does not type exceptions and likely never will due to JavaScript runtime semantics and the unchecked exception model.
  • The @throws JSDoc tag documents throw behavior but provides zero compiler enforcement or type safety.
  • Result types (Result<T, E>) and discriminated unions create verifiable error handling without language-level throw types.
  • Error discrimination patterns using instanceof and type guards allow safe exception handling in catch blocks when exceptions remain the chosen approach.
  • Teams must choose between exceptions with manual documentation (faster to write, harder to verify) and Result types (more verbose, compiler-verified).

Why TypeScript Still Doesn't Type Exceptions in 2026

TypeScript inherits JavaScript's unchecked exception model. Any function can throw any value at any time, and the runtime provides no compile-time guarantees about what gets thrown. Java and C# have checked exceptions where the compiler enforces throw declarations, but JavaScript does not, and TypeScript follows JavaScript semantics.

The language could theoretically add throw types as an optional static analysis layer. TypeScript already diverges from JavaScript in ways that require compilation (enums, namespaces before TypeScript 5.8's --erasableSyntaxOnly). Adding a throws keyword or enforcing @throws annotations would fit that pattern. The TypeScript team has chosen not to pursue this feature.

Three technical barriers prevent practical implementation of throw types in TypeScript:

Dynamic function references lose throw information under indirection. When a function gets assigned to a variable, passed as a callback, or returned from another function, TypeScript would need to preserve throw signatures through every layer of indirection. Higher-order functions and async operations create combinatorial explosion in the number of possible throw paths.

Third-party code has no throw annotations. The vast majority of npm packages ship without throw documentation. Even if TypeScript added throw types tomorrow, existing libraries would appear to throw nothing. The type system would require every developer to manually annotate every dependency, or accept a mass of implicit any exceptions that defeat the entire purpose.

JavaScript's throw accepts any type. Code can throw strings, numbers, null, or custom objects. A robust throw type system would need to model all possible thrown values, including edge cases where throw appears in expression position. The complexity of accurately representing JavaScript's throw semantics exceeds the benefit.

TypeScript 5.2 added decorator metadata (accessed via Symbol.metadata) that frameworks use to attach runtime information to classes. Decorator metadata does not extend to function throw signatures. TypeScript 5.8 introduced --erasableSyntaxOnly to restrict syntax to patterns that Node.js type-stripping can handle, but this targets import/export semantics and namespace elimination, not exception typing.

The official TypeScript handbook documents @throws in JSDoc but provides no mechanism to verify those annotations. The tag exists for human readers and documentation generators, not for the compiler.

The @throws JSDoc Tag: What It Provides and What It Doesn't

TypeScript recognizes the @throws JSDoc tag as valid documentation syntax. Developers write @throws {ErrorType} description above function declarations to document exception behavior. IDEs display this information in hover tooltips and generated documentation sites parse it. The compiler ignores it completely during type checking.

/**
 * Fetches user data from the API
 * @throws {NetworkError} when the request fails
 * @throws {ValidationError} when the response is invalid
 */
function fetchUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  // implementation
}

// This compiles without error despite missing try/catch
const user = await fetchUser("123");

The function signature carries throw information in JSDoc but the call site receives no type error. Developers who read the hover tooltip see the documented exceptions. Developers who skip the tooltip get no warning when they omit error handling. The pattern depends on discipline rather than verification.

JSDoc comments provide value for human communication. A well-documented codebase with consistent @throws annotations helps engineers understand error paths when reading code. Documentation generation tools like TypeDoc extract @throws tags into reference pages. These benefits matter for large teams maintaining complex systems.

The disconnect between documentation and enforcement creates a specific problem: stale annotations. When a function's throw behavior changes but the JSDoc comment does not get updated, the compiler never reports the mismatch. Callers continue seeing outdated throw documentation. Tests might catch the divergence if they cover error paths, but the type system provides no safety net.

TypeScript error handling documentation approaches

Some teams treat @throws annotations as required parts of their style guide and enforce them via linter rules. The eslint-plugin-jsdoc package includes a require-throws rule that demands JSDoc throw documentation on functions that contain throw statements. This catches missing documentation but does not verify that callers handle the documented exceptions.

The pattern works for teams that value documentation completeness and accept that verification happens during code review rather than compilation. For teams that need compiler-enforced error handling, different patterns become necessary.

Building Type-Safe Error Handling Without Language Support

Result types encode success and failure cases directly in return values. A function that can fail returns Result<T, E> where T represents success and E represents failure. Callers must explicitly unwrap the result to access the success value, forcing them to handle the error case.

type Result<T, E> = 
  | { ok: true; value: T }
  | { ok: false; error: E };

function parseConfig(data: unknown): Result<Config, ConfigError> {
  if (!isValidConfig(data)) {
    return { ok: false, error: new ConfigError("Invalid structure") };
  }
  return { ok: true, value: data as Config };
}

const result = parseConfig(rawData);
if (!result.ok) {
  // Compiler requires handling the error case before accessing value
  console.error(result.error);
  return;
}
// result.value is now safely typed as Config
processConfig(result.value);

The type system enforces error handling at compile time. Attempting to access result.value without checking result.ok produces a type error. The pattern eliminates silent failure propagation because every result must be explicitly unwrapped.

Rust and Go popularized this pattern in systems programming. The Rust standard library uses Result<T, E> as its primary error handling mechanism. Go functions commonly return (value, error) tuples. These languages prove that explicit result types scale to large production systems.

TypeScript libraries provide pre-built Result type implementations. The neverthrow package offers a chainable Result API with .map(), .mapErr(), and .andThen() methods for composing operations. The ts-results package provides similar functionality with a focus on zero-dependency size. Teams can adopt these libraries or implement their own Result type based on their needs.

import { Result, ok, err } from 'neverthrow';

async function fetchUserData(id: string): Promise<Result<User, NetworkError>> {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
      return err(new NetworkError(response.status));
    }
    const data = await response.json();
    return ok(data);
  } catch (e) {
    return err(new NetworkError(0, 'Connection failed'));
  }
}

// Chaining with automatic error propagation
const result = await fetchUserData('123')
  .andThen(user => validateUser(user))
  .andThen(user => enrichUserData(user));

if (result.isErr()) {
  handleError(result.error);
} else {
  processUser(result.value);
}

Result types add verbosity compared to exceptions. Every fallible operation returns a Result that must be unwrapped. Chaining multiple operations requires .andThen() calls or manual result checking. For teams working in exception-heavy codebases, converting to Result types represents a significant architectural shift.

The tradeoff favors type safety over brevity. Exception-based code can appear cleaner because errors propagate implicitly, but that implicit propagation creates the exact problem Result types solve. When error handling matters more than code conciseness, Result types deliver compiler-verified correctness.

Result Types vs Exceptions: The Practical Trade-Offs

Aspect Result Types Exceptions
Compile-time verification Required by type system Documentation only
Error propagation Explicit at every call Implicit through call stack
Refactoring safety Compiler catches all call sites Manual search required
Code volume Higher (wrapping overhead) Lower (implicit propagation)
Integration with existing code Requires conversion layer Works immediately
Performance overhead Negligible (return value) Negligible (modern VMs)
Team learning curve Moderate (new pattern) Minimal (familiar)

Result types force every error case to surface at the call site. When a function changes its error type from ConfigError to ConfigError | NetworkError, the compiler reports an error at every location that unwraps the result. This property makes large refactors safer because the type system identifies every affected call site automatically.

Exceptions propagate through intermediate callers without modification. A function that calls another function that might throw does not need to declare or handle the exception. The call stack unwinds until a catch block appears. This behavior reduces code volume because intermediate functions need no error-handling logic, but it also means errors can travel far from their source before getting caught.

Comparison of error propagation in Result types versus exceptions

Teams working in established codebases with thousands of exception-throwing functions face a migration challenge. Converting one function to return Result<T, E> requires updating every caller. Exceptions remain compatible with the existing architecture. For greenfield projects or isolated modules, Result types impose no integration cost.

Exception performance in modern JavaScript engines imposes negligible overhead under normal control flow. Throwing and catching exceptions costs more than returning a value, but the difference matters only in tight loops where exceptions occur frequently. Real applications rarely hit performance limits from exception handling. Result types have similarly negligible performance impact because they compile to plain object returns.

The learning curve for Result types affects teams differently based on their background. Engineers familiar with Rust, Go, or functional programming recognize the pattern immediately. Teams working exclusively in JavaScript/TypeScript need time to internalize the explicit error handling mindset. The pattern requires consistent adoption across a codebase to provide value.

Exception familiarity gives them an advantage for quick prototyping and small projects. Every JavaScript developer understands try/catch syntax. Result types require teaching the team a new pattern before they can use it effectively. For projects where time to market matters more than long-term maintainability, exceptions offer a faster path.

Error Discrimination Patterns That Actually Work in Production

Catching exceptions in TypeScript produces values typed as unknown. The type system provides no information about what gets thrown. Developers must narrow the caught value to specific error types before accessing error properties safely.

class NetworkError extends Error {
  constructor(public statusCode: number, message: string) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'NetworkError';
  }
}

class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(public field: string, message: string) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'ValidationError';
  }
}

function processRequest(data: unknown) {
  try {
    validateData(data);
    sendToServer(data);
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof NetworkError) {
      console.error(`Network failed with status ${e.statusCode}`);
      return;
    }
    if (e instanceof ValidationError) {
      console.error(`Validation failed on field ${e.field}`);
      return;
    }
    // Unknown error - rethrow or log
    throw e;
  }
}

The instanceof operator narrows the type of e within each conditional block. TypeScript understands that after e instanceof NetworkError passes, e has type NetworkError in that branch. This pattern works for class-based errors that extend Error or implement distinct prototypes.

Custom error classes should always extend Error and set a distinctive name property. This practice ensures stack traces remain accurate and error monitoring tools can distinguish error types. The built-in Error.prototype.name gets set automatically when using class syntax with extends Error.

Type guard functions provide an alternative to instanceof checks when errors do not share a common base class. A type guard returns a boolean and uses a type predicate to tell TypeScript what type the value has when the guard returns true.

interface APIError {
  code: string;
  message: string;
}

function isAPIError(e: unknown): e is APIError {
  return (
    typeof e === 'object' &&
    e !== null &&
    'code' in e &&
    'message' in e &&
    typeof (e as APIError).code === 'string'
  );
}

function handleResponse(response: unknown) {
  try {
    processResponse(response);
  } catch (e) {
    if (isAPIError(e)) {
      console.error(`API error ${e.code}: ${e.message}`);
      return;
    }
    console.error('Unknown error:', e);
  }
}

The type guard performs runtime validation that the caught value has the expected shape. This pattern works when integrating with third-party APIs that throw plain objects rather than Error instances. The guard must check every required property because unknown values can be anything.

Error discrimination flow using instanceof and type guards

Error discrimination patterns in TypeScript catch blocks

Some codebases throw string literals or plain objects instead of Error instances. These patterns work at runtime but complicate error handling. Catching a string provides no stack trace and no way to distinguish error types beyond string parsing. Modern code should always throw Error instances or subclasses.

The zod library provides a .safeParse() method that returns a discriminated union instead of throwing. This pattern bridges the gap between validation libraries that throw and Result-type error handling.

import { z } from 'zod';

const UserSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  email: z.string().email(),
});

function validateUser(data: unknown) {
  const result = UserSchema.safeParse(data);
  if (!result.success) {
    // result.error is a ZodError with detailed validation failures
    console.error(result.error.format());
    return null;
  }
  // result.data is typed as { id: string; email: string }
  return result.data;
}

The .safeParse() API demonstrates how libraries can provide both throwing and non-throwing variants. The standard .parse() method throws a ZodError on validation failure. The .safeParse() method returns { success: true; data: T } or { success: false; error: ZodError } without throwing. This gives callers the choice between exceptions and Result types per call site.

Documenting Throws Behavior for Teams and Tools

Teams that continue using exceptions need documentation strategies that scale. JSDoc @throws tags work when combined with linting rules that enforce their presence and code review processes that verify accuracy. The pattern relies on human discipline but provides value when applied consistently.

/**
 * Connects to the database with retry logic
 * @throws {ConnectionError} when all retry attempts fail
 * @throws {AuthenticationError} when credentials are invalid
 * @throws {TimeoutError} when connection exceeds deadline
 */
async function connectDatabase(config: DatabaseConfig): Promise<Connection> {
  // implementation
}

The eslint-plugin-jsdoc package includes rules that enforce @throws documentation. The require-throws rule checks that functions containing throw statements have corresponding @throws tags. Configuration options control whether the rule applies to all functions or only exported ones. Related tooling context shows how modern linters handle JSDoc validation.

Code review checklists should include verification that @throws tags match actual throw behavior. When a pull request modifies a function's error handling, reviewers check that JSDoc comments get updated accordingly. This manual process catches most documentation drift but depends on reviewer attention.

Documentation flow for throw behavior in team workflows

TypeDoc and similar documentation generators parse @throws tags into generated reference documentation. The official TypeDoc documentation (accessed via npm package typedoc version 0.26.x) shows that @throws tags appear in a dedicated "Throws" section of function documentation. This makes error behavior visible in generated API docs but does not affect compilation.

Some teams encode error types in function names as a lightweight alternative to comprehensive JSDoc. Functions named fetchUserOrThrow signal explicitly that they throw on failure, while tryFetchUser suggests they return null or undefined. This convention provides no type safety but improves code readability.

Error boundaries in React applications demonstrate a practical exception-based pattern that works without type system support. A component wraps children and catches errors that propagate during rendering. Related distributed context explores how error tracking spans service boundaries.

class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component<
  { children: React.ReactNode },
  { hasError: boolean; error?: Error }
> {
  state = { hasError: false, error: undefined };

  static getDerivedStateFromError(error: Error) {
    return { hasError: true, error };
  }

  componentDidCatch(error: Error, errorInfo: React.ErrorInfo) {
    logErrorToService(error, errorInfo);
  }

  render() {
    if (this.state.hasError) {
      return <ErrorFallback error={this.state.error} />;
    }
    return this.props.children;
  }
}

Error boundaries rely on React's lifecycle methods rather than TypeScript's type system. The pattern works because React guarantees when componentDidCatch gets called, eliminating the need for static analysis to track throw behavior through the component tree.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why doesn't TypeScript just add a throws keyword like Java?

JavaScript has unchecked exceptions and no runtime enforcement of throw declarations. TypeScript follows JavaScript semantics and avoids features that require fundamental runtime changes. The complexity of accurately modeling JavaScript's dynamic throw behavior through function references, callbacks, and async operations exceeds the benefit.

Can I use a compiler plugin to add throw type checking?

No compiler plugin system exists in TypeScript that allows custom type checking logic. The TypeScript compiler architecture does not support plugins that extend the type checker. Teams must work within the type system's built-in capabilities or use external tools like custom linters.

Do Result types work with async/await?

Result types work with async/await when the Promise resolves to a Result. Functions return Promise<Result<T, E>> instead of throwing. Callers await the Promise and then unwrap the Result with the same patterns used for synchronous code. The neverthrow library provides .asyncMap() and similar utilities for async Result composition.

How do I convert an exception-throwing library to use Result types?

Wrap library calls in adapter functions that catch exceptions and return Results. The adapter provides a typed boundary between exception-based external code and Result-based internal code. This pattern contains the exception handling at the integration point without requiring changes to the library itself.

What happens to stack traces when using Result types?

Result types preserve stack traces when the error case contains an Error instance. Creating errors with new Error() captures the call stack at that point. Result types simply return the error rather than throwing it, so the stack trace remains intact and accessible through the error's .stack property.

What to Do Until (If Ever) TypeScript Gets Throw Types

TypeScript will likely never support throw types given the language's design constraints and JavaScript's runtime semantics. The core team has not signaled any movement toward this feature in recent releases. Teams building production TypeScript applications must accept that exception typing will remain outside the type system's guarantees.

Result types provide the strongest alternative for codebases that need verifiable error handling. The pattern requires architectural commitment and training investment, but it delivers compile-time verification that exceptions cannot match. New projects should consider Result types from the start when error handling matters more than code brevity.

Exception-based codebases should combine @throws JSDoc with linter enforcement and code review processes. This approach lacks type system verification but provides human-readable documentation that scales to large teams. The pattern works when the team values familiar exception syntax and accepts manual verification during review.

Error discrimination using instanceof checks and type guards makes exception handling safer when exceptions remain the chosen approach. Every catch block should narrow the caught value to specific error types before accessing properties. This pattern prevents runtime errors from assumed error shapes while working within TypeScript's type system.

The library architecture patterns that underpin maintainable TypeScript projects apply equally to error handling strategy. Choose one approach and apply it consistently across the codebase rather than mixing patterns that create confusion at boundaries. The consistency matters more than the specific choice between Results and exceptions for most applications.

title: Ship /v2 of a Go API Without Forking the Service: Two HTTP Adapters, One Use Case
description:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Product wants /v2/orders/{id} to return customer instead of customer_name, and money as an integer instead of a float. Someone copies handlers/orders.go to handlers/v2/orders.go. Then the service it calls needs a different return shape, so OrderService gets copied to OrderServiceV2. Three months later a soft-delete bug gets fixed in v2 and nobody remembers v1 has the same bug. Your two versions now disagree about which orders exist.

A better copy won't save you. A version is a wire contract, and wire contracts belong at the edge. Stripe described this approach back in 2017: their API is written against the current version, and version change modules transform responses backward for older clients, which "keep older API versions abstracted out of core code paths." You don't need Stripe's machinery to get the same property in a Go service. Ports and adapters gives it to you for free.

In hexagonal terms, v1 and v2 are two driving adapters. Each owns its request and response types and the mapping to and from the domain. Both call the same use case through the same port, and the whole thing runs on the standard library.

The layout: one core, two doors

Here is the whole tree. order is the core. Everything under adapter is replaceable. The module needs nothing beyond the standard library:

module example.com/orders

go 1.22

orders/
├── go.mod
├── cmd/api/
│   ├── main.go
│   └── main_test.go
└── internal/
    ├── order/          # domain + ports + use case
    │   └── order.go
    └── adapter/
        ├── httpv1/     # driving adapter, old contract
        ├── httpv2/     # driving adapter, new contract
        └── memrepo/    # driven adapter, in-memory store

The domain holds money the way money should be held: an integer count of minor units plus a currency code. That float in v1's JSON was a wire decision, so it lives in the v1 adapter and nowhere else.

package order

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
)

var ErrNotFound = errors.New("order not found")

type Order struct {
    ID         string
    Customer   string
    TotalMinor int64 // 1999 = 19.99 in a 2-decimal currency
    Currency   string
    Deleted    bool
}

// Repository is the driven port.
type Repository interface {
    ByID(ctx context.Context, id string) (Order, error)
}

// Getter is the driving port. Both HTTP versions call it.
type Getter interface {
    Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (Order, error)
}

type Service struct{ repo Repository }

func NewService(r Repository) *Service {
    return &Service{repo: r}
}

func (s *Service) Get(
    ctx context.Context, id string,
) (Order, error) {
    o, err := s.repo.ByID(ctx, id)
    if err != nil {
        return Order{}, err
    }
    // The soft-delete fix lives here, once, for every version.
    if o.Deleted {
        return Order{}, ErrNotFound
    }
    return o, nil
}

Notice what this file does not know: JSON, HTTP, URL paths, version numbers. When v3 shows up, this file does not change.


Two driving adapters, one use case: the version lives at the door, not in the room.

The v1 adapter keeps the old contract, warts included

v1 promised clients customer_name and a float total. The adapter keeps that promise. It also does the division that v1 always did, which assumes two decimal places. For a zero-decimal currency like JPY, where Stripe's API takes 10 to mean 10 JPY, that division was already wrong. That is one of the reasons v2 exists, and it is a good reason not to "fix" v1 quietly: clients have coded around its behavior.

package httpv1

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "net/http"

    "example.com/orders/internal/order"
)

type orderResponse struct {
    ID           string  `json:"id"`
    CustomerName string  `json:"customer_name"`
    Total        float64 `json:"total"`
    Currency     string  `json:"currency"`
}

func toResponse(o order.Order) orderResponse {
    return orderResponse{
        ID:           o.ID,
        CustomerName: o.Customer,
        Total:        float64(o.TotalMinor) / 100,
        Currency:     o.Currency,
    }
}

type Handler struct {
    uc     order.Getter
    policy Policy
}

func New(uc order.Getter, p Policy) *Handler {
    return &Handler{uc: uc, policy: p}
}

func (h *Handler) Register(mux *http.ServeMux) {
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /v1/orders/{id}",
        deprecated(h.getOrder, h.policy))
}

func (h *Handler) getOrder(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    o, err := h.uc.Get(r.Context(), r.PathValue("id"))
    if errors.Is(err, order.ErrNotFound) {
        http.Error(w, "order not found", http.StatusNotFound)
        return
    }
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "internal error", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(toResponse(o))
}

v1 also has to tell clients it is going away. Two headers do the work. RFC 9745, published in March 2025 on the Standards Track, defines Deprecation as a structured-field date: an @ followed by Unix seconds, like Deprecation: @1688169599. It also defines a deprecation link relation that points at your migration docs. RFC 8594 defines Sunset, the moment the endpoint is expected to stop responding, as a plain HTTP-date. RFC 9745 adds one rule tying them together: the Sunset timestamp "MUST NOT be earlier than" the Deprecation timestamp.

All of that is wire behavior, so it goes in the v1 package:

package httpv1

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type Policy struct {
    Deprecated time.Time
    Sunset     time.Time
    DocsURL    string
}

func deprecated(next http.HandlerFunc, p Policy) http.HandlerFunc {
    dep := fmt.Sprintf("@%d", p.Deprecated.Unix())
    sun := p.Sunset.UTC().Format(http.TimeFormat)
    link := "<" + p.DocsURL + `>; rel="deprecation"`
    return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        h := w.Header()
        h.Set("Deprecation", dep)
        h.Set("Sunset", sun)
        h.Add("Link", link)
        next(w, r)
    }
}

The headers are set before next runs, so they are already in the header map when http.Error writes a 404 or 500. Clients that hit a missing order still learn the endpoint is going away. The .UTC() call matters: the http.TimeFormat docs say the time "must be in UTC for Format to generate the correct format."

The v2 adapter renames a field and fixes the money

v2 is a sibling package with its own DTO and its own mapping. It calls the same order.Getter.

package httpv2

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "net/http"

    "example.com/orders/internal/order"
)

type money struct {
    AmountMinor int64  `json:"amount_minor"`
    Currency    string `json:"currency"`
}

type orderResponse struct {
    ID       string `json:"id"`
    Customer string `json:"customer"`
    Total    money  `json:"total"`
}

func toResponse(o order.Order) orderResponse {
    return orderResponse{
        ID:       o.ID,
        Customer: o.Customer,
        Total: money{
            AmountMinor: o.TotalMinor,
            Currency:    o.Currency,
        },
    }
}

type Handler struct{ uc order.Getter }

func New(uc order.Getter) *Handler { return &Handler{uc: uc} }

func (h *Handler) Register(mux *http.ServeMux) {
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /v2/orders/{id}", h.getOrder)
}

func (h *Handler) getOrder(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    o, err := h.uc.Get(r.Context(), r.PathValue("id"))
    if errors.Is(err, order.ErrNotFound) {
        http.Error(w, "order not found", http.StatusNotFound)
        return
    }
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "internal error", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(toResponse(o))
}

Yes, the error branches look the same as v1's. Leave them duplicated. Error shape is part of the contract, and the day v2 moves to a JSON error body you want to change one file without a shared helper dragging v1 along. The duplication that hurts is duplicated business rules, and there is none here: the soft-delete check exists exactly once, in order.Service.

Mounting both on one ServeMux

Since Go 1.22, net/http.ServeMux patterns accept a method and wildcards, so GET /v1/orders/{id} is a complete route and r.PathValue("id") returns the segment. The routing announcement also notes that a GET pattern matches HEAD, and that when two patterns overlap the most specific one wins. Keep the go line in go.mod at 1.22 or later: the new matching is controlled by the httpmuxgo121 setting, and GODEBUG defaults follow the Go version in your go.mod.

The in-memory store is the driven adapter. It doubles as the test fake.

package memrepo

import (
    "context"

    "example.com/orders/internal/order"
)

type Repo map[string]order.Order

func (r Repo) ByID(
    _ context.Context, id string,
) (order.Order, error) {
    o, ok := r[id]
    if !ok {
        return order.Order{}, order.ErrNotFound
    }
    return o, nil
}

Wiring happens in one function, so the test can call the exact same code main runs:

package main

import (
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "time"

    "example.com/orders/internal/adapter/httpv1"
    "example.com/orders/internal/adapter/httpv2"
    "example.com/orders/internal/adapter/memrepo"
    "example.com/orders/internal/order"
)

var v1Policy = httpv1.Policy{
    Deprecated: time.Date(2026, 11, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC),
    Sunset:     time.Date(2027, 5, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC),
    DocsURL:    "https://api.example.com/docs/v2-migration",
}

func newMux(uc order.Getter) *http.ServeMux {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    httpv1.New(uc, v1Policy).Register(mux)
    httpv2.New(uc).Register(mux)
    return mux
}

func main() {
    repo := memrepo.Repo{
        "ord_1": {ID: "ord_1", Customer: "Acme GmbH",
            TotalMinor: 1999, Currency: "EUR"},
    }
    uc := order.NewService(repo)
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", newMux(uc)))
}

Count the places that know there are two versions: two Register calls and two packages. The service, the repository port and the domain type are shared, and none of them carry a version number.


Same order, two shapes on the wire. The mapping is the only thing that forks.

One table test, both versions, one fake repository

This is where the design pays rent. One fake repo, one mux, and a table that sends the same orders through both doors. The deleted-order row is the regression test for the bug from the opening: fix it once in the use case, and both versions return 404.

package main

import (
    "net/http/httptest"
    "strings"
    "testing"

    "example.com/orders/internal/adapter/memrepo"
    "example.com/orders/internal/order"
)

const v1Body = `{"id":"ord_1","customer_name":"Acme GmbH",` +
    `"total":19.99,"currency":"EUR"}`

const v2Body = `{"id":"ord_1","customer":"Acme GmbH",` +
    `"total":{"amount_minor":1999,"currency":"EUR"}}`

func TestOrdersBothVersions(t *testing.T) {
    repo := memrepo.Repo{
        "ord_1": {ID: "ord_1", Customer: "Acme GmbH",
            TotalMinor: 1999, Currency: "EUR"},
        "ord_2": {ID: "ord_2", Customer: "Gone Ltd",
            TotalMinor: 500, Currency: "EUR", Deleted: true},
    }
    mux := newMux(order.NewService(repo))

    tests := []struct {
        name, path, body string
        code             int
        deprecated       bool
    }{
        {"v1 found", "/v1/orders/ord_1", v1Body, 200, true},
        {"v2 found", "/v2/orders/ord_1", v2Body, 200, false},
        {"v1 missing", "/v1/orders/nope", "", 404, true},
        {"v2 missing", "/v2/orders/nope", "", 404, false},
        {"v1 deleted", "/v1/orders/ord_2", "", 404, true},
        {"v2 deleted", "/v2/orders/ord_2", "", 404, false},
    }

    for _, tc := range tests {
        t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {
            req := httptest.NewRequest("GET", tc.path, nil)
            rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
            mux.ServeHTTP(rec, req)

            if rec.Code != tc.code {
                t.Fatalf("code = %d, want %d", rec.Code, tc.code)
            }
            got := strings.TrimSpace(rec.Body.String())
            if tc.body != "" && got != tc.body {
                t.Errorf("body = %s\nwant  %s", got, tc.body)
            }
            dep := rec.Header().Get("Deprecation") != ""
            if dep != tc.deprecated {
                t.Errorf("Deprecation set = %v, want %v",
                    dep, tc.deprecated)
            }
        })
    }
}

Three things in that table are worth a second look. The body constants are the contract, written down: if someone reorders fields in a DTO or renames a JSON tag, a row fails. The Deprecation column proves the header is scoped to v1, including on its 404s. And the two deleted rows go through one rule in one place, which is the whole argument of this post in two lines of test data.

strings.TrimSpace is there because json.Encoder.Encode writes a trailing newline. The test goes through mux.ServeHTTP instead of calling the handlers directly, because r.PathValue is filled in by the mux during routing, and because you want the test to fail if a route pattern breaks.

Where this stops working

This pattern covers read-shape changes: renames, nesting, unit changes, header policy. It does not cover everything, and it is better to know the edges before you rely on it.

Behavior changes are the hard case. If v2 must validate an order differently, or charge a card at a different step, that is not a mapping. Put the choice in the use case as an explicit option the adapter passes in, with a name that says what it does rather than which version wants it. Stripe hits the same wall: their post describes flagging changes with side effects, turning their response transformation into a no-op, and handling them with checks elsewhere in the code.

Request bodies follow the same rule as responses. A POST /v2/orders adapter decodes its own DTO into a domain command. When v2 accepts amount_minor and v1 accepts a float, each adapter converts to TotalMinor before calling the core, and the v1 adapter is the one place that rounds.

On sunset day you remove internal/adapter/httpv1, delete one Register line, and drop the v1 rows from the table. If the domain had grown a V1Total field or an if version == 1 branch, you would be hunting through the core instead.

If this was useful

The move in this post (a version is an adapter, the use case is the product) is the same move Hexagonal Architecture in Go makes for databases, queues and third-party APIs. The book walks through the layout, the port boundaries and the persistence side, which is where most Go services start leaking SQL types into the core. If your /v2 folder is already a copy of /v1, it shows you how to pull the shared part back into the middle.

title: Seed the Chaos: Making Random Bugs Reproducible
description:
Every game that shuffles, spawns or rolls dice has a quiet problem: the bug that happened once and never again.

A tester sees the shop hand out the wrong reward. Nobody can make it happen twice. Without a way back to that exact run, the report is stuck: someone saw something, and nobody can prove what.

Randomness feels like the enemy of testing. It does not have to be. The same generator that makes a run unpredictable can make it exactly repeatable, if you keep one small piece of information: the seed.

A seed is a recipe, not a recording

Most engines let you set the starting seed of their random number generator. Godot's RandomNumberGenerator does. Give two runs the same seed and the generator produces the same sequence of numbers in both.

That gets you most of a replay, not all of it. An exact replay needs the same seed, the same code, the same engine version and the same inputs in the same order. Change any of them and the same seed tells a different story. A seed is the recipe for the randomness, not a recording of the run.

Two habits make seeds useful. Log the initial seed at the start of every run, meaning the seed the run began with, not the generator's later state. And log the build with it, so "cannot reproduce" at least means "cannot reproduce on this version".

Chaos, but on a schedule

Once every run has a seed, testing stops needing luck.

The practical setup is simple: an automated job plays seeded games and writes one line per failure - the seed it started from, the build, and the assertion that broke. The review comes down to three questions. Did anything fail? Does it fail again on the same seed and the same build? Is the failing state a real defect, or an expectation that aged?

On a quiet day the answers take minutes. On the day that matters, there is a reproduction already in hand instead of a theory.

The honest limits

Determinism covers logic. It does not cover timing, floating-point differences across devices, or the physics of a real thumb. A seeded replay can prove the shuffle behaved for that seed on that build. It cannot prove the game felt fair, any more than a passing screenshot proves a player understood the screen. I wrote about that boundary in an earlier piece (https://dev.to/kfiradut/a-test-report-should-say-what-it-cannot-prove-3i0i); it applies here with full force.

And some real defects stay intermittent even with seeds: race conditions, memory pressure, hardware quirks. A seed does not solve those. It gives every report somewhere concrete to start, instead of a shrug.

Why it is worth it

Reproducible randomness is not only for debugging. It is a design tool.

Balance questions stop being arguments from one lucky session. You can run a difficulty change across the same thousand seeds as the old one and compare what actually moved. The randomness becomes a fixed laboratory instead of weather.

Chaos is fine. Seed it first.

In my game projects, Instinct does much of the implementation and testing. I stay responsible for direction and for the decision to ship.

References:

  • RandomNumberGenerator - Godot Engine documentation: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_randomnumbergenerator.html
  • Random number generation - Godot Engine documentation: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/math/random_number_generation.html

title: Testing email flows in CI without sending email
description:
Email is usually the least tested part of a product because the test would send a real message to a real inbox. The workaround is a test doubles pattern that is easy to get wrong.

Assert on the intent, not the transport

Most suites mock the email client and assert that send was called. That passes while the template is broken. The useful assertion is on the rendered output: subject, recipient, and the presence of the token or link that the flow depends on.

Render in the test

Render the template with the same code path as production, then check the HTML and the text part both contain the expected URL. This catches the failure that matters most: a link that lost its base URL and now points at localhost.

Keep one real send per release

Mocks cannot catch DNS, authentication, or provider rejection. One real send per release to an internal address, with the headers checked for dkim=pass and a matching return-path, covers the gap that unit tests structurally cannot.

The detail that finds regressions

Snapshot the rendered message body and diff it in CI. Template edits that break variable substitution show up as a diff instead of as a customer complaint, and the diff is small enough to review.

Volanea exposes a render endpoint that returns the exact subject and body for given variables, so tests can assert on the real output.

title: A Save System Is a Promise, Not a Feature
description:
A player will never see your save code. They will feel the one time it fails.

Lost progress does not read like a technical problem to the person who lost it. It reads like a broken promise. The game said the progress counted, and then it did not.

In my game projects, Instinct does much of the implementation and testing. I stay responsible for direction and for the decision to ship. Save behavior sits exactly on that line: the assistant can build the mechanism, but the promise the mechanism keeps is a design decision. I want that promise written down before anyone writes code.

The failure is rarely the write

Most save systems write data correctly when they get the chance. The gap is timing.

A mobile game lives inside a lifecycle it does not control. The operating system can pause it, freeze it, or kill it to reclaim memory. A call arrives. The battery dies. The player swipes the app away in the middle of a reward animation because something in real life is more urgent than the next level.

If progress only reaches disk when a timer fires or when a scene closes politely, then every one of those exits is a small bet. Most days the bet wins. The day it loses, the player learns the game cannot be trusted, and that lesson is very hard to un-teach.

Write the promise in one sentence

Before choosing a mechanism, I want one sentence: what exactly must survive?

"Level progress and currency survive any exit, including a force-quit in the middle of an action." A sentence like that is short, but it rules things out. A timer that fires two seconds after a move does not satisfy it on its own. Neither does saving only when the player returns to the map.

The sentence also defines what is not promised. A half-finished animation does not need to resume. Cosmetic state can be regenerated. Being explicit here is what makes the real promise cheap enough to keep.

Save at decision points

The pattern I aim for is simple: when the game state changes in a way the player would call progress, that is a save point.

A level completed, a reward claimed, a purchase finished. If the save stays small, writing it often costs little. A few fields written at each decision point are usually a better bet than a full state dump written rarely.

Two mechanisms are worth naming. Writing to a temporary file and renaming it over the old one avoids the specific failure where a crash mid-write leaves a half-written file. It is not magic: durability still depends on the storage stack honoring the write, and the rename has to come after the write completes. Lifecycle callbacks are the second net, not the first. Android's onPause is a useful place to catch a background exit, but once the system decides to reclaim the process, no callback is guaranteed to run. A design that relies on callbacks alone is betting the promise on them.

Test the crash, not just the flow

A save you have not crash-tested is a hope.

The useful test is unglamorous: play, force-stop the app in the middle of the action, relaunch, and compare what survived with what the promise said should survive. Automate the boring version of it. Run it on the happy path and on the embarrassing paths: mid-reward, mid-purchase, mid-first-launch.

The honest limits

Even a good save design cannot guarantee that every byte reaches storage before the power is gone. What it can do is make that outcome rare, and make the promise explicit about what survives and what does not.

This is the same discipline as writing down what a test cannot prove. A persistence test that only exercises clean exits proves almost nothing about a phone in a pocket.

References:

  • Godot Engine documentation, Saving games: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/io/saving_games.html
  • Godot Engine documentation, FileAccess: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_fileaccess.html
  • Android Developers, The activity lifecycle: https://developer.android.com/guide/components/activities/activity-lifecycle

title: Storing email bodies without building a data swamp
description:
Email is the largest unstructured dataset most products own, and the default approach — dump the whole raw message into a database column — becomes a problem at around a hundred thousand messages.

Split the record

Store the metadata in the database: message id, thread id, participants, subject, timestamps, direction, and a pointer to the body. Store the raw message and the rendered parts in object storage keyed by message id. Listing an inbox then reads small rows, and opening one message reads one object.

Skew the schema

Bodies are large, variable, and rarely queried. Metadata is small, uniform, and queried constantly. Putting them in the same table means every index carries the weight of the part you never search.

Retention has to be per mailbox

Support conversations and agent inboxes have different legal expectations. If retention is a global setting, someone will eventually ask you to delete one conversation and you will have to write a migration instead of a delete.

The detail that makes search work

Index the extracted text, not the HTML. Indexing raw HTML puts tag names in your search results and multiplies the index size for no benefit. Extract once at ingest, store the extracted text next to the metadata, and search that.

Volanea keeps message metadata queryable and bodies addressable, so inbox listing stays fast as a mailbox grows.

title: Green tests, dead tripwire
description:
Here is a failure I had not thought about until someone asked me the right question.

You write a PreToolUse hook. It reads the tool call, decides the command is dangerous, and blocks it. You write unit tests for it, because a guard with no tests is a wish. The tests pass. Months go by and the hook never fires, which you read as good news, because nothing bad has happened.

Then one day you find out the harness renamed a field in the payload eighteen weeks ago, your hook has matched nothing since, and every one of your tests is still green. They're green because the test builds the payload itself, in the shape you believed the harness sends. The test and the hook agree with each other perfectly. Neither of them has spoken to the harness in months.

Green tests, dead tripwire. The guard and its tests share a belief, so the tests cannot see the belief go stale.

This is the same shape as a bug I wrote about last time, where a redaction tool verified its own output using the same wrong geometry it had used to draw with. Different domain, identical structure: a check built from the same assumption as the thing it checks is not a check, it's a second copy of your belief.

Why "it hasn't fired" tells you nothing

A guard has two states that look identical from the outside. Working and quiet, because nothing tripped it. Broken and quiet, because it cannot match anything any more.

Nothing in your workflow distinguishes them. You don't get a weekly report of hooks that ran. The absence of refusals feels like safety, and in the broken case it is precisely the opposite: you've been running unguarded while believing you were covered, which is worse than having no hook at all, because you'd have been more careful without one.

Every guard that encodes a fact about an external world has this problem. The payload shape of your agent harness. The name of a tool. Whether CI still runs the check your hook assumes runs. Those facts change without telling you, and the guard goes quiet rather than loud.

Fail closed, but not everywhere

The obvious fix is to fail closed. If this is a tool I'm guarding and the field I need isn't there, that's an anomaly, not an allow. Most hooks, mine included, default to allowing anything they can't parse, which is exactly backwards.

The question I got asked, and did not have a good answer for at first, was whether that means failing closed everywhere, or only for guards on irreversible things.

I now think irreversibility is the wrong axis. The right one is what happens when the hook declines to decide. Three modes, three correct failures:

Block mode: fail closed. The hook is certain from the input alone that the call is wrong. If it can't read the input, refuse. The fallback is a retry or a question, both cheap, and the false block you eat on the day the harness changes is the thing that tells you the shape moved. That one annoying refusal is the monitoring you never set up.

Warn mode: don't fail closed, and say why. A warn hook exists because the rule is a heuristic that will fire on legitimate work, so turning an unparseable payload into a wall contradicts its own design. Emit the warning anyway. And the detail I'd have got wrong: the warning has to say precisely that it couldn't read the input, rather than printing its usual generic text. A warning that can't name the file or the command, but talks as if it can, teaches the model to discount every future warning from that hook.

Auto-allow mode: already fails closed, for free. This is the mode nobody discusses. Hooks that pre-approve read-only commands so they never surface a permission prompt. If one can't parse the input, it simply doesn't allow, and you land on the normal prompt. The fallback is a human, which is exactly where you want to be.

So the rule I'd write now: fail closed wherever declining costs a prompt. Don't, wherever declining costs a block on legitimate work.

The fixture that lies to you

The other half is contract tests, and there's a trap in them.

Recording one real payload from an actual session and replaying it against the hook catches the rename before it costs you anything. Writing that fixture by hand does not, because a hand-written fixture is your belief about the payload shape stored in a second file. You now have two copies of the same assumption and a false sense of coverage. If you can't capture a real one, log the raw input on every invocation and go read it occasionally. Dull, works.

My own setup, honestly: two hooks have real unit tests, one with a table of about thirty adversarial command variants, and both assert the deny path rather than only the happy one. Neither has a recorded fixture. I haven't fixed it yet.

What I still don't have

The thing I'd actually want is a canary. A scheduled job that deliberately issues a known-bad call and asserts it gets refused, so a dead guard announces itself instead of waiting to be discovered. That's a cron and an assertion, it isn't hard, and I haven't built it, which I suspect means most people running a dozen hooks haven't either.

Most of this post came out of the comments on my last one rather than from me. @build996 pushed on which refusals an agent can actually act on, @max_quimby on hooks quietly becoming an unversioned rulebook nobody remembers the reasons for, @syntaxwanderer_26 asked the question that produced the whole fail-closed taxonomy and then supplied the warn-mode detail, and @doriansotpyrc asked how a rule earns promotion from prose into a hook, which I answered as: once means write the sentence, twice means the sentence isn't carrying it.

So, the part I'm stuck on. How would you detect a guard that has been dead for a month? A canary is the only honest answer I've got, and it only covers the failures you thought to simulate. If you've found something better, or you've had a tripwire die quietly and only noticed by accident, I'd like to hear it.

title: The LXD and MicroCloud Vulnerability That Turns a Public Certificate Into Host Root
description:
The LXD and MicroCloud Vulnerability That Turns a Public Certificate Into Host Root

The LXD and MicroCloud vulnerability disclosed by Canonical on October 28, 2026 lets an attacker authenticate as a trusted client without ever holding that client's private key, a flaw rated CVSS v4.0 10.0, the maximum possible. All it takes is network access to the management API and the trusted client's public certificate, which, unlike a private key, was never meant to be secret in the first place.

Jump to why a public certificate was enough if you only want the mechanism.

What LXD and MicroCloud Actually Got Wrong

LXD and MicroCloud, Canonical's tools for running and clustering Linux containers and virtual machines, authenticate clients to their HTTPS management API using mutual TLS. Ostorlab's technical writeup traces the bug to a single mismatch between what a TLS handshake proves and what the authentication code assumed it proved: a handshake only confirms the client holds the private key for the first certificate in its chain, the leaf. Everything else in that chain is client-controlled and unverified.

The vulnerable code looped over every certificate the client presented and checked each one against the trust store individually, rather than checking only the verified leaf. An attacker could therefore build a certificate chain out of their own leaf certificate plus the public certificate of someone the server already trusted, and the server would authenticate them as that trusted identity. Canonical's advisory confirms the resulting access follows the impersonated identity's actual permissions.

Why a Public Certificate Was Enough

This is the detail that makes the flaw worse than it first sounds. A public certificate is, by design, not a secret. The Hacker News reported that successful exploitation requires only HTTPS API reachability and a trusted client's public certificate, and security practitioners responding to that disclosure pointed out exactly where those certificates tend to live: in ~/.config/lxc, in CI runner configuration, in Ansible repositories, and in backups, none of which are typically treated as sensitive.

Canonical's own advisory goes further for MicroCloud specifically: an attacker who intercepts the public certificate of a node joining a cluster can later authenticate as that member. The resulting access, per Canonical, can include full control over containers, virtual machines, and storage volumes, and if the impersonated identity carries administrative rights, root execution on the host itself. An unrestricted LXD client is, functionally, root on the hypervisor.

The Part That Limits Real-World Exposure

A default, non-clustered LXD installation does not bind to a network port at all. It listens on a local Unix socket, gated by POSIX group membership rather than TLS, and the vulnerable HTTPS listener only activates once an administrator explicitly runs lxc config set core.https_address <ip>:<port>, typically on TCP 8443. The attack surface, in other words, exists specifically for clustered and remotely managed deployments, which is exactly where LXD and MicroCloud are most often used for anything resembling production infrastructure.

As of November 1, 2026, Ostorlab's advisory states no exploitation is known and the flaw is not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. That is a meaningfully different risk posture than an actively exploited bug, but a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass with no public proof-of-concept yet is not evidence of safety, it's a head start that won't last.

This Is the Second Time This Exact Check Failed

The CyberSec Guru's analysis draws a direct line to CVE-2024-6156, an earlier, lower-severity bug in the same authentication logic, limited at the time to PKI mode. CVE-2026-112816 is, in the analyst's words, "the same authentication boundary failing in a much more serious way," because the underlying flaw, trusting unverified certificate chain elements, was never fully closed the first time. The fix in Incus 7.6.0 and Canonical's patched LXD builds is specific: resolve identity from the first verified certificate in the chain only, after confirming it isn't empty, and stop looping over the rest.

What This Means If You Run Clustered Virtualization

Our verdict: patch immediately if you run LXD or MicroCloud with a network-exposed management API, and audit your trust store regardless, because the public certificates that grant trust are sitting in places, CI configs, Ansible repos, backups, that most teams don't treat as sensitive. A CVSS 10.0 score with no known exploitation yet is a narrow window, not a pass.

This bug doesn't tell you that clustering virtualization platforms is inherently unsafe. It tells you something narrower and more useful: when a single management API authenticates access to every container, VM, and storage volume in a cluster, the correctness of one authentication function becomes the entire security boundary for everything behind it. That's a structural property of centralized cluster control planes, not a one-off coding mistake, and it doesn't go away once this specific CVE is patched.

  • If you run an LXD or MicroCloud cluster with core.https_address set: patch to the fixed versions now (LXD 6.10.1, 5.21.9, 5.0.11, or 4.0.15 depending on track; MicroCloud 3.4.1 or 2.1.5; Incus 7.6.0), and until you confirm the patch landed, restrict the management listener to trusted hosts only.
  • Audit who holds your trust store's public certificates. They aren't secrets by design, which is exactly why they end up in places nobody locks down, and this bug shows that's a mistake.
  • If your own infrastructure relies on a single cluster-wide authentication boundary for isolation, this is a reminder to ask what happens when that one boundary has a bug, not whether it will.

FAQ

What is the LXD and MicroCloud vulnerability?

CVE-2026-112816 is a CVSS v4.0 10.0 authentication bypass in Canonical's LXD and MicroCloud, disclosed October 28, 2026. It lets an attacker with network access to the HTTPS management API authenticate as any trusted client by presenting that client's public certificate, without needing its private key, because the vulnerable code checked every certificate in a client's chain against the trust store instead of verifying only the cryptographically proven leaf certificate.

Can this vulnerability give an attacker root access to the host machine?

Yes, under specific conditions. Canonical's advisory states that if the identity an attacker impersonates has administrative privileges, the resulting access can include root execution on the host, because an unrestricted LXD client has functional control over the hypervisor. This requires the impersonated identity to already be privileged; impersonating a low-privilege client does not by itself grant host root.

Is the LXD and MicroCloud vulnerability being actively exploited?

As of November 1, 2026, no exploitation has been publicly confirmed and the flaw is not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, according to Ostorlab's advisory. No public proof-of-concept has been linked by the cited vendor advisories either. That status can change quickly for a bug this severe, so patching now rather than waiting for confirmed exploitation is the safer posture.

What We Checked Before Publishing

We pulled Canonical's own security advisory, Ostorlab's technical breakdown of the authentication flow, The Hacker News' disclosure summary, and The CyberSec Guru's historical comparison to CVE-2024-6156. We were not able to independently verify Canonical's internal timeline for when the flawed trust-loop logic was first introduced, so we've reported what the public advisories confirm rather than speculating about how long the window of exposure actually was.

I'm Rohit, founder of Krova Cloud: every Cube runs its own kernel behind a per-cube jailer sandbox, and we don't put a single cluster-wide management API in the critical path between a certificate and host root. That doesn't make centralized cluster control planes wrong for every use case, but it's a different trade-off than the one LXD and MicroCloud make, and this CVE is a clear look at what that trade-off can cost when one authentication function gets it wrong. More debugging stories at debugly.dev.
