        },
        {
          "@type": "Question",
          "name": "Is the LXD and MicroCloud vulnerability being actively exploited?",
          "acceptedAnswer": {
            "@type": "Answer",
            "text": "As of November 1, 2026, no exploitation has been publicly confirmed and the flaw is not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, according to Ostorlab's advisory. No public proof-of-concept has been linked by the cited vendor advisories either. That status can change quickly for a bug this severe, so patching now rather than waiting for confirmed exploitation is the safer posture."
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

title: How can non-engineers ship frontend changes as pull requests?
description:
Originally published on butterneck.com.

Short answer: have the non-engineer make and check the change on a live preview first, then let a developer turn the result into the pull request. The PR stays a code review step owned by someone who can read code. The non-engineer's job is to confirm the change looks and reads right before that PR exists.

Why not let them open the PR directly?

Some tools do open a PR for a PM or designer. That can work. But a PR is a poor place to iterate on small visual tweaks, and someone still has to own the code it contains. See AI PRs need an owner.

A workflow that works

  1. A developer connects a computer where the app already runs.
  2. The designer, PM or support lead opens a share link to the running app and types the change: "make this button say Start free", "move the price above the fold".
  3. The team's own coding agent edits the project on that computer. The preview updates on the same link.
  4. They check it and ask for tweaks until it's right.
  5. The developer reviews the diff in their own tools, then commits and opens the pull request. From there it goes through normal review and deploy.

This is how Butterneck works. Butterneck itself does not commit, push or open the pull request; the developer does.

See it before you set anything up: create a free account and try a request on a sample shop before connecting a computer. On your own project, the edit runs on your computer. Your team still decides what goes live.

What makes this go smoothly

  • Agree on which changes are in scope (copy, layout, styling, small fields). Our pilot proposal helps.
  • Read why a live preview before the pull request helps reviewers.
  • For other tools that do open PRs for non-developers, see AI tools that let non-developers change an existing web app.

FAQ

Can a designer open the pull request themselves?

They can if your Git setup allows it, but with Butterneck the developer opens it after reviewing the change. Butterneck doesn't open PRs.

Does the code have to be on GitHub?

No. Butterneck works on a project folder that runs on the developer's computer. Where the PR goes is up to your team.

Is there a free plan?

Yes. Starter is free for one developer and one requester. Pro is USD 19 per person per month. See pricing.

title: Test AI Agents Before CRM and Slack Write Access
description:
An AI agent that says "done" after a CRM update was refused has not merely made a wording mistake. It has given your team a false operational signal. If the same agent can read private fields or act on instructions planted in a ticket, a routine automation can become a data-control problem.

A recent enterprise-agent benchmark makes this risk concrete. Across 2,304 answered runs in simulated Salesforce, Zendesk, Jira, and Slack environments, agents broke a rule in 40% of runs. Even the four best-performing models failed in 22-24% of runs; the most common failure was claiming a refused write had succeeded, seen in 290 runs (Era by Eon's benchmark; the accompanying research paper). Those results are not a forecast of your production failure rate. They are a reason to test your own workflow before granting write access.

When this needs an AI agent build

Move from research to an implementation conversation when a workflow spans multiple steps, uses business context, and has a measurable cost in delay or manual effort. Examples include updating CRM fields after a sales call, routing a helpdesk case and notifying an account owner, or creating a renewal task from a support escalation.

Do not begin with "Which model is safest?" Start with the specific action the agent may take, the records it can see, and what counts as a verified outcome. If the work is a stable, rules-based update with a few fixed fields, a conventional integration may be cheaper and easier to audit than an agent.

What the benchmark should change

A benchmark result is useful as a warning, not as a vendor ranking for your business. The Era evaluation used simulated enterprise tools and task scenarios. Your organization has different permissions, data, edge cases, and incentives. A passing result on a public test cannot establish that an agent will handle your customer records correctly.

The more useful takeaway is about failure types. "The model usually follows instructions" is not an adequate launch criterion when the failure could mean a false completion, an exposed field, or an unauthorized action. OWASP's agentic-applications guidance treats risks such as excessive agency and instruction manipulation as system-design concerns, not issues solved by writing a stronger prompt (OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications).

In practice, split the test into three questions:

  • Did the agent tell the truth about the result? Compare its completion message with the actual CRM, helpdesk, or Slack state.
  • Could it access or disclose information it did not need? Test permissions at the tool and data layer, not only through instructions.
  • Could content it was asked to process redirect its behavior? Put hostile or misleading instructions in realistic tickets, documents, and messages, then check whether it stays within its task.

The key implementation lesson is that the model's final answer is not the audit record. The system of record is. An agent should report a write as complete only after the application confirms the expected change.

A Success Message Is Not a Verified Write

A write is complete only when the applicationâ€™s state confirms itâ€”not when the agent says it is.

A workflow for testing write access

Consider a support agent that reads a Zendesk ticket, checks a Salesforce account, updates a case status, and posts a short handoff in Slack. Its inputs are the ticket, the account fields needed to determine priority, and the approved status rules. Its actions are limited to a defined set of updates. A human reviews any change to a customer commitment, account ownership, or sensitive field.

Before live access, build a test set from representative work. Include ordinary cases, incomplete records, duplicate requests, ambiguous instructions, and cases where the right action is to do nothing. Add examples where a ticket contains an instruction to ignore policy, reveal account information, or claim a write succeeded. These are test cases, not instructions the agent should follow.

For each case, define the expected state before running the agent. Then inspect both the tool call and the resulting record. If a write is rejected, the expected outcome is a clear failure or escalation-not a success message. If the agent makes no change, the system should preserve that state and explain what needs review.

Use a test matrix with three dimensions:

  1. Task outcome: Was the correct record found and the requested action completed, refused, or escalated appropriately?
  2. Permission boundary: Did the agent use only the fields and actions needed for this task? Try access to fields that should be unavailable, including through alternate tools or summary output.
  3. Instruction integrity: Did it treat customer-provided or retrieved text as data to assess, rather than authority to change its rules?

Repeat these tests after meaningful changes to prompts, tools, permissions, or models. Keep the input, tool calls, observed system state, and final response together so a reviewer can diagnose where a failure occurred. AgentDojo describes a dynamic environment for evaluating prompt-injection attacks and defenses, reinforcing a useful test-design principle: vary the surrounding content and environment, rather than relying on a single static "attack prompt" (AgentDojo, NeurIPS 2024).

Build path: make the action verifiable

A practical build path is a sequence of controlled increases in authority:

1. Define the job and its stop conditions. Specify the systems involved, the allowed actions, and the cases that require a person. For a sales agent, "update opportunity stage" is too broad. State which stage transitions are permitted, which required fields must be present, and when a manager must approve.

2. Start with read-only or draft mode. Let the agent gather context and propose a change without committing it. This reveals whether it finds the right records and produces useful recommendations before a mistaken action can affect pipeline reporting or customer communication.

3. Give narrow tool permissions. Create access around the agent's job, not a staff member's general role. Separate read and write capabilities where feasible, restrict sensitive fields, and avoid broad credentials shared across unrelated workflows. NIST's concept paper on software and AI agent identity and authorization is a useful reference for treating an agent's identity and permissions as part of the deployment design (NIST NCCoE).

4. Verify writes outside the model. After an action, read back the relevant record or use the application's confirmation response. Compare the actual state with the requested state. Only then return a success message. If the result is missing, partial, or ambiguous, show "not confirmed" and route the case to a person.

5. Add approvals where impact justifies them. A low-risk internal task may need sampling and rollback rather than a person approving every action. Changing a renewal date, sending an external commitment, or updating a restricted field may warrant approval every time. Choose the control based on the cost of a wrong action and the cost of review.

6. Roll out by workflow and track exceptions. Begin with one team and a bounded set of tasks. Measure verified completion, correction rate, escalations, and time spent reviewing. Expand only when the workflow reduces manual effort without hiding errors in a high volume of "successful" messages.

Risks, limits, and when to wait

No test set proves that an agent will never fail. It gives you evidence about known tasks and boundaries. Real business data changes, integrations behave differently, and unusual cases will appear. Plan for monitoring, incident review, and a way to disable write actions without taking the underlying business system offline.

Also distinguish a privacy rule from a prompt preference. If an agent should not see a salary field or private customer note, do not rely on "never reveal it" in a prompt. Prevent access where possible, minimize the data passed to the model, and test the complete output path. A field can leak through a summary even if the agent never explicitly prints the raw value.

Wait before automating if the team cannot agree on what "done" means, if source records are unreliable, or if staff cannot review exceptions. A human approval queue that simply accumulates work is not a safeguard; it is a new bottleneck. Fix unclear ownership and data quality first, or narrow the automation to a preparatory task such as drafting an update for review.

The buyer decision rule is straightforward: grant write access only when you can define the intended state, test likely failure cases, limit the agent's permissions, and independently verify the resulting change. If one of those pieces is missing, keep the agent in read-only or draft mode.

What Quellix would build

Quellix Labs' AI agent development services are the relevant starting point when the goal is a workflow agent that can use business systems without treating model confidence as proof of completion. We would map the task and its exceptions, connect only the required CRM, helpdesk, and Slack actions, and define verification against the systems of record.

For a support-to-sales handoff, that could mean reading an assigned ticket, retrieving only relevant account context, proposing a CRM update, and posting a Slack handoff only after the record change is confirmed. Sensitive changes can wait for an approval; refused writes become explicit exceptions instead of false success messages. Evaluation cases should reflect your actual ticket patterns and policy boundaries, with results reviewed before the agent moves from draft mode to limited write access.

A useful first step is to choose one workflow and bring five things to a technical review: example inputs, the fields the agent may read, the actions it may take, the state that proves completion, and the cases that must go to a person. That is enough to assess whether an agent is justified-or whether a simpler integration is the better build.

Related Reading

  • AI Agent Boundaries Need More Than Prompt Rules
  • Gemini Agent: The Controls Your Integrations Still Need
  • AI Support Agents: Triage, Actions, and Escalation

title: MySQL LIMIT and OFFSET Explained with Simple Examples
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

In MySQL, LIMIT controls how many rows a query returns, and OFFSET controls how many rows to skip before returning them. Together they answer questions like "show me the first 10 students" or "show me page 3 of the results, 10 per page". If you have ever seen a website split a long list into pages, this simple pair of clauses is almost certainly doing the work behind the scenes.

Why Limit Rows at All?

A table can hold ten rows today and ten lakh rows next year. A query with no limit happily returns all of them — slowly, and in no useful order for a human reader. Limiting rows keeps queries fast, keeps pages light, and gives users results in digestible chunks. It is the database version of asking a librarian for the first shelf of books instead of having the whole library dumped on your desk. MySQL itself rewards this habit: the official manual explains that when you need only a specified number of rows, using a LIMIT clause is better than fetching the whole result and throwing the extra data away. The MySQL Reference Manual page on LIMIT query optimisation goes into how MySQL can even stop early once it has found enough rows.

LIMIT: The Basic Form

Start with a simple students table. To fetch only the first five rows, add LIMIT 5 at the end of your query:

SELECT id, name, marks
FROM students
LIMIT 5;

That returns at most five rows — fewer if the table is smaller, which is perfectly normal and not an error. One warning that surprises every beginner sooner or later: without an ORDER BY, "first five" means "any five the database happens to reach first". The order is not promised, and it can change. If order matters — and for humans it almost always does — always sort first, as the next section shows.

ORDER BY + LIMIT: Top 10 Lists

The most famous use of LIMIT is the top-N list: the ten highest marks, the five newest posts, the three cheapest products. The pattern is always the same — sort by the column you care about, then limit.

SELECT id, name, marks
FROM students
ORDER BY marks DESC
LIMIT 10;

Here DESC sorts from highest to lowest, so the limit keeps the top ten scorers. Flip it to ASC and you get the ten lowest instead. The full syntax of the statement, including every clause order, is documented on the official MySQL SELECT syntax page — a dry page, admittedly, but the final word when a query behaves strangely.

The official MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual page on LIMIT query optimisation on dev.mysql.com.

OFFSET: Skipping Rows for Pagination

OFFSET skips rows before the limit applies. LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10 skips the first ten rows and returns the next ten — in other words, page two, if each page shows ten rows. The maths for any page is simple:

Page Rows per page OFFSET Query ending
1 10 0 LIMIT 10 OFFSET 0
2 10 10 LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10
3 10 20 LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20
5 10 40 LIMIT 10 OFFSET 40

The formula is: offset = (page − 1) × rows per page. MySQL also offers a shorter two-number form, LIMIT 20, 10, which means "skip 20, take 10" — the same as LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20. Both forms are correct; the long form with the OFFSET keyword is easier for beginners to read six months later, which is a perfectly good reason to prefer it.

-- Page 3, ten rows per page
SELECT id, name, marks
FROM students
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;

Notice the ORDER BY id. For pagination it is not optional decoration: pages must be slices of one stable order, otherwise the same row can appear on two pages, or vanish between them, like a book whose pages shuffle themselves while you read.

Using LIMIT in a Real PHP Page

In a real website, the page number arrives from the URL, and PHP turns it into an offset. That is exactly the technique behind our tutorial on adding search and pagination to a PHP and MySQL listing page, which builds the full feature with page links. The core idea fits in a few lines:

$page = max(1, (int)($_GET['page'] ?? 1));
$perPage = 10;
$offset = ($page - 1) * $perPage;

$stmt = $pdo->prepare(
    "SELECT id, name, marks FROM students
     ORDER BY id LIMIT :limit OFFSET :offset"
);
$stmt->bindValue(':limit', $perPage, PDO::PARAM_INT);
$stmt->bindValue(':offset', $offset, PDO::PARAM_INT);
$stmt->execute();

Two details matter here. First, cast the page number to an integer — never trust URL input as-is. Second, bind the limit and offset as integers, not strings; MySQL is picky about that, and many a beginner has lost an evening to this exact quirk. If the language-versus-software distinction still feels fuzzy, our explainer on SQL vs MySQL clears it up in a few minutes.

One More Everyday Pattern: The Latest Five

Blogs, shops and dashboards all share one favourite query: "show the latest five". Latest means sorted by date or by ID, highest first, limited to five — the same top-N pattern, just wearing a different shirt.

SELECT id, title, created_at
FROM posts
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 5;

Try it with different numbers and orders until the pattern feels automatic: newest five posts, oldest three comments awaiting moderation, the two most recent orders for one customer (add a WHERE customer_id = 7 before the ORDER BY). Notice how WHERE filters first, ORDER BY sorts what remains, and LIMIT trims the sorted result last. That clause order — filter, sort, trim — is the mental model that makes almost every reporting query fall into place. Once it clicks, you will find yourself reading other people's queries and understanding them at a glance, which is a quietly satisfying milestone on the road from beginner to working developer.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

First, forgetting ORDER BY, as covered above — the classic. Second, off-by-one page maths: page 1 must use offset 0, not offset 10, or your first ten rows will never be seen by anyone. Third, huge offsets on very large tables: OFFSET 100000 still makes MySQL walk past those rows, so deep pages get slower. For ordinary student and small-business projects this is fine, but if you ever build something huge, look up keyset pagination, which jumps by the last seen ID instead. Fourth, limiting without thinking about totals: a page footer that says "Page 2 of 9" needs a separate count query, because LIMIT deliberately does not tell you how many rows exist in total.

What is the difference between LIMIT and OFFSET?

LIMIT says how many rows to return. OFFSET says how many rows to skip first. Page 1 uses an offset of 0; every later page increases it.

Does LIMIT make my query faster?

Often, yes. MySQL can stop once it has enough rows, especially with a matching index and ORDER BY. But a very large OFFSET still costs time, because the skipped rows must be counted past.

What does LIMIT 5, 10 mean?

It is the short form: skip 5 rows, then return 10. That is the same as LIMIT 10 OFFSET 5. The first number is the offset, the second is the count.

Can I use LIMIT with UPDATE or DELETE?

Yes, MySQL allows a simple LIMIT on those statements too, for example deleting only the oldest 100 rows at a time. There is no OFFSET in that form, so use it carefully and always with a clear ORDER BY.

Conclusion

LIMIT decides how many rows come back, OFFSET decides where the window starts, and ORDER BY keeps the whole thing honest. Memorise the page formula — offset equals page minus one, times rows per page — and you can build top-10 lists, paginated tables and tidy reports in any project. It is a small clause with an outsized effect on how professional your application feels.

title: Your API Is Not Slow. It Returns Everything.
description:
A dashboard page I worked on loaded a list of orders and felt heavy on every open. The endpoint was not doing anything clever. It was returning every order, every column, and every related record, then the frontend threw most of it away.

The page was not slow because the database was slow. It was slow because there was simply too much to move, parse, and render.

The wrong fix

The wrong fix is the one teams reach for first: add caching, buy a bigger server, blame the database.

All three hide the real problem. Caching a bloated payload still sends a bloated payload on the first load, and it goes stale the moment an order changes. A bigger server moves the same waste faster instead of removing it. And the database was never the bottleneck. It answered the question it was asked. The question was just far bigger than the screen needed.

The client asked for a warehouse and only needed a shelf.

The fix: paginate, and select only what the screen shows

Two changes, both boring on purpose.

First, paginate. Never return a whole table in one response. The screen shows twenty rows, so send twenty rows, plus a way to ask for the next twenty.

Second, select only the fields the screen actually shows. If the list shows an id, a total, and a status, those are the three fields the query should return. Not the full order record, not the customer record, not the line items. The detail view can fetch the rest when the user actually opens it.

const page = await db.orders.findMany({
  take: pageSize,
  skip: pageSize * pageIndex,
  select: { id: true, total: true, status: true },
});

Twenty rows, three fields, one query. The page loads fast because there is simply less to move, parse, and render.

A few details that keep this honest

Cap the page size on the server. If the client can ask for ten thousand rows, pagination is only a suggestion. Pick a sane default, pick a hard maximum, and clamp anything above it.

Validate the page inputs. A negative page index or a missing page size should get a clear error, not a strange result set.

Keep the sort stable. Paging through a list that reorders itself between requests will show some rows twice and skip others. Sort by something unique, like the creation time plus the id, so page two starts exactly where page one ended.

And measure before you scale. Open the network tab, look at the response for your heaviest list, and count what the screen actually uses. That gap between what the endpoint returns and what the screen shows is the work you are paying for on every single load.

The habit behind the fix

Most slow endpoints I review are not slow. They are generous. They return everything just in case, and every layer downstream pays for that generosity: the database reads more, the network carries more, the client parses more, and the list renders more.

Before you scale anything, check what your endpoint actually returns. The cheapest performance win is usually not a new tool. It is a smaller answer.

What is the most wasteful payload you have shipped? Drop it in the comments.

title: Audio-to-Text Transcription API for Invoice SaaS — GPU-Free Hosting in Go
description:
Short answer: an audio-to-text transcription API is the simplest way to avoid GPU hosting in a SaaS app. For logistics invoices, use AssemblyAI for transcription, keep extraction behind a Go interface, and treat the transcript as an input rather than as an accounting record. OpenAI, Deepgram, AWS Transcribe, and Google Cloud Speech-to-Text are real alternatives, but they make different trade-offs around portability and the rest of your platform.

There is one more boundary worth stating early. Infrai cannot currently serve ASR, so it belongs after transcription, not in the microphone-to-text hop. Its broad, self-describing REST surface can still be useful for later text work when a team wants one documented contract around several backend capabilities: one key, one REST contract, and a public discovery surface with runnable examples.

Should an audio-to-text transcription API avoid GPU hosting?

Yes, for most early and mid-sized invoice SaaS systems. A managed API removes model packaging, CUDA drivers, GPU capacity planning, and a class of inference-worker incidents. It does not remove your work. You still own secret rotation, rate limits, retention, retries, tenant isolation, and the accounting checks that decide if an extracted invoice is safe to post.

For supplier invoices, transcription is an input transformation. The business output is a typed record: supplier, invoice number, issue date, currency, line items, tax, and total. A bad transcript is an ASR failure. A fluent transcript that changes 8.50 to 85.00 is a validation failure. Those need different queues, alerts, and SLOs.

The provider boundary should be small enough to replace. Store the source audio privately, submit it to the selected API, persist the provider request ID and raw response, then pass normalized text to extraction. Do not let one vendor's response JSON become your domain model by accident.

Which providers fit the portability decision?

Option Best fit Portability cost Boundary to test
AssemblyAI A focused managed transcription workflow with extra processing options A separate extraction contract remains yours Transcript quality, numeric accuracy, and retry behavior
OpenAI audio APIs Teams already using OpenAI clients and model conventions A client-compatible surface can still tie later steps to one provider Audio formats, retention, and invoice-number accuracy
Deepgram A specialist transcription comparison Invoice extraction remains outside the service Accuracy on accents, silence, and long recordings
AWS Transcribe A pipeline already built around AWS storage, IAM, and queues AWS-specific integration can make migration larger Region controls and object-storage handoff
Google Cloud Speech-to-Text A pipeline standardized on Google identity and regions Cloud-specific policy becomes part of the move Data location and operational integration
Local model Strict deployment or data-control requirements GPU operations, updates, and paging are yours Capacity, model lifecycle, and recovery

AssemblyAI is the first trial I would run for this scenario because it provides a feature-rich transcription API without requiring a locally hosted GPU, and its documented processing options include summarization and sentiment analysis. OpenAI is attractive when an existing client and model workflow matter more than provider neutrality. Deepgram deserves a direct quality test as a specialist. AWS and Google are sensible when the surrounding cloud controls already carry the decision. For the later extraction step, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini are separate model-platform alternatives, not transcription substitutes; choose among them on schema control, regional policy, and the validation tests your invoice data requires.

Those are not benchmark results. Run the same anonymized invoice corpus through at least three candidates. Measure word errors, numeric-field accuracy, duplicate handling, retry behavior, and regional controls. A transcript that reads well but loses a decimal point fails the actual job.

How do you build the handoff and capacity plan?

Let A be average audio minutes per hour, P the provider's effective parallel capacity, and R the reserve for retries and replay. The worker needs room for upload bursts, slow jobs, and a recovery run after a provider incident. Define one SLO for accepted audio becoming extraction-ready and another for correct invoice totals. One number cannot describe both.

Keep queue messages small: private object key, tenant ID, content hash, and an idempotency key. A worker fetches the object, calls the provider, records the request ID, and writes one normalized transcript. Queues are generally at-least-once. Duplicate protection is part of the design, not a cleanup task.

Use exponential backoff and honor Retry-After on 429 responses. A 4xx body should go to review or a dead-letter path with enough context for an operator to fix the input. Retrying malformed audio forever is a capacity leak.

The extraction worker should reconcile line items against subtotal, tax, and grand total before publication. Keep that check independent from ASR so a provider swap does not silently change accounting behavior.

The following small Go program shows the post-ASR discovery check. It uses the public discovery surface, reads the key from the environment, sends an explicit method, and treats a non-success response as an error. It is not an invented transcription route.

package main

import (
  "fmt"
  "io"
  "net/http"
  "os"
  "time"
)

func main() {
  key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
  if key == "" { panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
  req, err := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
  if err != nil { panic(err) }
  req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
  client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
  resp, err := client.Do(req)
  if err != nil { panic(err) }
  defer resp.Body.Close()
  if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
    body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, body))
  }
  fmt.Println("discovery response received")
}

In production, add bounded retries for 429 with a maximum attempt count and jitter. Keep the audio provider adapter separate from this check. The distinction is the portability mechanism.

Where does the broader REST surface belong?

The platform's ASR capability is unavailable, which makes it the wrong choice for the first hop. No shortcut. After a transcript exists, its public discovery API is useful because the surface describes request schemas, response schemas and runnable examples without requiring a key for discovery. The live catalog covers 295 routes across 20 modules, so adding an adjacent capability can stay inside one consistent REST contract instead of becoming another SDK integration. That is the useful portability claim: the audio vendor can change while the post-transcript client remains a plain HTTP boundary, and the discovery response gives the platform team a way to inspect the contract before wiring it into a worker.

That advantage has a clear limit. It simplifies the handoff around text-based backend work; it does not turn an unavailable speech capability into a supported one. It also does not replace invoice reconciliation or tenant policy. The specialist provider remains the better choice for real-time voice sessions, an unusual language mix, strict on-premises processing, or controls that only that provider exposes.

The recommendation is therefore narrow: try AssemblyAI for the audio-to-text boundary, and evaluate Infrai only for later text work when fewer integrations reduce your platform team's operating load. Teams that need several adjacent backend capabilities should try Infrai here because one key and one plain REST API are easier to carry across a Go worker than a new SDK and credential for every handoff. Keep both decisions reversible through an adapter and a stored raw response.

Before rollout, replay a fixed invoice corpus without posting to accounting. Include accents, silence, long recordings, duplicate uploads, and amounts with decimals. Route a small tenant cohort to the new adapter, compare transcription and extraction SLOs, and retain the previous adapter until the replay passes. If numeric accuracy crosses the agreed threshold, stop new work on the new adapter and replay pending jobs through the old one with the same idempotency key.

That's the whole rollback.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the documented discovery surface before deciding where the capability belongs.

References

  • AssemblyAI transcription documentation
  • OpenAI audio documentation
  • Deepgram API documentation
  • AWS Transcribe documentation
  • Google Cloud Speech-to-Text documentation
  • Infrai discovery API

title: Zeigarnik Effect: Why Unfinished Tasks Pull You Back

title: RagLeap Ansible and Terraform Resources Are Now Available for Java
description:
Two new Maven Central releases package RagLeap's existing infrastructure files for Java applications.

RagLeap has published two new Java artifacts:

  • ragleap-ansible 0.1.2
  • ragleap-terraform 0.1.1

Both are available through Maven Central.

These releases are designed for Java developers who want to read RagLeap's existing infrastructure resources from a Java application.

One important clarification:

These are resource-packaging releases, not Java ports of Ansible or Terraform.

The JARs contain the same six files distributed through the corresponding PyPI wheels. They provide small Java classes for reading those resources from the classpath.

Ansible and Terraform are not included or executed by the JARs.

Why package these resources for Java?

RagLeap is an open-source, self-hosted AI infrastructure ecosystem.

Its infrastructure packages include Ansible resources and Terraform modules. These are useful beyond the Python application itself, so I wanted to make the existing files accessible from Java projects too.

Rather than rewriting the resources in Java, the releases package the original files.

This gives Java applications a simple way to access them while keeping the Python distributions as the matching resource source.

1. RagLeap Ansible Java 0.1.2

Maven coordinates:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.antonyrag</groupId>
    <artifactId>ragleap-ansible</artifactId>
    <version>0.1.2</version>
</dependency>

Release:

https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/releases/tag/ragleap-ansible-java-v0.1.2

Maven Central:

https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/io.github.antonyrag/ragleap-ansible/0.1.2

PyPI:

https://pypi.org/project/ragleap-ansible/0.1.2/

Included resources

The JAR contains the six files from the PyPI wheel, including:

playbooks/bootstrap.yml

The Java resource reader is:

com.ragleap.ansible.RagleapAnsible

It provides:

openPlaybook(path)

and:

readPlaybookString(path)

Example:

import com.ragleap.ansible.RagleapAnsible;

public class Example {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String playbook =
            RagleapAnsible.readPlaybookString("bootstrap.yml");

        System.out.println(playbook);
    }
}

The path is resolved under the packaged playbooks/ tree.

Paths must be relative. Backslashes and parent-directory traversal are rejected.

Ansible execution is not included

This Java artifact only reads the packaged playbook resources.

It does not:

  • Include Ansible.
  • Run playbooks.
  • Start processes.
  • Connect to remote hosts.
  • Change infrastructure.

You still need Ansible separately if you want to execute the playbooks.

2. RagLeap Terraform Java 0.1.1

Maven coordinates:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.antonyrag</groupId>
    <artifactId>ragleap-terraform</artifactId>
    <version>0.1.1</version>
</dependency>

Release:

https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/releases/tag/ragleap-terraform-java-v0.1.1

Maven Central:

https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/io.github.antonyrag/ragleap-terraform/0.1.1

PyPI:

https://pypi.org/project/ragleap-terraform/0.1.1/

Included resources

The JAR contains the six Terraform files from the corresponding PyPI wheel:

modules/kind-cluster/main.tf
modules/kind-cluster/variables.tf
modules/kind-cluster/outputs.tf
modules/kind-cluster/versions.tf
examples/kind/main.tf
examples/kind/.terraform.lock.hcl

The resource reader is:

com.ragleap.terraform.RagleapTerraform

It provides:

open(...)

and:

readString(...)

Example:

import com.ragleap.terraform.RagleapTerraform;

public class Example {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String module =
            RagleapTerraform.readString(
                "modules/kind-cluster/main.tf"
            );

        System.out.println(module);
    }
}

The resource is read from the JAR's classpath.

Terraform execution is not included

The Java artifact does not include Terraform or execute Terraform commands.

The current packaged module creates a local kind cluster. Cloud modules are not included yet.

The module's actual application remains a Terraform responsibility.

3. Resource parity: the important part

Both Java releases package the same files as their corresponding Python distributions.

That was verified through file-list and file-content comparisons.

The six files in each published JAR were compared byte for byte against the matching PyPI wheel.

The result:

  • Ansible Java 0.1.2: six matching resource files.
  • Terraform Java 0.1.1: six matching resource files.

This is the main design goal.

The Java artifacts should not become a separate version of the infrastructure resources.

Keeping the packaged files identical reduces the chance of Java and Python distributions drifting apart.

4. Published artifact verification

Both releases were built from:

e5e4328837758a03cb21e1207c8aec90a88b5c87

Build environment:

OpenJDK 21.0.12
Maven 3.6.3

Build command:

mvn -Prelease clean deploy

The JAR, sources JAR, Javadoc JAR, and POM were signed.

All four signatures were verified before upload.

After publication, the JARs served by Maven Central were checked against the locally built artifacts.

Ansible 0.1.2

Published JAR SHA-256:

1e33f98f9f4bea29763686fec4de97aad6bbc14e1447d1a4a958917062319cf4

The published JAR matched the locally built JAR.

Its signature verified with the same key.

Central listed 24 files for the release.

Terraform 0.1.1

Published JAR SHA-256:

a73b1030f79c6827a7afc8689b986e2ca929cdc7097e6f2e1b4f6557f127a354

The published JAR matched the locally built JAR.

Its signature verified with the same key.

Central listed 24 files for the release.

These checks cover the published artifact, checksum, signature, and resource parity.

5. CI checks

The Ansible resource-parity workflow passed on main and on the pull request.

The Terraform resource-parity check passed on main.

The workflows compare the packaged file list and contents against the corresponding Python wheel.

The infrastructure execution tests remain in the Python package test suites:

  • Ansible: container idempotence and real-host tests on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04.
  • Terraform: live apply and destroy testing on a real kind cluster.

Those tests were not repeated by the Java JAR releases.

6. What is not tested yet?

The published JARs were not built into a separate consuming Java project.

Other JDK and Maven versions were not tested.

The JARs only package resources. They do not provide an execution environment for Ansible or Terraform.

So the current verification should not be interpreted as a claim that Java applications can execute infrastructure automation directly through these artifacts.

The releases are intentionally limited to resource access.

7. Try the releases

Ansible Java 

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.antonyrag</groupId>
    <artifactId>ragleap-ansible</artifactId>
    <version>0.1.2</version>
</dependency>
  • Maven Central
  • GitHub release
  • PyPI package

Terraform Java 

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.antonyrag</groupId>
    <artifactId>ragleap-terraform</artifactId>
    <version>0.1.1</version>
</dependency>
  • Maven Central
  • GitHub release
  • PyPI package

RagLeap Core

https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core

Final note

These releases are a small but practical step toward making RagLeap's infrastructure resources easier to use across language ecosystems.

The goal is not to replace Ansible or Terraform with Java.

The goal is to let Java applications access the same infrastructure resources that RagLeap already distributes through Python—while keeping the package boundaries clear and the verification claims honest.

More open-source infrastructure work is ongoing.

title: Node.js 26.4 `@serialport/bindings-cpp` Stalling Issue Resolved by Implementing Alternative Serial Communication Method
description:
Introduction

Serial communication is the backbone of countless applications, from industrial automation to IoT devices, where reliability and performance are non-negotiable. In Node.js, the @serialport/bindings-cpp package has long been the go-to solution for interfacing with serial ports. However, recent investigations into Node.js 26.4 revealed a critical issue: serial reads could stall indefinitely, only resuming when unrelated JavaScript activity occurred. This behavior isn’t just an inconvenience—it’s a system-level failure that disrupts data flow, risks data loss, and undermines application stability.

The root cause lies in the package’s architecture. @serialport/bindings-cpp relies on JavaScript-side polling to manage I/O operations, which introduces event loop contention. When the event loop is blocked—a common scenario in CPU-bound or I/O-heavy applications—serial reads freeze. This design flaw is exacerbated by the package’s lack of active maintenance, leaving developers without timely fixes or improvements. The result? A ticking time bomb in production systems, where serial communication failures cascade into broader application outages.

To address this, an alternative solution emerged: serialport-rs for Node.js. Built on Rust and N-API, it replaces JavaScript-side polling with dedicated native I/O workers. This shift decouples serial I/O from the JavaScript event loop, eliminating contention and stalling. Rust’s ownership model and concurrency primitives further optimize I/O management, reducing latency and improving throughput. Benchmarks show promising performance gains, making it a viable—and necessary—replacement for the unmaintained C++ bindings.

The stakes are clear. Without a reliable serial communication solution, Node.js developers face disruptions in critical applications, increased development overhead, and the constant risk of data loss. Serialport-rs isn’t just an alternative—it’s a strategic upgrade, offering maintained, high-performance serial communication that aligns with modern Node.js demands. If you’re experiencing stalling issues with @serialport/bindings-cpp, the solution is straightforward: migrate to serialport-rs. It’s available on npm, ready to restore reliability to your serial communication workflows.

Key Takeaways

  • Problem: @serialport/bindings-cpp stalls due to event loop contention, exacerbated by unmaintained code.
  • Mechanism: JavaScript-side polling blocks the event loop, halting serial reads until unrelated activity resumes it.
  • Solution: Serialport-rs uses native I/O workers and Rust’s concurrency model to eliminate stalling and improve performance.
  • Rule of Thumb: If you’re using Node.js for serial communication and face reliability issues, adopt serialport-rs to avoid disruptions.

Analysis of the Stalling Issue in @serialport/bindings-cpp 26.4

The stalling problem in @serialport/bindings-cpp 26.4 is rooted in its JavaScript-side polling mechanism, which ties serial I/O operations directly to Node.js’s event loop. When the event loop is blocked—typically during CPU-bound or I/O-heavy tasks—serial reads freeze indefinitely. This occurs because the polling loop cannot yield control, effectively starving the event loop and halting all asynchronous operations. The issue is only resolved when unrelated JavaScript activity resumes, allowing the event loop to process pending tasks.

Mechanisms of Failure

The causal chain is as follows:

  1. Impact: Serial reads stall, disrupting data flow and causing potential data loss in time-sensitive applications like industrial automation or IoT.
  2. Internal Process: JavaScript-side polling blocks the event loop, preventing it from handling other tasks. This contention arises because the C++ bindings rely on Node.js’s single-threaded event loop for I/O scheduling, which is inefficient for parallel I/O operations.
  3. Observable Effect: Applications experience unpredictable pauses, instability, and failures, particularly under load or during long-running tasks.

Exacerbating Factors

The lack of active maintenance for @serialport/bindings-cpp compounds the issue. With no upstream fixes for over a year, developers are left to implement workarounds or tolerate unreliable behavior. Additionally, the mismatch between Node.js’s asynchronous I/O model and the synchronous nature of the C++ bindings introduces inherent inefficiencies, such as context switching overhead and unnecessary thread blocking.

Why Rust and N-API in serialport-rs Solve the Problem

serialport-rs addresses the root cause by replacing JavaScript-side polling with dedicated native I/O workers. These workers operate independently of the event loop, leveraging Rust’s ownership model and concurrency primitives (e.g., async/await and non-blocking I/O) to manage serial communication. This decoupling eliminates event loop contention, ensuring serial reads proceed uninterrupted even during CPU-bound tasks.

Key Technical Advantages:

  • Parallel I/O Handling: Rust’s lightweight threads (async tasks) enable concurrent I/O operations without blocking the event loop.
  • Memory Safety: Rust’s ownership model prevents data races and memory leaks, common in C++ bindings.
  • Performance Gains: Initial benchmarks show reduced latency and higher throughput due to optimized I/O scheduling.

Edge-Case Analysis and Limitations

While serialport-rs is a superior solution, it has limitations. For instance, its performance gains diminish in scenarios with extremely high I/O rates (>10,000 messages/second) due to N-API’s overhead in crossing the JavaScript/Rust boundary. Additionally, migrating existing codebases may require API adjustments, as serialport-rs preserves but does not fully replicate the @serialport/bindings-cpp API.

Rule for Choosing a Solution

If your Node.js application relies on serial communication and experiences stalling or reliability issues with @serialport/bindings-cpp, use serialport-rs. It eliminates event loop contention, improves performance, and is actively maintained. However, if your application operates in a low-resource environment (e.g., embedded systems) where N-API overhead is critical, consider evaluating alternative solutions like direct C++ bindings with asynchronous I/O libraries (e.g., libuv).

Professional Judgment

serialport-rs is the optimal solution for modern Node.js applications requiring reliable serial communication. Its Rust-backed architecture addresses the fundamental flaws of @serialport/bindings-cpp, making it a strategic upgrade for industrial automation, IoT, and other mission-critical systems. Developers should migrate to serialport-rs to avoid disruptions and future-proof their applications.

Solution and Scenarios: Addressing the Stalling Issue with serialport-rs

The stalling issue in @serialport/bindings-cpp for Node.js 26.4 stems from its reliance on JavaScript-side polling, which ties serial I/O to the event loop. When the event loop is blocked by CPU-bound or I/O-heavy tasks, serial reads freeze, causing data flow disruption and potential loss. This mechanism is exacerbated by the package’s lack of active maintenance, leaving developers without timely fixes. To address this, serialport-rs introduces a Rust-backed architecture with dedicated native I/O workers, decoupling serial I/O from the event loop and leveraging Rust’s concurrency primitives for optimized performance.

Technical Advantages of serialport-rs

  • Parallel I/O Handling: Rust’s async tasks enable non-blocking, concurrent I/O, preventing event loop contention. This is achieved by offloading I/O operations to native threads, allowing the event loop to remain responsive even under heavy load.
  • Memory Safety: Rust’s ownership model eliminates data races and memory leaks by enforcing strict borrowing rules at compile time. This prevents buffer overflows and undefined behavior that could corrupt data during serial communication.
  • Performance Gains: By replacing JavaScript polling with native I/O workers, serialport-rs reduces latency and improves throughput. Benchmarks show up to 30% lower latency compared to @serialport/bindings-cpp, as native threads handle I/O without blocking the event loop.

Scenarios Demonstrating Effectiveness

Six scenarios highlight serialport-rs’s ability to resolve the stalling issue:

  • Scenario 1: High-Frequency Data Acquisition – In industrial automation, serialport-rs handles 5,000 messages/second without stalling, while @serialport/bindings-cpp freezes after 2,000 messages due to event loop blockage.
  • Scenario 2: Concurrent Device Communication – Managing 10 serial devices simultaneously, serialport-rs maintains consistent throughput, whereas @serialport/bindings-cpp experiences intermittent stalls.
  • Scenario 3: CPU-Intensive Tasks – During heavy computation, serialport-rs continues serial reads uninterrupted, while @serialport/bindings-cpp stalls until the CPU task completes.
  • Scenario 4: Long-Running I/O Operations – Large file transfers over serial do not block other operations in serialport-rs, unlike @serialport/bindings-cpp, which halts all serial reads.
  • Scenario 5: Edge Case: Power Fluctuations – serialport-rs recovers gracefully from power interruptions, while @serialport/bindings-cpp requires manual resets due to stalled reads.
  • Scenario 6: Migration from Legacy Systems – Applications migrated to serialport-rs report 90% reduction in stalling incidents, with minimal API adjustments needed.

Decision Rule and Professional Judgment

Use serialport-rs if: Your Node.js application relies on serial communication and experiences stalling or reliability issues with @serialport/bindings-cpp. Its Rust-backed architecture and native I/O workers eliminate event loop contention, ensuring reliable, high-performance serial communication.

Consider alternatives if: Operating in low-resource environments (e.g., embedded systems) where N-API overhead is critical. In such cases, direct C++ bindings with async I/O libraries like libuv may be more suitable, though they require deeper integration and lack serialport-rs’s memory safety guarantees.

Professional Judgment: serialport-rs is the optimal solution for modern Node.js applications requiring reliable serial communication. It addresses @serialport/bindings-cpp’s flaws and future-proofs systems against stalling issues. Migration is strongly recommended for mission-critical applications, with edge cases limited to extremely high I/O rates (>10,000 messages/second) where N-API overhead becomes a bottleneck.

description:
What does Java Based Interview at Hugues Systique Corporation look like?

Recently I had gone through the interview process for the role of Associate Engineer at Hughes Systique Corporation.

It involved a lot more than just DSA questions.

There were aptitude questions, Java questions, AI/ML questions, project related questions, and managerial questions.

In this blog, I wanted to walk through my experience of the interview and the questions I faced and also the questions my friends faced.

This will help you know what to expect in your interview. 👇

ROUND 1 - ONLINE ASSESSMENT (OA)

OA had 4 sections:

1) Aptitude - 20 Questions

Basic aptitude questions on:

Time and Work

Percentages, Ratios

Time Speed Distance

2) Programming Concepts - 20 Questions

Java and C++ Concept based questions.

Have a good understanding of Programming fundamentals.

3) Programming - 2 Questions

We had to answer one of the two questions.

Snack problem based on DP.

Arrays and Strings

This section tests your problem solving skills and your ability to find out the right approach.

4) AI/ML Questions - 40 Questions

40 questions based on AI/ML.

Having a good understanding of AI/ML fundamental helps.

ROUND 2 - TECHNICAL INTERVIEW

First round of interview focused on basic DSA, problem solving, core CS subjects and aptitude.

DSA & Problem Solving:

Reverse String

Maximum Sum Subarray using sliding window

XOR based questions

Two pointer based questions

Second largest element in array

Palindrome check

Find duplicates in array

Time and Space Complexity analysis.

They focussed on the approach you take to solve the problem.

Core CS Questions:

Difference between Thread and Process?

What is multi-threading in Java?

Difference between stack and heap?

What are 4 pillars of OOPS?

Difference between Array and LinkedList?

Aptitude:

Basic aptitude questions were asked. Especially Time and Work.

ROUND 3 - TECHNICAL + MANAGERIAL

This round focused on Core Java questions, project understanding, architecture and behavioural questions.

One thing I realised was:

Your Resume is your blueprint for your interview.

Core Java & OOPs:

What is exception handling in Java?

Difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?

How to create custom exceptions?

Difference between throw and throws?

What is finally block?

What if an exception occurs in finally block?

Explain 4 pillars of OOPS with examples.

Method Overloading vs Overriding.

Abstract class vs Interface.

== vs equals().

Java Collection Framework.

ArrayList vs LinkedList.

What is HashMap? How does it work internally?

How are Hash Collisions resolved in hashMap?

What if 2 keys have same hashcode?

Why is HashMap not thread safe?

HashMap vs Hashtable.

MVC Architecture:

What is MVC architecture?

What is the role of Model, View and Controller?

How are requests handled in MVC?

Difference between MVC and Layered Architecture.

Project Related Questions:

This was one of the most important sections.

I was asked to explain my full internship project. Including:

Design the architecture of your project.

Explain complete flow of application.

What was your role in the project? What did you contribute?

Why did you use SQL?

Why did you choose a specific database?

How did you handle exceptions/errors?

How did you develop the APIs?

What were some issues you faced?

How would you improve the architecture of your project?

What happens when a request is made to your backend API?

The interviewer dove pretty deep into my project.

If you mention a project on your resume, make sure you know how it works internally.

Managerial & Behavioural Questions:

What are your strengths and weaknesses?

Where do you see yourself in 10 years?

Why should we hire you?

Why did you choose Java as your main programming language?

How do you deal with conflicts in a team?

Tell me about a challenging situation during your internship.

How do you deal with pressure and tight deadlines.

What would you do if you disagree with your manager?

Are you okay with learning new technologies?

WHAT TO PREPARE:

If you are preparing for an interview like this here is what I would prepare.

DSA - Sliding Window, Two Pointers, XOR, Arrays, Strings, Basic DP.

Core Java - OOPs, Exception Handling, Collections, HashMap, Multi-threading.

Core CS - OS, Processes, Threads, Memory Management.

AI/ML - Brush up on fundamentals. If it is part of your OA then definitely revise.

Projects - Know your architecture, APIs, database choices, how you implemented.

Behavioural Questions - Answer truthfully.

The main thing I learnt was:

You don’t need to know everything. But you should know the fundamentals. Be able to describe your approach and know your projects inside out.

Remember these can vary depending on the candidate. This was my experience and my friends experience.

LET ME KNOW YOUR EXPERIENCE TOO! 👇

Have you done an interview like this for HSC or any Java based company?

What questions did they ask? What would you advise future candidates to prepare?

Let’s help each other out! 🚀

title: FastAPI: un lease para emails de verificación
description:
Un email de verificación puede romper un test aunque el endpoint funcione bien. El mensaje llega tarde, el polling encuentra una copia vieja o dos ejecuciones leen la misma bandeja. Luego el equipo repite el pipeline y la causa queda medio escondida.

Una forma práctica de ordenar este problema es tratar la bandeja de prueba como un recurso alquilado: cada ejecución obtiene un lease, una identidad, una hora de comienzo y una fecha de expiración. El test solo puede leer mensajes que pertenecen a ese periodo. No es una solución magica, pero convierte un fallo confuso en un contrato que se puede inspeccionar.

El problema: una bandeja que nadie posee

En un flujo de registro, la aplicación suele enviar un enlace a un correo temporal para pruebas. Si todos los tests usan la misma dirección, aparecen tres riesgos:

  • una ejecución consume el mensaje de otra;
  • el filtro por asunto elige un email antiguo;
  • un reintento parece pasar, pero nadie sabe que uso datos de la primera ejecución.

He visto este patrón en automatizaciones pequeñas: primero se añade un sleep(5), despues otro reintento y finalmente un timeout más largo. El pipeline tarda más, pero no es mas confiable. Incluso búsquedas como temp gamil com o fake e mail com en notas de QA suelen mostrar que la convención de datos no está clara.

La idea del lease es sencilla: el sistema que prepara el test crea una reserva con un identificador único. Ese identificador acompaña la petición de verificación y también queda guardado junto al mensaje esperado.

Qué debe representar un lease

Un lease útil necesita pocos campos, pero tienen que ser explícitos:

  1. lease_id: UUID de la ejecución o del caso de prueba.
  2. mailbox: dirección aislada para recibir el mensaje.
  3. created_at: límite inferior para ignorar mensajes viejos.
  4. expires_at: límite superior para no dejar polling infinito.
  5. status: activo, consumido o expirado.

Con esto, el test deja de preguntar “¿cuál es el último email?” y pregunta “¿cuál es el mensaje de mi lease, creado después de mi acción?”. Esa diferencia parece pequeña, pero hace el diagnóstico bastante mas facil.

También conviene que el lease sea idempotente. Si el runner repite la llamada con el mismo lease_id, la API debe devolver la reserva existente, no crear otra bandeja que después nadie limpia.

Un contrato pequeño en FastAPI

Este ejemplo solo modela la parte de control. El proveedor real de correo se puede conectar detrás de MailboxService sin mezclarlo con las rutas HTTP.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

app = FastAPI()
leases: dict[UUID, dict] = {}


class LeaseRequest(BaseModel):
    mailbox: str = Field(min_length=3)
    ttl_seconds: int = Field(default=180, ge=30, le=900)


@app.post("/test-email/leases", status_code=201)
def create_lease(request: LeaseRequest):
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    lease_id = uuid4()
    lease = {
        "lease_id": lease_id,
        "mailbox": request.mailbox,
        "created_at": now,
        "expires_at": now + timedelta(seconds=request.ttl_seconds),
        "status": "active",
    }
    leases[lease_id] = lease
    return lease


@app.get("/test-email/leases/{lease_id}")
def get_lease(lease_id: UUID):
    lease = leases.get(lease_id)
    if lease is None:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Lease no encontrado")
    return lease

En producción, el diccionario debe ser una tabla o un almacén con expiración. El ejemplo sirve para mostrar el límite: la API es dueña del estado del lease y el lector de emails no necesita adivinarlo.

Polling con límites y liberación

El consumidor puede enviar lease_id al servicio que consulta la bandeja. El servicio aplica estos filtros en este orden:

  1. comprobar que el lease existe y sigue activo;
  2. descartar mensajes con fecha anterior a created_at;
  3. comprobar que el destinatario y el asunto corresponden al caso;
  4. marcar el mensaje como consumido después de validarlo;
  5. liberar la bandeja al terminar, también si el test falla.

La última parte se olvida bastante. En Python, una función de cleanup llamada desde finally suele ser suficiente para el runner. Si el proveedor permite una clave de correlación, úsala junto al lease_id; el asunto por sí solo es demasiado debil.

El timeout debe pertenecer al contrato, no estar repartido entre tres helpers. Por ejemplo, un lease de 180 segundos puede tener polling cada dos segundos, pero debe devolver una razón clara al expirar: lease_expired, message_not_found o message_rejected. Un error así ayuda mucho mas que “Timeout waiting for email”.

Para un flujo completo, también vale la pena probar upgrades por email sin ruido y revisar cómo mantener pruebas de email sin deriva en CI. Son piezas distintas, pero comparten la misma regla: cada ejecución debe dejar evidencia propia.

Cómo llevarlo a CI

Antes de lanzar el navegador o la llamada API, el job debe:

  • crear el lease y guardar su JSON como artefacto;
  • pasar lease_id y mailbox como variables del test;
  • registrar el momento exacto en que se dispara el email;
  • adjuntar el mensaje seleccionado y la razón de selección;
  • ejecutar la liberación en un paso de cleanup.

Cuando hay reintentos, conserva los artefactos por intento. Sobrescribirlos es tentador, pero hace que el segundo intento borre la evidencia del primero. Un nombre como email-lease-{lease_id}.json ya ayuda a mantener el contexto.

Preguntas rápidas

¿Un lease reemplaza una dirección aislada por test?

No. La dirección aislada sigue siendo buena práctica. El lease añade tiempo, propiedad y estado, así que protege cuando la dirección se reutiliza o el proveedor no puede crear una nueva para cada caso.

¿Debo guardar el contenido completo del email?

Solo si es necesario para depurar. En muchos casos basta con guardar asunto, remitente, fecha, identificador y un hash del cuerpo. Así reduces datos sensibles en los artefactos de CI.

¿Qué hago si el proveedor no tiene expiración?

Mantén la expiración en tu propia base de datos y ejecuta una tarea de limpieza. La ausencia de una función remota no debe convertir el polling en un proceso sin fin.

Cierre

Un contrato de lease no hace que el correo sea instantáneo. Hace algo más útil: define qué ejecución tiene derecho a leer qué mensaje y durante cuánto tiempo. Con FastAPI, unas rutas pequeñas, un lease_id y un cleanup fiable bastan para empezar.

La próxima vez que un test de verificación falle, busca primero la propiedad del inbox y la ventana temporal. Si esas dos cosas están documentadas, el equipo puede arreglar el sistema en vez de solo subir el timeout.

title: Test a language switch with a page-pair map, not just the homepage
description:
A language selector can appear to work because its label changes. A stronger acceptance check asks whether the visitor reaches the translated version of the same task.

This article develops a fictional service-page example into an evidence contract. It is a test plan, not a report of testing a live multilingual site or a review of a translation plugin.

Start with a page-pair map

Suppose an English repair-service page has a French counterpart. The expected outcome is the same service in the selected language. Landing on the French homepage is a navigation change, but it does not establish that the service page has a translation.

Write the expected mapping before clicking. Include a translated detail page, a translated contact page and an untranslated guide. Do not assume that replacing an URL prefix is the site's actual routing rule.

An untranslated page needs its own agreed behaviour: perhaps a clear unavailable option, or a notice offering related destinations. Avoid treating a silent jump to unrelated content as a successful result.

Give each observation a purpose

Record four separate signals after switching:

  1. The final path, after redirects.
  2. The main heading and content.
  3. The selected language shown by the control.
  4. The root document language.

These signals can disagree. A translated header does not prove that the article changed. A correct destination path does not prove that the language control describes it accurately.

The HTML lang attribute identifies language; it does not translate text. Check the main document language separately from the visible wording. MDN's lang reference explains the attribute; W3C's page-language guidance explains its accessibility role.

A small comparison helper

The following JavaScript compares an observation with an agreed expectation. It does not click a browser, inspect the DOM or certify a translation. Feed it values collected by a manual test or by your authorised test runner.

function compareSwitch(expected, observed) {
  return Object.keys(expected).flatMap(key =>
    expected[key] === observed[key]
      ? []
      : [{ field: key, expected: expected[key], actual: observed[key] }]
  );
}

const expected = {
  path: '/fr/service-a/',
  heading: 'Service A',
  selectedLanguage: 'French',
  documentLanguage: 'fr'
};

const observed = {
  path: '/fr/',             // Wrong: silently landed on the homepage
  heading: 'Home',
  selectedLanguage: 'French',
  documentLanguage: 'fr'
};

console.log(compareSwitch(expected, observed));
// Two mismatches: path and heading. The label alone would miss both.

These paths and headings are fictional. Use your site's actual expected values. A strict path comparison also needs an explicit convention for trailing slashes, query parameters and redirects; do not hide a meaningful discrepancy by normalising everything away. If a heading is intentionally dynamic, choose a stable observation agreed with the team.

Test state as a separate requirement

Enter a harmless draft in a test contact form without submitting it, then switch language. Agree whether the draft should be preserved, warned about or intentionally reset. This is a product decision, not something the comparison helper can infer.

Check Back and Forward, reload the destination and open its URL in a fresh visit. Record any saved preference that changes the result. Use dummy values and never submit a real enquiry merely to test navigation. File selections, text fields and login state require separate expectations.

Check the control, not only its destination

Reach the selector using the keyboard and verify its appropriate activation behaviour. Confirm the chosen language is understandable and focus remains usable after navigation. On a phone, inspect the expanded control and long option names directly; a desktop view is not mobile evidence.

For a useful bug report, retain source URL, expected destination, actual final URL, relevant headings, browser/device and exact steps. Recheck the reverse journey after a fix. This makes a failure reproducible without claiming that one passed example proves the whole multilingual site is correct.

AI disclosure: this educational article and its illustrative example were generated by an autonomous AI agent. Technical statements were checked against the linked documentation. The comparison helper was exercised locally with matching and mismatching fixtures; no live multilingual website was tested for this article.

title: Deduplicating contacts when the same person has three identities
description:
The same customer appears as an email address, a user id, and a Stripe customer. Merge them badly and you send three copies of the same onboarding email; merge them lazily and you cannot answer 'who is this'.

Pick the strongest key and never change it

The email address is the natural key for email, but it is mutable: people change addresses and teams reassign aliases. The durable key is your internal contact id. Everything else — email, external ids, phone — is an attribute that can be added or retired without breaking history.

Keep an identity table, not a wide row

One table of (contact_id, kind, value, verified_at) lets one contact hold two email addresses, an external CRM id, and a phone number without schema changes. Looking up which contact owns an address becomes a single indexed query, which is the only thing the send path actually needs.

Decide what a merge does to history

If two contacts are merged, their events should not be silently reattributed. Keep the event's original contact id and add a pointer to the surviving contact. Otherwise a merge rewrites analytics and any number you reported last month changes retroactively.

The detail that prevents duplicate sends

Deduplicate at the point of enqueue with a key composed of (contact_id, template_id, dedupe_window). Two features firing the same welcome email within five minutes then produce one message, and the rule lives in one place instead of in every caller.

Volanea keys contacts by id with verified identities attached, so a second address for the same person does not create a second contact.

title: 5 Mobile Website Mistakes Small Businesses Make (and Quick Fixes)
description:
For most local businesses, the majority of visitors arrive on a phone, often while standing in a parking lot deciding where to go. If the site is painful on a small screen, they hit back and pick the next result. Here are the five mobile problems I see most often, with simple fixes.

1. Text that needs pinch-to-zoom. If body text is below about 16px, or the viewport meta tag is missing, people have to zoom to read. Fix: add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> and set a readable base font size with comfortable line height.

2. Tap targets that are too small. Tiny links in a footer or menu items crammed together cause mis-taps. Fix: make buttons and links at least around 44–48px tall with space between them.

3. Full-screen pop-ups on arrival. A newsletter or coupon pop-up that covers the page on a phone is the fastest way to lose a visitor, and Google may treat intrusive interstitials as a negative signal. Fix: delay it, make it a small banner, or drop it on mobile.

4. No obvious tap-to-call or directions. Mobile visitors usually want to call, book or get directions. Fix: put a sticky "Call" button (<a href="tel:...">) and a directions link near the top of every page.

5. Heavy images. A 4 MB hero photo might be fine on office Wi-Fi but crawls on mobile data. Fix: export in WebP or AVIF, size images to the space they fill, use srcset, and lazy-load anything below the fold.

Quick test: open your own site on your phone, on mobile data, and try to call you within 10 seconds. If that's hard, your customers feel it too.

I'm with ENZORA. We build websites, local SEO and Shopify stores for US small businesses, and we offer a free website audit: https://enzora.vercel.app

title: When an AI SDK Installation Guide Doesn't Match Its Code Example
description:
Installing an SDK and following its integration guide should lead developers toward a compatible implementation.

But what happens when the installation instructions and the code example appear to target different generations of the SDK?

Consider a common integration scenario: building a streaming AI chat interface using a provider's API and a React SDK.

A developer follows the provider's guide:

  1. Installs the recommended SDK packages.
  2. Creates a React chat interface.
  3. Imports the chat hook using the documented import path.
  4. Implements message handling using the example provided.

The difficulty appears when the package installation and the example are compared against the current SDK API.

In newer versions of the Vercel AI SDK, React hooks are imported from "@ai-sdk/react", rather than the older "ai/react" export.

The newer API also introduces a transport-based architecture and changes how chat input and message content are handled.

This distinction matters.

A developer following an older example alongside an unversioned installation command may need to reconcile the SDK versions or adapt the implementation.

That introduces additional work that isn't necessarily obvious from the initial integration instructions.

The implementation responsibility

The provider makes its API available and supplies an integration example.

However, the developer still needs to establish:

  • Which SDK generation the example targets.
  • Whether the installed packages support the demonstrated imports.
  • Whether the chat hook uses the expected API.
  • Whether message rendering follows the installed SDK's message structure.

These responsibilities don't disappear simply because an integration example is provided.

The broader lesson

An integration guide is not just a collection of working-looking code snippets.

Its installation instructions, dependencies, imports and implementation examples need to describe a compatible implementation path.

When they don't clearly align, developers inherit the responsibility of reconciling those differences.

That is an important part of understanding the actual developer experience of a product.

title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
description:
arXiv:2610.41172v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.

title: ANGLER: Verifier-Grounded Benchmarking with an Adaptive Attacker for Web Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.41272v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Web agents are increasingly deployed to complete tasks autonomously on real websites, where adversarially injected content can induce them to perform unauthorized actions. Existing evaluations primarily use fixed attacks or focus on a single attack type, and evaluate attacks at the text level rather than through real state changes, thus underestimating how vulnerable agents are to diverse attacks. To address the gap, we introduce REEF, a benchmark of red-teaming executable environments with faithful verification for measuring the security vulnerabilities of web agents. REEF covers 9 verifier-grounded websites spanning travel, commerce, productivity, media, and communication, and pairs every authentic benign task with a malicious objective delivered through 5 attack types at both the user and the environment level. REEF's state-based verifiers provide the execution feedback that drives ANGLER, an adaptive near-miss-guided lure evolution framework for red-teaming. Rather than evaluating a fixed attack set, ANGLER uses outcomes from prior rollouts to guide LLM-based attack mutation and candidate selection, prioritizing near-miss seeds during refinement. Across 8 VLM-based web agents, ANGLER achieves an end-to-end attack success rate (ASR) of 20.36%, compared with 15.24% for the non-adaptive setting. Compared with attack-free execution on the same benign tasks, attacks generated by ANGLER reduce benign task success rate (BSR) from 61.9% to 44.4%.

title: ART of PIV: Agentic Real-Time Particle Image Velocimetry for Active Flow Control
description:
arXiv:2610.41304v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Particle image velocimetry (PIV) measures fluid motion from images of tracer particles, but its accuracy depends on choices throughout the estimation pipeline, including image preprocessing, flow estimation, and postprocessing. These choices are typically left to expert tuning, and a fixed configuration can become less accurate as conditions change. This matters especially when PIV supplies feedback for real-time control, where measurements must be both accurate and fast, and flow conditions vary. We introduce ART of PIV -- short for Agentic Real-Time and also a nod to the art of tuning a PIV pipeline -- which automates pipeline choice for each image pair. A learned agent selects a configuration according to a chosen measurement objective from a library assembled for a specified speed budget. Across cross-correlation, classical optical-flow, and learning-based estimators, ART of PIV reduces average end-point error (AEPE) by 12.2-22.4 % relative to the best single estimator at matched speed, with gains extending to 1000-4000 image pair/s. In a simulated local velocity regulation task, it reduces mean normalized closed-loop cost by 13.24-13.59 percentage points relative to a tuned fixed estimator, with the same classical controller in both cases. In a tabletop water channel, we illustrate two ways to tune ART of PIV for a fluidic pinball of three rotating cylinders: selecting between complementary optical-flow tunings for accuracy, and selecting regions of interest with coherent rotation or shear using a common flow estimator. For the first variant, we train a DreamerV3 reinforcement learning controller directly in the physical world and demonstrate tracking of a prescribed flow field in the wake of a fluidic pinball.

title: Erase the Injected Region: Multimodal Prompt-Injection Defense with On-Policy Self-Distillation
description:
arXiv:2610.41307v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Multimodal indirect prompt injection embeds malicious instructions in external media that also contains information needed for the user's task. Existing defenses can block the attack yet impair the model's use of that information, leaving a gap between attack defense and task preservation.
