title: How many fields does an inquiry form need before sales can quote?
description:
A buyer types "please send price for 500 pcs" into a contact form late at night. The next morning a rep replies with a list of questions: which model, which country, when do you need it. The buyer answers two days later, or doesn't, and somewhere in between a competitor sent a number.

Making the form longer does not fix that, and neither does making it shorter. The useful question is narrower: which answers does a price depend on? Everything else can move into the reply.

Write the quote before you design the form

Get the person who actually quotes prices to produce three quotes for three recent inquiries, from scratch, without reopening the original email thread. Note every question they had to answer in order to reach a number. That list is your field list, and it is usually shorter than the form you already have.

It tends to come out as five items: what the item is, how many, where it ships, when it is needed, and an address that reaches a human. Everything else is comfort.

Give each candidate field a job

Question Can the quote be produced without it? First form?
Model or part number No Required
Quantity No Required
Delivery country and city No — freight and tax move with it Required
Rough timing Sometimes Dropdown, with an empty default
Working email address No — there is nowhere to send the quote Required
Company name Only if you sell to companies exclusively Required in B2B, optional otherwise
Contact name No Optional
Phone No Optional, never required
Free-text message No Optional, marked as optional
Budget No — and asking too early costs the inquiry Leave out
How did you hear about us No Leave out, or ask on the thank-you page
Tax or VAT number No, that is an onboarding step Leave out

The test for anything not on this list: if a blank answer would not stop the quote, it belongs in the reply, not on the form. Budget is the one field people insist on and buyers rarely answer honestly at first contact — if the number matters, ask after you have shown you understand the requirement.

Friction is rarely the field count

Six clean fields convert better than four bad ones. What kills inquiries:

A required phone number, on a form used by buyers in another country who do not want a call. A country dropdown with every territory in it, on a phone. A required company name when the buyer is an individual sourcing one sample. A field that only accepts uploads, which fail on mobile data and give no feedback when they do. Validation that clears the form on error. A blank thank-you page that does not say what happens next.

Every one of those is fixable without removing a question sales needs.

The form itself

Plain HTML, labels outside the inputs, input types that bring up the right keyboard on a phone:

<form action="/inquiry" method="post">
  <label for="email">Work email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required>

  <label for="company">Company <span>(optional)</span></label>
  <input id="company" name="company" type="text" autocomplete="organization">

  <label for="item">Model or part number</label>
  <input id="item" name="item" type="text" required>

  <label for="qty">Quantity</label>
  <input id="qty" name="qty" type="text" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="off" required>

  <label for="dest">Delivery country and city</label>
  <input id="dest" name="dest" type="text" autocomplete="address-level2" required>

  <label for="when">When do you need it?</label>
  <select id="when" name="when">
    <option value="">Not sure yet</option>
    <option value="2w">Within two weeks</option>
    <option value="1m">This month</option>
    <option value="1q">This quarter</option>
  </select>

  <label for="notes">Anything else <span>(optional)</span></label>
  <textarea id="notes" name="notes" rows="4"></textarea>

  <p class="hp" aria-hidden="true">
    <label for="website">Website</label>
    <input id="website" name="website" type="text" tabindex="-1" autocomplete="off">
  </p>

  <button type="submit">Get a quote</button>
</form>

<style>
  .hp { position: absolute; left: -9999px; }
</style>

Notes on the choices. Quantity is type="text" with inputmode="numeric" rather than type="number", because number inputs change value on a scroll wheel and reject the way people write quantities. The timing dropdown has an empty first option so nobody is pushed into a false answer. The honeypot replaces a captcha: reject the submission server-side if website is not empty, and skip the whole puzzle that real buyers fail on a train.

If a file matters — a drawing, a bill of materials, a photo of a damaged part — ask for it in the confirmation, not on the form. By then the buyer has committed, and a link is easier than a failing upload widget.

Keep the form to one column on every screen size. Preserve what was typed when a validation error fires, and put the error next to the field that caused it.

Say what happens after submit

The thank-you page is part of the form. Two things belong on it: what you will send and when, and the one or two details that would speed it up if they have them to hand. "We reply within one working day with a price and lead time. If you have a drawing or a target price, send it to this address and we will include it."

That single paragraph removes most of the second round trip without adding a field.

Read the messages for a fortnight

The free-text box is a research tool. Read every message that arrives for two weeks and count how often the same question appears — "do you ship to X", "is this the same as model Y". Anything asked repeatedly is either a missing field, a missing explanation on the product page, or a shipping restriction nobody wrote down. Fix the page before you fix the form.

What to measure afterwards

The share of inquiries where the first reply could be the quote itself, with no clarifying email. And the share that reach your order system without anyone re-keying or chasing a missing detail. If both stay flat after trimming fields, the problem is upstream of the form — usually the product pages do not state what the buyer needs to know to describe their requirement.

Hand this to whoever builds it

  • Required: model or part number, quantity, delivery country and city, email.
  • Optional and visibly marked optional: company, name, free text.
  • No required phone number, no required budget, no captcha, no required upload.
  • Timing as a dropdown with an honest "not sure yet" option.
  • Validation that keeps the typed values, with the error beside the field.
  • A thank-you page that states the reply time and asks for attachments by return.
  • Someone reads the free-text box weekly for the first month.

title: When AI glasses could be a worthy headphones replacement
description:
착용 시간이 전부다 — 웨어러블 논쟁에서 시각 훈련 소프트웨어를 설계한 이유

AI 글래스가 이어폰을 대체할 수 있을까 — 엔가젯의 이 질문은 사실 웨어러블 전체에 던져진 질문입니다. 답은 "무엇에 쓰느냐에 달렸다". 그리고 그 답 뒤에는 더 냉정한 기준이 숨어 있습니다. 기기가 아무리 뛰어나도, 매일 오래 착용하지 않으면 아무 일도 일어나지 않는다는 것.

이 기준은 시각 훈련 영역에서 훨씬 잔인하게 작동합니다. 약시(lazy eye, amblyopia)를 가진 사람에게 훈련을 포기하게 만드는 건 대개 의지 부족이 아닙니다. 접착식 패치의 불편함, 적청 안경의 어지러움, 그리고 무엇보다 지루함입니다. 재미없는 훈련은 3주를 넘기지 못합니다. 개발자 관점에서 보면 이것은 기능 문제가 아니라 리텐션 문제입니다. 아무리 정교한 알고리즘도 사용자가 매일 헤드셋을 쓰지 않으면 실행되지 않습니다.

그래서 Seven Sports는 순서를 바꿔 접근했습니다. 훈련을 위해 콘텐츠를 찾는 대신, 이미 매일 보고 있는 콘텐츠를 훈련의 장으로 만들었습니다. Amblyotube는 Meta Quest(Quest 2, 3, Pro, 3S)에서 YouTube 스타일 영상을 보면서 눈마다 다른 시각 경험을 제공하는 시각 협응·주의력 훈련 소프트웨어입니다.

왜 VR인가 — 두 개의 독립 디스플레이

핵심은 하드웨어 구조에 있습니다. VR 헤드셋은 눈마다 독립된 아이피스(eyepiece)를 가지고 있고, 소프트웨어는 각 눈에 서로 다른 피드를 동시에 보낼 수 있습니다. Amblyotube는 이 구조를 그대로 활용해 양안 훈련(dichoptic vision training)을 구현합니다. 왼쪽 눈과 오른쪽 눈에 완전히 다른 렌더링 결과를 전달할 수 있다는 점이, 기존의 패치나 아나글리프(적청) 안경으로는 불가능했던 설계 공간을 열어 줍니다.

이 지점이 사실 시스템 설계에서 가장 흥미로운 부분입니다. 전통적인 시각 훈련 도구는 '하나의 화면'을 전제로 만들어졌습니다. 패치는 물리적으로 한쪽 눈을 가리고, 적청 안경은 색 필터로 두 눈을 분리합니다. 둘 다 하드웨어에 종속된 트릭입니다. 반면 VR은 렌더 파이프라인 단계에서 좌안과 우안에 서로 다른 프레임을 밀어 넣을 수 있습니다. 훈련 파라미터가 콘텐츠 위에 얹히는 소프트웨어 계층으로 올라오는 순간, 실험실에서나 가능했던 프로토콜이 거실로 내려옵니다.

작동 방식은 계층적으로 단순합니다.

첫째, 우세안 화면에는 조절 가능한 디지털 블러(Dominant Eye Shader)를 겁니다. 블러, 대비, 밝기, 감마, 불투명도(opacity)를 개별적으로 조정할 수 있고, 100% 불투명도에서는 사실상 완전한 디지털 패칭이 됩니다. 하지만 주 목표는 대개 '부분 투명'입니다. 두 눈이 동시에 시각 정보를 처리하도록 만드는 것이기 때문입니다.

둘째, 약시안 화면에는 AI Sharpener(MFBF 모드)가 동작합니다. 이 엔진은 영상 안의 사람 형상(얼굴과 몸)을 식별해, 약시안 쪽 뷰에만 선택적으로 샤프닝을 적용합니다. 여기에 시각적 악센트(Visual Accents)가 더해집니다. 사람 위에 부드러운 형광 황록색 하이라이트를 입히거나, 인체 실루엣을 따라 굵은 적색 외곽선을 그리는 식입니다. 펄스(Pulse) 컨트롤로 이 효과를 일정한 Hz와 깊이로 밝아졌다 어두워지는 '호흡' 리듬으로 만들 수도 있습니다. 목적은 명확합니다. 무시당하던 눈의 시각 피질이 대상에 다시 주의를 기울이도록 만드는 것.

여기서 한 가지 흥미로운 엔지니어링 트레이드오프가 있습니다. 왜 프레임 전체를 샤프닝하지 않고 '사람'만 골라 강조할까요? 계산 비용도 이유지만, 더 큰 이유는 주의(attention)의 방향입니다. 화면 전체를 자극하면 시각 시스템은 어디를 봐야 할지 모릅니다. 반면 사회적 대상 — 얼굴과 몸 — 은 인간 시각이 진화적으로 가장 먼저 반응하도록 설계된 신호입니다. 약시안이 무시하던 바로 그 신호를 인위적으로 증폭시키는 것이 핵심입니다. 영상 전체가 아니라 관심의 대상에 개입하는 것. 이것이 소프트웨어가 하드웨어 위에서 할 수 있는 가장 정직한 일입니다.

셋째, 선택적 Wedge Occlusion이 있습니다. 양쪽 시야 일부에 검은 쐐기 모양을 덮어, 각 눈이 장면의 서로 다른 부분만 보게 강제합니다. 이는 두 눈의 상이 충돌하는 양안 경쟁(binocular rivalry)을 줄이는 고전적 기법을 소프트웨어로 옮긴 것입니다.

넷째, 양안 융합 훈련입니다. 약시안에는 자연 배경(피부톤, 녹색, 파란색)과 확실히 구분되는 고채도 마젠타 핑크 원형 단서를, 우세안에는 은은한 중립 회색 점을 띄웁니다. 사용자가 시선을 따라가면 뇌는 두 신호를 하나로 합치려 시도하고, 이 과정에서 양안 융합과 입체 깊이 지각이 연습됩니다.

캘리브레이션이 곧 정확도다

엔지니어링에서 흔히 놓치는 부분이 초기 설정입니다. Amblyotube는 실행 시 어느 눈이 영향을 받았는지(좌/우)를 먼저 고르게 합니다. 이 선택이 틀리면 필터가 반대쪽 눈, 즉 우세안을 훈련시키게 됩니다. 정확도가 곧 결과를 좌우합니다. 센서 캘리브레이션이 틀어진 로봇이 정확한 동작을 못 하듯, 기준이 뒤집힌 훈련은 아무리 오래 해도 방향이 반대입니다.

난이도는 두 가지 경로로 정해집니다. 하나는 조건 프리셋(Mild / Moderate / Severe) — 각각 시력표 마지막 2줄, 3~5줄, 5줄 이상을 읽지 못하는 정도를 기준으로 우세안 셰이더와 약시안 샤프너의 기본 레벨을 자동으로 맞춥니다. 다른 하나는 내장 LogMAR 시력 확인 도구입니다. 가상 3미터 거리에서 표준 Landolt C 시표를 사용해 눈별로 최대 30회 시행, 임상 스테어케이스 알고리즘으로 logMAR 값을 산출하고, 감지된 경도에 맞춰 훈련 프로필을 자동 갱신할 수 있습니다. 사용자가 감으로 난이도를 정하지 않아도 되는 구조입니다.

리텐션을 위한 인터페이스 결정

세션은 30~40분, 최대 1시간을 권장합니다. 13세 이상 대상. 컨트롤 패널은 VR 안에서 크기 조절과 이동이 가능한 플로팅 패널이고, Meta Quest 컨트롤러와 핸드 트래킹을 모두 지원합니다. YouTube 검색창이 내장되어 있고, 네트워크 없이 재생 가능한 아동용 카탈로그(만화 등)도 미리 담겨 있습니다. Room View는 AR 패스스루 모드로, 가상 룸 대신 실제 방 위에 영상을 띄워 훈련할 수 있게 합니다. 재생, 일시정지, 탐색, 볼륨, 음소거, 언어 선택, 그리고 기본값 복원(Reset All) 버튼도 포함됩니다.

인터페이스 결정 하나하나가 리텐션을 향합니다. 플로팅 패널을 굳이 VR 공간 안에 띄운 이유는, 훈련 중 시선을 헤드셋 밖으로 빼지 않게 하기 위함입니다. 컨트롤러와 핸드 트래킹을 둘 다 지원하는 이유도 마찬가지입니다. 입력 방식에서 막히면 그 순간 세션이 끊기기 때문입니다. 오프라인 카탈로그는 네트워크가 불안정한 환경에서도 훈련이 멈추지 않게 하는 안전장치입니다. 화려한 기능이 아니라, 매일 켜지게 만드는 마찰 제거입니다.

한계를 명확히 두는 설계

중요한 전제가 있습니다. Amblyotube는 진단·치료·완치 수단이 아니라, 양안 협응과 깊이 지각을 돕는 보조적 시각 훈련 도구입니다. 전문 의료 지침을 대체하지 않습니다. 소프트웨어가 할 수 있는 일은 꾸준히 실행될 기회를 만드는 것, 그리고 그 기회를 매일의 콘텐츠 위에 얹는 것입니다. 이 경계를 분명히 긋는 것도 설계의 일부입니다. 과장된 약속은 리텐션을 만들지 못하고, 정직한 범위만이 오래 갑니다.

검사실이 아니라 거실에서, 패치가 아니라 좋아하는 영상 위에서 훈련이 일어나게 하는 것 — 웨어러블의 성패가 결국 착용 시간에서 갈린다면, 시각 훈련도 같은 규칙을 따를 수밖에 없습니다.

Meta Quest에서 Amblyotube를 만나보세요: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: Everything we changed when we rebuilt the token console — and the small annoyances we removed
description:
This is for people who launch tokens, add liquidity, run a presale or lock LP tokens — and who don't want to
read a smart-contract audit in order to do it. We just finished rebuilding the platform underneath, so here's
what actually changed for you, in plain terms, plus the small things we fixed that you'd otherwise notice only
as "huh, that used to be annoying."

Fifteen chains, one top bar

BNB Chain, Ethereum, Arbitrum, Polygon, Base, opBNB, Core, X Layer, Conflux eSpace, ApeChain, Morph, ECO,
Robinhood, ARC, plus the BNB testnet. Switching chains in the top bar carries the rest of the page with it:
which exchange and pool you're looking at, which fee steps that exchange offers, what a batch operation costs
in that chain's own coin. You don't re-enter anything, and nothing silently keeps the previous chain's
settings.

One honest boundary: Solana, TON, Sui and Tron are separate sites. This one is EVM chains only.

"I created the pool but I can't find it" used to be normal

Usually nothing had failed. Different exchanges have different fee steps — PancakeSwap's third tier is 0.25%,
Uniswap's is 0.3%. Ask one venue for the other's step and the pool you just made doesn't show up where you look
for it.

Now the fee options follow the exchange you picked, and the default is always a step that venue actually
offers.

For pools that are already live and out of balance there's repair liquidity (/tool/liquidity): it reads
the current reserves, works out how much each side is short, and deposits only the gap — you don't have to do
the ratio math or risk over-depositing.

Fewer confirmation popups, and failures you can act on

Multi-step flows used to make you confirm approvals one at a time, with a pause between each. They're bundled
now, so there's less clicking — and because the whole bundle is checked before it's broadcast, when something
goes wrong the message tells you which step failed instead of just "the transaction reverted."

Batch jobs also wait for each transaction to land before starting the next. That sounds obvious, but the
previous version started the next one while the earlier was still pending, and nodes rejected it. The kind of
"random" failure where retrying a minute later made it work was usually this.

Batch tools that point at the actual line

If you do airdrops, distributions or sweeps, you paste lists of addresses and amounts hundreds of rows long.
The rule we set for ourselves: one error per field, shown while you type, with a line number.

  • Fill a field and it checks immediately — you don't find out after pressing Confirm.
  • Bad address? It names the row. Nobody scans a 600-row box for row 481.
  • Duplicate addresses merge when you click away, so you don't pay the same wallet twice.
  • A limit that means "unlimited" displays as unlimited, not as a 77-digit number.

Neighbouring tools: migrate assets (/wallet/migrate) sweeps tokens and gas out of a batch of wallets with
a gas budget per wallet, and a paying wallet that checks its own balance before sending anything; spread
startup capital (/wallet/distribute) fans one funding wallet out to many, so your launch doesn't look like
one blob in the explorer. Change a scanning setting halfway through and the tool tells you the list you already
have is out of date.

Your private keys stay in your browser

The wallet vault encrypts locally before anything is saved, and a Passkey (face or fingerprint) can unlock it
instead of a password. Nothing is uploaded and no server holds your keys.

Two details that matter day to day:

  • Reloading the page doesn't lock you out again. The unlock lives in the current tab and expires after 15 minutes of inactivity, so you're not typing a password every refresh — and closing the tab really does end it.
  • There's a manual exit. A lock indicator in the top bar and a "lock now" button share that same 15-minute rule, so the interface can't show "locked" while a refresh quietly unlocks it.

Backups export as a CSV you can store somewhere else, not just to the clipboard — because "I copied 50 keys and
then closed the tab" has happened to everyone.

Also new, and worth five minutes

  • Vanity wallets (/wallet/vanity): want an address ending in 8888? Your browser searches for one locally. No transaction, no gas, and the result is an ordinary wallet — nothing special about it, just easy to recognise.
  • Bot workspace (/bot/robot): it picks the pool that's actually worth refreshing rather than the first one it finds; the wallet cap per round comes from one rule shared by the input box and the engine, so switching speed tiers adjusts your number instead of failing mid-run; and the run log survives a crash, so you can see what had already gone out.
  • Project website builder (/site): generate a landing page for your token and point your own domain at it with a CNAME record.
  • Contract calls (/tool/call) for changing parameters directly, token snapshot for holder lists, batch image upload for NFT artwork (returns ordinary https links plus IPFS addresses).
  • Read-only browsing: you can walk through the whole platform, including what your parameters would produce, without connecting a wallet.

The small things we spent real time on

These are the ones you'll notice without naming:

  • Changing language doesn't erase your form. Same page, Chinese to English, everything you typed stays. Move to a different page and it clears — on purpose, so half a form for one tool can't leak into the next.
  • Dates refuse the past and stop at the minute, so you can't schedule a lock for a time that already happened.
  • Long addresses are shortened with a copy icon, and hovering shows the whole thing — including names the chain gives back to us.
  • On a phone, dialogs slide up from the bottom with full-width stacked buttons, and fields are big enough that iOS doesn't zoom the page when you tap one.
  • Every fee is quoted in that chain's own coin, not in one fixed network's symbol.

What isn't finished

The AI-launch section is still labelled "in development" in the menu — we built part of it and pulled a piece
back out. Presale and IDO pages work today, but I'm not going to promise you a roadmap for them. And we verify
on the BNB testnet before mainnet, so if a flow behaves differently on a chain we test less often, tell us:
with fifteen chains live, your real transaction is a better test than ours.

Guides for each feature are under /en/guide, the FAQ is
/en/guide/faq, and the console is at gtokentool.com.

title: Suppression is a compliance surface, not a checkbox
description:
Most teams add a suppression list after their first complaint. The list is a table of addresses, and within a month nobody remembers why half of them are on it. That is a compliance problem, not a tidiness problem.

Every entry needs a reason and a scope

A hard bounce, a spam complaint, a manual block and an unsubscribe are four different facts with four different lifetimes. A hard bounce is permanent for that address. An unsubscribe is permanent for that channel but may not cover a transactional password reset somebody explicitly requested. A complaint usually means permanent for marketing and a manual review before anything else.

If the table only has (address, created_at) you cannot answer 'why is this blocked' in a support ticket, and you cannot safely unblock anything.

Normalise before you compare

Local parts are case sensitive in theory and case insensitive in practice for every provider your customers actually use. Lowercase the whole address for the suppression lookup, but store the address as the customer wrote it so the UI is not confusing. If you support plus-addressing, decide whether a suppression on user+tag@example.com blocks user@example.com. Most senders say yes and most customers expect no.

Check at send time, not at enqueue time

A message can sit in a queue for an hour. If suppression was checked when the job was created, an unsubscribe that arrived in between is ignored. Re-check immediately before the SMTP conversation, and treat the check as part of the send transaction.

Volanea keeps suppression scoped per project with the reason attached, and re-checks it at delivery time rather than at enqueue.

title: Renaming a column in SQL Server, and what it quietly breaks
description:
A column was misspelled when the table was created, and it has been Ammount ever since. The rename itself is one line:

EXEC sp_rename 'dbo.Invoice.Ammount', 'Amount', 'COLUMN';

Caution: Changing any part of an object name could break scripts and stored procedures.

That caution is the entire problem, stated once and never mentioned again. The rename succeeds. What breaks, breaks later, and in a different file.

Note the arguments: the old name is qualified with the table, the new name is not — write 'dbo.Invoice.Amount' as the second argument and you get a column called dbo.Invoice.Amount, brackets and all.

What follows the rename by itself

More than people expect.

Indexes keep working. The index still indexes the same column under its new name:

CREATE INDEX IX_Tag_Labell ON dbo.Tag (Labell);
EXEC sp_rename 'dbo.Tag.Labell', 'Label', 'COLUMN';

The index is intact and now covers Label. Its own name, though, is untouched — you are left with IX_Tag_Labell on a column called Label, which is how a schema starts lying about itself. Rename the index too:

EXEC sp_rename 'dbo.Tag.IX_Tag_Labell', 'IX_Tag_Label', 'INDEX';

Foreign keys keep working, and stay trusted — is_not_trusted remains 0. Nothing to do.

Unique constraints keep working, like indexes.

Default constraints keep working, and usually have nothing to rewrite — DEFAULT (0) is stored as ((0)) and names no column at all. The constraint's own name is untouched, so DF_Invoice_Ammount is still sitting on a column called Amount.

One case that refuses outright

A check constraint stops the rename dead:

CREATE TABLE dbo.ChkOnly (Id int NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    Qty int NOT NULL CONSTRAINT CK_ChkOnly_Qty CHECK (Qty >= 0));

EXEC sp_rename 'dbo.ChkOnly.Qty', 'Quantity', 'COLUMN';

Msg 15336, Level 16, State 1, Procedure sp_rename, Line 563
Object 'dbo.ChkOnly.Qty' cannot be renamed because the object participates in enforced dependencies.

The constraint's definition names the column, and SQL Server will not leave it pointing at a name that no longer exists. Drop it, rename, put it back:

ALTER TABLE dbo.ChkOnly DROP CONSTRAINT CK_ChkOnly_Qty;
GO
EXEC sp_rename 'dbo.ChkOnly.Qty', 'Quantity', 'COLUMN';
GO
ALTER TABLE dbo.ChkOnly ADD CONSTRAINT CK_ChkOnly_Quantity CHECK (Quantity >= 0);
GO

Those GOs matter. Without them the whole thing is one batch, the ADD CONSTRAINT is parsed before the rename has happened, and it fails with Invalid column name 'Quantity' — leaving you with the constraint dropped and the column renamed, which is the worst of the three states.

A schema-bound view refuses for the same reason, with the same message:

CREATE VIEW dbo.PaymentBound WITH SCHEMABINDING AS SELECT PaymentId, Ammount FROM dbo.Payment;
EXEC sp_rename 'dbo.Payment.Ammount', 'Amount', 'COLUMN';

Msg 15336, Level 16, State 1, Procedure sp_rename, Line 563
Object 'dbo.Payment.Ammount' cannot be renamed because the object participates in enforced
dependencies.

Both of these are the helpful outcome: they are the dependencies that will not let you break them. Everything in the next section breaks silently instead.

What does not follow

Views, stored procedures, functions and triggers hold your text, not a reference to the column. They are not updated, and they do not complain until something runs them:

SELECT * FROM dbo.InvoiceTotal;

Msg 207, Level 16, State 1, Procedure InvoiceTotal, Line 1
Invalid column name 'Ammount'.
Msg 4413, Level 16, State 1, Line 1
Could not use view or function 'dbo.InvoiceTotal' because of binding errors.

EXEC dbo.GetInvoice @Id = 1;

Msg 207, Level 16, State 1, Procedure dbo.GetInvoice, Line 1
Invalid column name 'Ammount'.

A deployment that renames a column therefore succeeds, reports no error, and leaves a procedure that fails the first time a customer calls it. That gap — between the change and the failure — is the whole risk of the operation.

Find them before you rename

Everything that uses the table:

SELECT referencing_schema_name AS SchemaName, referencing_entity_name AS UsesTheTable
FROM   sys.dm_sql_referencing_entities('dbo.Invoice', 'OBJECT');

SchemaName  UsesTheTable
----------  ------------
dbo         GetInvoice
dbo         InvoiceTotal

That is the list to read before you decide. It will not tell you which ones name the column, so after the rename, search the definitions for the old name:

SELECT OBJECT_SCHEMA_NAME(m.object_id) AS SchemaName,
       OBJECT_NAME(m.object_id)        AS ObjectName,
       o.type_desc                     AS Kind
FROM   sys.sql_modules AS m
JOIN   sys.objects AS o ON o.object_id = m.object_id
WHERE  m.definition LIKE '%Ammount%';

SchemaName  ObjectName  Kind
----------  ----------  --------------------
dbo         GetInvoice  SQL_STORED_PROCEDURE

Fix each one with ALTER VIEW or ALTER PROCEDURE, then run that query again. When it returns no rows, nothing left in the database names the old column. It is the only check at the end of this job that means anything.

Two caveats on it. It searches text, so a column named Code matches far too much — rename misspellings and distinctive names with confidence, and read the results rather than trusting the count. And it sees only what is stored in the database: your application's SQL, reports, ETL jobs and anything built with dynamic SQL are outside it entirely.

The safer shape, when the column is in use

A rename is instant and total: the old name is gone for every reader at the same moment. Where an application is deployed separately from its database, that is a window of failure you cannot close by sequencing.

The alternative takes longer and never breaks:

  1. Add the new column, and keep both written for a while.
  2. Move the readers across, one at a time, deploying as you go.
  3. Drop the old column when nothing names it.

Worth the extra deployments only where the downtime matters — but when it matters, nothing else does the job.

Knowing what points at the table

The lists above come from the database, which is a better source than memory. What they do not show is the shape of the thing: which tables point at this one, which columns join to what, and therefore how far a rename travels.

WoodFireERD draws that from your schema — pick the table, follow its relationships out as far as you want to look, and take the change out as an ordered migration script.

Originally published at woodfireerd.com. Every statement in it was run against a real SQL Server before publishing — the error messages are copied from the output, not from memory.

title: React Mastery Series — Part 1: React Fundamentals — From Zero to Components
description:
Welcome to the React Mastery Series!

This series is designed to take you from understanding the fundamentals of React to building modern, maintainable, and production-ready applications.

Whether you're a JavaScript developer exploring React for the first time or someone looking to strengthen your frontend fundamentals, this series will help you understand not only how React works, but also why it works the way it does.

In this first article, we'll focus on the foundations:

  • What React is
  • Why React was created
  • The problems React solves
  • Declarative vs. imperative programming
  • Understanding the DOM
  • Single Page Applications
  • The component-based architecture
  • Creating your first React application
  • Building your first components

Let's get started!

Table of Contents

  1. What Is React?
  2. Why Was React Created?
  3. The Problem with Traditional DOM Manipulation
  4. Declarative vs. Imperative Programming
  5. What Is the DOM?
  6. What Is a Single Page Application?
  7. React Is a Library, Not a Framework
  8. The Component-Based Architecture
  9. Understanding React's Rendering Process
  10. Setting Up Your React Environment
  11. Creating Your First React Application
  12. Understanding the Project Structure
  13. Your First React Component
  14. Component Composition
  15. Practical Example: Building a User Profile
  16. Understanding React's Mental Model
  17. Common Beginner Mistakes
  18. What We Learned
  19. What's Next?
  1. What Is React?

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces.

It was originally developed at Facebook, now Meta, and is used to create interactive web applications.

React allows developers to build interfaces using reusable pieces called components.

Instead of manually updating individual DOM elements whenever something changes, React lets us describe what the UI should look like based on the current data.

Consider a simple website:

Hello World

This is straightforward HTML.

Now imagine a dashboard containing:

  • A navigation bar
  • A sidebar
  • A profile section
  • A list of products
  • Notifications
  • Search functionality
  • Interactive filters

Managing all of these elements manually can become difficult.

React helps us organize the interface into smaller, reusable components.

For example:

function App() {
return (






);
}

Each component represents a specific part of the interface.

This makes applications easier to maintain, reuse, and scale.

  1. Why Was React Created?

To understand React, we first need to understand the problems developers faced when building complex interfaces.

Imagine you're building an online shopping application.

The interface contains:

  • A product list
  • A shopping cart
  • A total price
  • A checkout button

When a user adds a product to the cart, several things need to change:

  1. The cart contents update.
  2. The number of items changes.
  3. The total price changes.
  4. The UI reflects the new data.

Using traditional DOM manipulation, you might manually update each element.

const cartCount = document.querySelector(".cart-count");

cartCount.textContent = 3;

This works for simple applications.

However, imagine dozens of components depending on the same data.

Now you must carefully coordinate every DOM update.

This creates several problems:

  • UI logic becomes scattered.
  • DOM updates become difficult to maintain.
  • Bugs become harder to track.
  • Components become tightly coupled.
  • Reusing UI logic becomes more complicated.

React provides a different approach.

Instead of manually updating every affected element, you update the application state and describe the UI based on that state.

React handles the necessary rendering work.

  1. The Problem with Traditional DOM Manipulation

Let's build a small example using plain JavaScript.

0


Increment

JavaScript:

const countElement = document.getElementById("count");

const button = document.getElementById("increment");

let count = 0;

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
count++;

countElement.textContent = count;
});

This is perfectly valid JavaScript.

But notice what we are doing:

  • Keeping track of the count manually.
  • Finding the DOM element.
  • Listening for an event.
  • Updating the DOM manually.

For a small example, this is fine.

But imagine an application with hundreds of interactive elements.

You would need to manually synchronize:

  • Application data
  • DOM elements
  • Event handlers
  • UI states

This is where maintaining consistency becomes difficult.

React changes this approach by making the UI a function of data.

Conceptually:

Application State
↓
React Components
↓
UI

When the state changes, React determines what needs to be updated.

  1. Declarative vs. Imperative Programming

This is one of the most important concepts to understand before learning React.

Imperative Programming

Imperative programming describes how to perform a task.

You provide instructions step by step.

Example:

const heading = document.createElement("h1");

heading.textContent = "Hello React";

document.body.appendChild(heading);

We explicitly tell the browser:

  1. Create an element.
  2. Set its text.
  3. Add it to the document.

Declarative Programming

Declarative programming describes what the result should look like.

function App() {
return

Hello React

;
}

We describe the desired UI.

React handles the underlying DOM operations.

The difference

Imperative| Declarative
Describes how to do something| Describes what should happen
Requires manual DOM operations| React manages DOM updates
UI logic can become scattered| UI is described through components
Developer coordinates updates| React manages rendering

React's declarative model becomes especially powerful when the UI depends on changing data.

  1. What Is the DOM?

DOM stands for Document Object Model.

When a browser loads an HTML document, it creates a structured representation of that document.

For example:


Hello


Welcome to React



The browser represents this document as a tree.

Conceptually:

Document
|
└── html
|
└── body
|
└── div
|
├── h1
|
└── p

This structure allows JavaScript to interact with the document.

For example:

document.querySelector("h1").textContent = "Updated";

This changes the DOM.

React works with the browser DOM through its rendering system.

You usually don't need to manipulate DOM elements manually when building ordinary React interfaces.

  1. What Is a Single Page Application?

A Single Page Application, or SPA, is a web application that typically loads an initial HTML document and then updates its interface dynamically as users interact with it.

Traditional multi-page applications often navigate by requesting a new HTML document from the server.

In a typical SPA:

  1. The browser loads the application.
  2. JavaScript initializes the UI.
  3. User interactions update the interface.
  4. Navigation may happen without a full document reload.

For example:

User opens application
↓
Initial HTML loads
↓
JavaScript initializes
↓
React renders the UI
↓
User interacts
↓
UI updates

React is commonly used to build SPAs.

However, React is not limited to SPAs.

React can also be used with frameworks such as Next.js that support server rendering and other rendering strategies.

  1. React Is a Library, Not a Framework

This distinction is important.

React focuses primarily on building user interfaces.

It provides:

  • Components
  • Rendering
  • State
  • Hooks
  • UI composition

But React itself doesn't prescribe a complete solution for every application concern.

For example, React doesn't include a complete built-in routing system.

You may use additional tools:

Requirement| Common Solution
UI| React
Routing| React Router
Server rendering| Next.js or another framework
Client state| React state, Zustand, Redux Toolkit
Server state| TanStack Query
Forms| React Hook Form
Styling| CSS, Tailwind CSS, CSS Modules

You don't need all these tools when starting React.

Learn React fundamentals first.

  1. The Component-Based Architecture

Components are the foundation of React.

A component is a reusable piece of UI.

For example, a website might contain:

Application
│
├── Navbar
│
├── Sidebar
│
├── Dashboard
│ ├── Statistics
│ ├── Chart
│ └── RecentActivity
│
└── Footer

Each part can be implemented as a separate component.

This approach is called component-based architecture.

Why components?

Components help us:

  • Reuse UI
  • Separate responsibilities
  • Organize code
  • Maintain applications
  • Build complex interfaces from smaller pieces

Imagine building a dashboard without components.

You might end up with one enormous function containing hundreds of lines of JSX.

With components, each section can have its own logic and structure.

A component should have a clear responsibility

For example:

function Navbar() {
return

Navigation;
}

function Footer() {
return

Footer;
}

function App() {
return (
<>

Main content

</>
);
}

This is easier to understand than placing everything inside one component.

  1. Understanding React's Rendering Process

At a high level, React applications follow this pattern:

State or Props Change
↓
React Renders Components
↓
React Determines Necessary Updates
↓
React Commits Updates
↓
Browser Displays the UI

Let's simplify this.

Imagine a counter displaying:

0

The user clicks a button.

The state changes to:

1

React renders the component again using the new state.

React then determines what changes are necessary in the browser DOM.

The important idea is:

You describe the UI. React manages the rendering process.

Rendering a component does not necessarily mean that React changes the DOM.

React may render a component and determine that the resulting DOM is unchanged.

We'll explore rendering and reconciliation in more detail later in this series.

  1. Setting Up Your React Environment

Before creating a React application, make sure you have Node.js installed.

Node.js allows JavaScript tools to run outside the browser.

Check your versions:

node -v
npm -v

You should see version numbers.

If Node.js is not installed, download it from the official website:

https://nodejs.org

For modern React development, Vite is a common choice.

Vite provides:

  • A development server
  • Fast startup
  • Hot Module Replacement
  • Build tooling
  1. Creating Your First React Application

Let's create a React project using Vite.

Run:

npm create vite@latest react-mastery

Choose:

Framework: React
Variant: JavaScript

If you want TypeScript, choose the TypeScript variant instead.

Then:

cd react-mastery
npm install
npm run dev

Vite will start a development server.

You can open the local URL displayed in your terminal.

Your application should now be running.

What is Hot Module Replacement?

Hot Module Replacement, or HMR, allows Vite to update parts of your application during development without requiring a complete page reload in many situations.

This makes the development experience faster.

For example, when you change a component, Vite can update the application while preserving certain existing state.

  1. Understanding the Project Structure

A typical Vite React project looks like this:

react-mastery/
│
├── public/
│
├── src/
│ ├── assets/
│ ├── App.jsx
│ ├── App.css
│ ├── index.css
│ └── main.jsx
│
├── index.html
├── package.json
└── vite.config.js

Let's understand the important files.

App.jsx

This is usually where the main application component lives.

function App() {
return

Hello React

;
}

export default App;

main.jsx

This is the entry point that connects React to the browser DOM.

import { StrictMode } from "react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";

import App from "./App.jsx";

createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render(



);

index.html

Vite provides an HTML document containing a root element.

React renders the application inside this element.

  1. Your First React Component

Let's create a simple component.

function Welcome() {
return

Welcome to React!

;
}

export default Welcome;

This is a React function component.

Let's break it down.

function Welcome()

We define a JavaScript function named "Welcome".

return

Welcome to React!

;

The function returns JSX.

React uses this returned description to render the UI.

Now use the component in "App.jsx":

import Welcome from "./Welcome";

function App() {
return (




);
}

export default App;

Notice the syntax:

We use the component like a JSX element.

This is one of the fundamental ideas of React.

  1. Component Composition

Component composition means combining smaller components to create larger interfaces.

Let's create three components.

function Header() {
return

My Application;
}

function MainContent() {
return

Welcome to the dashboard;
}

function Footer() {
return

© 2026 My Application;
}

Now compose them:

function App() {
return (
<>




</>
);
}

The final interface is created from smaller components.

This approach makes your code easier to read and maintain.

Why not create one giant component?

A giant component often becomes difficult to:

  • Understand
  • Debug
  • Test
  • Reuse
  • Maintain

Breaking it into smaller components improves organization.

However, don't create a component for every single HTML element.

Components should represent meaningful pieces of UI or reusable behavior.

  1. Practical Example: Building a User Profile

Let's build a small React application using multiple components.

Step 1: Create the Profile component

function Profile() {
return (


src="https://placehold.co/100"
alt="User avatar"
/> 
  <h2>Hamed Farazi</h2>

  <p>Frontend Developer</p>

  <button>View Profile</button>
</div>

);
}

export default Profile;

Step 2: Create the App component

import Profile from "./Profile";

function App() {
return (


Team Members

  <Profile />
</div>

);
}

export default App;

The "App" component uses the "Profile" component.

Step 3: Reuse the component

function App() {
return (


Team Members

  <Profile />
  <Profile />
  <Profile />
</div>

);
}

Now we have three profile cards.

This demonstrates component reuse.

However, all three profiles currently display the same information.

In the next part of this series, we'll learn how to make components dynamic using Props.

  1. Understanding React's Mental Model

The most important thing to understand when learning React is its mental model.

React applications are built around a few fundamental ideas:

Components describe the UI

function Greeting() {
return

Hello

;
}

Props provide inputs

function Greeting({ name }) {
return

Hello, {name}

;
}

State represents changing data

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

React renders the UI based on these inputs

Conceptually:

Props + State
↓
React Component
↓
UI

When props or state change, React can render the component again.

This is the core mental model behind React.

Instead of manually updating the interface, you describe how it should look for the current data.

  1. Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Thinking React is HTML

JSX looks like HTML, but it is JavaScript syntax transformed into JavaScript.

const element =

Hello

;

This isn't ordinary HTML.

Mistake 2: Thinking React automatically makes everything faster

React helps manage UI rendering, but it doesn't guarantee that every application will be faster than manually written JavaScript.

Performance depends on architecture, rendering behavior, and implementation.

Mistake 3: Creating one massive component

Break your UI into meaningful components.

Mistake 4: Learning advanced hooks too early

Don't begin with "useMemo", "useCallback", or complex state management.

First understand:

  • Components
  • Props
  • State
  • Events
  • Rendering

Mistake 5: Memorizing syntax without understanding the mental model

The goal isn't to memorize every React API.

The goal is to understand how React describes and updates interfaces.

  1. What We Learned

In this article, we covered the fundamentals of React:

  • React is a JavaScript library for building UIs.
  • React uses a declarative programming model.
  • Components are reusable pieces of UI.
  • React manages rendering and DOM updates.
  • JSX allows HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript.
  • React applications can be built using Vite.
  • Components can be composed to create larger interfaces.
  • Props and state will help make components dynamic.

These concepts form the foundation of everything else in React.

  1. What's Next?

In Part 2: JSX, Props, State & Events, we'll explore the concepts that make React applications interactive.

We'll cover:

  • JSX in depth
  • JavaScript expressions inside JSX
  • Props and destructuring
  • Passing data between components
  • State with "useState"
  • State updates
  • Event handling
  • Conditional rendering
  • Rendering lists
  • Keys
  • Practical examples

By the end of Part 2, you'll understand how to build dynamic React components instead of static interfaces.

Continue the React Mastery Series

Part 1: React Fundamentals — From Zero to Components

Part 2: JSX, Props, State & Events

Part 3: React Hooks — Complete Practical Guide

Part 4: React Forms & API Integration

Part 5: React Architecture & Best Practices

Part 6: React Performance Optimization

Part 7: React Internals — Virtual DOM, Fiber & Reconciliation

Part 8: Modern React 19 Features

Part 9: Routing & State Management

Part 10: Testing React Applications

If you're learning React, share what you're currently working on in the comments.

Let's build better React applications together.

Happy coding!

React #JavaScript #FrontendDevelopment #WebDevelopment #ReactJS

title: How to Plan a Small Brochure Website: Pages, Content and Launch
description:
A small brochure website has a simple job: help a visitor understand who you are, what you offer and how to reach you. It can be a single page with clear sections or a small collection of pages. The right choice depends on the services and questions you need to explain, not on a required number of menu items.

This guide walks through a practical page map, the content to prepare and the checks to run before launch. It is intended for a freelancer, small workshop or business owner making an initial site.

Decide what the site needs to do

Write down your audience and the main action you want a visitor to take. A consultant may want a project enquiry; a local repair shop may want a customer to arrange an appointment. List the questions someone needs answered before they take that step.

A brochure site can be a good fit for presenting services, examples and contact details. If visitors need to select products, pay, track delivery or manage an account, document those flows before choosing a tool. A few descriptive pages may not be enough.

Launching a site does not automatically bring enquiries. A clear offer, working contact route and a plan to reach an appropriate audience all matter.

Choose one page or several

A single page can work for one main service, a short introduction, a few examples and contact information. Menu items can link to sections of the same page. Keep the route to key information short enough that a visitor does not have to scroll through a long sequence of decorative sections.

Separate pages can help when services have different conditions, examples need detail or readers must compare options. Each page should answer a distinct question with enough useful information. Avoid empty pages added only to make the menu look bigger.

A sample page map

Imagine a fictional bicycle repair workshop. This is a teaching example, not a description of an actual business. It might start with four pages:

Page Visitor's question Useful content
Home What does the workshop do and how can I get in touch? Brief offer, main services, service area and contact
Services What can I request and how is work agreed? Service descriptions and how estimates are made
Work examples Has the workshop handled a similar task? A few real examples with permitted images and context
Contact How do I reach the team and when can I expect an answer? Working channels and hours or location when applicable

An appointment-only business without a public office should not invent one. A solo professional could place the same material in sections of one page instead.

Make the home page specific

Near the top, explain who you serve and what you do. Offer one clear next step, such as viewing services or discussing a task. Include a location or service area when it affects availability. Test the button or link: it should lead to a working section or contact channel.

For the fictional workshop, “City bicycle repairs by appointment,” paired with its real service area, tells visitors more than “the best service for everyone.” Only publish claims about timing, experience or results that you can support.

Below the introduction, provide short summaries of key services, how the work proceeds and selected evidence. The home page does not need to contain every detail; it should point clearly to the next relevant answer.

Explain services and conditions

Use the language your customers use. For each service, describe who it helps, what the work includes, what falls outside the scope and how timing and cost are agreed.

If you cannot quote a fixed price in advance, explain the process honestly: for example, an initial assessment may precede an agreed estimate. The precise conditions should come from the business's actual practice, not a generic template.

One service may deserve its own page if it needs substantial explanation. A group of closely related offerings may fit in one services page. Test the structure with a person who has not built the site: can they find the answer without guessing?

Show evidence without inventing it

An “about” section should explain who performs the work and which relevant experience or capabilities they bring. It need not be a long biography. Update it when the team or service changes.

For examples of work, describe the original task, what you did and a result you can substantiate. Obtain permission when a project includes a client's information or protected material. If you do not have a public case study yet, show your process or label a demonstration as hypothetical. Do not invent customers, testimonials or outcomes.

Use testimonials with appropriate permission and preserve their context. A photograph and caption should not imply that you performed work you did not do.

Make contact easy

Provide only channels you actually monitor: for example, an email address or telephone number. Add working hours or an expected response process if you can meet it. An in-person service may need an address and directions; a remote service may need a service area or time zone.

If you add a form, ask only for information needed to respond. Decide who receives the message and what the visitor sees on success or failure. Submit a test from a phone and a computer, confirm that the message arrives and provide another contact route if the form fails.

Before adding analytics, maps, forms or third-party widgets, identify what information they process and what notices or settings are appropriate for your circumstances. Requirements depend on location and processing; seek qualified advice when needed.

Build and publish in four steps

1. Prepare content first

Gather the offer, services, actual conditions, contact details and images you have permission to use. Draw a simple map of what appears first, where detail lives and how a visitor returns to contact. Draft the content before choosing animations or decorative effects.

2. Choose a creation method

A page builder with reusable blocks may suit someone who wants to edit a few pages without code. A CMS can provide a more configurable content workflow. Static files or custom development may fit a team comfortable with a repository and deployment process. Test the particular tool against your own editing task rather than relying only on a feature list.

Check whether you can use your domain, edit titles and contacts, export content, restore a backup and hand access to another person. Compare both launch and ongoing costs.

3. Arrange domain, hosting and access

Choose a readable domain and ensure the responsible owner controls the account. Understand renewal terms and how to change providers. Choose hosting or a service appropriate for the build method and follow its instructions for the domain and secure connection.

Limit access, protect accounts and store recovery information safely. Establish how the site is backed up and how restoration is tested. Never publish test passwords or private administration details.

4. Assemble and test

Apply the page map, use consistent menu labels and link services, examples and contact information. On a phone, verify that menus open, text is readable without horizontal scrolling and buttons can be used comfortably.

Give each page a descriptive title and useful description. Provide meaningful alternative text for informative images. Avoid duplicating pages merely to repeat search phrases. These steps support clarity; they do not guarantee search placement.

Before and after launch

Open the site in several browsers and on a phone. Check spelling, current conditions, addresses, links and buttons. Submit a test enquiry and verify receipt. Ask someone unfamiliar with the project to find a service and contact you; observe where they hesitate.

After publication, recheck the final address, secure connection, images and any restrictions on test or private material. Do not change access rules blindly. Assign an owner to update contact information and conditions, manage domain renewal and verify backups.

A short checklist

  • The audience, offer and main visitor action are clear.
  • You chose which information belongs in sections and which needs separate pages.
  • Services, examples and contacts are accurate and current.
  • You have appropriate permission for project material, images and testimonials.
  • The form and an alternative contact method work.
  • Mobile navigation, links, page titles and meaningful image alternatives have been checked.
  • The owner controls the domain, access, renewal and backups.
  • Someone is responsible for enquiries and future updates.

Start with the smallest structure that answers real customer questions. Add pages when they have a clear purpose and enough useful content to support it.

title: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX terminated because a duplicate key was found
description:
You make a column unique on a table that has been in use for a while:

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX UX_Account_Email ON dbo.Account (Email);

Msg 1505, Level 16, State 1, Line 1
The CREATE UNIQUE INDEX statement terminated because a duplicate key was found for the object name
'dbo.Account' and the index name 'UX_Account_Email'. The duplicate key value is (a@x.com).

The message names exactly one value. It is the first collision found, not a report — there may be one more or four hundred, and fixing the named one just gets you the next message.

A unique constraint fails the same way, with an extra line, because a constraint is an index underneath:

ALTER TABLE dbo.Account ADD CONSTRAINT UQ_Account_Email UNIQUE (Email);

Msg 1505, Level 16, State 1, Line 1
The CREATE UNIQUE INDEX statement terminated because a duplicate key was found ...
Msg 1750, Level 16, State 1, Line 1
Could not create constraint or index. See previous errors.

Two nulls are a duplicate

This is the part that surprises people, and it is why the message so often reads The duplicate key value is (<NULL>):

INSERT dbo.Account VALUES (4, NULL), (5, NULL);

Two rows with no email at all will defeat a unique index. In comparisons, NULL = NULL is unknown; for a unique index, SQL Server treats nulls as equal to each other, so exactly one row may have no value. That is the opposite of what most people expect from "the email must be unique", where the intention is nearly always unique when there is one.

The fix for that case is a filtered index:

SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX UX_Account_Email ON dbo.Account (Email) WHERE Email IS NOT NULL;

Now any number of rows may have no email, and the ones that do have one must differ.

SET QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON matters. It is on by default in SQL Server Management Studio and in most application connections, which is why this is rarely seen interactively — but it is off by default in sqlcmd, so a migration script run that way fails on the filtered index and only on the filtered index:

Msg 1934, Level 16, State 1, Line 1
CREATE INDEX failed because the following SET options have incorrect settings: 'QUOTED_IDENTIFIER'.

Put the SET at the top of the script and it applies to the whole batch.

List every duplicate, not just the first 

SELECT Email, COUNT(*) AS Rows_, MIN(AccountId) AS KeepThisOne
FROM   dbo.Account
WHERE  Email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC;

Email      Rows_  KeepThisOne
---------  -----  -----------
a@x.com    2      1

Leave the WHERE Email IS NOT NULL out if you are building an unfiltered index and need the nulls counted too.

To see the whole rows rather than the values — usually what you need, because the decision is which row survives:

WITH Duplicated AS
(
    SELECT *, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY Email) AS CopiesOfThisEmail
    FROM   dbo.Account
    WHERE  Email IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT *
FROM   Duplicated
WHERE  CopiesOfThisEmail > 1
ORDER BY Email, AccountId;

Choosing what to keep

"Keep the lowest id" is the usual reflex and it is often wrong. The oldest row may be an abandoned signup while the newest is the account in daily use. Before deleting anything, ask what points at these rows:

SELECT OBJECT_NAME(parent_object_id) AS ReferencingTable, name AS ForeignKey
FROM   sys.foreign_keys
WHERE  referenced_object_id = OBJECT_ID('dbo.Account');

Every table in that list has rows pointing at an account id you are about to remove, and they need repointing at whichever row you keep — before the delete, or the delete fails on the foreign key.

When the duplicates are genuinely the same thing and nothing references them, this deletes all but one of each:

WITH Ranked AS
(
    SELECT AccountId, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Email ORDER BY AccountId) AS Copy
    FROM   dbo.Account
    WHERE  Email IS NOT NULL
)
DELETE FROM Ranked WHERE Copy > 1;

Run it as a SELECT first. ORDER BY AccountId is the decision about which copy survives, and it is the only line in there worth arguing about.

A gentler order of work

Adding the index last is the reflex, and it means the cleanup and the constraint are the same deployment. The alternative is to add the filtered unique index first against the rows that are already clean, which stops the duplicates growing while you decide what to do with the ones you have.

Seeing it before you run it

What makes this change expensive is never the index; it is the rows pointing at the ones you are about to merge, in tables you did not know were involved.

WoodFireERD draws that for you — pick the table, follow what points at it, and take the change out as an ordered script with the index, the constraint and the clean-up steps in the order they have to run.

Originally published at woodfireerd.com. Every statement in it was run against a real SQL Server before publishing — the error messages are copied from the output, not from memory.

title: Spring Boot @Transactional: 7 Interview Traps That Catch Experienced Developers
description:
Most backend developers have put @Transactional on a service method and moved on. It usually works, which is exactly why interviewers like it. A few follow-up questions show quickly whether you know what the annotation does or just where to put it.

Here are seven of those follow-ups, with answers written the way I'd say them out loud. Everything assumes Spring Boot 3.x (Spring Framework 6.x), Jakarta Persistence, Hibernate 6 and Java 17-21.

1. "Why didn't my @Transactional method start a transaction?"

The usual cause is self-invocation.

Spoken answer: "Spring applies @Transactional through a proxy. Callers get the proxy, the proxy opens the transaction, then delegates to the real object. If a method inside the same class calls another annotated method with this., that call never goes through the proxy, so the annotation is ignored."

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository orderRepository) {
        this.orderRepository = orderRepository;
    }

    public void placeOrders(List<Order> orders) {
        for (Order order : orders) {
            saveOrder(order); // same as this.saveOrder(order): no proxy, no transaction
        }
    }

    @Transactional
    public void saveOrder(Order order) {
        orderRepository.save(order);
    }
}

Fixes, in the order I'd suggest them: move saveOrder into a separate bean and inject it, use TransactionTemplate for programmatic control, or switch to AspectJ weaving if you really need it. Self-injecting the bean with @Lazy also works, but it's a workaround most reviewers won't love.

2. "Can I put @Transactional on a private or final method?"

Spoken answer: "With the default proxy mode, no for private, and no for final. Spring Boot uses class-based (CGLIB) proxies by default, which work by subclassing your bean and overriding methods. A private method can't be overridden, and neither can a final one, so no transaction is applied."

Two details make this answer stand out:

  • Since Spring Framework 6.0, protected and package-private methods can be transactional with class-based proxies. Before that, only public methods counted. With interface-based JDK proxies, the method still has to be public and declared on the interface.
  • A final method on a proxied bean is a nasty bug. The call runs on the proxy instance itself, whose injected fields are usually null, so you can get a NullPointerException instead of a missing transaction.

3. "My method threw an exception. Why did the data still commit?"

Spoken answer: "By default Spring rolls back only on RuntimeException and Error. A checked exception, like IOException or your own PaymentFailedException extends Exception, does not trigger rollback. The transaction commits whatever was written before the exception."

Fixes:

  • @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) on the method or class.
  • Since Spring Framework 6.2 you can change the default globally with @EnableTransactionManagement(rollbackOn = RollbackOn.ALL_EXCEPTIONS).

A related follow-up: if you catch the exception inside the method and don't rethrow it, Spring never sees it, so it commits. And if an inner REQUIRED method throws a runtime exception that the outer method catches, the shared transaction is already marked rollback-only. The outer commit then fails with UnexpectedRollbackException. That surprises people the first time they see it.

4. "REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW: when would you use each?"

Spoken answer: "REQUIRED is the default. If a transaction already exists, the method joins it; if not, it starts one. Everything commits or rolls back together. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the current transaction and starts an independent one, which commits or rolls back on its own."

A real use case: recording a failed payment attempt. You want the audit row saved even when the payment transaction rolls back.

@Service
public class PaymentAuditService {

    private final PaymentAuditRepository auditRepository;

    public PaymentAuditService(PaymentAuditRepository auditRepository) {
        this.auditRepository = auditRepository;
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void recordFailure(Long orderId, String reason) {
        auditRepository.save(new PaymentAudit(orderId, reason));
    }
}

PaymentService.charge() runs in its own REQUIRED transaction, calls paymentAuditService.recordFailure(...) (a different bean, so the proxy applies), then throws. The charge rolls back, and the audit row stays.

The catch worth mentioning: REQUIRES_NEW needs a second database connection while the first one is suspended. Under load, heavy use of it can exhaust a small connection pool.

5. "What does readOnly = true actually do?"

Spoken answer: "It's a hint, and with Hibernate it has real effects. Spring sets the Hibernate session to manual flush mode and marks it read-only, so Hibernate skips dirty checking and doesn't keep snapshots of loaded entities. That saves memory and CPU on big reads. By default Spring also passes the read-only flag to the JDBC connection, and some drivers and databases use it for optimisations, or a routing data source can send those calls to a read replica."

What it doesn't do: it isn't a security guarantee. Whether a write fails depends on the driver and the database, so don't rely on it to block writes. Use it on query methods so you get the performance benefit, and keep writes in methods without it.

6. "Two users update the same row at once. What happens?"

This is the lost update problem. Both transactions read balance 1,000, one adds 200, the other subtracts 100, and whichever commits last wins. One change disappears.

Spoken answer: "@Transactional uses Isolation.DEFAULT, which means the database's default: READ COMMITTED on PostgreSQL and Oracle, REPEATABLE READ on MySQL InnoDB. READ COMMITTED does not stop a read-modify-write lost update. You can raise isolation, but in a JPA application the common fix is optimistic locking with a version column."

@Entity
public class Account {

    @Id
    private Long id;

    private BigDecimal balance;

    @Version
    private Long version;

    public void deposit(BigDecimal amount) {
        this.balance = this.balance.add(amount);
    }
}

Hibernate adds WHERE version = ? to the update. If another transaction changed the row first, zero rows are updated and Spring throws ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException. You then retry or return a conflict to the client. When conflicts are frequent, like a hot counter, pessimistic locking with @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) on a repository query can be the better choice.

7. "Why do I get LazyInitializationException, and why doesn't it happen in my controller?"

Spoken answer: "A lazy association is loaded only when you touch it, and that needs an open Hibernate session. If you access order.getItems() after the transaction and session are closed, for example in a mapper or a scheduled job, you get LazyInitializationException."

It often doesn't show up in controllers because Spring Boot enables Open Session in View by default (spring.jpa.open-in-view=true). The session stays open for the whole web request, so lazy loading works in the controller and during JSON serialisation. Boot logs a warning about it at startup for a reason: it hides N+1 queries and holds a connection for the whole request.

Better fixes: fetch what you need inside the service with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection, and set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false so problems show up in tests instead of production.

public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {

    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "items")
    Optional<Order> findWithItemsById(Long id);
}

Quick revision checklist

  • Self-invocation skips the proxy. Call through another bean or use TransactionTemplate.
  • Private and final methods aren't proxied. Protected and package-private work on class-based proxies since Spring 6.0.
  • Default rollback is unchecked exceptions and errors only. Use rollbackFor, or rollbackOn = ALL_EXCEPTIONS on Spring 6.2+.
  • A caught inner exception can still mark the transaction rollback-only and give you UnexpectedRollbackException.
  • REQUIRES_NEW is for work that must survive the outer rollback, like audit logs. It costs an extra connection.
  • readOnly = true turns off Hibernate dirty checking and flushing. It's not a write lock.
  • Default isolation comes from the database. Use @Version against lost updates.
  • Fetch lazy data inside the transaction and consider turning off open-in-view.

Which of these has bitten you in a real project? I'd like to hear about it in the comments.

title: I built a Mac app in Rust that turns the edges of the trackpad into controls
description:
My MacBook trackpad has four edges I never touch. Meanwhile I kept reaching for the menu bar to change the volume or the brightness. So I built Brink, a free menu bar app that turns those edges into controls:

  • Right edge: slide for volume
  • Left edge: slide for brightness
  • Top edge: slide for keyboard light
  • Bottom edge: swipe to skip a track
  • Top-right corner: double-tap to mute

It shows the same HUD as the keyboard keys, ticks under your finger as you slide, and keeps the pointer still while you do it. Here's how it works.

Reading raw touches

NSEvent gestures can't tell you that a finger is resting 3 mm from the right edge. You only get scrolls and swipes once macOS has already decided what the gesture is. Brink reads raw contact frames from the private MultitouchSupport framework instead: MTDeviceCreateList, MTRegisterContactFrameCallback, MTDeviceStart. Each frame lists every finger's normalized position, so the app can tell when a touch starts in an edge zone.

Every symbol is resolved with dlopen/dlsym. A private API can change, so a missing symbol turns the feature off instead of crashing the app.

Telling a slide from a scroll

This is the hard part. A finger near the edge might be the start of a slide, an ordinary two-finger scroll, a palm, or a tap. The engine is a small state machine:

enum State {
    Idle,
    Candidate { zone: Zone, id: i32, x0: f32, y0: f32, t0: f64, frozen: bool, corner: bool },
    Sliding(Slide),
    Lost { slide: Slide, since: f64 },
    Spent { frozen: bool },
}
  • Candidate: one finger landed in a zone. It becomes a slide once it moves along the edge by more than SLIDE_START, a swipe after SWIPE_DISTANCE, or a tap if it lifts quickly without moving.
  • Lost: trackpads drop a finger for a frame or two mid-slide, so the slide waits 180 ms for the finger to come back before ending.
  • Spent: a second finger arrived, or the gesture belongs to someone else. Brink ignores everything until all fingers lift.

A watchdog tick ends any slide that stops receiving frames. It's pure logic with no system calls, so the tests feed it synthetic frames.

Making it feel native

  • HUD: volume and brightness changes are posted as system-defined NSEvents carrying the media-key codes (NX_KEYTYPE_SOUND_UP and friends) through CGEventPost. macOS draws its own HUD, exactly as if you'd pressed the key. With Shift and Option held you get quarter steps, just like the keyboard.
  • Haptics: MTActuatorCreateFromDeviceID and MTActuatorActuate fire a light tick on every step, so you can feel the slider.
  • Holding the pointer still: while a slide is live, an event tap (CGEventTapCreate) swallows mouse-moved and drag events, so the cursor doesn't drift across the screen as your finger travels.

The panel

Brink itself is Tauri 2 with a Rust core. The menu bar panel is a WebView styled as liquid glass, and on macOS 26 it sits on a real NSGlassEffectView. To keep the text readable on any wallpaper, the backdrop is toned per pixel and a feathered mask darkens just the area behind the labels.

Shipping

  • Universal binary (Apple silicon and Intel), signed and notarized
  • Auto-updates with Tauri's updater and minisign-signed releases
  • Homebrew: brew trust muhammadalims/tap && brew install --cask muhammadalims/tap/brink

It's free, and it runs on macOS 13 or later: zerowing.in/brink

If you try it, I'd love to hear where the gesture detection gets it wrong for you, especially palm rejection on the bigger trackpads.

title: Testing callback ref cleanup on the same DOM node and in TypeScript
description:
A React callback ref can return a cleanup function as well as receive a DOM node. This capability, added in React 19, was tested through ResizeObserver registration and disconnection.

Unmounting is only part of the behavior. Even when the same DOM node remained, changing the callback reference ran the previous cleanup and the next registration.

Return disconnection from the callback that creates the observer

This function creates a callback ref and records its activity. With legacy: false, it returns cleanup. With true, it disconnects when called with null.

function makeTrackedRef(legacy) {
  let observer;
  function disconnect() {
    observer.disconnect();
    trace.active.delete(observer);
    trace.events.push('cleanup');
  }
  return node => {
    if (node === null) {
      trace.events.push('null');
      if (observer) disconnect();
      return;
    }
    observer = new ResizeObserver(() => {});
    observer.observe(node);
    trace.active.add(observer);
    trace.events.push('attach');
    if (!legacy) return disconnect;
  };
}

The fixture creates a real browser ResizeObserver and observes the node. trace.active tracks observers whose disconnection has not been recorded. Resize notification counts are not part of this comparison.

The test compares preserving a callback with creating a new one on every render:

export function RefExperiment({ stable, legacy }) {
  const [tick, setTick] = useState(0);
  const stableRef = useMemo(() => makeTrackedRef(legacy), [legacy]);
  const ref = stable ? stableRef : makeTrackedRef(legacy);
  return <section>
    <button id="rerender" onClick={() => setTick(previous => previous + 1)}>Render {tick}</button>
    <div id="observed" ref={ref}>Observed node</div>
  </section>;
}

Clicking the button rerenders the parent while the target div remains the same node. The root is then unmounted to verify cleanup.

A different callback triggers cleanup on the same node

Build and callback construction Initial log Log added by rerender Log added by unmount
Production, same callback, returns cleanup attach None cleanup
Production, new callback, returns cleanup attach cleanup → attach cleanup
Production, same callback, cleans up on null attach None null → cleanup
Development root Strict Mode, same callback, returns cleanup attach → cleanup → attach None cleanup
Development root Strict Mode, new callback, returns cleanup attach → cleanup → attach cleanup → attach cleanup
Development root Strict Mode, same callback, cleans up on null attach → null → cleanup → attach None null → cleanup

All 6 conditions had one tracked observer after initial processing and after rerender, then 0 after unmount. Even the version creating new callbacks paired setup with cleanup, so observers did not accumulate in this implementation.

The callback ref reference distinguishes returned cleanup, cleanup and reattachment when callbacks change, and the extra development cycle. No null call appeared in the returned-cleanup version's logs. Do not expect a second copy of the same cleanup through a null callback.

Direct comparison of node references before and after rerender confirmed that the DOM node stayed the same. Callback activity and DOM replacement are separate observations.

An implicit value return can fail type checking

Type behavior was also checked with TypeScript 7.0.2, @types/react 19.3.0, strict checking, and react-jsx.

import React from 'react';
const nodes = new Map<string, HTMLDivElement | null>();
export const view = <div ref={node => nodes.set('preview', node)} />;

Map.set returns the Map, so this callback did not satisfy the required void-or-cleanup return type and produced TS2322. A cleanup written as () => nodes.delete('preview') also produced TS2322 because it returns a boolean.

The version using a block and returning no value from cleanup passed:

import React from 'react';
const nodes = new Map<string, HTMLDivElement>();
export const view = <div ref={node => {
  if (!node) return;
  nodes.set('preview', node);
  return () => { nodes.delete('preview'); };
}} />;

This type comparison corresponds to the change described in the React 19 upgrade guide. When the operation is storing a node in a Map, avoid forwarding the Map operation's return value as the ref callback result.

Separate cleanup behavior from state-update loops

An existing article examined a ref callback that repeatedly updated state in an image preview. This experiment leaves state updates out of the observer callback and compares callback identity with cleanup timing. It does not establish that returning cleanup fixes arbitrary state-update loops.

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with React and React DOM 19.3.0, Node.js 24.15.0, esbuild 0.28.2, macOS arm64, and Headless Chrome 152 and no React Compiler. The production cases also had a Strict Mode wrapper, but did not run the extra development cycle. Observer counts come from fixture registration and disconnection records, not measurements of the browser's internal resource usage.

The fixture code, logs for the 6 conditions, and 3 type-checking cases separate changes to the DOM node from changes to the callback reference.
