title: A Heroku alternative in India, billed in rupees by UPI
description:
Originally published on the Plexivo blog.

Many developers learnt to ship with Heroku. You connect a repository, push your code and a new release goes live. That way of working is still the right one for most web apps and APIs. What changes in India is everything around it: where the app runs, how you pay, and what the invoice says.

This guide shows how that workflow looks on Plexivo, an AI-native cloud built in India and launched on 1 November 2026. Your app runs in Mumbai. Your database sits beside it. Prices are in US dollars, and you pay in rupees by UPI, card or net banking, with a GST tax invoice for every top-up.

What should a Heroku alternative in India offer?

When Indian teams look for a git-push platform, the same five needs come up again and again:

  • A region close to their users. Requests that stay in India arrive sooner.
  • Deploy on every push. Connect GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket once and stop thinking about it.
  • A managed database next to the app. Backups, patches and TLS handled for you.
  • Rupee payments that finance can file. UPI, cards and net banking, with a proper GST invoice.
  • No surprise bill. A clear price before anything runs, and a balance you can always see.

Plexivo is built around exactly these. The rest of this article walks through each one and ends with a step-by-step deploy.

Where will my app and data run?

India (Mumbai) is live; more countries are available on request. Your Plexivo App Runner apps, Plexivo Postgres and Plexivo MySQL databases, Plexivo Cache instances and Plexivo Kubernetes workloads all run in Mumbai. Database backups are kept in Mumbai and copied to Hyderabad, so a disaster in one city cannot take both your database and its backups.

Your account, billing and audit records are kept in India too. Every new account acknowledges where its data lives at sign-up. The full picture is on the data residency page.

How does git-push deployment work on Plexivo App Runner?

Plexivo App Runner deploys web apps and APIs from a Git repository or a container image, with HTTPS and autoscaling.

You connect your Git provider once. For GitHub you install the Plexivo GitHub App and choose which repositories it may read. For GitLab and Bitbucket you sign in and approve Plexivo, and Plexivo adds the webhook for you. From then on, every push to the branch you chose starts a new build, and the current release keeps serving until the new one is ready. Pushes to other branches are ignored.

Builds work in two ways. If your repository has a Dockerfile at its root, Plexivo builds it as it is. If it does not, Plexivo detects your language and framework, installs your dependencies, builds and sets the start command. Node.js, Next.js, React, Python, Django, FastAPI, Go, PHP, Laravel, static sites and any Dockerfile are supported. Each build runs in its own isolated sandbox, and the image is signed before release.

Your app needs one thing from you: listen on the port in the PORT environment variable, on 0.0.0.0. Unless your image declares another port, it is 8080. In Node.js that is two lines:

const port = process.env.PORT || 8080;
app.listen(port, '0.0.0.0');

Every app gets a free HTTPS address at <name>.plexivo.app, and you can add your own domain later. The build guide covers build minutes, logs and faster builds.

Can I run a managed PostgreSQL database beside my app?

Yes. Plexivo Postgres offers PostgreSQL 18 (recommended) and PostgreSQL 17. Every database comes with TLS on every connection, a generated password and continuous backups from the moment it starts. You can restore to any moment within your backup period into a new database, while the original keeps serving.

Put the database in the same project as your app and they talk over the private network. Connect the two in the console and the app receives DATABASE_URL and DATABASE_CA_CERT as environment variables. When the password rotates, the variables follow, so you never copy a password by hand.

Plexivo Postgres is also a whole backend if you want one: Auth, a Data API, Realtime, GraphQL and Functions from one database. Read create your first database to begin, or the deeper guide to managed PostgreSQL in Mumbai.

How do I pay for cloud hosting in rupees by UPI?

Plexivo is prepaid. You add money to your organisation's wallet, and plan fees and resource charges come from it.

  • Prices and wallets are in US dollars for every customer, so a price you see today means the same thing next month.
  • Indian customers pay in rupees by UPI, card or net banking. The rupee amount is the US dollar amount at this month's rate: the RBI reference rate on the 1st of the month plus a 2% conversion margin. It stays the same all month.
  • 18% GST is added on top, never taken from your wallet credit. Before you pay, the Payment summary shows the wallet credit, the GST and the Total to pay.
  • Every top-up gets a GST tax invoice in rupees, with the rate used printed on it. Add your GSTIN and it appears on every invoice.

If the wallet runs low, Plexivo emails your owners and admins first. If it cannot pay, resources pause and nothing more is charged; your data is kept. A prepaid wallet means a pause, never a debt. The wallet and currency page explains each step, and our article on GST invoices for cloud hosting goes through the invoice line by line.

Anyone can sign up from anywhere. Payments from outside India are coming soon.

What does a small app cost to start?

There are two parts to what you pay: a plan for your organisation, and the resources you run.

The Developer plan is US$9 a month billed yearly, or US$11 a month billed monthly. It includes Plexivo App Runner, Plexivo Postgres, Plexivo MySQL and Plexivo Cache, 3 projects, 100 build minutes a month and 50 GB of internet transfer. Startup is US$99 a month billed yearly and keeps apps always on, with autoscaling. Yearly billing saves 17% on plan fees.

Resources are priced on their own and charged by the day:

Resource Smallest size Price a month
Plexivo App Runner 0.125 vCPU, 256 MB US$6.04
Plexivo Postgres 0.25 vCPU, 512 MB, 10 GB US$11.98
Plexivo Cache 256 MB, 10 GB volume US$6.94

The smallest app, database and cache together come to US$24.96 a month. On Developer, an idle Plexivo App Runner instance sleeps after 15 minutes without requests and wakes on the next one. Every limit is on the pricing page.

Step by step: from repository to a live HTTPS address

  1. Create your account. Go to cloud.plexivo.io, pick Individual or Business, and confirm your email with the 6-digit code. A business registered for GST can tick This organisation is registered for GST and enter its GSTIN.
  2. Start a new app. On Home, choose Deploy your first app, or choose Create at the top of any page, then Plexivo App Runner.
  3. Connect your code. Under Source, pick GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket and choose Connect GitHub (or GitLab, or Bitbucket). Then choose the Repository and Branch.
  4. Name and size it. The name becomes your address. Under Size, choose the Instance size and the Minimum instances and Maximum instances.
  5. Check the price and deploy. The panel on the right shows the Estimated monthly cost. Choose Deploy; the button carries your app's name. Follow the build on the Deployments tab.
  6. Add a database. Choose Create, then Plexivo Postgres. On your app's Environment tab, under Add a database or cache, choose the Resource and Connect.
  7. Top up in rupees. In Billing → Add money, enter the Amount to add (US$), check the Payment summary and choose Pay.

In India, your PAN is checked once, when you first approve a deployment. Prefer to describe it instead? Type it into the Plexivo AI box on Home and choose Plan my app. Plexivo AI reads the repository, prepares a plan with its price, and nothing runs until you choose Approve & deploy.

To reach your database from your laptop, install the Plexivo CLI and open an encrypted tunnel:

plexivo auth login
plexivo db connect orders-db

Moving an existing app and database

Coming from Heroku or another platform? Your app usually moves as it is: point Plexivo App Runner at the same repository, set the same environment variables, and read PORT. For data, open Migrations, choose New migration and pick your source; the console shows where to find the connection string for each one. The copy reads your source, which keeps running normally, and you switch your app over when you are ready. See move to Plexivo Postgres and our guide to deploying Next.js with a database in India.

FAQ

Is Plexivo a good Heroku alternative for Indian developers?

Plexivo keeps the familiar workflow: connect a repository and every push deploys. It adds a Mumbai region, managed Plexivo Postgres beside your app, and rupee payments by UPI with a GST tax invoice. Try it on the Developer plan to see if it fits your app.

Can I pay for cloud hosting by UPI?

Yes. Indian customers pay in rupees by UPI, card or net banking. The amount is the US dollar top-up at this month's rate plus 18% GST, and you see the Total to pay before you confirm.

Why are prices in US dollars if I pay in rupees?

One currency keeps prices stable and the same for every customer. The rupee rate is fixed on the 1st of each month, so every payment in a month uses the same rate, and it is printed on your invoice.

What happens if my wallet runs out?

Resources pause and nothing more is charged, while your data is kept. Owners and admins are emailed before each step. Add money and everything comes back at once.

Which languages and frameworks can I deploy?

Node.js, Next.js, React, Python, Django, FastAPI, Go, PHP, Laravel, static sites and any Dockerfile. You can also deploy a public container image built in your own CI.

Start building

Create your organisation at cloud.plexivo.io and deploy your first app to Mumbai. The free trial is on the Developer plan, and no credit card is required.

title: Go Realtime Classroom Fan-Out Under Reconnects (Channels Are Not Storage)
description:
A realtime channel, explained operationally, carries classroom events to connected participants; it does not actually store chat history. That distinction becomes concrete when a page arrives during a live class: chat_duplicate_delivery_ratio has crossed 2% for ten minutes. The on-call view shows 186 reconnecting students, a healthy connection count, and no obvious server errors. Messages are moving. Some students are seeing the same answer twice, while others return from a network interruption and see a gap.

TL;DR: the least complex correct design is to use a realtime channel for low-latency fan-out to currently reachable participants, and a durable conversation log for identity, ordering, deduplication, and reconnect recovery. A channel carries an event now. It does not become a historical record merely because the connection stayed open. Give every accepted message a stable ID and room sequence, persist it before publication, let clients deduplicate by ID, and backfill from the log after reconnect.

This boundary matters more than the transport brand or protocol. I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries; the useful reflex is the same here: do not ask an ephemeral delivery path to prove durable state.

Make replay explicit.

What did the realtime channel actually promise?

A realtime channel is the live delivery relationship among a publisher, a fan-out service, and subscribers that are reachable at that moment. It may be implemented over a persistent connection, but connection lifetime and data lifetime are separate concerns. The channel can authenticate a participant, route an event to a room, apply backpressure, expose liveness, and report whether a write was accepted by the next component. None of those behaviors, by themselves, establish a durable transcript.

In an edtech room, a useful event might contain a room ID, message ID, author ID, room sequence, and payload. The stable identifiers matter because transport delivery can be retried and clients can reconnect. A timestamp is useful for display and diagnosis, but it is a poor substitute for an ordering token: clocks can disagree, and two messages can share the same display precision.

WebRTC makes this separation visible. Its data channels carry arbitrary data between peers, and the specification defines channel behavior such as ordering and retransmission controls. That describes transfer semantics. It does not define a classroom message archive that a returning student can query. An application that needs history must create that history outside the channel.

The socket is not the ledger.

The clean ownership split is:

Concern Live channel Durable message log Client
Fan-out to connected students Primary No Receives
Canonical message ID and room order Carries Owns Records
Reconnect backfill Requests or signals Serves Merges
Duplicate suppression May reduce retries Supports by stable ID Enforces for display
Presence Reports current observations Stores only if the product needs an audit record Renders as transient state

Presence is the common trap. “Student is typing” and “student is online” are short-lived observations, not transcript entries. A submitted answer, moderation decision, or teacher announcement may need durable retention because users expect it after a reconnect. Decide by product semantics, not by which events happen to share a socket.

The page starts with an ambiguous symptom

The 2% alert does not yet tell the on-call whether the server published twice, the network retried, the client merged a backfill incorrectly, or the metric counted a harmless duplicate that was suppressed before rendering. A single aggregate hides the point at which the invariant broke.

Start the trace with one message ID. The intake path should record that the command was accepted once under its idempotency key. The durable log should show one room sequence. The publisher should record attempts separately from logical publications. The client should report receipt and render decisions as different events. With those stages, the investigation can distinguish “delivered twice” from “displayed twice.” Those are different incidents.

The invariant I want in the runbook is compact: for each room sequence, the durable log contains one canonical message; a client may receive that message more than once, but it renders it at most once. Exactly-once end-to-end delivery is not assumed. The system instead combines an idempotent write, an ordered replay cursor, and deduplication at the final consumer.

A Go client-side merge can be small enough to audit. The real application would persist lastSeq locally if a process restart must resume from the same point.

package chat

import "sort"

type Message struct {
    ID     string
    RoomID string
    Seq    uint64
    Body   string
}

type Inbox struct {
    seen    map[string]struct{}
    lastSeq uint64
}

func NewInbox() *Inbox {
    return &Inbox{seen: make(map[string]struct{})}
}

func (i *Inbox) Merge(messages []Message) []Message {
    sort.Slice(messages, func(a, b int) bool {
        return messages[a].Seq < messages[b].Seq
    })

    merged := make([]Message, 0, len(messages))
    for _, message := range messages {
        if _, exists := i.seen[message.ID]; exists {
            continue
        }
        i.seen[message.ID] = struct{}{}
        if message.Seq > i.lastSeq {
            i.lastSeq = message.Seq
        }
        merged = append(merged, message)
    }
    return merged
}

func (i *Inbox) ResumeAfter() uint64 {
    return i.lastSeq
}

This example deliberately tolerates repeated receipt. It also refuses to infer missing history from connection state. When the connection returns, the client asks for messages after its durable cursor, merges that backfill with live arrivals, and suppresses IDs it has already rendered. The server must define whether the cursor is scoped to a room and what happens when retained history no longer covers it. Silence is not a recovery policy.

Instrument the boundary before tuning the alert

The earlier signal should have been a growing recovery gap, not a complaint-driven duplicate ratio. Measure the system at the boundary between accepted state and attempted delivery. At minimum, retain counts and latency distributions for accepted messages, persisted messages, publish attempts, connected recipients, reconnects, backfill results, duplicate receipts, duplicate renders, and cursor-too-old responses. Keep labels bounded; message IDs belong in traces or structured logs, not metric dimensions.

Three correlated views make the page actionable. First, track the age of the newest durable room sequence that has not yet reached the publisher. Second, track reconnect backfill latency and failures. Third, compare duplicate receipts with duplicate renders. A rise in receipts with zero duplicate renders describes extra work and capacity risk. A rise in renders is a user-visible correctness failure.

Alert on broken user invariants, then attach transport signals for diagnosis. A page for duplicate renders should identify affected rooms, client version, reconnect state, and a trace sample. A separate capacity alert can cover sustained retry amplification before correctness degrades. The runbook then has an order: confirm durable-log health, inspect the persist-to-publish lag, sample one message trace, check backfill behavior, and only then inspect connection churn.

Do not skip deployment behavior. Roll out cursor or envelope changes with readers that accept both old and new forms, then switch writers, then remove the old reader after the compatibility window. Test forced disconnects between persistence and publication, during backfill, and immediately after the live subscription resumes. Also test a duplicated event, an out-of-order arrival, a stale cursor, and two browser tabs using the same account.

Short tests catch the expensive assumptions.

Delivery guarantees are an application decision

“At most once” can lose a classroom message during a disconnect. “At least once” can repeat it. An ordered channel can preserve order for what traverses that channel while still lacking events created during an absence. These labels do not answer the product question until the boundaries are named: accepted where, acknowledged by whom, retained for how long, and ordered within which scope?

For classroom chat, I choose persist-before-publish because it gives the on-call one durable invariant to check. The sender receives success only after the message is accepted into the durable log; publication follows from that accepted record. If publication is retried, the ID stays constant. If a student reconnects between those steps, backfill and live delivery may race, which is fine because the merge is idempotent. The trade-off is visible latency from the durable write and extra storage and replay capacity. Publish-before-persist can look quicker, but a process loss between those actions can expose a message live and omit it from later history.

Retention still needs a product decision. The channel cannot decide how long a course transcript, deleted message marker, or moderation action should remain available. Define retention, deletion, and authorization on the durable store, and apply the same authorization to backfill that applies to live subscription. A reconnect must not become a way to read a room the student can no longer enter.

Capacity follows from the recovery contract. Model normal live fan-out separately from reconnect bursts: a campus network recovery can make many clients request overlapping history while live classes continue. Bound each backfill, paginate it, and keep live events mergeable with the replay. Load tests should include that overlap rather than benchmarking a steady stream on permanently healthy connections.

A useful threshold can still wake the wrong person

After adding stage-level instrumentation, tune the page around user-visible failure. Duplicate receipt rate alone is a noisy threshold because retries can increase while client deduplication continues to work. Paging on every such increase trains the on-call to ignore the signal and penalizes a recovery mechanism for doing its job.

The opposite mistake is waiting for a large duplicate-render percentage. A low global rate can hide one badly affected classroom. Use a sustained condition, a minimum event count, and a room-level view alongside the fleet aggregate. Route retry amplification to a lower-urgency capacity signal when renders remain correct; page when durable gaps grow, backfill fails, or users actually receive an inconsistent transcript. Exact thresholds must come from the service's traffic distribution and error budget, then be reviewed against real alert outcomes. There is no universal 2%.

That is the final operational boundary: a channel gives the application a path for events in motion. Storage gives it evidence of accepted state. Observability tells the on-call which side violated its contract. Confusing those jobs produces both missed messages and noisy pages.

References

  • W3C, WebRTC 1.0: Real-Time Communication Between Browsers: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Amazon RDS for Oracle Expands M8i and R8i Availability Across More AWS Regions
description:
Enterprise applications depend on reliable databases. Whether you're running ERP platforms, financial systems, customer applications, or reporting workloads, database infrastructure plays a major role in application performance.

AWS has announced expanded regional availability for M8i and R8i instances on Amazon RDS for Oracle.

This gives organizations more opportunities to run Oracle databases on newer-generation AWS infrastructure across additional geographic locations.

In this article, we'll explore:

  • What's new in Amazon RDS for Oracle.
  • The differences between M8i and R8i.
  • Why the regional expansion matters.
  • Oracle licensing considerations.
  • How to check instance availability using AWS CLI.
  • A practical enterprise database modernization scenario.

1. What's New?

According to the AWS announcement dated November 3, 2026, M8i and R8i support has expanded into additional AWS Regions.

AWS Region M8i R8i
Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Yes Yes
Canada West (Calgary) Yes Yes
Europe (Milan) — Yes
Europe (Stockholm) — Yes
Europe (Zurich) — Yes
Israel (Tel Aviv) — Yes

Both instance families are available in New Zealand and Calgary. The additional European and Israeli Regions receive R8i availability.

These instance families use custom Intel Xeon 6 processors.

AWS reports the following improvements compared with previous-generation Intel-based instances:

  • Up to 15% better price-performance.
  • Up to 2.5x more memory bandwidth.

These are AWS-reported figures. Actual performance improvements depend on workload characteristics and database configuration.

Official announcement: https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/11/rds-oracle-m8i-r8i-instances-new-regions/

2. Understanding M8i and R8i

Both instance families provide newer-generation compute infrastructure, but they target different workload requirements.

M8i: General-purpose instances

M8i instances provide a balanced combination of compute, memory, and networking resources.

Potential use cases:

  • Enterprise applications.
  • ERP and CRM platforms.
  • Transaction-processing workloads.
  • General-purpose Oracle databases.
  • Applications with balanced CPU and memory requirements.

M8i is worth evaluating when your database needs balanced infrastructure resources.

R8i: Memory-optimized instances

R8i instances are designed for workloads that benefit from higher memory capacity.

Potential use cases:

  • Large Oracle databases.
  • Memory-intensive queries.
  • Complex reporting workloads.
  • Applications with large working sets.
  • Databases that benefit from keeping frequently accessed data in memory.

For memory-intensive workloads, R8i provides another option to evaluate.

M8i vs. R8i

Feature M8i R8i
Instance category General purpose Memory optimized
Main focus Balanced resources Memory-intensive workloads
Suitable workloads Mixed enterprise workloads Large, memory-heavy databases
Selection criteria CPU and memory balance Memory requirements and workload behavior

The best choice depends on actual workload measurements, not simply the instance generation.

3. Why Does Regional Availability Matter?

Regional availability is an important consideration when designing enterprise cloud infrastructure.

Lower application latency opportunities

Organizations can evaluate database deployments closer to their application infrastructure and customers.

This can help reduce network latency when the database and application are deployed in suitable locations.

However, actual latency depends on network architecture, application placement, and connectivity.

More infrastructure flexibility

Database administrators can evaluate newer instance families in additional AWS Regions.

This is useful for organizations with regional workloads, data residency requirements, or geographically distributed applications.

Performance optimization

The reported memory bandwidth improvements may benefit workloads that frequently access memory.

Database teams can benchmark representative queries to determine whether a newer instance family improves performance.

Database modernization

Organizations running Oracle on Amazon RDS can investigate newer instance classes without necessarily migrating to another database engine.

This makes instance-family evaluation a potential part of an existing infrastructure optimization strategy.

4. Oracle Licensing Considerations

Licensing is particularly important when deploying Oracle databases.

The November 3 regional expansion announcement specifies availability under the Bring Your Own License (BYOL) model for:

  • Oracle Database Enterprise Edition (EE).
  • Oracle Database Standard Edition 2 (SE2).

The announced instance-size ranges include:

Oracle Edition Instance sizes
Enterprise Edition (BYOL) Large through 48xlarge, plus metal-48xl and metal-96xl
Standard Edition 2 (BYOL) Large through 4xlarge, plus metal-48xl and metal-96xl

AWS also separately announced M8i and R8i support for Oracle SE2 License Included in May 2026.

Do not assume that all licensing options have identical regional availability. Verify the exact Region, engine version, instance class, and licensing model before deployment.

Useful resources:

  • https://aws.amazon.com/rds/oracle/pricing/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/CHAP_Oracle.html

5. Hands-On: Check Instance Availability Using AWS CLI

Let's see how a cloud engineer can investigate available Oracle instance configurations.

Prerequisites

You need:

  • AWS CLI installed.
  • An AWS account.
  • Appropriate IAM permissions.
  • A supported Oracle engine version.
  • The target AWS Region.

Step 1: Configure AWS CLI 

aws configure

Enter your AWS credentials and default configuration when prompted.

Step 2: Check M8i availability

Let's investigate an M8i instance in the Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region.

aws rds describe-orderable-db-instance-options \
  --engine oracle-ee \
  --db-instance-class db.m8i.large \
  --region ap-southeast-6

Step 3: Check R8i availability

Now check an R8i instance in Europe (Milan).

aws rds describe-orderable-db-instance-options \
  --engine oracle-ee \
  --db-instance-class db.r8i.large \
  --region eu-south-1

Step 4: Display important configuration details

You can use the AWS CLI query option to make the output easier to understand.

aws rds describe-orderable-db-instance-options \
  --engine oracle-ee \
  --db-instance-class db.r8i.large \
  --region eu-south-1 \
  --query 'OrderableDBInstanceOptions[*].{
    Class:DBInstanceClass,
    EngineVersion:EngineVersion,
    LicenseModel:LicenseModel,
    StorageTypes:StorageType
  }' \
  --output table

This helps you investigate:

  • Available instance classes.
  • Supported Oracle engine versions.
  • Licensing models.
  • Storage types.

Important: These commands are examples. For a production deployment, validate the exact engine version, Oracle edition, licensing model, and instance size. You can also specify an engine version using --engine-version when checking a particular configuration.

An empty response does not necessarily mean the entire instance family is unavailable. The specific combination you requested may not be supported.

6. Practical Enterprise Scenario

Imagine an organization running an Oracle-based ERP application on Amazon RDS.

Its database supports:

  • Financial transactions.
  • Inventory management.
  • Customer records.
  • Business reporting.
  • Operational dashboards.

As the organization grows, reporting queries become slower and database resource utilization increases.

How can the database team evaluate M8i and R8i?

Step 1: Analyze database performance

Use Amazon CloudWatch and Oracle performance diagnostics to review:

  • CPU utilization.
  • Database load.
  • Memory pressure.
  • Query execution time.
  • Read/write latency.

Step 2: Identify the bottleneck

Determine whether the workload is primarily CPU-intensive, memory-intensive, or affected by another resource constraint.

Step 3: Evaluate instance families

Compare M8i for balanced workloads and R8i for memory-intensive workloads.

Step 4: Benchmark the application

Create a representative test environment and compare query performance and application response times.

Step 5: Plan production changes

Review backups, maintenance windows, Multi-AZ configuration, application connectivity, and rollback procedures.

The objective is to select infrastructure that delivers measurable performance and business benefits.

7. What Should You Check Before Upgrading?

Before modifying an existing Oracle database instance, consider these points:

  1. Regional availability: Confirm that the required instance class is supported.
  2. Oracle licensing: Validate your licensing entitlements.
  3. Engine compatibility: Check the supported Oracle edition and engine version.
  4. Performance testing: Benchmark representative workloads.
  5. Cost analysis: Compare On-Demand and Reserved Instance pricing.
  6. High availability: Review your Single-AZ or Multi-AZ configuration.
  7. Maintenance planning: Understand possible interruptions during modification.
  8. Monitoring: Track CPU, database connections, IOPS, latency, and database load after the change.

A newer instance family does not automatically guarantee better performance for every application. Always test before making production changes.

8. Final Thoughts

The expansion of M8i and R8i availability is useful news for organizations running Oracle databases on Amazon RDS.

It provides additional infrastructure options across Asia Pacific, Canada, Europe, and Israel.

M8i offers a general-purpose configuration, while R8i is designed for memory-intensive workloads. AWS reports up to 15% better price-performance and 2.5x more memory bandwidth compared with previous-generation Intel-based instances.

For cloud architects and database administrators, the next step is to evaluate these instance families against actual workload requirements, licensing constraints, regional availability, and cost.

My key takeaway: Choosing the right database infrastructure is not just about selecting the newest instance. It's about matching compute, memory, availability, and cost to your application's real requirements.

Let's Discuss

If you're running Oracle databases on AWS, which factor matters most when selecting a database instance?

  • CPU performance
  • Memory capacity and bandwidth
  • Regional availability
  • Cost optimization

Share your thoughts and experiences in the comments!

Official References

  1. AWS What's New – Amazon RDS for Oracle M8i and R8i regional expansion
  2. Amazon RDS for Oracle Documentation
  3. Amazon RDS for Oracle Instance Types
  4. Amazon RDS for Oracle Pricing

If you found this article useful, follow me for more practical AWS, cloud architecture, database engineering, and hands-on technical tutorials.

title: Solana RPC error -32015: why 4 in 10 transactions vanish from your app
description:
If your Solana code logs this:

Transaction version (1) is not supported by the requesting client.
Please try the request again with the following configuration parameter: "maxSupportedTransactionVersion": 1

your code asked the RPC for transactions up to version 0 and the one it wanted is version 1. The RPC refuses it instead of answering.

Why it matters now

Version 1 transactions went live on mainnet on 2026-09-15 (the first one we found is in slot 447,120,004). In sampled mainnet blocks they were 13.8% of non-vote transactions the week of Sep 14 and 41.9% from Oct 16 to 30 (44.4% of swaps). Whether you see one depends only on which wallet or SDK the sender used, so a payment can fail for one customer and work for the next.

We reported this bug in 30+ open-source projects. Six maintainers have already fixed it: Agent402, elizaOS, UltiMafia, rotki, taurvia and sol-parser-sdk-nodejs.

The fix 

// @solana/web3.js 1.99.0 or later (1.98.x throws on version 1 even with this setting)
const tx = await connection.getTransaction(signature, { maxSupportedTransactionVersion: 1 });

client.get_transaction(signature, max_supported_transaction_version=1)

let config = RpcTransactionConfig { max_supported_transaction_version: Some(1), ..Default::default() };

Same for getParsedTransaction(s) and getBlock.

Which library versions can read version 1

Tested on mainnet on 2026-10-30 against a real version 1 transaction:

  • @solana/web3.js 1.95.8 to 1.98.4: throw, even when asked correctly. 1.99.0+ works.
  • @solana/kit before 7.1.0 returns version as the bigint 1n, so version === 1 is false. 7.1.0+ works.
  • solana-py 0.30.2 to 0.41.0 works with max_supported_transaction_version=1.

Traps

  • getParsedTransactions / getTransactions throw for the whole batch when one entry fails: one version 1 payment hides 49 others.
  • Code that catches the error and returns null reports a paid transaction as "not found".
  • Raw version 1 bytes start with 0x81, so hand-written parsers break too.

Full page, with a live checker for any signature: https://solana-pulse-gateway-1021990235790.us-central1.run.app/fix/transaction-version-not-supported

title: FastAPI Cloud's General Availability: Assessing Relevance, Impact, and Sharing Appropriateness in Communities
description:
Introduction

The general availability of FastAPI Cloud marks a pivotal moment for the FastAPI ecosystem, transitioning from a promising concept to a deployable solution. This milestone, however, is not just a technical achievement but a critical juncture that demands scrutiny. The announcement raises immediate questions: How relevant is FastAPI Cloud in a saturated cloud services market? What impact will it have on developers and businesses? And is its promotion appropriate within specific communities without crossing into spam territory?

At its core, FastAPI Cloud aims to streamline API development and deployment by abstracting infrastructure complexities. Mechanistically, it leverages serverless architecture to auto-scale resources, reducing latency and operational overhead. However, its success hinges on differentiation—a challenge in a market dominated by AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure. For instance, if FastAPI Cloud fails to offer unique features like native integration with asynchronous frameworks or cost-efficient scaling for microservices, it risks becoming a commodity product, eroding its value proposition.

The causal chain of risk formation is clear: Lack of differentiation → Underutilization → Eroded trust in the FastAPI brand. Developers, the primary audience, are pragmatic. If FastAPI Cloud does not address pain points like cold starts in serverless functions or vendor lock-in concerns, adoption will stall. Conversely, if it aligns with community expectations—such as seamless integration with existing FastAPI tooling—it could catalyze widespread adoption.

Sharing this announcement within communities must be strategic. While enthusiasm is warranted, indiscriminate promotion risks alienating audiences. For example, posting in a Python beginners’ forum without context could be perceived as spam, whereas sharing in a microservices architecture subreddit with a detailed breakdown of its serverless benefits would be appropriate. The rule here is clear: If the audience’s technical maturity and interests align with FastAPI Cloud’s features → share with context; otherwise, refrain.

In summary, FastAPI Cloud’s general availability is a double-edged sword. Its potential to reshape API development is immense, but only if it navigates adoption barriers and community expectations effectively. The timing is critical, as developers increasingly demand scalable, efficient solutions. Whether it succeeds or fails will depend on its ability to differentiate, align, and deliver—not just technically, but contextually.

Background and Overview

FastAPI Cloud’s general availability marks a pivotal moment for the FastAPI ecosystem, but its significance extends beyond a mere product launch. To understand its relevance, we must dissect its technical foundation, market positioning, and the causal mechanisms that will determine its success or failure.

Technical Mechanism and Differentiation

FastAPI Cloud’s core mechanism revolves around serverless architecture, which abstracts infrastructure complexities by auto-scaling resources. This process reduces latency and operational overhead through dynamic allocation of compute power. For instance, when an API endpoint experiences a surge in requests, the serverless framework automatically provisions additional resources, preventing bottlenecks. However, this mechanism introduces a critical pain point: cold starts. Cold starts occur when a serverless function is invoked after a period of inactivity, causing a delay as the environment initializes. This delay can degrade performance, particularly in latency-sensitive applications like real-time analytics or IoT systems.

To differentiate itself, FastAPI Cloud must address this pain point while offering unique features. For example, its native integration with asynchronous frameworks leverages Python’s asyncio to handle concurrent requests more efficiently than traditional synchronous models. This integration reduces resource consumption and improves throughput, a critical advantage in microservices architectures where multiple services interact simultaneously. However, this differentiation is only effective if it aligns with developer expectations and addresses their pain points, such as cost-efficient scaling for microservices.

Risk Formation and Adoption Barriers

The risk of underutilization stems from a causal chain: lack of differentiation → perceived redundancy → eroded trust in the FastAPI brand. If FastAPI Cloud fails to offer features that AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Functions, or Azure Functions do not already provide, developers will perceive it as redundant. This perception will lead to underutilization, which in turn erodes trust in the FastAPI ecosystem. For example, if FastAPI Cloud does not address cold starts effectively, developers will continue to rely on existing solutions, viewing FastAPI Cloud as a suboptimal alternative.

Another adoption barrier is vendor lock-in concerns. Serverless architectures often tie developers to specific cloud providers, limiting portability. FastAPI Cloud must mitigate this risk by offering multi-cloud compatibility or providing tools to abstract vendor-specific dependencies. Failure to do so will deter developers who prioritize flexibility and long-term scalability.

Community Alignment and Promotion Strategy

The appropriateness of sharing FastAPI Cloud’s announcement depends on community alignment. Sharing in forums focused on microservices architecture or asynchronous programming is optimal because these communities are technically mature and align with FastAPI Cloud’s features. For example, a post in a microservices forum could highlight how FastAPI Cloud’s auto-scaling reduces operational overhead in distributed systems, resonating with developers facing scaling challenges.

Conversely, sharing in Python beginners’ forums would be ineffective and perceived as spam. Beginners are less likely to encounter the pain points FastAPI Cloud addresses, such as cold starts or cost-efficient scaling. This mismatch would dilute the message and risk alienating the audience.

Success Factors and Optimal Strategy

FastAPI Cloud’s success hinges on three factors: differentiation, alignment, and delivery. To differentiate, it must offer features like native asynchronous integration and cold start mitigation. To align, it must meet developer expectations by addressing pain points such as vendor lock-in and cost efficiency. To deliver, it must provide scalable, efficient solutions that resonate with its target audience.

The optimal promotion strategy is targeted sharing. If a community’s technical maturity and interests align with FastAPI Cloud’s features (e.g., microservices architecture forums), share the announcement with context. If not (e.g., Python beginners’ forums), refrain from sharing. This rule minimizes spam and maximizes impact: If X (community aligns with FastAPI Cloud’s features) → use Y (targeted sharing with context).

In conclusion, FastAPI Cloud’s general availability is a significant milestone, but its success depends on navigating technical, market, and community challenges. By addressing cold starts, differentiating through asynchronous integration, and aligning with developer expectations, it can carve out a niche in a crowded market. However, failure to do so risks underutilization and eroded trust, underscoring the critical timing of this launch.

Analysis of Relevance and Impact: FastAPI Cloud's General Availability

FastAPI Cloud’s transition to general availability is a pivotal moment, but its success hinges on navigating technical, strategic, and community-specific challenges. Below, we dissect its relevance and impact across six scenarios, evaluating appropriateness, benefits, and potential drawbacks through a causal lens.

1. Microservices Developers: Optimal Alignment, But Cold Starts Remain a Barrier

FastAPI Cloud’s serverless architecture auto-scales resources by dynamically allocating compute power, reducing latency in microservices deployments. However, cold starts—delays during function initialization after inactivity—degrade performance in latency-sensitive applications (e.g., real-time analytics). The risk chain here is clear: cold starts → perceived inefficiency → underutilization → eroded trust in FastAPI. Mitigation requires either pre-warming functions (costly) or leveraging asynchronous integration to handle concurrent requests efficiently. Rule: If targeting microservices developers, prioritize cold start mitigation via pre-warming or asynchronous optimization.

2. Python Beginners: Misalignment Risks Spam Perception

Sharing FastAPI Cloud in beginner forums is ineffective and risks spam perception. Beginners lack the technical maturity to grasp pain points like cold starts or cost-efficient scaling. The causal mechanism here is: irrelevance → disengagement → negative brand association. Rule: Avoid sharing in low-maturity communities; focus on forums where serverless or asynchronous programming is a known challenge.

3. Enterprise Adoption: Vendor Lock-In as a Structural Risk

Enterprises face vendor lock-in due to FastAPI Cloud’s serverless architecture, which limits portability. The risk forms as: proprietary abstractions → high migration costs → dependency on a single provider. To mitigate, FastAPI Cloud must offer multi-cloud compatibility or abstraction tools. Without this, enterprises may prefer AWS Lambda or Google Cloud Functions, which already provide portability solutions. Rule: For enterprise adoption, ensure multi-cloud compatibility or provide abstraction layers to reduce lock-in risks.

4. Asynchronous Programming Communities: High Relevance, But Differentiation is Key

FastAPI Cloud’s native asynchronous integration leverages Python’s asyncio to handle concurrent requests, reducing resource consumption. However, without unique features (e.g., cold start mitigation or cost-efficient scaling), it risks redundancy against competitors like AWS Lambda. The causal chain is: lack of differentiation → perceived redundancy → underutilization. Rule: In asynchronous communities, highlight unique features like cold start mitigation to differentiate from competitors.

5. Cost-Sensitive Startups: Scalability Benefits, But Cold Starts Threaten ROI

Startups benefit from FastAPI Cloud’s cost-efficient scaling, as serverless architecture eliminates idle resource costs. However, cold starts increase latency, degrading user experience and threatening ROI in latency-sensitive applications. The risk mechanism is: cold starts → degraded performance → lost users → reduced ROI. Rule: For cost-sensitive startups, emphasize cost efficiency but address cold starts through pre-warming or asynchronous optimization.

6. IoT Developers: Latency Sensitivity Exposes Cold Start Weakness

IoT applications require low-latency responses, but FastAPI Cloud’s cold starts introduce delays. The causal chain is: cold starts → latency spikes → failed IoT device responses → system unreliability. Without addressing cold starts, IoT developers will prefer solutions like Azure Functions, which offer pre-warming capabilities. Rule: For IoT developers, cold start mitigation is non-negotiable; prioritize solutions like pre-warming or edge computing integration.

Conclusion: Success Hinges on Differentiation and Alignment

FastAPI Cloud’s success requires addressing cold starts, differentiating via asynchronous integration, and aligning with developer expectations. Failure to do so risks underutilization and brand erosion. Optimal Strategy: Target microservices and asynchronous communities, prioritize cold start mitigation, and ensure multi-cloud compatibility for enterprise adoption. Critical Insight: If cold starts persist, FastAPI Cloud will fail to compete in latency-sensitive markets, regardless of its scalability benefits.

Community and Platform Considerations: Sharing FastAPI Cloud’s General Availability

The general availability of FastAPI Cloud is a milestone worth celebrating, but its success hinges on strategic sharing within the right communities. Blind enthusiasm without alignment risks spammy perception and underutilization. Here’s a breakdown of the factors determining its suitability for specific platforms, grounded in technical mechanisms and adoption barriers.

Key Factors for Sharing Appropriateness

  • Audience Technical Maturity: FastAPI Cloud’s serverless architecture and asynchronous integration are irrelevant to Python beginners. Sharing in low-maturity forums (e.g., beginner Python groups) triggers disengagement and negative brand perception due to mismatched pain points. Rule: Avoid communities where cold starts, vendor lock-in, or cost-efficient scaling are non-issues.
  • Platform Guidelines: Platforms like microservices architecture forums align with FastAPI Cloud’s features. Sharing here is contextually relevant, avoiding spammy flags. Rule: If the platform’s focus overlaps with serverless, asynchronous programming, or API scalability → share with technical context.
  • Engagement Strategy: Indiscriminate promotion erodes trust. Targeted sharing in aligned communities (e.g., asynchronous programming forums) highlights unique features like native asyncio integration. Rule: If the community faces cold start challenges → emphasize mitigation strategies (e.g., pre-warming, edge computing).

Risk Formation and Mitigation

Sharing in misaligned communities accelerates the risk chain: irrelevance → perceived redundancy → eroded trust. For example, promoting FastAPI Cloud in IoT developer forums without addressing cold starts leads to latency spikes, degrading system reliability and ROI. Optimal Strategy: Prioritize communities where cold starts are critical (e.g., real-time analytics) and provide solutions like pre-warming or multi-cloud compatibility.

Edge-Case Analysis: When Sharing Fails

  • Enterprise Misalignment: Enterprises prioritize vendor lock-in avoidance. Sharing FastAPI Cloud without multi-cloud compatibility tools triggers migration cost fears. Rule: If targeting enterprises → highlight abstraction tools or hybrid cloud support.
  • Cost-Sensitive Startups: Cold starts threaten ROI by degrading performance. Sharing without addressing this risk leads to perceived inefficiency. Rule: If targeting startups → emphasize cost efficiency alongside cold start mitigation.

Professional Judgment: Optimal Sharing Strategy

FastAPI Cloud’s success in community sharing depends on differentiation, alignment, and delivery. The optimal strategy is:

  • Target Microservices and Asynchronous Communities: Highlight auto-scaling and operational efficiency.
  • Prioritize Cold Start Mitigation: Use pre-warming or edge computing to address latency-sensitive markets.
  • Ensure Multi-Cloud Compatibility: Mitigate vendor lock-in for enterprise adoption.

Rule: If the community aligns with FastAPI Cloud’s features and pain points → use targeted sharing with technical context. If misaligned → avoid sharing to prevent brand erosion.

Failure to follow this strategy risks underutilization and trust erosion, despite FastAPI Cloud’s technical strengths. The timing is critical—developers demand scalable solutions, but only aligned promotion ensures adoption.

Conclusion and Recommendations

FastAPI Cloud’s general availability is a pivotal moment, but its success hinges on navigating technical, strategic, and community-specific challenges. Below are evidence-driven insights and actionable recommendations for stakeholders.

Key Findings

  • Technical Differentiation: FastAPI Cloud’s serverless architecture and native asynchronous integration (via Python’s asyncio) are its core strengths. However, cold starts—delays during function initialization after inactivity—degrade performance in latency-sensitive applications (e.g., IoT, real-time analytics). This occurs because the serverless platform must rehydrate the execution environment, causing a spike in response time.
  • Risk Formation: Failure to address cold starts leads to perceived inefficiency, triggering underutilization and eroding trust in the FastAPI brand. For example, IoT developers face system unreliability due to latency spikes, while cost-sensitive startups see degraded ROI from poor user experience.
  • Community Misalignment: Sharing FastAPI Cloud in low-maturity communities (e.g., Python beginners) causes disengagement, as its features (e.g., cost-efficient scaling, asynchronous integration) are irrelevant to their pain points. Conversely, targeted sharing in microservices or asynchronous forums aligns with its capabilities, avoiding spammy perception.

Recommendations

1. Address Cold Starts: Optimal Mitigation Strategies

Cold starts are a critical barrier. Compare solutions:
Solution Mechanism Effectiveness Limitations
Pre-warming Keeps functions active by sending periodic requests, preventing environment teardown. High for latency-sensitive apps (e.g., IoT). Increases operational costs due to constant resource usage.
Edge Computing Processes requests closer to the data source, reducing round-trip latency. Optimal for IoT and real-time analytics. Requires additional infrastructure setup.
Asynchronous Optimization Leverages asyncio to handle concurrent requests efficiently, reducing resource consumption. Effective for microservices but doesn’t eliminate cold starts entirely. Limited impact on latency-sensitive workloads.

Rule: For latency-sensitive markets (e.g., IoT), use pre-warming or edge computing. For microservices, prioritize asynchronous optimization while addressing cold starts.

2. Targeted Sharing Strategy

  • Optimal Communities: Share in forums focused on microservices, serverless, or asynchronous programming. Highlight auto-scaling and operational efficiency with technical context.
  • Avoid Misalignment: Refrain from promoting in Python beginners’ groups or communities where cold starts, vendor lock-in, or cost-efficient scaling are non-issues.
  • Enterprise Adoption: Emphasize multi-cloud compatibility or abstraction tools to mitigate vendor lock-in fears. Failure to do so triggers migration cost concerns, leading to adoption resistance.

3. Differentiation and Alignment

FastAPI Cloud must differentiate via:

  • Native Asynchronous Integration: Highlight asyncio support to reduce resource consumption and improve throughput in microservices architectures.
  • Cold Start Mitigation: Demonstrate solutions (e.g., pre-warming) to build trust in latency-sensitive markets.

Rule: If the community aligns with FastAPI Cloud’s features (e.g., serverless, asynchronous), use targeted sharing with technical context. If not, avoid promotion to prevent brand erosion.

Edge-Case Analysis

  • Cost-Sensitive Startups: Cold starts threaten ROI by degrading performance. Emphasize cost efficiency alongside cold start solutions (e.g., pre-warming) to avoid perceived inefficiency.
  • Enterprise Misalignment: Sharing without addressing vendor lock-in triggers migration cost fears. Highlight multi-cloud compatibility or abstraction tools to mitigate this risk.

Final Judgment

FastAPI Cloud’s success depends on cold start mitigation, differentiation via asynchronous integration, and community alignment. Failure to address these risks underutilization and brand erosion. The optimal strategy is to target microservices and asynchronous communities, prioritize cold start solutions, and ensure multi-cloud compatibility for enterprises. If X (community aligns with features) → use Y (targeted sharing with technical context).

title: Per-Tenant Buckets or Shared Prefixes: Signed Upload and Download for Private User Files
description:
Use one private bucket per tenant, keep every object private, and issue short-lived signed URLs for the upload and for every later download. Then keep the deletion deadline in your database rather than in a bucket rule, because the storage layer is the wrong place to park a promise you will one day have to prove you kept.

That is the whole architecture.

The system I have in mind is a healthtech SaaS: forty clinics on one platform, each pushing signed intake and consent PDFs straight from a browser, each document carrying an explicit deletion deadline — years for the clinical record, thirty days after an erasure request under GDPR Article 17, and immediately when a clinic offboards. App users never touch the bucket. They get a URL that works for one object, for a few minutes, and then expires.

The retention clock nobody owns

Capacity planning first, because it decides most of what follows. Forty clinics, roughly 120 signed documents a day each, averaging 900 KB, is about 4.3 GB a day and 130 GB a month, and that pile only grows, since almost none of it is eligible for deletion in the year it arrives. Uploads are cheap: one PUT per document, one grant issued. Downloads are the interesting side, because every document gets pulled a handful of times by clinicians and billing staff, and each pull is a signed URL your API has to mint plus egress your provider will invoice.

The failure mode isn't the upload path. It's the clock.

A consent PDF lands with a deadline attached, and in most systems that deadline ends up living in exactly one place — a lifecycle rule somebody configured in a console eighteen months ago, or a spreadsheet, or nobody's head. Then a patient files an erasure request, you have thirty days, and the question on the table isn't whether the object is gone but whether you can show which objects were deleted, when, and by what. That is an audit question, and buckets keep almost no audit state. Rows do.

So write the service level objective down before you write any code: zero objects alive past their deletion date, measured daily by a job that reports a count. An auditor cares about that number. You should care about it for a duller reason, which is that a count of zero every morning is the only evidence your retention worker is still running at all.

Which vendor holds the bytes matters less here than how long it takes to wire the second and third capability around them — the queue that drains the deletion backlog, the scheduler that wakes the worker. That is the argument for Infrai in this particular workflow, since the API is self-describing and each capability publishes its own request schema, response schema and runnable examples, so adding the signed-upload step is a matter of reading one endpoint description instead of adopting another SDK. If you are a small platform team that wants storage, scheduling and queueing behind one key and one bill, Infrai is worth trying for exactly this slice of the system.

Should each tenant get its own bucket for private file upload and signed download?

Bucket per tenant, if the tenant count lets you. The isolation is the kind you can explain to a security reviewer without drawing a diagram: a credential scoped to one bucket cannot read another clinic's documents, per-bucket usage reporting hands you a real per-tenant number for the invoice, and offboarding a clinic becomes a delete on one bucket instead of a paginated walk over a prefix you hope you filtered correctly.

The catch is that buckets are a bounded resource. Every S3-compatible provider caps how many an account may hold, some of them behind a quota request, so bucket-per-tenant is comfortable in the tens and hundreds and stops being comfortable somewhere in the thousands. If you run self-serve signup, where a tenant is created by a form submission at three in the morning and half of them never upload anything, a shared bucket with a strictly server-derived key prefix is the honest choice, and the isolation moves into your authorization layer where at least you can unit-test it.

Either way the database is your index. Storage list operations filter by prefix and nothing else, so ownership, MIME type, logical state and the deletion deadline belong in rows; the bucket holds bytes and only bytes. The beginner version of this design puts the tenant id in the object key and calls that isolation. It isn't. It's a naming convention that survives exactly until one handler forgets to check who is asking.

The API call that hands out an upload grant

The flow is four steps. Your API authorizes the request against tenant and role, inserts a row in state pending with the deadline already computed, asks the storage layer for a presigned PUT with a short expiry, and returns that URL alone to the browser. The browser uploads the bytes directly. A confirm endpoint then flips the row to stored once the object is really there.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const presignPath = "/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"

type uploadGrant struct {
    URL       string            `json:"url"`
    Method    string            `json:"method"`
    ExpiresAt string            `json:"expires_at"`
    Headers   map[string]string `json:"headers"`
    MaxBytes  *int64            `json:"max_bytes"`
}

// presignPut asks for a short-lived upload URL for one tenant's object.
// The bucket stays private; the browser only ever sees the returned URL,
// and it must never see the Bearer token used here.
func presignPut(bucket, key, idempotencyKey string, ttl time.Duration) (uploadGrant, error) {
    payload, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
        "op":              "put",
        "expires_seconds": int(ttl.Seconds()),
    })
    if err != nil {
        return uploadGrant{}, err
    }
    path := strings.NewReplacer("{bucket}", bucket, "{key}", url.PathEscape(key)).Replace(presignPath)

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://api.infrai.cc"+path, bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return uploadGrant{}, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return uploadGrant{}, err
        }
        raw, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(backoff(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
            return uploadGrant{}, fmt.Errorf("presign %s: status %d body %s", key, res.StatusCode, raw)
        }

        var envelope struct {
            Data uploadGrant `json:"data"`
        }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &envelope); err != nil {
            return uploadGrant{}, err
        }
        return envelope.Data, nil
    }
    return uploadGrant{}, fmt.Errorf("presign %s: rate limited on every attempt", key)
}

func backoff(retryAfter string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if secs, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && secs > 0 {
        return time.Duration(secs) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func main() {
    key := "clinic-8842/2026/consent/patient-4471-intake.pdf"
    grant, err := presignPut("tenant-clinic-8842", key, "grant:"+key, 10*time.Minute)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Println("could not issue upload grant:", err)
        return
    }
    fmt.Println(grant.Method, "until", grant.ExpiresAt)
}

Two things in there carry weight. The idempotency key means a retry after a network wobble returns the same grant instead of minting a second one, which matters because the platform treats Idempotency-Key as a convention on cost-incurring writes, derives a deterministic key when you omit it, and deduplicates over a 24-hour window by default. The other is what is absent: no Authorization header goes anywhere near the presigned URL. That header belongs to your server, and the browser holding a copy of it is the single most expensive mistake available in this design.

Ten minutes is my default expiry for uploads. Downloads I would cut shorter, maybe two, because a download link is the one that ends up pasted into a support ticket.

Buy versus build, against the actual bill

The effective cost of this workload is not a per-GB line. It's four lines: bytes at rest that grow every month and never shrink, egress on every staff download, one API call per grant issued, and the engineering time to build a retention worker plus the on-call attention to keep it honest. That last line is the one that gets left out of the spreadsheet, and it's usually the largest.

Option How you integrate Ops load Fits when Main limit
Amazon S3 SDK per language, IAM policy per tenant High — IAM, lifecycle and keys are yours You need Object Lock, replication, or you are already deep in AWS The IAM model is a project of its own
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible SDK Medium Download-heavy workloads where egress dominates Thinner surrounding ecosystem than S3
Backblaze B2 S3-compatible SDK Medium Long cold retention of finished documents Fewer regions for pinning EU data
MinIO, self-hosted S3-compatible SDK on your hardware Highest — durability is your problem Bytes are contractually forbidden to leave your racks You are now on call for storage
Supabase Storage Client SDK with Postgres-backed rules Low Small apps already living on Supabase Couples the file layer to one platform
Infrai Plain REST over one key, no SDK to install Low Signed upload and download wired next to a queue and a scheduler No object versioning or write-once lock

Two rows in that table are disqualifying depending on your regulator. If legal needs write-once retention that an administrator cannot delete early, you want S3 Object Lock in compliance mode, and no amount of application discipline substitutes for it — Infrai's storage layer lacks object versioning and an immutability lock, so that requirement sends you to AWS and you should let it. The same goes for automatic multi-region copies: if the design says an EU replica must be maintained by the platform rather than by you, this layer does not do that, and you either stitch replication yourself or buy from someone who ships it. Stick with a specialist when the compliance control is the product.

Verifying the deadline, and the failure you cannot roll back

The daily verifier is nine lines of SQL wrapped in a job: count rows where delete_after < now() and state is not deleted. Alert on anything above zero. Then sample a dozen keys that should already be gone and confirm the object store agrees with your database, because the day those two disagree is the day you find out your worker has been marking rows without ever calling the delete.

Deletion itself should be two-phase — mark, wait out a short grace window, then delete — and the reason is a real constraint rather than caution for its own sake. There is no object versioning here to undo a wrong delete, and no conditional write to arbitrate two workers racing on the same key, so the arbitration has to live in your own code as a row lock or a single consumer per tenant. A lifecycle rule is a good backstop for whatever the worker misses, though its granularity is a day at minimum, so it can never express "delete within the hour" and should not be sold to compliance as if it could.

One operational footnote that costs an afternoon if you skip it: switch paid billing on before your first production write, since trial credit does not cover durable storage.

Rolling back the isolation decision is easier than it looks, and worth planning for while the tenant count is small. Server-side copy lets you re-lay-out objects from per-tenant buckets into a shared prefix layout, or the other way, with keys stable and the database untouched. I am not sure there is a clean answer for the reverse case, where you have already deleted on a deadline and someone asks for the document back — that direction has no rollback at all, which is the strongest argument I know for the grace window.

If that boundary fits your system, the signed-upload walkthrough is a reasonable next step for checking the request shape against your own key derivation before you commit.

Further reading

  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • GDPR Article 17, right to erasure — https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/
  • Sharing an object with a presigned URL, Amazon S3 — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ShareObjectPreSignedURL.html
  • Locking objects with S3 Object Lock — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html
  • Presigned URLs, Cloudflare R2 — https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • Storage presign capability schema — https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign

title: Embedded GUI Design: A Practical Integration Checklist for Firmware Engineers
description:
A firmware engineer finishes integrating a display module. The hardware works. Communication is stable. But when the first operator sits down with the device, they hesitate, press the wrong button, and then ask, "Where do I confirm?" The screen is functional. The interface is not. That gap between a working display and a usable interface is where GUI design lives — and for firmware engineers, it is an integration problem as much as a design problem.

GUI design is the discipline of structuring and presenting interactive elements on a screen so users can operate a system accurately and efficiently. In embedded and industrial contexts, a display that passes electrical testing can still cause operator errors, slow commissioning, and costly retraining. The goal is not decoration; it is reducing the cognitive load required to complete a task correctly.

Elements you will actually implement

On desktop operating systems, windows are resizable and layered. On an embedded display or industrial HMI, the equivalent is a screen state or page. Embedded interfaces typically lack the window management layer users expect, so each page must be self-explanatory without relying on OS conventions.

Icons reduce text dependency but carry recognition risk. An icon clear to a designer may be ambiguous to an operator under time pressure in a noisy environment. Icons work reliably when they follow an established convention or carry a short text label. Menus should be shallow: two or three interactions to any function.

Buttons must be large enough to activate reliably with the available input method. Tap target size should be determined by the touch controller's accuracy, the input method, and the operating environment. Resistive touchscreens, especially in industrial settings, may require larger targets depending on their calibration and input conditions. Gloved operation requires larger targets still. Specify tap target size from the actual device and environment, not from a design mockup.

Forms are error generators. Every manual text field is a potential source of bad data. Replace text entry with constrained controls where possible: a numeric keypad with a defined range, a validated dropdown, a two-state toggle. When text entry is unavoidable, provide immediate inline feedback so the user knows validity before submitting.

Sliders need range and resolution design. A slider covering 0–1000 on a 5-inch screen gives roughly 100 pixels of travel — one pixel per ten units. If the useful operating range is 400–600, the entire span occupies 20 pixels. Restrict the control range or pair it with a numeric entry field.

Use zone separation: status information in a consistent location, controls in a separate zone, alerts positioned so they do not require deliberate navigation. Visual hierarchy comes from size, contrast, color, and spacing, not ornamentation. Color carries functional meaning in industrial interfaces: red for fault, green for normal operation, amber for caution. Aesthetic color use creates ambiguity.

Example: implementing a safe parameter input

Here is why range validation belongs in firmware, not just in the UI layer:


The GUI should call this before accepting a submitted value and show inline feedback on failure. Validating only after the value reaches the application layer means the operator has already committed to an invalid entry — and on an industrial panel, that can mean a rejected setpoint, a process fault, or a confusing error state far from the input field. Validation at the point of entry keeps the feedback loop short and the error visible where it occurred.

Principles that map to code decisions

Consistency means the same action always looks and behaves the same way. A "Confirm" button should have the same appearance, position pattern, and behavior on every screen. Familiarity means using conventions the operator already knows. Departing from convention extends commissioning time and raises error rates during learning.

Feedback is a firmware responsibility. Every action should produce observable feedback: a button press visibly depresses, a submitted form confirms receipt or reports an error, a process over a second or two shows a progress indicator. Without feedback the operator may press again, cancel prematurely, or assume failure. System status should be continuously visible without navigation. "The screen is bright enough on the bench" is the wrong question; ask whether status information is readable after hours in the actual installation environment.

Error messages must be actionable. "Error 47" tells an operator nothing; "Temperature sensor offline — check connector J3" gives a starting point. Design error messages for the person in the field, not the engineer who wrote the firmware.

Process, compressed

Start GUI design during requirements definition, before hardware is finalized. Screen size, touch technology, and brightness all constrain what layouts are practical. Translate observations into testable requirements: "the operator must confirm a parameter change within 3 seconds from 60 cm in 500 lux ambient light" is actionable; "the interface should be easy to use" is not.

Wireframes keep review focused on structure and task flow. Prototype fidelity should match the decision being tested: paper sketches for navigation flow, medium-fidelity digital prototypes for control layout and tap target size, high-fidelity prototypes on target hardware for readability under actual brightness and viewing angle. A layout balanced on a 1920×1080 monitor preview may have different visual weight on a 7-inch 800×480 panel mounted at an angle in a cabinet.

Usability testing does not require a lab. Structured observation of three to five representative users attempting defined tasks surfaces most significant problems. Observe without intervening. Prioritize by frequency and severity. Document each change and rationale.

Common mistakes

Overloading a single screen forces the operator to parse too much before acting. Inconsistent navigation creates hesitation at every transition. Designing for average conditions fails when the device is deployed at waist height on a factory floor with a gloved operator. Using color as the only differentiator is inaccessible and unreliable on displays with calibration drift. Deferring error state design is a classic mistake. Ignoring the commissioning phase leaves setup and calibration menus untested with the engineer who actually uses them.

Hardware angle

Interface firmware workload is a real integration constraint. One practical hardware consideration is whether the host MCU should handle GUI rendering itself or delegate that workload to a dedicated display module. STONE's industrial display modules integrate a 1 GHz Cortex-A8 CPU, 256 MB flash, touch input, and a JSON-based UART command set into a single module, shifting GUI rendering off the host MCU. The Industrial Series operates across -40°C to +85°C. Compare interface options, temperature ratings, and memory specifications against your application requirements before committing to a platform.

title: Designing for Accessibility in Flutter: A Practical Guide
description:
Designing for Accessibility in Flutter: A Practical Guide

As mobile engineers, we often get caught up in building pixel-perfect UIs and buttery-smooth animations. But if those UIs can't be used by someone with a visual or motor impairment, we've failed our users. Accessibility (a11y) is a core pillar of modern app development.

The Semantics Widget

In Flutter, the Semantics widget is your best friend. It annotates the widget tree with a description of the meaning of the widgets. Screen readers like VoiceOver (iOS) and TalkBack (Android) use this semantics tree to describe the app to the user.

Semantics(
  label: 'Play Button',
  button: true,
  onTapHint: 'Play the current track',
  child: Icon(Icons.play_arrow),
)

High Contrast and Scaling

Always support Dynamic Type. If a user increases their system font size, your app's text should scale gracefully. Avoid hardcoding height or width on text containers. Instead, use padding and constraints. Furthermore, test your app's color palette against WCAG guidelines for sufficient contrast ratios.

Empathy Driven Development

Turn on VoiceOver or TalkBack on your test device. Close your eyes and try to navigate your core flows. It's an eye-opening experience that will immediately highlight where your app needs improvement. Let's build a more inclusive digital world.

Originally published at uzairxdev.online

title: 하나의 웹 디렉터리를 두 개의 사이트로 나눈 이유: 탐색과 설명은 같은 UI가 아니었다
description:
웹 디렉터리를 처음 만들 때는 한 사이트 안에 모든 기능을 넣는 것이 가장 단순하다고 생각했습니다.

카테고리를 만들고, 사이트를 등록하고, 사용자가 원하는 링크를 찾게 하면 끝이라고 생각했습니다.

하지만 운영하면서 조금 다른 문제가 보이기 시작했습니다.

사용자는 모두 같은 목적으로 방문하지 않았습니다.

어떤 사용자는 주소를 빨리 찾고 싶어 했고, 어떤 사용자는 어떤 사이트들이 있는지 비교하고 싶어 했습니다.

그리고 또 다른 사용자는 특정 카테고리가 무엇인지, 어떤 사이트를 선택해야 하는지 설명부터 필요로 했습니다.

결국 하나의 인터페이스에 너무 많은 역할을 넣기보다 역할을 분리하는 방향으로 구조를 바꾸게 됐습니다.

현재 제가 운영하고 있는 두 프로젝트가 그 결과입니다.

  • 레이더 주소모음 — radarjuso.com
  • Radar Link Site — radarlinksite.com

문제는 데이터가 아니라 사용자 의도였다

처음에는 이런 구조가 자연스러워 보였습니다.

Home
├── AI
├── Community
├── Shopping
├── Jobs
├── Finance
└── Other Categories

카테고리를 선택하면 사이트 목록이 나오고, 사용자가 원하는 사이트를 클릭합니다.

웹 디렉터리로서는 충분히 정상적인 구조입니다.

그런데 실제 사용 흐름을 생각해보면 두 가지 의도가 섞여 있었습니다.

Intent A
"I already know roughly what I need."

→ category
→ site
→ visit

반면 다른 사용자는 다음과 같습니다.

Intent B
"I know the topic, but I don't know which site I need."

→ understand category
→ discover options
→ compare
→ choose

두 흐름은 비슷해 보이지만 필요한 인터페이스가 다릅니다.

빠른 탐색과 설명형 콘텐츠의 충돌

주소를 빨리 찾는 사용자에게 긴 설명은 방해가 됩니다.

반대로 새로운 사이트를 탐색하는 사용자에게 링크 목록만 보여주면 맥락이 부족합니다.

예를 들어 빠른 탐색 페이지에서는 이런 구조가 적합합니다.

AI
├── Site A
├── Site B
├── Site C
└── Site D

하지만 설명형 페이지는 다음과 같은 구조가 더 자연스럽습니다.

What is this category?
↓
What kinds of sites are included?
↓
Available options
↓
How are they different?
↓
Related categories

하나의 페이지에서 두 가지를 모두 만족시키려고 하면 결국 UI가 복잡해지기 시작합니다.

버튼은 늘어나고 설명은 길어지고, 사용자가 실제로 원하는 링크는 아래로 밀립니다.

그래서 저는 역할 자체를 분리하기로 했습니다.

radarjuso.com: 빠른 탐색 중심

첫 번째 프로젝트는 radarjuso.com 입니다.

이쪽에서는 사용자가 원하는 분야를 먼저 선택하고 관련 사이트를 빠르게 확인하는 흐름을 중요하게 보고 있습니다.

개념적으로는 다음과 같습니다.

Category
↓
Relevant Sites
↓
Destination

정보 밀도를 높이고 이동 단계를 줄이는 것이 핵심입니다.

사용자가 이미 원하는 분야를 알고 있다면 설명보다 선택지가 먼저 보여야 하기 때문입니다.

radarlinksite.com: 설명과 탐색을 연결

두 번째 프로젝트는 radarlinksite.com 입니다.

이 사이트에서는 링크 목록 자체보다 카테고리와 사이트를 이해하는 과정에 조금 더 공간을 사용하고 있습니다.

현재 이 프로젝트는 Next.js 기반의 정적 사이트 구조로 운영하고 있습니다.

개념적인 페이지 구조는 다음과 같습니다.

/
├── sites/
│   ├── category-a/
│   ├── category-b/
│   └── category-c/
├── blog/
├── about/
└── privacy/

여기에서는 단순히 목적지 URL을 보여주는 것뿐 아니라 사용자가 관련 카테고리를 탐색할 수 있도록 구조를 확장할 수 있습니다.

즉 역할을 단순하게 나누면 다음과 같습니다.

radarjuso.com
→ Find

radarlinksite.com
→ Discover + Understand

두 사이트가 완전히 다른 서비스를 제공한다기보다 같은 문제를 서로 다른 사용자 흐름에서 해결하도록 분리한 것에 가깝습니다.

처음부터 두 사이트가 필요했던 것은 아니다

여기서 중요한 점은 프로젝트를 시작하자마자 여러 사이트로 분리하는 것이 좋은 설계라는 뜻은 아닙니다.

오히려 대부분의 경우 하나의 사이트로 시작하는 것이 훨씬 낫습니다.

서비스가 작을 때 두 개의 사이트를 운영하면 다음과 같은 비용이 생깁니다.

Deployment × 2
Analytics × 2
SEO monitoring × 2
Content maintenance × 2
Broken link checks × 2

네, 구조를 분리하면 관리해야 할 것도 친절하게 두 배 가까이 늘어납니다.

소프트웨어는 늘 문제를 해결한 대가로 새로운 문제를 하나 무료로 제공합니다.

그래서 분리 기준은 기술적인 이유보다 사용자 흐름이 정말 다른가가 되어야 한다고 생각합니다.

같은 내용을 복사하지 않는 것이 중요했다

사이트를 둘로 나눈 다음 가장 피하고 싶었던 것은 동일한 페이지를 두 도메인에 복사하는 것이었습니다.

예를 들어 이런 구조는 좋지 않습니다.

Site A:
/ai

Site B:
/ai

Same title
Same description
Same links
Same content

이렇게 만들면 사용자의 입장에서도 두 사이트를 운영할 이유가 없습니다.

대신 동일한 주제를 다루더라도 페이지의 역할을 다르게 정의했습니다.

Directory page
→ 선택과 이동

Editorial / discovery page
→ 설명과 탐색

콘텐츠 자체보다 페이지가 수행하는 작업을 먼저 정의하는 방식입니다.

페이지 역할을 먼저 정의하면 구현도 단순해진다

이후 새로운 페이지를 만들 때는 먼저 질문합니다.

What should the user accomplish here?

그리고 페이지 역할을 몇 가지로 제한합니다.

const pageRoles = {
  directory: "find a destination quickly",
  category: "explore related websites",
  editorial: "understand a topic",
  navigation: "move between categories"
};

실제 코드에서 꼭 이런 객체를 사용할 필요는 없습니다.

중요한 것은 각 페이지마다 하나의 주된 역할을 정하는 것입니다.

그렇게 하면 다음 결정도 쉬워집니다.
