title: Designing a Thumbnail Annotation System: Text, Arrows, and Intent
description:
A thumbnail editor needs intent, not just controls

Font pickers and arrow buttons look like small interface features. In a thumbnail workflow, they can create a large usability problem: a creator can change five visual properties without ever stating what the text or arrow is supposed to do.

That produces a familiar review comment: “Make it pop.” It is hard to implement, hard to compare, and almost impossible to test.

For a public-UI design memo, it is useful to model these elements as annotations. A text treatment explains a short idea. An arrow marks a particular visual target. Both should have a reason that survives outside the editor.

Start with two explicit contracts

At the interface level, a text annotation needs a message and a readability condition. An arrow annotation needs a target and a direction. The following is a design proposal, not a claim about the implementation of any public tool:

type TextAnnotation = {
  content: string;
  role: "hook" | "context" | "number";
  weight: 400 | 700 | 900;
  spacing: number;
  separation: "none" | "outline" | "shadow";
};

type ArrowAnnotation = {
  style: "straight" | "curved" | "hand-drawn";
  targetLabel: string;
  rotation: number;
  contrastChecked: boolean;
};

The useful part is not the field list itself. It is the review question it enables. A reviewer can ask, “What is this arrow pointing at?” instead of “Does the red arrow look exciting enough?”

The public YouTube Thumbnail Font Generator provides a good visible example of why text needs several separate controls. Weight, size, letter spacing, fill color, outline, shadow, and background transparency affect different aspects of a phrase. Bundling them into one “boldness” slider would make comparison vague.

Why a one-change review loop matters

If a team changes typeface, size, outline, and copy at once, the final candidate might look better, but the team learns very little. The next thumbnail starts from the same uncertainty.

Use a controlled loop instead:

  1. Lock the short hook.
  2. Compare two weights at the intended feed size.
  3. Lock the better weight and compare spacing.
  4. Add outline or shadow only when the background requires separation.
  5. Record the reason for the selected variant.

The point is not to create an A/B-testing claim without data. It is to create a repeatable design review. A candidate can be rejected because the hook loses shape against a bright background, not because someone “doesn’t like it.”

Arrows should reference a meaningful target

An arrow has a simpler contract and a stricter failure mode. If the target does not carry the video’s story, the arrow is visual noise.

A Thumbnail Arrow Generator exposes straight, curved, and hand-drawn choices, with color and advanced controls. The visible page also describes an upload-or-blank-canvas workflow and a transparent PNG output. That gives a frontend team a helpful surface model: an arrow can be handled as an independently positioned layer rather than baked into the background.

The contract should still prevent two common failures:

  • an arrow ending on empty space;
  • several arrows competing to define the primary subject. 
function canExportArrow(arrow: ArrowAnnotation) {
  return arrow.targetLabel.trim().length > 0 && arrow.contrastChecked;
}

This is only illustrative logic. A production UI may use coordinates, masks, or object detection instead. The design principle stays the same: asking for a target label makes ambiguity visible before export.

State transitions worth discussing

An editor can keep the review trace lightweight:

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Brief
  Brief --> TextVariant: choose hook
  TextVariant --> ArrowVariant: confirm readable text
  ArrowVariant --> Preview: select target
  Preview --> TextVariant: revise one property
  Preview --> Export: promise is clear

The diagram is not an observed product architecture. It is a way to reason about when a creator has enough information to move forward.

The preview state is especially important. A high-resolution canvas encourages tiny fixes that disappear in a feed. A practical review asks what survives at small size: the primary object, the hook, and the arrow’s endpoint. If all three cannot be named quickly, reduce the number of active signals.

Interface acceptance checks

For a similar feature, I would start with these checks:

Area Acceptance question
Copy Is the hook short enough to compare as a single visual unit?
Text Does changing weight preserve the actual phrase?
Separation Is outline or shadow selected because of the background, not habit?
Arrow Can the creator name the highlighted target?
Preview Does the target remain visible at mobile feed size?
Fidelity Does the target appear in the actual video?

The last row cannot be verified by an editor alone. It needs human review against the footage. That limitation matters more than any styling control.

Thumbs AI is most useful in this framing as an ideation surface: a creator can compare typography and arrow direction after writing a clear visual brief. It does not replace a content review or prove an improvement in click-through rate.

The broader lesson for UI design is modest: expose expressive controls, but pair them with a question that makes each control accountable. “Which weight?” is a preference. “Can the viewer read this phrase before the scene overwhelms it?” is a product requirement.

title: Confidential Computing's Real Tax: SEV-SNP vs TDX vs H100 Confidential Mode
description:
Confidential computing has spent a decade as a compliance checkbox and is now being pulled into production by a concrete commercial need: customers who will not send data to a model they cannot verify. The pitch is clean. Encrypt memory so the host cannot read it, attest the software stack so the customer knows what is running, and let them trust the math instead of the operator.

The pitch is also incomplete, because every one of those guarantees costs throughput, and the cost is not evenly distributed across the stack. Some of it is nearly free. Some of it is 30% and no amount of tuning removes it.

Part One: What memory encryption actually costs

AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX both encrypt guest memory with a key the hypervisor does not hold, and both use hardware AES engines in the memory controller to do it. Published benchmarks put the CPU-side overhead in the low single digits for memory-bound workloads, and near zero for compute-bound ones.

That is the part people hear, and it is genuinely good news: if your workload is a CPU service, confidentiality is almost free. A database, an API server, a batch job — the tax is a rounding error, and the operational complexity is a boot parameter and an attestation flow.

The trouble starts when the workload is not a CPU service.

Part Two: Where the tax concentrates

Three places.

Attestation itself. Every confidential VM must produce a report the relying party verifies, and that report has to be tied to a key the guest generates. The flow is a round trip: guest generates key, requests report, sends report to verifier, verifier checks signature chain against the vendor's root, returns a token, guest unwraps a secret. That is one to three seconds of latency at startup, which matters for autoscaling and for anything that spawns short-lived workers.

IO. Confidential VMs cannot trust the hypervisor's device emulation, so virtio has to be protected: shared memory regions, bounce buffers, an encrypted channel. Every network packet and every disk block takes an extra copy. For a workload that moves a lot of bytes, this is where a double-digit percentage disappears.

GPUs. This is the expensive one. H100 confidential computing mode encrypts the PCIe path between host and device and adds bounce buffers for every transfer. Published figures from early access show roughly 10-20% throughput loss for large-model inference, and worse for small-batch workloads where the transfer is a larger fraction of the step.

Part Three: The number that decides adoption

Combine the throughput loss with the price of confidential SKUs and you get an effective cost premium. My model: about 4-5% for CPU-only confidential VMs, around 22% for H100 confidential mode, and up to 38% for confidential GPU SKUs that also carry a price premium.

Now compare that to willingness to pay. Regulated workloads — health records, financial positions, anything under a data processing agreement with an audit clause — will pay a large premium because the alternative is not running the workload in the cloud at all. Workloads outside that category will not, because the benefit is invisible to their users.

So the market splits cleanly: confidentiality is a compliance product, not a performance product. Teams that adopt it for architectural elegance rather than a specific contractual requirement end up paying 22% for a property nobody asked for.

Part Four: The architecture that makes it affordable

Three patterns that work.

Split the workload. Put the CPU-side orchestration, the tokenisation, and the business logic in a confidential VM where the tax is 4%, and send only the tensor operations to the confidential GPU. Most of the data-handling surface is then protected at near-zero cost, and the expensive part does the minimum work necessary.

Batch hard on the GPU. The confidential-mode overhead is dominated by transfers per kernel launch, so larger batches amortise it. A confidential H100 at batch 1 is a bad deal; at batch 64 it is close to a plaintext H100 at batch 32 in cost per token.

Cache attestation results. Do not re-attest on every request. Attest once per instance, cache the token with a TTL, and treat the instance as trusted until the TTL expires. This turns a startup cost into an infrastructure cost.

Part Five: The thing to measure before you commit

Benchmark your own workload, not the vendor's. The published overhead figures are for large-batch inference and memory-bound microbenchmarks; your workload is probably neither.

Specifically measure three things: tokens per second at your production batch size, p99 latency including the encrypted transfer, and the number of times per hour your autoscaler would need to attest a new instance. The third number is the one that surprises people, because a scale-to-zero design can attest hundreds of times a day.

Then compare the premium to the deal. If a customer's contract requires verifiable execution, the 22% is a cost of goods. If it does not, you are buying insurance against a threat model your customer has not articulated.

The transferable lesson

Every security property is a trade against a threat model, and the trade only makes sense when the threat is named. Confidential computing names it precisely: the cloud operator. If that is not a threat you are contractually obligated to address, the tax buys nothing.

The broader pattern is that hardware security features arrive with uneven costs. Encryption of memory is cheap because it is a wide, parallel operation. Encryption of a serial interconnect is expensive because it is on the critical path of every transfer. Knowing which side of that line a feature sits on tells you more about its adoption curve than any marketing deck.

title: Spot vs Reserved GPUs: The Utilisation Number That Decides Everything
description:
The first thing every team does when the GPU bill gets uncomfortable is look at spot pricing. The discount looks enormous, often 60-70% off on-demand, and the arithmetic seems obvious: move the training job to spot, save most of the money.

Then the job gets interrupted twice in an afternoon, and someone discovers that a distributed job with a lost rank does not resume, it restarts. The discount evaporates into recomputation, and the team goes back to reserved capacity convinced that spot is a trap.

Neither instinct is right. Spot is a good deal for some workloads and a bad deal for others, and the variable that separates them is not the discount, it is the duty cycle and the checkpoint cost.

Part One: The crossover

Model it properly. A reserved instance costs a fixed amount per hour whether you use it or not. A spot instance costs less per hour but has an interruption probability, and each interruption costs you the work since the last checkpoint plus the restart time.

My model uses a 40% average spot discount, 6% hourly interruption probability, and a 90-second checkpoint overhead on a 40 GB state. The result: below roughly 65% duty cycle, spot is cheaper per GPU-hour delivered. Above it, reserved wins, and the gap widens quickly because interruptions are proportional to time, not to useful work.

65% is the number to remember, and almost nobody measures their actual duty cycle before choosing. Teams assume 100% because that is what the capacity is for, then run at 40% because of queueing, data loading and idle time between experiments.

Part Two: Checkpointing is the only real control

The discount is not a lever. The interruption rate is not a lever. The checkpoint interval is, and it is the one parameter teams set by habit rather than arithmetic.

Checkpoint every thirty minutes and an interruption costs you fifteen minutes of work on average, plus restart. Checkpoint every two minutes and an interruption costs you one, but you write 40 GB every two minutes, which is 1.2 TB an hour of object storage traffic and a measurable hit on the training loop.

At the numbers above, the lost GPU-minutes per hundred hours fall from 900 with no checkpointing to 85 at a two-minute interval, while the checkpoint write overhead rises from zero to 26 minutes per hundred hours. The sum has a minimum near two minutes. That minimum is where you should be, and it is not where most jobs are.

The write overhead is the part that surprises people. A 40 GB checkpoint at 500 MB/s takes 80 seconds, which is longer than the interval you wanted. The fix is incremental or sharded checkpoints, and if your framework does not support them, that is a stronger argument against the framework than any benchmark.

Part Three: The workloads that should never be on spot

Three categories.

Long single-GPU jobs with no checkpoint support. If the job cannot resume, the expected cost of an interruption is the whole job. At 6% hourly interruption, a ten-hour job has a 46% chance of being interrupted at least once. Half your runs die.

Tightly coupled multi-node training. One lost rank means a collective operation stalls, and depending on the framework the whole job either restarts or hangs until a timeout. The effective interruption rate multiplies by the number of nodes.

Anything with a latency SLO. Serving on spot means a fraction of your requests fail at exactly the moment your provider needs capacity back, which is correlated with when everyone else needs capacity back.

Part Four: The workloads that should always be on spot

Batch inference over a fixed corpus. Checkpoint at the shard boundary, which is free, and interruptions cost nothing because the unit of work is small.

Hyperparameter sweeps. Each trial is independent and short. A killed trial is a lost trial, not a lost job, and the scheduler just resubmits.

Data preprocessing. Idempotent, restartable, and the bottleneck is IO anyway.

The pattern: spot is for work whose unit of completion is small relative to the interruption interval. If a unit of work takes longer than the mean time between interruptions, spot is a bet against yourself.

Part Five: The hybrid that most teams should run

Reserve a floor that covers your steady-state load, and put the burst on spot with a fallback to on-demand when spot capacity is unavailable. The floor should be the capacity you use more than 70% of the time, not your peak.

Two operational details matter more than the split. First, tag every spot instance with the job and the checkpoint location, so a reaper can restart it automatically without a human reading logs. Second, track interruptions per thousand GPU-hours as a first-class metric. If it drifts above your model's assumption, the crossover moves and your reservation decision is stale.

The transferable lesson

Discounts are priced for the inconvenience they cause, and the inconvenience is variance. Any time a vendor sells you something cheaper in exchange for unreliability, the correct analysis is expected cost including recovery, not unit price.

The teams that run cheap GPU fleets are not the ones that found a better discount. They are the ones that made their work restartable in small units, which made the discount usable. Cheap capacity is not a purchasing decision, it is an engineering property of the workload, and you build it before you buy it.

title: A100 vs H100: is the H100 worth it for LLM training?
description:
The H100 is worth it when it finishes your training job at least as many times faster as it costs more per hour. On Nodus the NVIDIA H100 SXM is listed at $2.60/hr and the A100 80GB at $1.09/hr, so the H100 must run 2.39 times faster to be the cheaper way to finish. Large BF16 or FP8 training usually gets there; small, memory-bound or poorly fed jobs often do not.

That ratio is the whole decision, and it changes with each provider's price list. Under the line, the A100 gives you the cheaper finished job. Over it, the H100 gives you a cheaper job that also finishes sooner.

How much faster is an H100 than an A100 on paper?

Between 1.50 and 3.17 times, depending on which part of the chip your job leans on. Every number here comes from NVIDIA's own spec tables for the A100 80GB SXM and the H100 SXM.

A100 80GB SXM H100 SXM H100 ÷ A100
BF16 Tensor Core, dense 312 TFLOPS 989.5 TFLOPS 3.17x
FP8 Tensor Core, dense Not supported 1,979 TFLOPS New on H100
Memory 80 GB HBM2e 80 GB Same capacity
Memory bandwidth 2,039 GB/s 3,350 GB/s 1.64x
NVLink per GPU 600 GB/s 900 GB/s 1.50x
Max power 400 W Up to 700 W 1.75x

NVIDIA lists H100 Tensor Core figures with sparsity (1,979 BF16 and 3,958 FP8 TFLOPS). Dense training gets half of those, which is what the table shows.

These ratios bracket what a real job sees. A job limited by matrix math, like a large model at a big batch size, moves toward the 3.17x compute ratio. A job limited by moving bytes, like a small model, a short sequence or heavy optimizer traffic, moves toward the 1.64x bandwidth ratio. Neither number is a benchmark, and a slow data loader holds both GPUs to the same speed.


The Nodus price ratio sits between the bandwidth ratio and the compute ratio, so your workload decides the winner.

When does the H100 cost less per finished job?

When your measured speedup beats the hourly price ratio. The rule is one division: H100 price per hour divided by A100 price per hour. If the H100 finishes the job faster than that multiple, it is the cheaper choice.

The ratio depends on where you run. We divided each provider's own listed rates for the 80 GB A100 and the H100 SXM:

Where A100 80GB per hour H100 SXM per hour Speedup the H100 needs
Nodus $1.09 $2.60 2.39x
RunPod (Pods, A100 SXM) $1.79 $3.99 2.23x
Modal ($0.000694 and $0.001097 per second) $2.50 $3.95 1.58x

Sources: Nodus pricing, RunPod pricing, Modal pricing. Prices checked November 2, 2026.


A cheap A100 rate raises the bar the H100 has to clear.

On Modal the H100 wins almost by default, because its premium over the A100 is small. On Nodus the A100 is cheap enough that the H100 has to earn its place with a compute-bound job.

What does that look like for a real fine-tune?

Take a fine-tune that needs 20 hours on one A100 80GB. On Nodus that is 20 x $1.09 = $21.80. The same job on one H100 at the three speedups that matter:

H100 speedup H100 hours H100 cost on Nodus
1.64x (bandwidth-bound) 12.20 h $31.71
2.39x (breakeven) 8.38 h $21.80
3.17x (compute-bound, at the spec ceiling) 6.31 h $16.40


A memory-bound job costs 45% more on the H100; a compute-bound one costs 25% less.

The spread is large. Picking the wrong GPU for this job costs between $5.40 and $9.91, before you count the hours you wait. On Modal the same job runs $49.97 on the A100 and $48.16 on an H100 at only 1.64x, which is why the answer flips between providers.

How do you measure your own speedup in 30 minutes?

Run a short probe of your real training script on each GPU and compare steady-state throughput. Keep the model, batch size, sequence length and data identical. Skip the first few dozen steps, because compilation and warm-up distort them.

Add a timer to your loop that prints tokens or samples per second every 50 steps. Then launch the probe twice with a hard spending cap, using the nodus run flags from the Nodus Jobs guide:

nodus run --name probe-a100 --gpu A100-80GB --image nodus/pytorch --max-cost 1.00 --timeout 20m -- python train.py --max-steps 300
nodus run --name probe-h100 --gpu H100 --image nodus/pytorch --max-cost 1.00 --timeout 20m -- python train.py --max-steps 300

At listed rates, 15 minutes costs $0.27 on the A100 and $0.65 on the H100. Divide the H100's tokens per second by the A100's. Compare that number with the breakeven for where you will run the full job.

If you want FP8, test it as a third probe. FP8 only exists on the H100, and NVIDIA credits its Transformer Engine with up to 4x faster training than the prior generation on GPT-3 175B. That is NVIDIA's projection for a very large model, so check that your loss curve holds before you count on it.

Where is the A100 the better choice?

The A100 wins whenever your job cannot keep an H100's Tensor Cores busy. These are the common cases:

  • Small models and LoRA fine-tunes on 7B to 13B models, where batches are small and memory traffic dominates.
  • Data pipelines that cannot feed the GPU faster. If an A100 already waits on the loader, an H100 waits longer.
  • Code pinned to FP16 or TF32 kernels that predate Hopper, or libraries without FP8 support.
  • Long runs without a deadline, where a lower cost matters more than finishing sooner.
  • Power or rack limits on your own hardware: 400 W per A100 against up to 700 W per H100.

Memory is a tie. Both have 80 GB, so a model that does not fit on an A100 80GB will not fit on an H100 SXM either. For more memory per GPU you need an H200 or a B200, and our VRAM guide for 70B models shows the math.

When is the H100 clearly worth it?

Pay for the H100 when time matters or the job is compute-bound. Pretraining and continued pretraining, full fine-tunes of 30B and larger models, long sequences and FP8 recipes all push toward the compute ratio.

Multi-GPU jobs lean the same way. NVLink is 1.5x faster on the H100, so gradient and tensor-parallel traffic between 8 GPUs costs less time. For why the H100 holds its price in the first place, see why the H100 is so expensive.

A deadline can also justify an H100 below the breakeven. At 1.64x, our 20-hour job finishes 7.8 hours sooner for $9.91 more.

How do you let Nodus pick between A100 and H100?

List both types in the Job and set a cost cap. The Nodus GPU guide says the scheduler picks among the accepted types by expected cost to finish.

apiVersion: nodus.dev/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: finetune
spec:
  image: nodus/pytorch
  command: [torchrun, train.py]
  resources:
    gpu: {type: [A100-80GB, H100], count: 8}
  timeout: 24h
  maxCostUSD: "250.00"

If your probe already settled the question, pin one type instead, for example --gpu H100:8. Run nodus apply -f job.yaml --dry-run=server -o estimate first to see the offering, the expected cost and the startup time without spending anything. For an 8-GPU launch with torchrun, our multi-GPU PyTorch guide walks through the setup.

FAQ

Is the A100 better than the H100?

Not on any performance spec; it only draws less power. The A100 is the better value when your job runs less than about 2.4 times faster on the H100 at Nodus list prices.

Is the A100 40GB worth considering for LLM training?

Only for small models or LoRA on 7B-class models with short sequences. Its 40 GB fills quickly once you add optimizer states and activations, so most LLM training plans should start from the 80 GB version.

Can I train in FP8 on an A100?

No. The A100 has no FP8 Tensor Cores, so FP8 recipes fall back to BF16 or fail. The H100 adds FP8 through its Transformer Engine.

Do H100 PCIe-based cards match the H100 SXM?

No. NVIDIA lists the PCIe-based H100 NVL at 1,671 BF16 TFLOPS with sparsity against 1,979 for the SXM, and 600 GB/s NVLink against 900 GB/s. On Nodus, H100 accepts any variant, while H100-SXM or H100! pins the SXM version.

Does a cheaper A100 rate still pay off if the run gets interrupted?

Only if the run resumes from a checkpoint. A restart from zero repeats the work and erases the saving. Nodus restores the latest checkpoint on new capacity, which our checkpointing guide covers.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: AI SDK 7.0.160 Started Enforcing dataPartSchemas. Your Loading States Might Now Throw
description:
If you pass dataPartSchemas to useChat and bump ai to 7.0.160 or later, a chat that worked yesterday can end up in status: 'error' with a TypeValidationError. You didn't change anything. Your schemas just started running.

What changed

useChat and Chat accept dataPartSchemas, keyed by the bare part name (weather for a data-weather part). The stream processor looked the schema up by the full chunk type (data-weather), so the lookup always missed and streamed data parts were never validated. That's issue #24241, fixed in PR #24298 and shipped in ai 7.0.160: "Invalid data parts now raise a TypeValidationError."

So a patch release turned on a check that was configured but never ran.

What I ran

I didn't want to guess at the edge cases, so I drove the Chat class from @ai-sdk/react with a fake transport that replays fixed UI message chunks. No model, no network. useChat runs on that same class (its chat option even takes an existing Chat instance), so the stream handling is the same code path. I ran the same script against ai 7.0.159 with @ai-sdk/react 4.0.163, ai 7.0.162 with @ai-sdk/react 4.0.166, and ai 6.0.322 with @ai-sdk/react 3.0.325, all with zod 4.6.7 on Node 20.19.2.

Stream 7.0.159 7.0.162
Valid data-weather part ready ready
city: 42, then some text ready, bad data kept in parts, text arrives error, no assistant message at all
Loading update without weather, then the final value ready error, earlier text kept, final value lost
Transient part that fails the schema ready, onData called error, onData not called
data-notice part with no schema ready ready

On 6.0.322 every row matched the 7.0.159 column: bad data went through without an error.

The one that'll bite: progressive updates

The streaming data docs use a progressive pattern: write { city, status: 'loading' } first, then write to the same id again with the real value. The docs type weather as optional (weather?: string), which fits that pattern. But if your zod schema was written for the finished shape, the loading chunk fails now. Here's the excerpt from my test script (start and end are the start/finish chunks, text() writes one text part, and run() sends a message through Chat with these chunks):

const strictSchemas = {
  weather: z.object({
    city: z.string(),
    weather: z.string(),
    status: z.enum(['loading', 'success']),
  }),
};

// Case 3: a loading update, then the final value under the same id
await run('3 loading update without weather, then final', [...start,
  ...text('t0', 'Checking...'),
  { type: 'data-weather', id: 'w1', data: { city: 'Berlin', status: 'loading' } },
  { type: 'data-weather', id: 'w1', data: { city: 'Berlin', weather: 'sunny', status: 'success' } }, ...end]);

On 7.0.162 this ended with Type validation failed for message.parts[2].data (data-weather, id: "w1"). The "Checking..." text that streamed before it stayed in the message, the final value never arrived, and chat.status was error.

Every chunk is checked, not just the last one per id. Transient parts too, even though they never land in message.parts.

The fix

Make the schema describe every state the server actually sends. A discriminated union keeps the final shape strict:

const unionSchemas = {
  weather: z.discriminatedUnion('status', [
    z.object({ status: z.literal('loading'), city: z.string() }),
    z.object({ status: z.literal('success'), city: z.string(), weather: z.string() }),
  ]),
};

With this schema the same stream finished with status: ready on both versions, and the part ended up as { city: 'Berlin', weather: 'sunny', status: 'success' }.

Before you upgrade, I'd do three things:

  1. Search the client for dataPartSchemas.
  2. For each data-* type in there, check every writer.write() on the server against its schema, including loading, progress and transient writes.
  3. Make sure the UI shows error from useChat. In my runs a failed part stopped the whole response, so a silent failure here looks like a chat that just stops.

Data parts with no schema aren't checked at all, so a schema-less type won't start failing.

I'd rather have the error than let city: 42 slip into message.parts without a word, which is what 7.0.159 did. Have you hit this one after updating, or were your schemas already matching what the server sends?

References

  • ai 7.0.160 release notes
  • Issue #24241: useChat/Chat never validates streamed data parts against dataPartSchemas
  • PR #24298: validate streamed data parts against dataPartSchemas
  • AI SDK docs: Streaming custom data
  • AI SDK docs: useChat reference

title: AI Image Lifecycle Policies for Property Management: Go Signals for Large-File Recovery
description:
Short answer: the useful lifecycle policy for AI-generated property images is governed by four clocks: access frequency, large-file recovery time, retention obligations, and the capacity of the restore workers. Keep frequently opened images hot. Move inactive images to an archive only if the resulting restore path still meets the recovery SLO, and delete them only after the regional retention and legal-hold checks pass.

The least complex implementation is a small set of lifecycle classes with an observable decision record. For example, an image attached to an active maintenance case can stay hot while a listing-generation intermediate becomes cold after its workflow closes. The exact day count is a product and compliance decision, not a universal storage setting.

For a small platform team, Infrai is worth trying for the policy write and recovery worker when one bearer key and one plain HTTP contract matter more than storage-native immutability. Its public discovery surface can expose the request schema before deployment. That is a conditional fit, not a blanket storage recommendation.

That distinction matters during an incident. The page should fire while the restore queue is becoming unsafe, not after a tenant's selected snapshot has already disappeared. For a platform team, I would choose the storage service only after measuring p95 image size, concurrent restores, and the recovery SLO. A lifecycle rule that works for thumbnails can fail badly for full-resolution inspection images.

The page fires before the image is lost

Start with what the on-call engineer sees: the oldest restore job keeps getting older, large-file throughput falls below the recovery target, or repeated attempts receive rate-limit responses. A deletion event is a poor first signal because it describes an irreversible outcome rather than the pressure that caused it.

Work backward from that page to the earlier instrumentation. Each restore record should carry a snapshot identifier, object key, region, lifecycle class, object size, queue age, attempt count, request ID, and last successful restore test. Those fields make it possible to distinguish a cold object that is behaving as designed from a recovery backlog that is consuming the SLO budget.

Keep tenant images private. Deliver them with a presigned URL after the application has authorized the viewer; do not put a service bearer token on that returned URL. This is also where the storage boundary becomes important: the available surface has no object versioning or object lock, so an overwrite that must be reversible or immutable needs naming discipline and coordination in a database or queue outside the object store.

There are three clocks to keep separate:

  • The access clock: how often users or workflows open the image.
  • The recovery clock: how quickly a selected snapshot must become usable, including queue delay and transfer time.
  • The retention clock: how long a regional law, contract, or internal policy requires the record to remain available.

The shortest clock does not automatically decide the policy. A legal retention period can outlive access by months, while a strict recovery SLO can rule out an archive tier even for an image that is rarely opened. Automation should evaluate the clocks together and leave an inspectable decision rather than silently applying object age as the only input.

Which factors should control an AI image lifecycle policy?

Usage pattern is the starting point, not the conclusion. A generated room image for an active tenant maintenance case may be opened repeatedly by residents, property staff, and contractors. A discarded generation intermediate may have no operational value after the final image is accepted. Treating both objects alike creates either unnecessary hot storage or an unsafe restore path.

Large files make the throughput calculation less forgiving. Capacity planning should use the p95 object size, expected concurrent restores, the number of snapshots a worker must process, and the recovery SLO. An average image size hides the tail that determines whether a selected snapshot can be restored during a busy reconciliation window. Archive retrieval, network transfer, retries, and queue delay all consume the same recovery budget. I would keep the capacity record alongside the lifecycle policy revision, because a policy that was safe for 100 concurrent restores is not automatically safe after the portfolio doubles; the worker count, transfer headroom, and queue-age threshold must be reviewed together, and the restore test must exercise the largest representative objects rather than a convenient thumbnail.

The alert is not the policy.

Compliance is a boundary condition, not a storage tier. Regional retention law may constrain where data is kept or how long it remains, while deletion obligations may require evidence that the deletion occurred. The policy service should receive a reviewed mapping from tenant region and record class to a lifecycle class. NIST SP 800-66 Rev. 2 is useful background for organizations handling regulated health information, but it does not replace legal review for property-management records.

I initially treated “archive after 30 days” as a sensible default. That rule is attractive because it is easy to explain and easy to automate. It is also a weak proxy for whether the data has stopped mattering. The correction is to combine access history with workflow state, then test one selected snapshot from every lifecycle class on a schedule. The number 30 remains an example of a policy input, not a recommendation.

The measurable constraint is the one-day floor: lifecycle expiration is not an hourly cleanup mechanism. That matters for short-lived generation intermediates, which need an application-level cleanup decision if their useful life is measured in hours.

What should an alert-to-action path measure?

The page should represent sustained risk, not a single transient failure. A useful policy is to page on a sustained recovery-SLO breach together with queue age, while a single failed attempt becomes a lower-severity event. A threshold set too low produces pages for short bursts and trains the team to ignore them. A threshold set too high allows a regional backlog to consume the recovery budget before anyone acts.

Retries need the same discipline. Standard queues are at-least-once, so the consumer must treat a repeated restore instruction as normal and use a deterministic idempotency key derived from the tenant and snapshot identifiers. On HTTP 429, back off exponentially and honor Retry-After when it is present. A retry that creates a second restore operation is a consumer defect, even when the storage service returned the correct rate-limit response.

For a lifecycle write, the worker should record the intended class and policy revision before calling the storage API, then record the response status and request ID. If the process dies after the remote write and before the local acknowledgement, the same idempotency key must make the retry safe. That is the difference between retry logic and a recovery design.

The route below is intentionally small. The current lifecycle request schema should be discovered and supplied through INFRAI_LIFECYCLE_JSON; keeping the body outside the example avoids inventing fields that are not part of the verified route facts. The code uses private storage by policy and assumes image delivery will use a separately authorized presigned URL.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    body := os.Getenv("INFRAI_LIFECYCLE_JSON")
    if apiKey == "" || body == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_LIFECYCLE_JSON are required")
    }

    const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/bucket/set_lifecycle/property-images"
    const idempotencyKey = "property-images/lifecycle/policy-2026-10-26"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, endpoint, bytes.NewBufferString(body))
        if err != nil {
            cancel()
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        cancel()
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if retryAfter := res.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(retryAfter)); parseErr == nil {
                    delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("lifecycle request failed: %s: %s", res.Status, responseBody))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(responseBody))
        return
    }
}

The example does not send the authorization header to any presigned object URL. It also does not treat a 2xx response as proof that the recovery workflow is healthy; the worker still needs to observe the subsequent restore test and queue age. Lifecycle rules are useful only when their effects are visible.

For readers who prefer to inspect the request outside a Go worker, this is the same call shape. The body is still supplied by the verified discovery schema rather than guessed here:

// curl --request POST \
//   --url https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/bucket/set_lifecycle/property-images \
//   --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \
//   --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
//   --header "Idempotency-Key: property-images/lifecycle/policy-2026-10-26" \
//   --data "$INFRAI_LIFECYCLE_JSON"

One key and one HTTP contract: where does it help?

There is a credible reason to consider a unified REST surface for this workflow. Storage, image processing, and adjacent backend work can use one bearer key and one base URL, which removes a class of secret-rotation and invoice-reconciliation work from the platform team's monthly routine. That is operationally useful, but it expands the trust boundary: one provider now sits across more of the recovery path, and independent failure domains become less independent.

The second advantage is different. A plain HTTP interface means a Go restore worker can call the service without installing an SDK, while the public discovery surface exposes capability schemas without a key. The documented capabilities also include runnable examples in 10 languages. In a lifecycle workflow, that reduces the friction of keeping a worker, a policy reconciler, and a test utility on the same request contract. Discovery is not a substitute for integration tests, but it makes the request shape inspectable before deployment.

The breadth is real: 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. That can make a small platform team faster when the workflow crosses storage and other backend services. It can also make the provider a larger dependency, so I would treat the breadth as a workflow simplifier rather than as evidence that the storage primitives are stronger than a specialist's.

The comparison is therefore about boundaries, not a winner:

Option Useful fit for this workflow Operational boundary
Infrai A Go worker that wants one HTTP contract and one credential across storage and adjacent backend calls No object versioning, object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud batch migration; the storage vendor coverage does not include GCS or B2
Amazon S3 Teams that prioritize mature object-storage controls, including WORM-oriented designs through the AWS ecosystem Processing, queueing, and observability remain separate service contracts to operate
Google Cloud Storage GCP-native teams that need regional storage workflows and Google-managed integrations The rest of the restore pipeline still has its own APIs, credentials, and failure modes
Azure Blob Storage Azure-native teams that want lifecycle management inside an Azure-centered platform Portability depends on the surrounding Azure integration and its operational contracts

Infrai is the recommendation for a team that specifically values one key plus a plain, self-describing REST contract for the storage-to-worker handoff, and that can accept application-level coordination for immutability and replication. The one-key advantage reduces credential and billing glue; the HTTP and discovery advantage reduces SDK and request-shape friction. Those are concrete benefits for this recovery workflow, not a claim that every property-management archive belongs there.

Where a specialist is the better choice

Use S3 or another specialist when the requirement is financial-grade immutability, automatic cross-region replication, or a browser upload flow that needs independently managed CORS rules. This storage surface has no versioning or object lock, no automatic cross-region replication, no cross-cloud batch migration tool, and no public set_cors route for self-service browser uploads. Strict concurrent writes also need a queue or database because there is no If-Match conditional write.

That is the central limitation and trade-off: Infrai is not suitable when the storage layer itself must provide WORM retention, object history, or replication as a native guarantee. In those cases, choose S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage according to the required regional and compliance controls, and keep the processing and queue integrations separate.

The lifecycle boundary has its own limits: the minimum expiration period is one day, there is no automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments, and metadata cannot be searched server-side beyond prefix filtering. Those constraints should appear in the design review, especially for large-file workloads where abandoned multipart uploads can accumulate outside the normal object-age policy.

The practical decision rule is narrow. Keep hot images hot when access frequency and recovery SLO require it. Archive only after a measured restore test shows enough throughput headroom. Delete only after compliance and legal-hold checks, with an auditable worker decision. Choose the unified API when one key and one HTTP contract remove meaningful operational glue; choose a specialist when immutability, replication, or storage-native browser controls are the primary risk.

If that boundary matches your system, start with the Infrai storage guide and validate the policy against a selected snapshot before rollout.

Further reading

  • NIST SP 800-66 Rev. 2, Implementing the HIPAA Security Rule: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/66/r2/final
  • Amazon S3 Object Lifecycle Management: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • Google Cloud Storage Object Lifecycle Management: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle
  • Azure Blob Storage lifecycle management: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/lifecycle-management-overview
  • Infrai storage discovery surface: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.multipart.create

title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
description: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

title: Choosing Matter Gateway Development Boards: A Hardware and Validation Checklist
description:
Gateway shopping lists grow quickly: a Linux board, a Bluetooth kit, a debugger, a serial adapter, a packet sniffer, power supplies, cables and breakout boards. Each item seems useful.

Then you start connecting them. One board is missing a pin. A firmware image targets a different chip. Another tool turns out to be unnecessary for the experiment in front of you. You have bought the hardware, but still cannot assemble the connection you wanted to test.

Our project bridges Bluetooth Mesh devices into Matter. A Linux host handles Matter and device mapping; a Silicon Labs module runs the Bluetooth Mesh stack; Telink-based lights and switches sit downstream. The PC prototype already connects to Apple Home, and we have built a Linux system image. Flashing the target board, testing real Silicon Labs–Telink Mesh interoperability and verifying the complete system are still ahead.

That makes my purchasing rule straightforward: each purchase should help answer a specific unresolved question.

Draw the connection before buying hardware

An operation in Apple Home should follow this path:

Apple Home
    ↓ Matter over the local network
Linux host: device mapping, commands, state synchronization
    ↓ UART / BGAPI
Silicon Labs module: Bluetooth Mesh NCP firmware
    ↓ Bluetooth Mesh
Telink device: light or switch

When someone presses the device's physical button, its new state must travel back and update Apple Home.

This diagram prevents a few common purchasing mistakes. The Matter connection in this design uses Ethernet or Wi-Fi. The downstream radio network is Bluetooth Mesh. Bluetooth Mesh and Thread are different protocols, despite both being mesh networks.

Using Matter here does not automatically require a Thread development kit or a Thread border router. Those become relevant if we later develop or connect Matter-over-Thread devices. Apple Home controllers, home hubs and software versions should follow Apple's current compatibility requirements.

Built-in Bluetooth on a Linux board also does not automatically replace our NCP. It normally comes with a different driver and host software arrangement. Our architecture places the Mesh stack on a separate module and accesses it through BGAPI; replacing that layer means evaluating the software interface and stack as well.

Start with the Bluetooth experiment

The PC-and-phone prototype let us work on Matter before the hardware arrived. The next useful purchase should establish whether the Silicon Labs module can control the Telink devices as required.

An existing PC can remain the host. Connect the Silicon Labs kit through its supported serial interface or a suitable USB-to-UART adapter. Get provisioning, control and status reporting working before moving the host to a Linux board. That gives each failure fewer possible causes.

Item What to check Question it answers
Silicon Labs development kit Exact chip and board IDs, Mesh NCP example support, programming and serial interfaces Can the intended SDK and firmware run on this hardware?
Telink board or controllable light sample Reflashable firmware, known Mesh models, factory-reset procedure Do provisioning, model control and status reporting interoperate?
Programmer/debugger Whether the kit includes it and whether it connects to this target Can we flash, recover and inspect the firmware?
USB data cable, power supply and wiring Data capability, power specifications, connectors and signal levels Are power and connections reliable?
USB-to-UART adapter, if needed Exposed flow-control pins and logic levels Can the host communicate with the NCP?

One device board running a standard on/off model is enough to start. Observing its LED is easier than immediately connecting a mains-powered light.

After the smallest setup works, add a second node, dimming and multi-channel devices to exercise group control, multiple elements and different models. One working node proves the basic procedure; it says little about network capacity or long-term reliability.

Match the Silicon Labs board to the firmware

A search for an “xG24 development board” produces kits with different chips, connectors and accessories. “BG24 module” in a design document is not a precise enough order specification.

Our planned module is in the BGM240 family. Before ordering, match the production module, the evaluation board's chip, the SDK version and the example project. Sharing “24” in their names does not mean two boards can run the same firmware binary.

I would confirm five things:

  1. Can the chosen Bluetooth Mesh SDK create the required NCP project for this exact board?
  2. Are the provisioner and required client models covered by examples or documented configuration?
  3. Does the target meet the project's Flash, RAM and component requirements?
  4. Does the kit include a debugger or development mainboard? What else is needed if buying a radio board separately?
  5. Where are UART, flow-control, reset and debug signals, and can an external host reach them?

A working Bluetooth example establishes support for that example. We need Bluetooth Mesh NCP specifically, so I would ask the supplier to identify the corresponding board and project.

The NCP application and its bootloader are also separate components. Flashing through a debugger proves that programming path. If the Linux host will later update the module over UART, we must also check the bootloader, pins, update-entry procedure and compatible firmware combination.

A complete kit may cost more than a bare board, but included debugging, serial access and documentation can save a lot of piecemeal setup.

A USB-to-UART chip name is not enough

Small FT232- or CP2102-based adapters are easy to buy without much thought. Some expose only TX, RX, ground and power. Even if the chip supports other signals, inaccessible pins on the finished adapter are no help.

For this design, I would choose an adapter exposing TX, RX, RTS, CTS and GND, then confirm driver support at the required baud rate. Check the finished board's pinout and schematic.

RTS/CTS coordinates the two ends of the connection. Wire signals according to their direction and both board manuals. The NCP configuration, host settings and physical wiring must agree: an endpoint waiting for flow control that is not connected may never communicate normally.

Hardware flow control reduces loss caused by an overwhelmed receiver. It does not provide error checking or retransmission. Electrical interference, wiring faults and parser errors still need their own diagnosis. Whether flow control is enabled depends on both ends; our hardware plan reserves the necessary connections.

Check voltage levels too. A board's UART might use 1.8V or 3.3V. A “3.3V/5V” jumper may select only the adapter's power output, without changing TX/RX logic levels.

Before ordering, establish the signal voltage, exposed flow-control pins and supported baud rates. TTL UART and RS-232 are not directly interchangeable. If the target already has its own supply, decide whether to connect the adapter's power pin according to the board's power design.

Choose the Linux board for its SDK and usable interfaces

We already compared processors in the RK3506, RK3562, RK3576 and RDK X5 article. Purchasing is now about development conditions.

Route Useful for Check before buying
RK3562 board The planned standard gateway platform Vendor BSP, UART pin muxing, flow control, Wi-Fi drivers and module availability
RK3506 board Evaluating a smaller configuration once functionality works 32-bit toolchain, measured memory use, storage layout and security support
RDK X5 Continuing our existing SDK and system-image work Board revision, image compatibility, flashing and interface configuration
Existing Linux computer or board Host-program and serial-protocol development Program compatibility and suitable serial or USB connections

We do not need all four. RK3562 is the planned standard product platform, while system-image work began with the X5 SDK. An existing platform can answer useful questions before the final hardware is selected.

I want four things from a Linux board supplier.

A rebuildable SDK: download access, version, build environment, toolchain and board configuration. A preinstalled image alone leaves us dependent on the supplier when trimming the system or changing drivers.

A usable application UART: a processor having many UARTs does not guarantee that a full TX/RX/RTS/CTS set reaches an accessible header. Check pin sharing and device-tree configuration. Keep the debug console separate so boot logs do not enter the NCP protocol stream.

A recovery path: flashing interface, recovery mode, debug console and partition documentation. When a custom image fails to boot, these become more valuable than extra compute performance.

Networking and persistent storage suited to the system: check IPv6, local discovery, Wi-Fi drivers and where configuration and device data survive reboots. Routers, VLANs, client isolation and firewalls can interfere with discovery. This is separate from purchasing public IPv6 service from an ISP.

Our earlier Buildroot work found IPv6 disabled in the default configuration. Booting successfully and reaching the internet are only the beginning of checking a Matter gateway.

Buy sniffers and logic analyzers when needed

The original topic notes included an nRF52840 Dongle. I would not make it mandatory in the first order.

Tools such as nRF Sniffer for Bluetooth LE can help observe radio traffic. Supported hardware, firmware and capture methods must match the tool version. Mesh analysis also depends on the bearer, encryption, keys and decoding software.

Buying a Bluetooth dongle does not automatically make all Mesh application traffic readable. Buy it once a problem really requires radio-level observation and the tool supports the traffic of interest. It also does not automatically serve as a Thread sniffer or the gateway's NCP.

A logic analyzer is useful for UART activity: bytes on the line, flow-control transitions and the stream around a fault. Choose input levels, channel count and sampling capability appropriate for the actual signals.

For the first experiments, capture serial logs, command responses, Mesh status events and timestamps. Add electrical or radio observation when those logs leave a specific question unanswered.

Test each layer after the boards arrive

Stage Work Evidence that this layer works
Development kit Flash supported firmware; connect serial, reset and debugger Stable communication and expected startup events or version information
Minimal Mesh network Provision and configure through a supported host example or tool Device operates and returns status
State in both directions Operate the device's physical button The host receives the change
Our host program Implement commands, responses and events Add, control, query and remove the same device
Matter bridge Map the device to Matter endpoints Apple Home controls it and receives device-side changes
Linux integration Move to the target board; configure startup, networking and UART Correct startup and restoration of device identity and persistent data
Recovery Restart host, module and device separately; disconnect network and power Explain the displayed state during failure and recover control and synchronization

Sending a command and completing a physical operation are different milestones. A successful serial write means bytes reached the serial subsystem. An NCP response must be interpreted according to the operation it acknowledges. Device state needs the relevant Mesh Status, observation of the device and agreement with the Matter display.

If Apple Home immediately shows a light as on while the real light remains off, the test has not passed. With optimistic state updates, also unplug the device and test response timeouts: the interface should not retain an incorrect state indefinitely.

Split recovery tests as well. Recovering from a host reboot does not prove module replacement works. A retained device list does not prove keys, sequence numbers and network state are handled correctly. Module replacement and network restoration need dedicated reliability work.

How I would place the orders

First, buy a Silicon Labs kit that supports the intended NCP firmware and one controllable Telink device board. Fill gaps in power, cables and programming access. Use the PC to establish provisioning, model control and status reporting.

Second, add the target Linux board and migrate the working host program. Confirm the SDK, complete UART interface and recovery procedure, preferably within a vendor ecosystem that can also support the future production module.

Then increase device variety and count. Test multi-channel switches, dimming, disconnections and recovery. Buy specialist capture and measurement tools as problems justify them.

Here is a supplier request you can reuse:

We are building a Linux-hosted gateway with a Bluetooth Mesh NCP. Please provide the exact board model and hardware revision, matching SDK and example project, required programming/debugging accessories, and the pinouts and logic levels for UART, RTS/CTS, reset and debug. For the Linux board, please also confirm UART device-tree configuration, system rebuild instructions and recovery flashing.

Clear answers make a board worth considering. A useful development setup helps resolve firmware compatibility, interoperability, return status and recovery one question at a time. Once those are understood, cost reduction and a custom carrier board become much better-informed decisions.

Working on Silicon Labs NCP, Telink interoperability or Linux UART integration? Get in touch.

References: Silicon Labs Bluetooth Mesh API, RDK documentation, Luckfox Lyra RK3506, nRF Sniffer for Bluetooth LE.

title: Building the Linux System for a Matter Gateway: RDK X5 SDK and Buildroot in WSL
description:
The previous post covered writing the gateway program in Rust with rs-matter. Right now it runs on a PC. To turn it into a gateway you can actually sell, one layer is still missing: the gateway's own Linux system.

Dev boards usually ship with an Ubuntu image that works the moment you plug them in. Most people's first instinct: just install the gateway program on Ubuntu and call it done?

Fine for development. Not for production. This post documents how we built the D-Robotics RDK X5 SDK inside WSL and used Buildroot to produce the gateway system image, plus a few pitfalls you only find by actually doing it.

Why not just use Ubuntu

The D-Robotics X5 SDK itself offers two root filesystems: an Ubuntu 22.04 image for development and Buildroot for production. For a gateway, the difference is obvious:

Ubuntu image Custom Buildroot system
Size Several GB A few hundred MB; the system partition is only 250MB
What's inside A full desktop-grade set of packages Only what you choose to include
Boot services Lots, and you're not sure which are running Every one is visible and removable
Updates apt, package by package Whole system image replaced; with A/B partitions you can roll back
Security review You have to justify a pile of software you don't use Small attack surface, easy to explain

A gateway sits in someone's home and nobody logs into it for years. What it needs: start the gateway program at boot, a read-only system that can't be corrupted by writes, and automatic fallback to the previous version if an update fails. All of that is standard practice in Buildroot; on Ubuntu you'd have to fight to strip things down.

Why start on the RDK X5

In the main processor selection post, we put the RDK X5 under "works, but not a good fit for a gateway": 10 TOPS of AI compute that a gateway will never use, and a relatively high cost.

But it has one very practical advantage: the SDK is publicly downloadable, with official documentation for building, system trimming, secure boot, A/B OTA and OP-TEE secure storage. Rockchip's SDK is also Buildroot-based and works much the same way. So for the system customization step, we used the best-documented SDK, the X5's, to get the whole workflow running end to end first.

A caveat up front: this post covers an image that has been built but not yet flashed and tested on a board. Flashing and real-world runs come in a later post once the board arrives.

Environment: a dedicated WSL distro

X5 SDK LNX6.1.176_PL5.1_V2.0.0 requires Ubuntu 22.04 and takes about 9.5GB once extracted. My daily driver is Ubuntu 24.04 and I didn't want the SDK's dependencies mixed in, so I installed a separate distro with its virtual disk on the D drive:

wsl --install -d Ubuntu-22.04 --name x5build --location 'D:\wsl\x5build' --no-launch

When running wsl commands from Git Bash, prefix them with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1, otherwise Git Bash rewrites paths starting with / into Windows paths.

Main components in the SDK:

Component Version
Linux kernel 6.1.176
U-Boot 2022.10
ATF 2.8
Buildroot 2025.02
Root filesystem glibc, SysV init
Cross toolchain ARM GNU Toolchain 11.3 (aarch64), bundled with the SDK

Fetching the code, installing dependencies and the first full build:

B=https://archive.d-robotics.cc/downloads/sdk/LNX6.1.176_PL5.1_V2.0.0/board_support_package
curl -O $B/platform_source_code.tar.gz.md5sum
curl -C - --retry 5 -O $B/platform_source_code.tar.gz   # 约 4.1GB，断了能续传
md5sum -c platform_source_code.tar.gz.md5sum
tar -I pigz -xf platform_source_code.tar.gz && cd platform_source_code

sudo build/install_host_deps.sh
sudo tar -xf toolchain/arm-gnu-toolchain-11.3.rel1-x86_64-aarch64-none-linux-gnu.tar.xz -C /opt/

./bd.sh lunch 8   # board_x5_soc_debug_config.mk
./bd.sh           # 第一次完整编译，约 12 分钟

lunch 8 is the debug configuration, with adb and debugging tools; for production you switch to the release configuration, lunch 9.

Watch the memory too: my global WSL limit is 8GB, while the SDK recommends 16GB. For now I'm only building the gateway and repackaging, and 8GB is enough. If you later need to build all of Buildroot from source and run short on memory, change memory= in C:\Users\<用户名>\.wslconfig and then run wsl --shutdown. Note that this shuts down every WSL distro.

Building the gateway program into the system

I wrapped the whole flow in a script, so after a code change it's a single line on Windows:

wsl -d x5build -- bash /mnt/d/<项目目录>/x5/build.sh

The script does a few things: syncs the source, cross-compiles the gateway program, drops it into the root filesystem and repackages the image. A few details along the way are worth mentioning.

Sync the source into the Linux filesystem before building

The project code lives on the Windows D drive, which is /mnt/d inside WSL. Building Rust directly under /mnt/d is much slower, because every file access crosses into the Windows filesystem. So the script first uses rsync to copy the code into a directory on WSL's own filesystem (excluding target and .git), and builds there.

The glibc target, not musl

Back during main processor selection, we planned to build a statically linked binary with aarch64-unknown-linux-musl that would work on both Rockchip and D-Robotics.

On the X5 we switched to aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, with the linker pointed at the SDK's bundled GCC 11.3:

CARGO_TARGET_AARCH64_UNKNOWN_LINUX_GNU_LINKER=/opt/arm-gnu-toolchain-11.3.rel1-x86_64-aarch64-none-linux-gnu/bin/aarch64-none-linux-gnu-gcc \
  cargo build --release --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu

The reason is that the X5's root filesystem is glibc to begin with. Linking with the SDK toolchain, whose glibc is older than the one in the firmware, guarantees the binary runs on the board, with no musl compatibility issues to deal with.

Overlay directory: restore first, then layer on top

The SDK provides a root filesystem overlay directory, system/buildroot/prebuilt/boot-utils-runtime; anything placed there goes into the image as-is. Our own files live in the project's x5/overlay/.

On its first run, the script backs up the SDK's original overlay directory as a snapshot. On every build after that, it restores the snapshot first, then layers our files on top.

The benefit is reversibility: delete a file from x5/overlay/ and the image goes back to the SDK original, with no leftovers from the previous build.

Disabling boot services we don't need

Disabling services also works through the overlay: drop in a script with the same name containing only exit 0 to replace the SDK's original init script. So far we've disabled:

Service Why it's disabled
S50telnet Plaintext remote login, which doesn't meet cybersecurity regulations like the EU's EN 18031 or the UK's PSTI
S40bluetoothd The module's built-in Bluetooth isn't used; Bluetooth Mesh goes through a separate Silicon Labs module
S65ptp4l, S66phc2sys PTP precision time sync, which a gateway doesn't need
S90cam-service Camera service
S99iiod IIO sensor service

sshd and adb stay for now during development and get disabled for production.

Autostart: the pitfall behind a single &

The gateway program has to start automatically at boot and restart if it crashes. The X5 uses SysV init, so an /etc/init.d/S95gateway script does the job.

First thing to watch out for: there's no bash on the board. Starting with V2.0.0, the X5 SDK no longer ships bash, so system scripts must be POSIX sh.

The second pitfall is subtler. The most obvious approach is to put the supervisor loop in the background in the init script:

while true; do /usr/bin/gateway; sleep 2; done &

Looks fine. But at boot, when rcS finishes running all the init scripts and exits, it sends a hangup signal to the background processes it started, and the loop gets killed along with it. The gateway program starts for a split second at boot, then vanishes.

The right way is start-stop-daemon -b, which detaches the daemon from rcS's session:

LOOP="cd /userdata/gateway && while true; do /usr/bin/gateway </dev/null 2>&1 | logger -t gateway; sleep 2; done"
start-stop-daemon -S -b -m -p /var/run/gateway.pid -x /bin/sh -- -c "$LOOP"

If the program exits abnormally, it restarts after 2 seconds, and its output goes to the system log via logger. There's no logread on the X5; logs are in /userdata/log/kernel/message, so use grep gateway to find them. Gateway data goes in /userdata/gateway/data/: that partition is writable, while the system partition is read-only.

Two SDK defaults you must change

IPv6 is off in the kernel by default

This was the nastiest pitfall of the whole process.

The X5 SDK's default kernel config says # CONFIG_IPV6 is not set, in both hobot_x5_soc_defconfig and hobot_x5_soc_perf_defconfig.

And Matter is built on IPv6: mDNS for device discovery and the communication between Apple Home and the gateway all go over IPv6. With the SDK's default kernel, the gateway program starts, but Apple Home will never find it.

The script checks both configs, flips them to CONFIG_IPV6=y if needed, and rebuilds the kernel with ./bd.sh boot. This needs re-checking whenever you move to a new SDK version.

Partition table: dropping the 700MB app partition

The SDK's default partition table includes a 700MB app partition that holds nothing but D-Robotics sample programs, which the gateway has no use for. The script uses a small bit of Python to remove it from x5-soc-debug-gpt.json and x5-soc-release-gpt.json.

Once the partition table changes, you need a full rebuild to generate a new GPT. The script checks whether the change has already been made and skips it if so, so it doesn't do a full build every time.

With it gone, the system partition is 250MB and userdata is only 50MB. 50MB is enough for the gateway's device table and Matter data for now, but it must be re-planned around real requirements before production.

What comes out

File Purpose
out/product/emmc_disk.img Full eMMC image, flashable via fastboot, DFU or TFTP
out/product/emmc_disk.simg Sparse image, smaller, but doesn't work with DFU
out/product/uart_usb/ Bootloader firmware for flashing blank chips
out/product/*.img Individual per-partition images

The xburn flashing tool is in software_tools/download_tools/ in the SDK download directory.

Still to do

Building the image is only the first step. Before production, there's still:

  1. Flash and test on a board: autostart, IPv6, Matter commissioning and logging all need a run-through on real hardware.
  2. A/B partitions and OTA: the SDK comes with seamless A/B updates. ./bd.sh otapackage generates full and delta update packages, and the device side provides a C interface in libupdate.so; our program handles downloading and calling it. But the default is a single partition, so the partition table has to be changed to enable it. That way there's no need to integrate RAUC or SWUpdate separately.
  3. Switch to the release configuration: remove adb and the debugging tools, disable sshd.
  4. Secure boot: the verification at each stage after U-Boot has to switch to our own signing keys, burned into eFuse. Burning eFuse is irreversible, so validate on a handful of samples first.

Wrapping up

Looking back, what took time in this step wasn't the build commands themselves; the SDK's bd.sh wraps them up nicely. What really took time were the defaults: IPv6 off in the kernel, no bash on the board, background processes killed by rcS, a 700MB sample partition stuffed into the partition table. None of them throws an error. They just make the gateway quietly stop working at some step.

Next up: once the board arrives, flash the image and hook up the Silicon Labs Bluetooth module, so the gateway controls a Bluetooth Mesh light on real hardware for the first time.

If you're also building gateways or IoT devices on the D-Robotics X5, Rockchip or another Buildroot SDK, I'd love to compare notes: linktr.ee/weiyii

title: Building a Matter Gateway in Rust: Bridging Devices to Apple Home
description:
In the previous post, we paired a prototype gateway with Apple Home using a computer and a phone. This time, let's look at the Rust code behind the Matter side. The project uses rs-matter. Real Bluetooth Mesh interoperability, the Linux board and large deployments remain untested.

A gateway is not one big light

The gateway appears as a Matter node. Endpoint 0 provides its root functions, endpoint 1 is the aggregator, and each bridged light gets its own endpoint. The device types and clusters tell the controller what each device is and can do: Descriptor, On/Off, Bridged Device Basic Information and Groups are included in this prototype.

Mapping endpoints to devices

A small device table holds the endpoint ID, device address, name, on/off state and reachability. When Apple Home asks to turn on endpoint 2, the gateway finds the matching device address and sends a command downstream. Real products need additional provisioning, security and recovery data.

Commands and state reports

The prototype updates its local state optimistically when a command arrives, sends the command, and uses a subsequent status report to correct the state. If the device never responds, the display may temporarily be wrong. Timeouts, retries, polling and offline detection still need work.

The reverse path matters too: a physical switch can change the light. The gateway matches the incoming device address, updates the endpoint state and notifies Matter subscribers. In the phone demonstration, repeated identical broadcasts are deduplicated to avoid restoring stale state. Those plaintext broadcasts are only a demo, not a real Mesh test.

Adding devices and surviving restarts

Devices can be added or removed while the prototype runs. It assigns increasing endpoint IDs instead of immediately reusing a deleted ID, reducing the risk of confusing controller state. Long-term allocation and recovery still need design and testing.

The device mapping is saved locally, while rs-matter has its own persistent store. The mapping is written to a temporary file before replacement; this reduces the chance of corrupting the old file but is not a complete power-failure guarantee. Actual device state must be confirmed again, and real Mesh keys need a secure backup and recovery plan.

What has been tested?

The demonstration verified pairing with Apple Home, displaying and controlling simulated bridged devices, simulated status reports, and basic addition, removal and restart behavior. It has not verified the real Mesh network, operation on the target Linux board, failure recovery or hundreds of devices. Test credentials are not production certification.

The Rust release profile enables size optimization, LTO and symbol stripping. One previous desktop build was about 2.3 MB; other targets and configurations need their own measurements. Next we will replace the simulation with real hardware and test the control and reporting paths.
