title: The model that wouldn't be forced
description:
When Anthropic released Opus 5.5 I was massively looking forward to it. It's a big step up on the Opus line, and the estate's chat adapters were going to get it the moment I could wire it in.

Then I read the release notes, and there it was, a few paragraphs down: the model now refuses forced tool use. That's a slightly awkward thing to read when forcing a tool is how you've been getting structured answers out of it for months!

The trick

A fair chunk of the estate asks a model a question and hands the reply to code and not to a person, so it has to arrive as JSON in a known shape (I've made the case for that before, and I still stand by it). In go/chat that's Ask: you give it a question and a type, it derives a JSON Schema from the type, and it fills your struct.

The Claude adapter, go/chat-anthropic, did that with a bit of sleight of hand. It offered the model one tool, called submit_response, whose input schema was your schema, and then forced the model to call it. The tool never ran. It was only there so the answer would arrive as a tool call's arguments, which the API validates against the schema. This is the old version, trimmed to the part that matters:

params.Tools = []anthropic.ToolUnionParam{
    {
        OfTool: &anthropic.ToolParam{
            Name:        toolName,
            Description: anthropic.String(c.cfg.SchemaDescription),
            InputSchema: inputSchema,
        },
    },
}
params.ToolChoice = anthropic.ToolChoiceUnionParam{
    OfTool: &anthropic.ToolChoiceToolParam{
        Type: "tool",
        Name: toolName,
    },
}

If you've ever had a card forced on you by a magician, it's the same move. You think you're picking any card you like, and the magician has made very sure there's only one you can pick. And like any decent trick it needed a bit of stagecraft round the back to keep going: the API insists a tool call is followed by a tool result, so after each answer the adapter wrote a fake one into the conversation, a constant whose content was the single word "recorded" (yes, really).

And it worked a treat on every model I'd pointed it at.

The volunteer stopped playing along

Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 turn it down before they've even started. Ask either of them with a forced tool and you get this back, on both:

HTTP 400 {"type":"error","error":{"type":"invalid_request_error",
  "message":"tool_choice: type \"tool\" and \"any\" are not supported for this model."}}

Now, "the model refuses" makes it sound like the model looked at the request and declined, and it never got that far. This is the API turning down the shape of the request for those two models, the same way it would turn down a malformed field. (Opus 5 and Fable 5 still accept it, so it's a change in the newest models and nothing to do with thinking being on by default.)

So Ask with a schema was broken on the newest models, one of which was already in the adapter's catalogue.

Not the fix I went in with

My first instinct came straight from the release notes, which suggested setting the tool mode to auto instead and still getting schema adherence out of it. So I went and read up on it.

The migration guide has three routes, depending on why you were forcing a tool in the first place: steering the model towards a real tool (use auto and name it in the prompt), guaranteeing schema-valid arguments for a real tool (strict under auto), and, the last one, if the forced call existed only to get JSON back, replace it with structured outputs. That last one was my case, to a tee. submit_response had never run once. The old code even called it "a structured-output device rather than a real tool" in its own comments.

By the time I'd written the spec (0024) I'd talked myself out of my auto idea, and I think for the right reason. auto wasn't flaky (it called the tool two times out of two when I tried it), but it would have kept the fake tool, kept the fake "recorded" result, and added a retry loop on top for the day auto decided not to bother. The line I ended up putting at the top of it says it better than I managed in the first draft: the reply should be valid against the schema because the API constrained it, not because the model chose to comply.

No card at all

So the fix (d203fed) doesn't force anything. The schema now travels in output_config.format, the Messages API's structured outputs, and the model is offered no tool at all. The new version is shorter, which I always take as a good sign:

func (c *Claude) applyResponseSchema(params *anthropic.MessageNewParams) error {
    raw, err := json.Marshal(c.cfg.ResponseSchema)
    if err != nil {
        return errors.Wrap(err, "marshalling the response schema")
    }

    var schema map[string]any
    if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &schema); err != nil {
        return errors.Wrap(err, "decoding the response schema")
    }

    delete(schema, "$schema")
    delete(schema, "$id")

    params.OutputConfig.Format = anthropic.JSONOutputFormatParam{Schema: schema}

    c.logger.Debug("Claude response schema", "schema", string(raw))

    return nil
}

The fake tool result went with it, so a conversation's history now records a question and an answer instead of a pretend tool call. No per-model switch either: they all take the new path, since they all accepted it when I tested.

The spike that waited a week for money

The testing nearly didn't happen on time. The spec was drafted in late September, and the spike that was meant to prove it failed on every call, with the API telling me my credit balance was too low (given the month I'd been having with bills, that felt about right). I topped it up the following week, with a firm note to keep the testing lean, and it ran in thirty-odd small calls.

All fifteen models in the catalogue accepted the format and came back schema-valid, and then it turned up something I wouldn't have guessed. The first draft of the spec folded the schema's description into the request, which seemed harmless, helpful even. With that description in, Opus 5.5 returned perfectly valid JSON with the arrays empty... three times out of three. Without it, the same request came back complete four times out of four! So the adapter now sends the caller's schema as given and adds nothing to it.

The first conformance test for the new behaviour passed against the unchanged adapter, which should have been impossible. The old SetTools, it turns out, threw the schema away whenever you gave the client real tools, so the test was looking for the absence of a tool and finding it for completely the wrong reason. That earned a second test case, and fixed a bug that hadn't been reported along the way.

The trick's over

I don't think forcing a tool was ever wrong, as such. At the time it was the cleverest way I had of getting a guaranteed shape back, and it served the estate well for months. But a trick that needs the volunteer to play along is only ever one release away from falling flat, and this time the volunteer had read the instructions. These days I tell the API the shape I want and it holds the model to it, no card required.

Originally published at phpboyscout.uk on 3 November 2026.

title: The transactional outbox: stop losing events between your database and Kafka
description:
This is one of the most common bugs in event-driven systems, and it hides in two innocent lines:

orderRepository.save(order);                 // 1. commit to the database
kafkaTemplate.send("orders", orderCreated);  // 2. publish the event

If the process dies between line 1 and line 2 — a deploy, an OOM kill, a lost connection to the broker — the order exists, but the event never goes out. Billing never bills, the warehouse never ships, and nothing errors, because from every service's point of view nothing happened.

Swapping the lines doesn't help. Publish first, and if the database commit then fails you've announced an order that doesn't exist.

The underlying problem is a dual write: two systems, no shared transaction. You can't make a Postgres commit and a Kafka publish atomic without distributed transactions, which most teams rightly avoid. But you can make two writes to the same database atomic. That's the whole idea of the outbox.

The pattern


The business write and the event are committed together; publishing happens afterwards, as often as needed. Explore the interactive diagram

  1. In the same transaction as the business change, insert a row into an outbox table describing the event.
  2. A separate relay reads new outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka.
  3. Once Kafka acknowledges, the relay marks the row as published (or deletes it).

If the service crashes after the commit, the outbox row is still there and the relay publishes it later. If the transaction rolls back, the outbox row rolls back with it. The event exists if and only if the order does.

The table and the write 

CREATE TABLE outbox (
    id            BIGSERIAL    PRIMARY KEY,
    aggregate_id  TEXT         NOT NULL,      -- e.g. the order id; used as the Kafka key
    event_type    TEXT         NOT NULL,      -- OrderCreated, OrderCancelled, ...
    payload       JSONB        NOT NULL,
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    published_at  TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished ON outbox (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

@Transactional
public Order placeOrder(PlaceOrder cmd) {
    Order order = orders.save(Order.from(cmd));
    outbox.save(new OutboxEvent(order.getId(), "OrderCreated", toJson(order)));
    return order;   // both rows commit together, or neither does
}

The partial index keeps the relay's query fast no matter how many published rows you keep around.

Relay option 1: polling

The simplest relay is a scheduled loop:

@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)
@Transactional
public void relay() {
    List<OutboxEvent> batch = jdbc.query("""
        SELECT id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload
        FROM outbox
        WHERE published_at IS NULL
        ORDER BY id
        LIMIT 100
        FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
        """, outboxRowMapper);

    for (OutboxEvent e : batch) {
        kafka.send("orders", e.aggregateId(), e.payload()).get();   // wait for the ack
    }
    jdbc.update("UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = ANY(?)", ids(batch));
}

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets you run several relay instances: each one locks a batch and the others skip it instead of waiting or double-publishing. Using aggregate_id as the Kafka key keeps all events for one order on one partition, so consumers see them in order.

Polling is easy to understand, needs no new infrastructure, and its latency (half a second here) is fine for most business events.

Relay option 2: change data capture

If you need lower latency or you don't want polling load on the database, use change data capture: a tool like Debezium reads the database's replication log (the Postgres WAL, the MySQL binlog) and publishes each new outbox row. Debezium even ships an "outbox event router" that maps outbox columns onto Kafka topics and keys.

The trade-off is operational: you now run Kafka Connect and Debezium, and you need to manage replication slots so they don't hold back WAL cleanup. For a team already running Kafka Connect it's the better relay. For a team that isn't, polling is usually enough to start.

The part people forget: duplicates

The outbox guarantees at-least-once, not exactly-once. If the relay publishes a batch and crashes before marking it published, the next run publishes it again. So consumers must be idempotent:

  • Give every event a unique ID (the outbox id, or a UUID in the payload).
  • In the consumer, record processed event IDs in the same transaction as the consumer's own side effect, and skip IDs it has already seen.

That's the same idea as idempotency keys for APIs, applied to messages — see Idempotency keys: making retries safe for money.

Operating it

  • Clean up. Delete published rows older than a few days with a scheduled job, or partition the table by day and drop old partitions.
  • Alert on the oldest unpublished row. now() - min(created_at) WHERE published_at IS NULL is the single best health metric: if it grows, events are stuck.
  • Keep payloads self-contained. Put the data consumers need in the event, rather than making every consumer call back to your API — otherwise you've rebuilt the coupling the events were meant to remove.

Takeaways

  • "Commit, then publish" is a dual write, and it loses events on crashes.
  • Write the event into an outbox table in the same transaction; publish it afterwards.
  • Relay by polling with SKIP LOCKED to start; move to CDC when latency or load demands it.
  • The outbox is at-least-once: consumers must de-duplicate.

title: Converting Excel Worksheets to Images in Java: A Practical Look
description:
Excel workbooks are designed for data manipulation and analysis, but there are scenarios where a static image is more appropriate. Whether you are generating report snapshots for a web dashboard, embedding table data into an email, or archiving records in a format that prevents accidental edits, converting worksheets to images is a practical requirement. In Java, this task is not natively supported by the standard library. While Apache POI is the de facto standard for reading and writing Excel files, it does not include a rendering engine to produce visual output. This is where third-party libraries come into play.

This article examines the practical aspects of converting Excel content to images in a Java environment using Spire.XLS for Java as an example tool. It covers the library's approach to rendering, the code required for common conversion scenarios, and the trade-offs developers should consider.

Why Convert Excel to an Image?

Before diving into implementation, it is worth understanding the contexts where this conversion is beneficial. Excel files, while rich in data, are not always the most portable format for presentation. An image file (PNG or JPEG) can be viewed on any device without spreadsheet software, embedded directly into HTML without complex browser rendering, and shared without exposing the underlying formulas or raw data structure.

Common use cases include generating visual snapshots for automated reporting systems, creating thumbnails for document management systems, or preparing data for platforms that only accept image uploads. The key constraint is that the conversion must preserve the visual fidelity of the original sheet—cell formatting, merged regions, and layout must remain intact.

How the Library Handles Rendering

Spire.XLS for Java operates as a standalone library that does not require Microsoft Office or Excel to be installed on the host machine. It includes its own rendering engine that interprets Excel formatting and outputs it to standard Java BufferedImage objects or directly to files. This is a relevant architectural characteristic for server-side applications where installing Office is impractical or prohibited by licensing.

The library supports two primary conversion modes: saving an entire worksheet as an image, or extracting a specific range of cells. For scenarios requiring higher output quality, the library exposes DPI (dots per inch) settings through its ConverterSetting class, allowing developers to adjust resolution for print-oriented outputs. Chart objects within worksheets can also be converted independently, which is useful when the visual element of interest is a graph rather than the raw data table.

Converting a Worksheet to an Image

The most straightforward operation is converting an entire worksheet. The workflow involves loading the workbook, selecting the desired sheet by index, and invoking the save method.

import com.spire.xls.*;

public class ExcelToImage {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();
        workbook.loadFromFile("input/sample.xlsx");

        Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);
        sheet.saveToImage("output/sheet_image.png");

        workbook.dispose();
    }
}

This method produces a PNG file representing the used range of the worksheet. The library determines the output dimensions based on the content and default rendering settings. For many internal reporting needs, this level of simplicity is sufficient. However, developers should be aware that very large worksheets may result in correspondingly large image files, which could impact performance in memory-constrained environments.

Extracting Specific Cell Ranges

In many reporting workflows, only a subset of the sheet is relevant. Exporting the entire sheet introduces unnecessary whitespace and can make the output image difficult to read when embedded in documents or web pages. The library provides an overload that accepts row and column indices to define a rectangular region.

import com.spire.xls.Workbook;
import com.spire.xls.Worksheet;
import javax.imageio.ImageIO;
import java.awt.image.BufferedImage;
import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;

public class RangeToImage {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Workbook workbook = new Workbook();
        workbook.loadFromFile("input/sample.xlsx");

        Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);

        // Convert from row 1, column 1 to row 7, column 4
        BufferedImage image = sheet.toImage(1, 1, 7, 4);
        ImageIO.write(image, "PNG", new File("output/range_image.png"));

        workbook.dispose();
    }
}

The toImage method returns a BufferedImage, giving the developer full control over the output format and any subsequent processing. This approach is particularly useful for generating summary tables or extracting a single report section from a larger financial model.

Controlling Output Resolution

The default rendering DPI may be adequate for screen display but insufficient for printing or high-density displays. The library allows explicit configuration of horizontal and vertical DPI before conversion. This setting affects the pixel dimensions of the output while maintaining the same physical layout proportions.

Workbook workbook = new Workbook();
workbook.loadFromFile("input/sample.xlsx");

workbook.getConverterSetting().setXDpi(300);
workbook.getConverterSetting().setYDpi(300);

Worksheet sheet = workbook.getWorksheets().get(0);
sheet.saveToImage("output/high_res.png");

Setting the DPI to 300 or higher is a standard practice for print-oriented outputs. It is important to note that higher DPI values increase memory consumption during rendering and produce larger file sizes, so the choice should be driven by the target medium rather than arbitrary quality preferences.

Practical Considerations and Limitations

While the library simplifies the conversion process, developers should evaluate several factors before integrating it into a production system.

Formatting Fidelity: The library renders cell styles, fonts, and borders with reasonable accuracy, but complex Excel features such as conditional formatting, data bars, or sophisticated custom number formats may not translate perfectly. Testing with representative files from the actual business domain is essential.

Font Availability: Since the rendering happens in the Java Virtual Machine, the fonts used in the Excel file must be available on the host system. If a specified font is missing, the library will substitute another, potentially altering text layout and causing content to overflow cell boundaries. On Linux servers, this often requires explicit installation of common fonts.

Licensing and Cost: Spire.XLS is a commercial product. While a free version exists, it imposes restrictions such as watermarks or limits on the number of rows processed per file. For projects with strict budget constraints or high-volume processing requirements, the licensing terms must be carefully reviewed. Open-source alternatives using Apache POI combined with manual Graphics2D rendering exist, but they require substantially more development effort to handle formatting and layout correctly.

Memory Management: Loading large Excel files and rendering them to high-resolution images can consume significant heap memory. The Workbook object should be disposed of explicitly after use to release resources, especially in long-running server processes.

Conclusion

Converting Excel worksheets to images in Java is a solvable problem with the right library. Spire.XLS for Java offers a direct API that handles the rendering complexity, supporting full-sheet conversion, range extraction, and DPI configuration without requiring Office dependencies. The approach is suitable for server-side automated reporting and archival workflows where visual fidelity is important, but the Excel application itself is not available.

Developers should approach this capability with an understanding of its boundaries. Font dependencies, the commercial nature of the library, and the inherent differences between spreadsheet rendering and browser/print rendering mean that output quality should be validated against specific use-case requirements. For simple tables and standard formatting, the library performs reliably. For highly complex or highly customized spreadsheets, a proof-of-concept phase with actual production files is recommended before committing to a particular solution.

title: ISC Stormcast For Tuesday, November 3rd, 2026 https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10162, (Tue, Nov 3rd)
A Tiny Regex Bug in Adyen's Java Library, and How My Fix Shipped in SDK v42.0.0
description:
In my last posts I wrote about why I started open source and about my first merged PR in Zalando Logbook. This one is about a PR in the Adyen Java API Library, and it is a good example of how a very small bug can hide in plain sight.

What is the Adyen Java library?

Adyen is a global payments company, and this library is how Java applications talk to Adyen's APIs. The whole SDK has to build the correct base URL for every service, for both test and live environments. If that URL is wrong, the payment call goes to the wrong place.

The bug

The method createBaseURL in Service.java swaps test URLs for live URLs. It used String.replaceFirst() to do that.

Here is the catch: replaceFirst() takes a regex, not a plain string. In regex, a dot . means "any character". So a URL part like pal-test.adyen.com was not matching a literal dot. It was matching any character in that position.

Simplified, it looked like this:

// Before: the dots are treated as "any character" because this is a regex
url = url.replaceFirst("pal-test.adyen.com", "pal-live.adyen.com");

For normal URLs it worked fine, which is exactly why nobody noticed. But a URL that only looks similar, with other characters where the dots should be, could still be transformed by mistake.

The fix

The fix was small. I replaced the affected replaceFirst() calls with String.replace(), which matches plain text with no regex at all:

// After: plain literal matching, no regex wildcard risk
url = url.replace("pal-test.adyen.com", "pal-live.adyen.com");

I updated the pal-, checkout- and device-api- blocks. I left the two calls without dots (-live to -test and back) as replaceFirst() on purpose, because they were not affected by this issue.

I also added a test, testLivePalUrlOnlyMatchesLiteralDots(), using a URL shaped like pal-testXadyenYcom. It looks like the real endpoint but has no literal dots, so it must not be transformed. The test proves the fix and protects against the bug coming back.

What the review taught me

  • Keep the scope tight. The maintainer said he thought about asking me to use .replace in the other places in the method for consistency. Then he decided it was not necessary, because it was unclear whether that would cause some other issue. A good reviewer is careful about changes that were not asked for. It reminded me to fix the bug I was given, not everything I could.
  • Formatting is part of the PR. The project had recently enforced code formatting, and my PR was blocked until I ran mvn spotless:apply. A tiny thing, but it taught me to run the project's formatter and checks before pushing, every time.
  • Tests are the real proof. My first version of the test was not strong enough, and I improved it so the URL structurally matched the real one with non-dot separators. A test should fail without your fix, otherwise it proves nothing.

The PR was approved and merged, and the change shipped in SDK v42.0.0. Seeing something I wrote inside a release of a payments SDK was a good feeling. The change was small, but real people who use the library get it.

What I would tell someone starting out

  1. Small bugs are good first PRs. You do not need a big feature to make a real contribution.
  2. Read the project's contributing rules and run its formatter and tests before you push.
  3. Write a test that fails without your fix.
  4. Do not widen the scope. Fix what the issue asks for.

Proof of my work

Everything here is public, so you can check it yourself:

  • Adyen/adyen-java-api-library #1952: the regex fix (merged, shipped in v42.0.0)
  • The original issue #1838
  • zalando/logbook #2301: StatusCodeBasedSink and LevelBasedHttpLogWriter (merged)
  • PicnicSupermarket/error-prone-support #2275: merged after review
  • Sionna Visualizer: my side project, a 6G + AI dashboard (live demo)
  • My GitHub: all my repos and contributions

Next post: my PR in Picnic's error-prone-support, and what working with a strict reviewer taught me.

If you are a maintainer, a recruiter or a team looking for someone who learns in public and likes to collaborate, my DMs are open. Tell me in the comments if you have hit a regex surprise like this one.

title: Building a Zero-Dependency Key-Value Engine in 5 Languages (Rust, Go, TypeScript, Swift, Kotlin)
description:
Modern distributed software is polyglot. A cloud backend might have microservices written in Go, low-latency data pipelines in Rust, web APIs in TypeScript/Node, iOS clients in Swift, and Android/JVM services in Kotlin.

Yet, when working across different language ecosystems, caching semantics are wildly fragmented:

  • Eviction policies behave differently ($O(1)$ LRU vs probabilistic vs FIFO).
  • Concurrency models handle mutex contention and clock drift inconsistently.
  • Dependency bloat drags dozens of third-party packages into otherwise clean microservices.

To solve this, we engineered KVDock natively across 5 languages with zero external dependencies in core and unified memory/concurrency semantics.

Here is what we learned building high-performance key-value engines across Rust, Go, TypeScript, Swift, and Kotlin.

1. Rust (kvdock-rs): Monotonic Clocks & Zero Lock Contention

In systems programming, relying on wall-clock time (SystemTime) for TTL eviction is dangerous because NTP clock synchronizations or leap seconds can cause erratic cache expirations.

In kvdock-rs, we enforce TTL using monotonic Instant:

use kvdock_rs::{KVDock, MemoryAdapter};
use std::time::Duration;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let adapter = MemoryAdapter::new(10_000);
    let dock = KVDock::new(adapter).with_default_ttl(Duration::from_secs(60));

    // Single-flight stampede coalescing in Rust
    let session = dock.get_or_set("user:session:101", || async {
        fetch_user_from_db().await
    }).await;
}
  • Concurrency: Thread-safe KVDock<A> backed by read-write locks for sub-microsecond concurrent reads.
  • Eviction: True $O(1)$ LRU with doubly-linked intrusive pointers.

2. Go (kvdock-go): Generics & Singleflight Mutexes

Go 1.18+ generics revolutionized type-safe caching without interface{} type assertions:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "time"
    "github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock-go"
)

type UserSession struct {
    UserID string
    Role   string
}

func main() {
    dock := kvdock.New(kvdock.WithMemoryAdapter(10000), kvdock.WithTTL(60 * time.Second))

    // Generic type-safe get or set
    val, err := kvdock.GetOrSet[UserSession](dock, context.Background(), "user:101", func() (UserSession, error) {
        return queryUserFromDB()
    })
}
  • Concurrency: Combines atomic operational telemetry with internal single-flight deduplication to ensure concurrent Goroutines requesting the same missing key coalesce into a single execution.

3. TypeScript (kvdock): Zero Dependencies & Universal Runtimes

JavaScript runtimes are now fragmented across Node.js, Bun, Deno, and Cloudflare Workers:

import { KVDock, TieredDock } from "kvdock";
import { MemoryAdapter } from "kvdock/adapters/memory";
import { RedisAdapter } from "kvdock/adapters/redis";

const dock = new TieredDock({
  l1: new MemoryAdapter({ maxSize: 10_000 }), // In-memory L1 (< 0.05ms)
  l2: new RedisAdapter({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL }), // Distributed L2
  l1TTL: 15_000
});
  • Key Innovation: Zero runtime dependencies in core. Tree-shakeable dual ESM/CJS exports with single-flight promise coalescing that reduces database stampedes by 99.9%.

4. Swift (kvdock-swift): Swift 6 Concurrency & Actor Isolation

In modern Swift, data races are caught at compile-time using structured concurrency:

import KVDockSwift

let dock = await KVDock(
    adapter: MemoryAdapter(capacity: 10_000),
    defaultTTL: .seconds(60)
)

// Actor-isolated thread-safe access
let user = try await dock.getOrSet("user:profile") {
    try await fetchUserProfile()
}
  • Uses ContinuousClock for nanosecond monotonic TTL expiration.

5. Kotlin (kvdock-kt): Access-Order LRU & Coroutines

On the JVM and Android, coroutine compatibility and low memory overhead are paramount:

import com.kvdock.KVDock
import com.kvdock.adapters.MemoryAdapter
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.minutes

val dock = KVDock(MemoryAdapter(maxSize = 10_000), defaultTTL = 1.minutes)

val order = dock.getOrSet("order:7788") {
    fetchOrderFromDatabase()
}

The Polyglot Ecosystem on GitHub

Explore the source code, benchmarks, and architectures:

  • TypeScript Engine: github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock
  • Rust Engine: github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock-rs
  • Go Engine: github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock-go
  • Swift Engine: github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock-swift
  • Kotlin Engine: github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock-kt

⭐ Star the repos & follow @zisam-glitch for deep dives into low-latency systems architecture!

title: USA SMS Receipt Alerts: Testing Settlement Evidence Before Selecting a Messaging API
description:
Choose the SMS provider whose evidence you can reconcile to a settled payment before comparing notification features. For a marketplace order receipt, that means preserving the settlement reference, the receipt intent, and the provider message identifier as separate records.

TL;DR: Twilio, Bandwidth, and Vonage are credible USA SMS API choices for alert notifications; evaluate them against the same settlement-replay experiment. Include Infrai when consolidating backend credentials and billing matters, provided a polling-based evidence workflow meets your requirements. An accepted message is insufficient evidence that the receipt reached its recipient.

How should USA SMS API services preserve evidence for receipt notifications?

The decision is to create one durable receipt intent per settled payment and notification purpose, then reconcile transport evidence independently. This exactly-once mindset belongs at the ledger boundary: a provider's response cannot establish that payment settled, and a successful submission cannot establish that a recipient read a receipt. Keep those claims separate.

For the proposed experiment, use synthetic marketplace order order-4107, payment payment-882, and settlement reference settlement-19. Submit that settlement twice, then submit an unsettled payment. The identifiers are test inputs, not observations from a production system. Keep phone numbers and payment credentials out of the fixture; use controlled destinations during the subsequent provider evaluation.

Replay is ordinary.

A useful audit trail must answer which settlement authorized the receipt, which content revision was selected, what submission was attempted, and which subsequent observations changed the recorded messaging state. Store timestamps alongside those observations, with the provider identifier when one has been returned. An absent observation remains unknown; promoting it to delivered would turn a reconciliation gap into a false compliance assertion.

US A2P 10DLC compliance also needs a separate review. Twilio publishes documentation for that process, but a messaging API and its delivery records do not establish the marketplace's compliance by themselves. Decide what registration, consent evidence, retention, and access controls your particular traffic requires with the responsible compliance owner; this article supplies an engineering test, not a legal determination.

Compare the evidence boundary before selecting the API

Infrai's primary operational attraction here is one key and one bill across backend services, reducing credential administration and the pile of invoices attached to a marketplace's receipt workflow. Its public discovery surface supplies request and response schemas without requiring a key, which gives an evaluator a second concrete benefit: inspecting integration contracts before writing an adapter. One REST API also lets the receipt worker use plain HTTP without installing another SDK, keeping transport dependencies small when the worker only needs a status read.

A marketplace team should try Infrai for receipt-status reconciliation when it already wants consolidated backend access and can accept polling, because credential consolidation and public schema discovery remove distinct operating and integration tasks. This is a conditional recommendation. The experiment must still establish whether its evidence fits the team's requirements.

Infrai offers one REST API with no SDK to install: plain HTTP requests let the Go reconciliation worker use its standard library for status reads. Its unified API provides a simple interface across 295 routes and 20 modules, so a team integrating several backend capabilities can reuse the same transport conventions. This SDK-free integration removes an additional client dependency. That broad backend coverage matters only if the marketplace needs other services through the same integration boundary; a dedicated SMS system should not count unused modules as a benefit.

The interface is simple but powerful in a specific, testable sense: public discovery is self-describing, and runnable examples in 10 languages accompany every documented capability. Start with the Go example when reviewing the receipt adapter, then compare the request against the schema. This is contract-review assistance, not evidence of delivery.

Candidate Reason to include it Boundary to evaluate with the same fixture
Twilio Popular US APIs, flexibility, and a strong reputation for operational reliability make it a reasonable reference candidate. Use its US A2P 10DLC documentation in the compliance review; reputation cannot replace evidence from your own receipt workflow.
Bandwidth Its domestic USA SMS rate positioning makes it relevant to a marketplace with substantial US traffic. Require the same settlement linkage and evidence review before letting commercial terms decide the result.
Vonage Bulk discounts and promotions can matter when assessing a larger notification workload. Check the current offer separately; a promotion does not demonstrate reconciliation quality or compliance suitability.
Infrai Consolidated credentials and billing, with public discovery schemas, suit a team integrating several backend services. Messaging event observations use a pull model; test whether your polling interval and evidence handling satisfy the receipt requirement.
Amazon SES A separate candidate for an email-receipt evaluation if that channel enters scope. Keep it outside this SMS ranking; this experiment establishes no email delivery or compliance conclusion.

Pricing and features belong in the procurement record, but this comparison deliberately has no unit-price ranking. Ask for current terms against the same traffic assumptions after the evidence gate passes; the supplied commercial distinctions do not support a claim that any candidate is universally cheapest.

There is a real trade-off in the last row. Pull-based observation gives the worker an explicit reconciliation schedule, while putting freshness and repeated-read handling in the application. If immediate event push is mandatory, a specialist messaging integration that demonstrates that behavior in evaluation is the better choice. Also assess geographic abuse controls and country-based spending cutoffs in the business layer rather than assuming the transport settles that policy.

Put the settlement invariant on the critical path

The following complete Go program exercises the local decision boundary without sending a message. Save it as main.go and run it with Go. It creates a receipt intent from a settled payment, rejects a conflicting settlement reference, and checks that replay does not create a second intent. No provider behavior is simulated as a successful delivery.

package main

import (
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

type Settlement struct {
    PaymentID string
    Reference string
    Settled   bool
}

type Receipt struct {
    PaymentID string
    Reference string
    Purpose   string
}

type Gate struct {
    intents map[string]Receipt
    audit   []string
}

func (g *Gate) Observe(s Settlement) (bool, error) {
    if !s.Settled {
        g.audit = append(g.audit, "held:"+s.PaymentID)
        return false, nil
    }
    if s.PaymentID == "" || s.Reference == "" {
        return false, errors.New("missing settlement identity")
    }
    key := s.PaymentID + ":order-receipt"
    if prior, ok := g.intents[key]; ok {
        if prior.Reference != s.Reference {
            g.audit = append(g.audit, "conflict:"+s.PaymentID)
            return false, errors.New("settlement reference conflict")
        }
        g.audit = append(g.audit, "replay:"+s.PaymentID)
        return false, nil
    }
    g.intents[key] = Receipt{s.PaymentID, s.Reference, "order-receipt"}
    g.audit = append(g.audit, "intent:"+s.PaymentID)
    return true, nil
}

func main() {
    g := Gate{intents: make(map[string]Receipt)}
    settled := Settlement{"payment-882", "settlement-19", true}
    created, err := g.Observe(settled)
    if err != nil || !created {
        panic("first settlement must create an intent")
    }
    created, err = g.Observe(settled)
    if err != nil || created {
        panic("replay must reuse the intent")
    }
    created, err = g.Observe(Settlement{"payment-883", "", false})
    if err != nil || created {
        panic("unsettled payment must remain held")
    }
    _, err = g.Observe(Settlement{"payment-882", "settlement-20", true})
    if err == nil || len(g.intents) != 1 || len(g.audit) != 4 {
        panic("conflict or audit invariant failed")
    }
    fmt.Println("local invariant checks passed")
}

This is an executable invariant demonstration, not a production outbox. Its map and audit slice disappear when the process exits, and they provide no concurrency protection. A production implementation needs a durable unique constraint for the receipt identity and an atomic transaction that records both the intent and its audit entry; otherwise, two settlement consumers can each pass a local existence check and submit duplicate receipts.

The sender belongs after that transaction.

Use the intent identity to correlate every attempt, and inspect the chosen operation's actual idempotency contract before enabling automatic retries. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a default 24-hour deduplication window; that bounded convention does not replace a marketplace's durable record of an older settled payment. Nor does it prove that every capability shares the same retry semantics. Public discovery exposes operation-level schemas and idempotency information, which should become inputs to the adapter review.

A particularly consequential trap is the ambiguous submission: the worker loses its response after the provider may have accepted the request. Marking that attempt as definitively failed and creating another receipt intent destroys the very identity the settlement gate preserved. Keep the attempt unresolved until the documented provider contract supplies a safe reconciliation or retry decision.

Run the same experiment against every candidate

The local program establishes only the first boundary. Next, connect each candidate to the same controlled receipt fixture, preserving the intended text revision and correlation identity, and record observations without interpreting acceptance as delivery. For Infrai, inspect discovery first, then exercise SMS submission and the documented status lookup as one measured leg of this experiment. Use polling for its event observations and retain the raw evidence alongside your application interpretation.

This second standalone Go program performs that status read. Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_SMS_ID to your own key and an existing test message identifier before running it. It prints the response without guessing its schema; the adapter must interpret the documented response contract before assigning an application state. Keep raw evidence in restricted audit storage rather than a general application log. The call is read-only, uses an explicit method, and bounds rate-limit retries under an overall deadline.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    key, id := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("INFRAI_SMS_ID")
    if key == "" || id == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_SMS_ID")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    endpoint := strings.Replace("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/status/{id}", "{id}", url.PathEscape(id), 1)
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if requested := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if requested := time.Until(date); requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Set a proposed evidence-freshness target of 60 seconds before running the trial. That number is an experimental requirement, not a provider latency claim or a guarantee of carrier delivery. A 10-second polling interval is one test configuration; record actual observation times and decide whether that interval is operationally acceptable.

Use these pass/fail criteria consistently:

  1. Two copies of the same settled-payment fixture produce one durable receipt intent; the unsettled fixture produces none.
  2. A conflicting settlement reference is held for review, and the audit record preserves the conflict without replacing the original receipt identity.
  3. Every attempted submission is linked to its receipt intent. A missing response is retained as an unresolved attempt until the documented retry or reconciliation rule can be applied.
  4. Observed messaging states remain distinguishable from ledger settlement and submission acceptance. Re-reading the same evidence does not create another receipt.
  5. Evidence available through the integration is recorded within the proposed freshness target, or the candidate fails that target. Pending transport states remain pending.
  6. The compliance owner can retrieve the agreed registration, consent, content, and delivery evidence for the test receipt, with each gap explicitly identified.

These are acceptance criteria, not reported benchmark results. Record a failure when the evidence cannot answer a required question, even if a handset visibly received the message. Conversely, a test cannot establish general carrier reach or long-term reliability from a single controlled destination.

The decision rule is strict: exclude any integration that fails a mandatory invariant or evidence requirement, then compare integration effort and commercial terms among the survivors. If the polling configuration passes, Infrai's consolidated access may justify selection. If it fails, changing the provider or revising the requirement requires an explicit architecture decision; silently reclassifying stale evidence as current is unacceptable.

Rejected option: submit directly from the payment handler

Reject synchronous SMS submission as the sole record of a marketplace receipt. A payment handler can finish its financial work while the notification outcome remains uncertain; coupling those outcomes makes a messaging response look like a settlement decision and leaves replay behavior dependent on the transport.

The direct approach still has a valid use case for a disposable demonstration using synthetic payments, where losing notification state is acceptable and no durable compliance evidence is required. That boundary does not fit the receipt system evaluated here.

Keep the durable intent and reconciliation record even when a provider offers convenient submission semantics. If consolidated access and a pull-based evidence boundary fit your system, start with the Infrai documentation.

References

  • Twilio US A2P 10DLC compliance documentation
  • Bandwidth messaging documentation
  • Vonage SMS API documentation

title: What migrating a Vuetify 2 dashboard to Vue 3 actually took
description:
Vue 2 reached end of life on 31 December 2023. Vuetify 2 followed on 25 January 2025. If your admin panel still runs on them, it gets no security fixes, and every SOC 2 or ISO 27001 review asks why.

To show what the move involves, I migrated a well-known open-source app in public: Creative Tim's Vuetify Material Dashboard (MIT, 1.3k GitHub stars). The full branch is here: https://github.com/SayedEsmail/vuetify-material-dashboard. Every commit handles one concern and lists the breaking changes it fixed, so the commit log reads as the migration plan. I wrote the plan, did the work with an AI coding assistant, and reviewed every change myself at the end.

The starting point

  • Vue 2.6, Vuetify 2.2, Vuex 3, Vue Router 3, Vue CLI 4 on webpack 4.
  • 33 single-file components and 5,620 lines of JavaScript and Vue.
  • 553 lines of custom SASS written against Vuetify 2's internal class names.

The target was Vue 3.5, Vuetify 3, Pinia, Vue Router 4 and Vite.

Step 0: delete before you migrate

Seven of the 33 components could not be reached. Five views had no route, and two components were only used by those views. A form-validation library was registered globally and never used. The test suite still asserted the Vue CLI scaffold text, so it could never pass.

Deleting that first removed a third of the code before any migration work started. It is the cheapest saving in every migration, and an audit finds it in an afternoon.

Why Vuetify 2 projects can't migrate "gradually"

The usual Vue 2 path is the @vue/compat build: run on Vue 3 in compatibility mode, then fix warnings one by one. That path is closed when the app uses Vuetify 2, because Vuetify 2 cannot run on Vue 3 at all. The UI layer has to move in one step.

So the order matters:

  1. Tooling first: Vue CLI to Vite, then the new dependency set.
  2. App bootstrap: createApp, createVuetify, the i18n adapter.
  3. State and routing: Vuex to Pinia, Router 3 to 4. These are mechanical.
  4. Vue-2-only plugins: the chart wrapper had no Vue 3 version, so it became a 56-line local component on Chartist 1.x.
  5. Vuetify, from the outside in: layout shell, then the shared component library, then the views.
  6. The custom CSS layer last.

Where the real work is

Component APIs changed a lot, but those changes are well documented: v-list-item-content is gone, activator slots give props instead of on and attrs, v-tabs-items became v-window. I hit 43 distinct breaking changes and logged each one. That list is now the checklist I run in every audit.

The expensive surprises were elsewhere:

  • Custom CSS on framework internals. 470 lines targeted classes like .theme--light, .v-size--default and .v-card__text. Not one of them exists in Vuetify 3. Nothing errors. The styles silently stop applying.
  • Behaviour that changed without an error. In Vuetify 3, a navigation item linked to / stays highlighted on every page unless you mark it exact. Alerts now clip anything positioned outside them. The build stays green and the UI is subtly wrong.
  • Bugs that were already there. The theme colour picker never reached dark mode because it read a property that was never defined. Turning the sidebar image back on stored the value true instead of an image URL. Neither was caused by the migration, but a migration is when someone finally reads every line.

The result

  • Vue 3.5, Vuetify 3.13, Pinia, Vue Router 4, Vite 8, ESLint 10.
  • 26 components, 3,644 lines of JavaScript and Vue, and 350 lines of SASS in one file.
  • The same 8 routes and the same behaviour, minus the two bugs above.
  • A test suite that runs: every route renders in the full layout with zero Vue warnings.

What I'd tell a team planning this

  1. Run an inventory first. Dead code, undeclared dependencies and tests that can't pass are common, and they change the scope.
  2. Budget for CSS and visual QA, not only for component syntax.
  3. If you use Vuetify 2, plan the UI layer as one cut-over, behind a feature branch, with route-level smoke tests in place before you start.
  4. Decide the target versions up front. Vuetify 4 is out now. Going to Vuetify 3 first is still the shorter step from Vuetify 2, and 3 to 4 is a much smaller change.

If your product still runs on Vue 2, Nuxt 2 or Vuetify 2, I do a fixed-price migration readiness audit: a written report with the dead code, the breaking changes that apply to your codebase, the risks, and a fixed quote for the migration.

title: Moderation API Timeout Handling: Idempotent Retries and Recovery Boundaries
description:
A moderation timeout is a delivery problem before it is a classification problem. Retry a bounded set of transient failures with exponential backoff, give every attempt a deadline, and make the final decision explicit: allow, hold for review, or reject. For a marketplace, that state matters more than squeezing another attempt into the same request window.

TL;DR: keep the synchronous path short, log timeout and rate-limit details, and move uncertain content to a durable review state. A local fallback can keep the queue moving, but it should not silently turn an unavailable remote classifier into an approval.

For a marketplace already operating several backend services, Infrai fits the surrounding workflow: one REST API, one key, one bill, and per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata. It has no dedicated moderation endpoint, so use that fit for orchestration and cost visibility, not as a claim that it replaces a specialist moderation API.

The retry is not the decision.

What did the timeout actually change?

The dangerous assumption is that a timeout means the moderation request was never seen. It may have reached the provider and only lost its response. Retrying a write-like moderation workflow without a stable request identity can produce duplicate work, inconsistent audit records, or two different decisions for the same marketplace comment.

The operational invariant is simple: one content revision gets one decision record, while delivery may have several attempts. Store a content revision ID, an attempt count, the provider request ID when available, and the final state. Keep the retry policy separate from the business decision.

I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so my first question is not “how many retries should this client make?” It is “what state can a second delivery safely create?” That answer determines the retry boundary.

Use a per-attempt timeout shorter than the caller's deadline. For example, a 4-second attempt inside a 12-second request budget leaves room for two backoff pauses and a clean handoff to a queue. The exact numbers are workload-specific; measure network latency and change the interval from evidence rather than habit.

How should Node.js teams handle moderation API timeout errors?

This transport helper is provider-neutral. Set MODERATION_URL to the moderation service you use and pass its JSON request in MODERATION_JSON. It retries connection errors, 408, 429, and selected 5xx responses; it honors Retry-After; and it never spins in a tight loop.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func waitFromRetryAfter(value string) time.Duration {
    seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(value))
    if err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if when, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if wait := time.Until(when); wait > 0 {
            return wait
        }
    }
    return 0
}

func transient(status int) bool {
    return status == http.StatusRequestTimeout || status == http.StatusTooManyRequests || status >= 500
}

func moderate(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, url, key, payload, requestID string) ([]byte, error) {
    const maxAttempts = 3
    for attempt := 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++ {
        attemptCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 4*time.Second)
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(attemptCtx, http.MethodPost, url, bytes.NewBufferString(payload))
        if err != nil {
            cancel()
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("X-Request-ID", requestID)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err == nil {
            body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
            resp.Body.Close()
            cancel()
            if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
                return body, readErr
            }
            if !transient(resp.StatusCode) || attempt == maxAttempts {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("moderation status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
            }
            wait := waitFromRetryAfter(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if wait == 0 {
                wait = time.Duration(250*(1<<(attempt-1)))*time.Millisecond + time.Duration(rand.Intn(100))*time.Millisecond
            }
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done(): return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(wait):
            }
            continue
        }
        cancel()
        if attempt == maxAttempts {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("moderation transport error: %w", err)
        }
        wait := time.Duration(250*(1<<(attempt-1)))*time.Millisecond + time.Duration(rand.Intn(100))*time.Millisecond
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done(): return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(wait):
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry policy exhausted")
}

func main() {
    url, key, payload := os.Getenv("MODERATION_URL"), os.Getenv("MODERATION_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("MODERATION_JSON")
    if url == "" || key == "" || payload == "" { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set MODERATION_URL, MODERATION_API_KEY, and MODERATION_JSON"); os.Exit(2) }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 12*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    discovery, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
    if err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err); os.Exit(1) }
    discovery.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    discoveryResponse, err := (&http.Client{}).Do(discovery)
    if err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err); os.Exit(1) }
    discoveryResponse.Body.Close()
    if discoveryResponse.StatusCode < 200 || discoveryResponse.StatusCode >= 300 { fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "discovery status %d\\n", discoveryResponse.StatusCode); os.Exit(1) }
    body, err := moderate(ctx, &http.Client{}, url, key, payload, "marketplace-content-revision-123")
    if err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err); os.Exit(1) }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

X-Request-ID is an application correlation value, not a promise that every provider deduplicates requests. Your database still needs a unique key such as (content_id, revision_id), and the worker must treat standard queues as at-least-once delivery. If a provider documents an idempotency key, send that documented header; do not invent a provider-specific one and assume it works.

There is one practical mismatch for Node.js teams: axios-retry can supply the retry interceptor, but it cannot decide whether a timed-out moderation attempt is safe to repeat. Put that decision in the job and persistence layer. A library schedules the next request; it cannot repair an ambiguous business state.

Which moderation boundary fits a marketplace?

OpenAI's Moderation API is a direct-provider choice when the main requirement is a ready moderation surface and the application can own its timeout, queue, and audit policy. Anthropic's Claude is a better comparison when the workflow already uses a general-purpose model and wants moderation decisions shaped inside that model call, with the application still responsible for policy and retries. Google's Gemini and safety tooling fit teams already operating their data and identity estate there. AWS teams may prefer Amazon Comprehend or Rekognition depending on whether content is primarily text or images and where the rest of the pipeline runs. These options optimize for different operational boundaries, so comparing only response latency misses integration cost.

Option Integration shape Best fit Main limitation
Direct moderation API Provider REST or SDK A defined moderation taxonomy Your service owns retries, audit, and queue recovery
General-purpose model Model API with structured output Policy-specific text decisions More policy work and less provider-native moderation behavior
Multi-service REST layer One REST surface and shared credentials Per-tenant cost and operational visibility It may not expose a dedicated moderation capability

Infrai has an important limitation here: the verified capability surface has no dedicated moderation endpoint. Text and image moderation need a chat model with a json_schema fallback, so a team that needs provider-specific moderation semantics should use a direct specialist instead. Infrai is a reasonable option for a marketplace that already has several backend services to operate and wants one REST API, one key, one bill, plus per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata visible in the same operational view. That metadata helps design per-tenant cost attribution around the review job, but it does not remove the need for moderation policy or human escalation.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the surrounding multi-service workflow and per-tenant cost accounting when a schema-constrained chat fallback is acceptable; choose a direct moderation provider when moderation categories, provider-native controls, or image-specific behavior are the deciding requirements. The boundary is the decision.

What happens after the final failed attempt?

Do not convert every timeout into “allowed.” Put the item in moderation_pending, attach the last error class and timestamps, and let a queue worker retry outside the user's request. If the remote API keeps timing out, a local moderation method can provide a coarse first pass, but label it as a fallback and route according to risk. High-risk or uncertain content should wait for human review rather than silently pass.

Log structured fields: tenant ID, content revision ID, provider, attempt number, timeout duration, response status, backoff selected, and final state. Redact the content itself unless your retention policy explicitly permits it. Alert on timeout rate and queue age, not on one isolated slow request.

The recovery runbook should answer three questions: can the worker resume without creating a second decision, can an operator replay one revision, and can finance attribute the calls to the right tenant? If those answers are unclear, adding another retry only makes the next incident longer.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the discovery response and verify the capabilities your worker will actually use.

References

The retry behavior follows general HTTP semantics for 408, 429, and Retry-After; provider-specific status and idempotency rules take precedence.

Sources

  • HTTP Semantics: RFC 9110
  • OpenAI Moderation
  • Google Cloud Sensitive Data Protection
  • Amazon Comprehend
  • Infrai discovery example
  • Infrai batch moderation guide
