title: Day 26 of My React Learning Journey 🚀 | useEffect Hook and Component Lifecycle
description:
I learned about the useEffect Hook in React and created an e-commerce website. I also learned about component lifecycle and dependency arrays.

1. What is useEffect?

useEffect is a React Hook that allows us to synchronize a component with external systems, such as APIs, timers, browser events, and other external resources.

It is commonly used to perform side effects in React components.

Syntax

`import { useEffect } from 'react';

useEffect(() => {
// Side effect code
}, [dependencies]);
`

2. Why do we use useEffect?

  • We use useEffect for tasks such as:
  • Fetching data from an API.
  • Setting up timers.
  • Adding event listeners.
  • Synchronizing with external systems.
  • Cleaning up resources when they are no longer needed.

3. Component Lifecycle

A React component has three commonly discussed lifecycle stages:

Mounting

Mounting happens when a component is created and displayed on the screen for the first time.

Updating

Updating happens when a component renders again because its state or props have changed.

Unmounting

Unmounting happens when a component is removed from the screen.

4. Types of Dependency Arrays in useEffect

There are three common ways to use the dependency array.

1. Empty Dependency Array []

useEffect(() => {
console.log("Component mounted");
}, []);

Runs after the initial render.

Does not run again because of ordinary state or prop updates.

2. Dependency Array with a Value [count]

useEffect(() => {
console.log("Count changed");
}, [count]);

Runs after the initial render.

Runs again whenever count changes.

3. Without a Dependency Array

useEffect(() => {
console.log("Component rendered");
});

Runs after every render.

4. Cleanup Function

A cleanup function is returned from inside useEffect.

It is useful for cleaning up resources, such as timers and event listeners.

useEffect(() => {
console.log("Effect executed");

return () => {
    console.log("Cleanup executed");
};

}, []);

The cleanup function runs when the component unmounts. When dependencies change, the previous cleanup also runs before the next effect.

What I Learned Today

  • What the useEffect Hook is.
  • Why we use useEffect in React.
  • Component lifecycle: Mounting, Updating, and Unmounting.
  • The three types of dependency arrays.
  • How cleanup functions work.

I also created an e-commerce website as part of my React practice. Every day, I am learning new concepts and improving my understanding of React!

title: PDFBox 3 in Java: Line Breaks, Page Breaks and Unicode
description:
A 60-row statement drawn with Apache PDFBox needs Java code to decide where page 1 ends, and a cover letter needs Java code to decide where each line breaks. Apache PDFBox is the Apache Software Foundation's PDF library for Java, and its 3.0.8 release has been on Maven Central since 11 July 2026. We wrote this for teams producing documents with it, and it covers the issues that show up once the first real templates go through it, each one with run output or the project's own documentation behind it.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

Who Decides Where a Line Breaks?

The calling code does. PDFBox accepts neither HTML nor CSS. The project FAQ calls it low-level, offering text and image drawing but no API above that for laying out pages or flowing paragraphs. A paragraph is therefore a list of lines the program builds itself by measuring words with getStringWidth, which returns widths in 1/1000 units of text space.

import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.PDDocument;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.PDPage;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.PDPageContentStream;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.common.PDRectangle;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.font.PDType0Font;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class DrawWrappedLetter {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        String body = "Thank you for your order. The parcel left our warehouse in Gdańsk this morning "
                + "and should reach you within three working days. Reply to this letter if any item is missing.";

        try (PDDocument document = new PDDocument()) {
            PDPage page = new PDPage(PDRectangle.LETTER);
            document.addPage(page);
            PDType0Font font = PDType0Font.load(document, new File("fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf"));
            float fontSize = 12;
            float margin = 72;
            float maxWidth = page.getMediaBox().getWidth() - 2 * margin;

            // Each showText call draws one line, so the program measures words and decides the breaks itself.
            List<String> lines = new ArrayList<>();
            String line = "";
            for (String word : body.split(" ")) {
                String candidate = line.isEmpty() ? word : line + " " + word;
                if (font.getStringWidth(candidate) / 1000 * fontSize > maxWidth) {
                    lines.add(line);
                    line = word;
                } else {
                    line = candidate;
                }
            }
            lines.add(line);

            try (PDPageContentStream content = new PDPageContentStream(document, page)) {
                content.beginText();
                content.setFont(font, fontSize);
                content.setLeading(fontSize * 1.4f);

                // PDF coordinates start at the bottom left, so the first baseline sits one margin below the top edge.
                content.newLineAtOffset(margin, page.getMediaBox().getHeight() - margin);
                for (String text : lines) {
                    content.showText(text);
                    content.newLine();
                }
                content.endText();
            }
            document.save("letter.pdf");
            System.out.println("Lines: " + lines.size());
        }
    }
}

It printed Lines: 3 and saved a 7,336-byte letter.pdf on a 612 by 792 point US Letter page, the paragraph broken into three lines inside one-inch margins. A dozen lines of Java do the job a browser does for a <p> element, and they handle only plain words, with no hyphenation, justification, bold runs or links. For richer layouts the FAQ sends readers elsewhere, to Apache FOP when the source is XML, or to add-on layout projects like Boxable and easytable that sit on top of PDFBox.

Page Breaks Are Tracked by Hand

The same applies one level up. newLine moves the baseline down by the leading and nothing more, so a table longer than the page keeps drawing below the bottom edge unless the program opens a new page itself.

import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.PDDocument;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.PDPage;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.PDPageContentStream;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.common.PDRectangle;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.font.PDType1Font;
import org.apache.pdfbox.pdmodel.font.Standard14Fonts;

import java.io.IOException;

public class ManualPagination {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        float margin = 50;
        float leading = 16;
        PDType1Font font = new PDType1Font(Standard14Fonts.FontName.HELVETICA);

        try (PDDocument document = new PDDocument()) {
            PDPageContentStream content = null;
            float y = 0;

            for (int row = 1; row <= 60; row++) {
                // The program tracks the baseline itself and opens a new page once it has dropped below the bottom margin.
                if (content == null || y < margin) {
                    if (content != null) {
                        content.endText();
                        content.close();
                    }
                    PDPage page = new PDPage(PDRectangle.A4);
                    document.addPage(page);
                    content = new PDPageContentStream(document, page);
                    content.beginText();
                    content.setFont(font, 11);
                    content.setLeading(leading);
                    y = page.getMediaBox().getHeight() - margin;
                    content.newLineAtOffset(margin, y);
                } else {
                    content.newLine();
                    y -= leading;
                }
                content.showText("Line " + row + "    " + String.format("%.2f", row * 1.25));
            }

            // Each page's content stream has to be closed before the document is saved.
            content.endText();
            content.close();
            document.save("paginated-statement.pdf");
            System.out.println("Pages: " + document.getNumberOfPages());
        }
    }
}

The run printed Pages: 2, with rows 1 to 48 on the first A4 page and rows 49 to 60 on the second, all inside the page bounds. Repeating a header row, keeping a row's cells together or adding a page number would each be more code of the same kind. Without the y < margin check, rows keep going below the bottom edge of the first page, still present in the content stream and invisible in a viewer.

Names Like Łódź and Gdańsk Need PDType0Font

The letter above loads Noto Sans through PDType0Font.load for a reason. With the Standard 14 Helvetica, which needs no font file and is created in 3.x through new PDType1Font(Standard14Fonts.FontName.HELVETICA), showText on the word Gdańsk threw an IllegalArgumentException reporting that U+0144 ('nacute') is not available in Helvetica's WinAnsiEncoding, and Łódź failed the same way on U+0141. The FAQ's fix for that message is the Type 0 font, which PDType0Font.load(PDDocument, File) embeds as a subset of the TrueType file. Any service printing customer names or addresses with letters like these has to ship and load font files for each script it needs.

What Moving From 2.x to 3.x Changes

The 3.0 migration guide lists the API changes that stop 2.x code compiling. PDDocument lost its load methods to the new Loader class, the Standard 14 fonts lost their static fields, and a StreamCacheCreateFunction took the place of the MemoryUsageSetting parameter. Merging shows the new signature.

import org.apache.pdfbox.io.IOUtils;
import org.apache.pdfbox.multipdf.PDFMergerUtility;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;

public class MergeInvoicePack {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        PDFMergerUtility merger = new PDFMergerUtility();
        merger.addSource(new File("invoice.pdf"));
        merger.addSource(new File("statement.pdf"));
        merger.setDestinationFileName("invoice-pack.pdf");

        // The stream cache argument arrived in 3.x, and a memory-only cache suits small inputs.
        merger.mergeDocuments(IOUtils.createMemoryOnlyStreamCache());
    }
}

With a one-page invoice and a three-page statement as sources, it wrote a four-page, 10,381-byte invoice-pack.pdf. IOUtils lives in the separate pdfbox-io module that 3.0 introduced, which Maven pulls in with pdfbox alongside fontbox and commons-logging 1.4.0. A 2.x codebase has to rewrite every PDDocument.load call, font field and memory setting before it compiles against 3.0.8, or stay on the 2.0 line, which published 2.0.37 to Maven Central on 15 July 2026.

Security Advisories by Version

Ten CVE records appear on the PDFBox security page, and a fixed release exists for each. Scores are the ones NVD displays, from NIST for the older records and from CISA's ADP program for the 2026 pair.

  • CVE-2026-33929, CVSS 4.3 from CISA ADP: A path traversal in the ExtractEmbeddedFiles example and an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-23907, affects 2.0.24 to 2.0.36 and 3.0.0 to 3.0.7 and is fixed in 2.0.37 and 3.0.8.
  • CVE-2026-23907, CVSS 5.3 from CISA ADP: The original path traversal in that example, affects 2.0.24 to 2.0.35 and 3.0.0 to 3.0.6 and is fixed in 2.0.36 and 3.0.7.
  • CVE-2019-0228, CVSS 9.8 from NIST: XML external entity processing through a crafted XFDF file in 2.0.14, fixed in 2.0.15.
  • CVE-2016-2175, CVSS 7.8 from NIST: XML external entity processing through a crafted PDF in 1.8.0 to 1.8.11 and 2.0.0, fixed in 1.8.12 and 2.0.1.
  • CVE-2018-8036 and CVE-2018-11797, CVSS 6.5 and 5.5 from NIST: A parser loop and a long page-tree computation on crafted files, fixed in 2.0.11 and 2.0.12.
  • CVE-2021-27807, CVE-2021-27906, CVE-2021-31811 and CVE-2021-31812, CVSS 5.5 each from NIST: Infinite loops and out-of-memory errors on crafted files, fixed in 2.0.23 for the first two and 2.0.24 for the last two.

The project footnotes the 2026 pair as affecting only the examples module, but the NVD record for the later one lists the main apache:pdfbox CPE as vulnerable below 2.0.37 and 3.0.8, which is why NVD-based scanners raise it on the core artifact. Upgrading pdfbox to 3.0.8 or 2.0.37 clears all ten, and code copied from ExtractEmbeddedFiles needs the change from pull request 427. Maven Central has no fixed build of pdfbox-examples, though, since that artifact ends at 3.0.7 and 2.0.36. One more point from the same page affects upload services. Under the project's policy, crafted files that throw unchecked exceptions, loop without end or use memory out of proportion fall outside its security scope, and applications reading untrusted PDFs in volume are expected to set their own timeouts and memory caps.

Rendering the Statement From HTML Instead

Teams whose letters and statements already live as HTML can hand them to IronPDF for Java, Iron Software's commercial PDF library, which takes the layout and font work above off the Java side. It renders HTML with a full Chromium engine, so line breaks, table widths and page breaks follow the markup and its CSS, a TrueType file named in an @font-face rule of an HTML file embedded in our 2026.10.1 run with Łódź and Gdańsk intact, and page JavaScript runs when setEnableJavaScript is on, with setWaitFor delaying the render for a set time or a network-idle signal. The calls are PdfDocument.renderHtmlFileAsPdf for an HTML file or renderHtmlAsPdf for a string, then PdfDocument.merge, extractAllText or getSecurity() on the result before saveAs.

The Maven coordinate is com.ironsoftware:ironpdf, and Maven Central lists ten 2026 releases of it up to 2026.10.1 from 1 October 2026. A free trial key covers a test against your own templates, and the generation settings example walks through the render options.

The PDFBox Checklist in Short

PDFBox 3.0.8 leaves line wrapping, page breaks and Unicode font loading to the calling code, takes no HTML or CSS, asks 2.x code to be rewritten for its 3.x API and carries ten CVE records that 3.0.8 and 2.0.37 fix. For teams with HTML templates, we point to IronPDF for Java as the solution, with guides to merging PDFs and filling PDF forms on the same document object.

What reached your team first with PDFBox, the layout code, the fonts or the scanner report?

Apache PDFBox, PDFBox and Apache FOP are trademarks of The Apache Software Foundation, we have no affiliation with the foundation, and the details here rest on the project's own pages and on NVD and Maven Central records.

Drafted with AI. Code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team against Apache PDFBox 3.0.8, with IronPDF method names checked against com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.10.1, on 2 November 2026.

title: Eclipse BIRT 4.25 Reports: Page Totals, PDF/A and JDK 21
description:
We ran Eclipse BIRT 4.25.0, the Eclipse Foundation's Java reporting engine, released on 9 September 2026, on JDK 25, checked its advisory records, and wrote down each problem that came up. Some come from how BIRT lays out HTML, some from the release itself, and one from an old artifact still sitting on Maven Central. Each item below has the run output or the record behind it, who it hits, and the fix BIRT offers where there is one.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

Does BIRT Render Flexbox, Grid or JavaScript?

It does not, and the reason is structural. Every IReportEngine method that opens an input takes a design or a stored report document, which means an existing HTML page has no way in until someone rebuilds it as a .rptdesign. Inside a design, HTML can fill a text item, and BIRT's own layout code positions it. This test design packs a flex row, a CSS grid and a document.write script into a single text item, adds a 150-row table, and writes its footer with value-of page variables.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<report xmlns="http://www.eclipse.org/birt/2005/design" version="3.2.23">
    <data-sources>
        <script-data-source name="Generated"/>
    </data-sources>
    <data-sets>
        <script-data-set name="Rows">
            <list-property name="resultSetHints">
                <structure>
                    <property name="position">1</property>
                    <property name="name">line</property>
                    <property name="dataType">string</property>
                </structure>
            </list-property>
            <property name="dataSource">Generated</property>
            <method name="open"><![CDATA[counter = 0;]]></method>
            <method name="fetch"><![CDATA[if (counter == 150) return false;
counter++;
row["line"] = "Row " + counter;
return true;]]></method>
        </script-data-set>
    </data-sets>
    <page-setup>
        <simple-master-page name="Simple MasterPage">
            <property name="type">a4</property>
            <page-footer>
                <text>
                    <property name="contentType">html</property>
                    <text-property name="content"><![CDATA[Page <value-of>pageNumber</value-of> of <value-of>totalPage</value-of>]]></text-property>
                </text>
            </page-footer>
        </simple-master-page>
    </page-setup>
    <body>
        <text>
            <property name="contentType">html</property>
            <text-property name="content"><![CDATA[<div style="display:flex"><div style="width:50%">Flex left</div><div style="width:50%">Flex right</div></div>
<div style="display:grid; grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr"><div>Grid A</div><div>Grid B</div></div>
<script>document.write("Written by script");</script>
<p>After the script tag</p>]]></text-property>
        </text>
        <table>
            <property name="dataSet">Rows</property>
            <list-property name="boundDataColumns">
                <structure>
                    <property name="name">line</property>
                    <expression name="expression" type="javascript">dataSetRow["line"]</expression>
                </structure>
            </list-property>
            <column/>
            <detail>
                <row>
                    <cell><data><property name="resultSetColumn">line</property></data></cell>
                </row>
            </detail>
        </table>
    </body>
</report>

The class below runs it in two steps, storing a .rptdocument first and rendering the PDF from that document.

import java.util.logging.Level;

import org.eclipse.birt.core.framework.Platform;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.EngineConfig;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.IRenderTask;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.IReportDocument;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.IReportEngine;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.IReportEngineFactory;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.IRunTask;
import org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.api.PDFRenderOption;

public class IssueReportTwoStep {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        EngineConfig config = new EngineConfig();
        config.setLogConfig(null, Level.WARNING);
        Platform.startup(config);
        IReportEngine engine = ((IReportEngineFactory) Platform
                .createFactoryObject(IReportEngineFactory.EXTENSION_REPORT_ENGINE_FACTORY))
                .createReportEngine(config);

        try {
            // Run once into a report document, so the page count is known before rendering.
            IRunTask run = engine.createRunTask(engine.openReportDesign("known-issues.rptdesign"));
            run.run("known-issues.rptdocument");
            run.close();

            IReportDocument document = engine.openReportDocument("known-issues.rptdocument");
            System.out.println("Pages: " + document.getPageCount());
            IRenderTask render = engine.createRenderTask(document);
            PDFRenderOption options = new PDFRenderOption();
            options.setOutputFormat(PDFRenderOption.OUTPUT_FORMAT_PDF);
            options.setOutputFileName("known-issues-two-step.pdf");
            render.setRenderOption(options);
            render.render();
            render.close();
            document.close();
        } finally {
            engine.destroy();
            Platform.shutdown();
        }
    }
}

Console output was Pages: 4, and known-issues-two-step.pdf, at about 3 KB, shows the layout problem on page one. All four boxes from the flex row and the grid sit one per line at the same 6.5 mm left offset, so no columns formed, and no page contains the string Written by script. The 4.25.0 source lines up with that. Its DisplayManager registers sixteen display keywords, among them block, inline, list-item and the table types, and none of them is flex or grid, and the code that turns HTML into PDF content skips over script nodes. Teams moving HTML templates or script-drawn charts into BIRT feel this most. The BIRT answer is to redo the layout with designer grids and tables, and to draw charts with BIRT's chart engine.

Why Does the Footer Say Page 2 of 2?

That same footer gave two different results depending on the task. Run as above, through IRunTask and then IRenderTask, the four pages read Page 1 of 4 to Page 4 of 4. Run through a single IRunAndRenderTask, every page claimed to be the last one, from Page 1 of 1 up to Page 4 of 4, the total keeping pace with the current page. Single-task runs of any multi-page report with this footer are affected. Besides the two-step run, the designer's auto-text items for page number and total page print the right count in one task, which a separate run of the design confirmed with Page 2 of 4 on page two.

Why Does PDF/A Output Stop on Times-Roman?

Archival output is a property of the design. BIRT's PDF emitter README names it PdfEmitter.Conformance (since 4.16), and in the XML it is one line under <report>.

<property name="pdfConformance">PDF.A1B</property>

Adding just that line to known-issues.rptdesign and pointing the two-step class at the copy got as far as Pages: 4. Rendering then failed. A warning came first (Times not embeddable), then an EngineException whose cause, PdfXConformanceException, named Times-Roman as unembedded, and the PDF on disk was 0 bytes. Times-Roman is a base-14 font that BIRT references without embedding, so a design left on the default font cannot become PDF/A as it stands. Two fixes exist in BIRT itself, an embeddable font such as Arial set on the report style, or the PdfEmitter.PDFA.FallbackFont setting from the README. The Arial route came to roughly 35 KB, and veraPDF 1.30.3 accepted it as PDF/A-1b.

Why Won't BIRT 4.25 Compile on JDK 17?

The 4.21.0 release notes record the change that moved BIRT's bundles to JavaSE-21, and every engine jar with code in it since then is compiled to class file version 65. The 4.20.0 engine still targeted Java 11. Point a JDK 17 compiler at a 4.25.0 project and it stops at the first BIRT import, because javac reads Platform.class as version 65 where it can load at most 61. Teams still on Java 11 or 17 upgrade the JVM first, or hold at 4.20.0, the last Java 11 release.

The Maven layout adds two more issues. Central's all-in-one birt-runtime artifact has not moved past 4.9.0 from May 2022, so a 4.25.0 build lists the engine modules one by one, and a missing module surfaces only when a report runs.

  • Without org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.emitter.pdf, the run step still prints Pages: 4, and render() then ends in UnsupportedFormatException because no PDF writer is installed.
  • Without org.eclipse.birt.report.engine.script.javascript, data engine creation fails during the run step on No such script extension : javascript., so no PDF is written.

The bundled 4.25.0 runtime comes from the Eclipse download site instead, as a zip of 290,887,286 bytes. The project's license is the Eclipse Public License 2.0.

Is the BIRT Report Viewer Affected by CVEs?

Yes, in older builds, and one of those builds is still the newest Viewer on Maven Central. NVD records four BIRT CVEs, all in the Report Viewer, the servlet application that serves reports over HTTP, each scored by NIST and none disputed.

  • CVE-2021-34427, CVSS 3.1 score 9.8: Crafted query parameters write a remotely reachable JSP into the viewer folder, through 4.8.0.
  • CVE-2023-0100, CVSS 3.1 score 8.8: A tampered Host header lets the viewer fetch a report from an absolute HTTP path, from 2.6.2 until the 4.13 fix.
  • CVE-2019-11776, CVSS 3.1 score 6.1: Reflected XSS through a viewer URL parameter, versions 1.0 to 4.7.
  • CVE-2009-4521, CVSS 2.0 score 4.3: Cross-site scripting in the __report parameter of birt-viewer/run, before 2.5.0.

Exposure depends on where the Viewer is fetched from. Search Central for org.eclipse.birt.report.viewer and the newest hit is 4.9.0, uploaded 2 May 2022, a version that GHSA-4grc-q4fj-45p8 places inside the CVE-2023-0100 range. Deployments built from that coordinate carry the flaw. A patched birt.war ships inside the 4.25.0 runtime zip on the Eclipse download site. On 2 November 2026, OSV showed no advisories against the 4.25.0 engine or any of the 70 jars it pulled into the test build.

For reports that can start as HTML, IronPDF for Java is a commercial library our team builds that avoids the layout and footer issues above. Chromium does the drawing, and in our 2026.10.1 run a flex row and a grid each split into two columns while a script wrote its line. Java 8 and later can use it through a single Maven dependency, com.ironsoftware:ironpdf, which fetches the Chromium engine on first run or from a platform ironpdf-engine artifact, and Central lists ten 2026 versions up to 2026.10.1 from 1 October. A free trial covers evaluation.

Footers come from addTextFooter, which stamps {page} and {total-pages} onto the finished document, and saveAsPdfA with PdfAVersions.PdfA1b writes PDF/A. The PDF lands in a file or a byte array for the caller, so nothing like the Report Viewer has to be deployed.

Where These BIRT Issues Leave a Java Team

A JDK 21 floor, a Maven layout that needs hand-picked modules, no flex or grid display values, dropped scripts, a page total that depends on the task, PDF/A refusing the default Times font and a 2022 Viewer on Central with a known CVE are the issues to check before a BIRT upgrade, especially for a report that already exists as HTML.

IronPDF for Java renders that kind of report from a template on Java 8 or later, with rendering done in the separate engine process the IronPdfEngine guide describes.

Eclipse BIRT is a trademark of the Eclipse Foundation, we have no affiliation with the Foundation, and the versions, advisories and run results above rest on public records and our own test runs from 2 November 2026.

Drafted with AI. BIRT code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team against Eclipse BIRT 4.25.0 and com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.10.1 on 2 November 2026.

title: # 230,756 Requests/Second. And Breeze Is Much More Than a Fast Go Framework. 🚀
description:
What if your Go web framework could deliver exceptional performance while providing an entire ecosystem for building, operating, and scaling modern applications?

Meet Breeze v2.2.

Built on gnet. Engineered for throughput. Designed for production.

⚡ Let's talk numbers.

Breeze v2.2 (Go 1.27) has achieved:

Concurrent Connections Requests / Second
64 230,756
256 207,333
512 198,196

Nearly 200K requests per second, even at 512 concurrent connections.

And how does it compare with other Go frameworks on The Benchmarker?

Go performance comparison

Framework 64 256 512
Breeze v2.2 230,756 207,333 198,196
web 205,272 187,397 178,910
fasthttp 182,167 166,243 158,145
Fiber 178,319 162,992 155,733
Hertz 173,885 154,279 143,920

At 64 connections, Breeze delivers:

  • 12.4% more throughput than the next-highest Go entry.
  • 26.7% more than fasthttp.
  • 29.4% more than Fiber.
  • 32.7% more than Hertz.

And the advantage remains across all three concurrency levels.

🧠 Performance is in the architecture.

Breeze is built around an event-driven gnet engine, with:

  • Inline execution for non-blocking handlers.
  • O(1) exact-path routing, dynamic parameters and wildcards.
  • Opt-in zero-copy request-header handling.
  • Pooled contexts, requests, responses and buffers.
  • Configurable worker pools with backpressure policies for blocking operations.

But here's where Breeze becomes more interesting.

🏗️ More than an HTTP framework.

Breeze brings an extensive set of production-ready capabilities into one ecosystem:

HTTP & Security

  • High-performance HTTP server, routing, request binding and validation.
  • 12 built-in middlewares: CORS, rate limiting, compression, ETag, logging, recovery, security headers, JWT and more.
  • OAuth2 / social login with Google, GitHub, Microsoft and Discord, including PKCE.
  • Graceful shutdown and static file serving.

Real-time & Application Development

  • Native WebSocket server and client, with connection lifecycle management and broadcasting.
  • Server-side templates, layouts, reusable components, SPA navigation, partial rendering and i18n — without a frontend framework.
  • Built-in byte-range video streaming, seeking, caching and signed URLs.

Backend Infrastructure

  • Typed, reflection-free event bus with priorities, filters, asynchronous dispatch and metrics.
  • Durable workflows with retries, timeouts, parallel DAG execution, Saga compensation and crash recovery.
  • SQL migrations and a gnet-based outbound HTTP client.
  • JSON-RPC 2.0 server, including batches and notifications.
  • gRPC server/client code generation.

Developer Experience

  • Rails-style CLI for project scaffolding and feature integration.
  • 23 modular breeze add features.
  • Code generators for resources, handlers, models, events, listeners, workflows, middleware, WebSockets, views, jobs and gRPC.
  • OpenAPI generation, interactive Scalar documentation and LLM-readable documentation.
  • Docker support and runnable examples.

Observability & Production Operations

  • Integrated live dashboard with request monitoring, RPS, latency, memory and goroutine metrics.
  • Per-request profiling, route explorer and API explorer.
  • Database browser, ORM query monitoring, cache, queue and scheduler monitoring.
  • Logs, health checks, video monitoring and Fleet views.
  • Built-in observability, diagnostics and distributed tracing across services, with W3C trace propagation, topology visualization and root-cause analysis.

AI-Native Development

  • Native MCP integration in three forms: standalone generator, read-only application runtime and in-process server.
  • Approximately 40 MCP tools for project scaffolding, code generation, feature integration, Go toolchain execution and live service inspection.
  • Auto-MCP: expose explicitly tagged, authenticated application routes as AI-callable tools.

All of this in one MIT-licensed Go ecosystem.

🚀 But performance isn't the only reason to choose Breeze.

A fast server is valuable.

But a framework that also helps you build APIs, manage workflows, handle real-time communication, monitor production, trace distributed services, generate code, document APIs and integrate AI agents is a much bigger proposition.

Less infrastructure to assemble. Fewer disconnected tools. More capabilities in one cohesive ecosystem.

That's the vision behind Breeze.

And we're still improving it.

The goal isn't just to build another fast Go framework.

It's to build a better foundation for modern Go applications.

Explore Breeze

https://web-frameworks-benchmark.vercel.app/

https://web-frameworks-benchmark.vercel.app/result?l=go

💻 Source code:
https://github.com/nelthaarion/breeze

https://nelthaarion.github.io/breeze/

Breeze v2.2 — Performance is the beginning, not the whole story.

title: React.js ~useEffectEvent~
description:
About useEffectEvent

useEffectEvent is a React hook for situations where you want to read the latest props or state from inside an Effect, but you don't want the Effect to re-run when those values change.

The problem it solves

For example, suppose you want to connect to a chat room and show a notification using the current theme when the connection is established.

function ChatRoom({ roomId, theme }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const connection = createConnection(roomId);
    connection.on('connected', () => {
      showNotification('Connected', theme);
    });
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
  }, [roomId, theme]); // Including theme causes a reconnect every time the theme changes
}

If you leave theme out of the dependency array, you get a lint error; if you include it, simply switching the theme triggers a reconnection. The connection should only be re-established when roomId changes.

Writing it with useEffectEvent 

import { useEffect, useEffectEvent } from 'react';

function ChatRoom({ roomId, theme }) {
  const onConnected = useEffectEvent(() => {
    showNotification('Connected', theme);
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const connection = createConnection(roomId);
    connection.on('connected', () => {
      onConnected();
    });
    connection.connect();
    return () => connection.disconnect();
  }, [roomId]); // Don't include onConnected in the dependency array
}

Inside onConnected, you can always read the latest theme, but the Effect does not re-run when theme changes.

How to think about it

  • An Effect Event separates the "reactive" part of an Effect (synchronization that responds to changes in roomId) from the "non-reactive" part (logic that only reads the latest values at that moment).
  • An Effect Event is a function that always "sees" the latest props and state from each render, so the latest values are used whenever the Effect calls it.

Rules for using it

  1. Call it only from inside an Effect. Don't call it during rendering, and don't pass it to other components or hooks. Don't use it outside Effects, such as in event handlers; use a regular function there instead.
  2. Don't put it in the dependency array. An Effect Event is not a stable reference, and it isn't something to include in dependencies. The latest version of eslint-plugin-react-hooks understands this rule.
  3. Don't use it just to silence dependency warnings. First ask, "Should this code really react to changes?" Then extract only the parts that shouldn't react. Pushing a value that should be reactive (such as roomId) into an Effect Event will cause bugs.

Typical use cases

  • Logging or showing a notification when a connection or subscription completes (uses the latest state, but no reconnection is needed)
  • Reading the latest values inside callbacks for timers or event listeners
  • Sending analytics, such as including the latest cart contents when the user navigates between pages

Note

useEffectEvent became a stable API in React 19.2. In earlier versions it was experimental and cannot be used. We recommend checking your React version and keeping your ESLint plugin up to date.

title: How We Eliminated Cache Stampedes in Node.js & Bun with Single-Flight Coalescing
description:
Every engineer who has scaled a high-traffic backend has lived through this nightmare:

You have an expensive endpoint (e.g., aggregating leaderboard data or rendering a personalized dashboard). To protect your database, you cache the result with a 60-second TTL.

Everything runs smoothly until the key expires while receiving 1,500 requests per second.

Within a 50-millisecond window, hundreds of concurrent requests see a cache miss. All of them immediately hammer the primary database simultaneously to recompute the same data. Your connection pool saturates, CPU spikes to 100%, latency explodes, and your server crashes.

This is the thundering herd / cache stampede problem.

The Traditional (Fragile) Workarounds

  1. Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch algorithm): Recomputes the value before it expires based on an exponential probability. While effective, it wastes backend CPU cycles recomputing keys that may never be accessed again.
  2. Distributed Mutex Locks (Redlock): Acquiring a distributed lock before computing. This introduces noticeable network roundtrip latency and runs the risk of deadlocks if a worker dies mid-flight.

The Zero-Overhead Alternative: Single-Flight Promise Coalescing

Instead of locking distributed infrastructure, we can coalesce concurrent requests in-process at the execution runtime layer.

When Key A is requested and misses the cache:

  1. Check if an execution promise for Key A is currently in-flight.
  2. If YES: Do not touch the database. Return the existing promise and await it.
  3. If NO: Register a new in-flight promise, execute the database fetcher, cache the result, resolve all awaiting callers, and deregister the promise in a finally block. 
// How KVDock implements zero-overhead single-flight coalescing:
const running = this.inFlight.get(key);
if (running) {
  this.metrics.stampedeCoalesced++;
  return (await running) as T;
}

const run = (async () => {
  try {
    const cached = await this.get<T>(key);
    if (cached !== null) return cached;
    const fresh = await fetcher();
    await this.set(key, fresh, options);
    return fresh;
  } finally {
    this.inFlight.delete(key);
  }
})();

this.inFlight.set(key, run);
return (await run) as T;

⚡ Real-World Benchmark: 1,000 Concurrent Requests

We ran a controlled benchmark under 1,000 concurrent requests to an uncached endpoint with 25ms simulated database query latency:

Metric Traditional Caching KVDock (getOrSet) Net Improvement
Incoming Requests 1,000 1,000 Same Load
Database Queries Executed 1,000 queries (Herd) 1 query (Single-Flight) 99.90% DB load reduction
Coalesced Waiting Callers 0 999 Zero lock contention
Connection Pool Exhaustion 💥 Saturated 🟢 Baseline Stable Zero connection contention

Open Source & Polyglot

We built this into KVDock — an open-source, zero-dependency caching engine with multi-tier storage (L1 RAM + L2 Persistent):

  • Zero runtime dependencies in core
  • Multi-tier caching with automatic backfill
  • Cross-runtime support across Node.js, Bun, Deno, and Cloudflare Workers
  • Native polyglot implementations in Rust (kvdock-rs), Go (kvdock-go), Swift (kvdock-swift), and Kotlin (kvdock-kt)

⭐ Explore the code & star on GitHub: github.com/zisam-glitch/kvdock

👤 Follow the maintainer: @zisam-glitch for low-latency systems engineering deep dives!

title: Building an Authorization Gateway for AI Agents: A Practical Architecture
description:
AI agents are increasingly capable of interacting with external APIs and enterprise systems.

But consider this scenario:

You build an AI agent that can access Gmail, update Salesforce, and interact with cloud infrastructure.

How do you prevent it from performing an action that the requesting user was never authorized to perform?

A common mistake is to give the agent a service account with broad permissions.

That makes implementation easier, but it creates a significant security risk.

Let's explore a better approach: an authorization gateway for AI agents.

*1. The architecture
*
Instead of allowing agents to communicate directly with enterprise APIs, route actions through an authorization gateway.

User Request
|
v
AI Agent
|
v
Action Request
|
v
Authorization Gateway
|
+---- Identity Validation
|
+---- Policy Evaluation
|
+---- Permission Check
|
v
Enterprise API
|
v
Audit Event

The agent proposes an action. The gateway determines whether that action is authorized.

The agent should not be responsible for granting itself permission.

*2. Define an agent identity
*
An agent needs an identity that is independent of its LLM provider.

*Example:
*
{
"agent_id": "crm-agent-001",
"owner": "sales-platform",
"environment": "production",
"allowed_actions": [
"customer.read",
"customer.update"
]
}

In a production implementation, identity records should be maintained in a trusted registry rather than accepted directly from an agent request.

*3. Define an action request
*
Every action should carry enough information for the gateway to evaluate it.

{
"agent_id": "crm-agent-001",
"principal_id": "employee-123",
"task_id": "task-987",
"resource": "customer/456",
"action": "customer.update"
}

The principal_id must be established through a trusted authentication and delegation process. It must not simply be trusted because the agent included it in JSON.

*4. Implement a basic policy check
*
A simplified Python example:

AGENT_POLICIES = {
"crm-agent-001": {
"customer.read",
"customer.update"
}
}

def authorize_action(agent_id, action):
allowed = AGENT_POLICIES.get(agent_id, set())

if action not in allowed:
    return {
        "authorized": False,
        "reason": "Action not permitted"
    }

return {
    "authorized": True,
    "reason": "Policy allows action"
}

This demonstrates the basic decision, but it is not production-grade authorization.

A real gateway must also validate the authenticated principal, delegation, resource ownership, tenant boundaries, credential scope, and applicable contextual policies.

*5. Add a human approval boundary
*
Not every action should be treated equally.

*For example:
*

  • Action
  • Suggested policy
  • Read a customer record
  • Automatic if authorized
  • Update a customer record
  • Automatic with scoped permission
  • Send an external email
  • Approval based on policy
  • Delete a customer account
  • Explicit approval
  • Modify production infrastructure
  • Strong approval controls

Human approval should be enforced by the gateway, not merely requested through an LLM prompt.

*6. Add audit logging
*
Every authorization decision should produce an event.

{
"event_type": "agent.authorization",
"agent_id": "crm-agent-001",
"task_id": "task-987",
"action": "customer.update",
"resource": "customer/456",
"decision": "ALLOW",
"timestamp": "2026-11-02T12:00:00Z"
}

Production systems should also capture the authenticated principal, policy version, correlation ID, execution result, and relevant delegation metadata.

Avoid logging access tokens, secrets, or unnecessary sensitive customer data.

*7. What should a production implementation add?
*
The simplified example is a starting point. A real enterprise authorization gateway should include:

  • OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect integration.
  • Short-lived, scoped credentials.
  • Token exchange or equivalent delegated authorization.
  • Centralized policy management.
  • Resource-level authorization.
  • Agent identity registration and revocation.
  • Rate limits and execution budgets.
  • Tamper-resistant audit storage.
  • Human approval workflows.
  • Multi-tenant isolation.

It should also ensure that a delegated agent cannot obtain broader permissions than the original authorization allows.

*8. Why this matters
*
Agent frameworks will continue to evolve. LLM providers will change. New orchestration technologies will emerge.

But enterprise security cannot be tightly coupled to a particular model or agent framework.

An independent authorization layer creates a consistent security boundary across different agent implementations.

*The key architectural principle is simple:
*
An AI agent may decide what action it wants to perform, but a trusted authorization layer must decide whether it is allowed to perform it.

That separation could become one of the foundational requirements for enterprise agent infrastructure.

What approach are you taking to identity and authorization in your agent implementations?

About the Author

Ashwin Giridharan writes about Cloud & Enterprise Architecture, AI Infrastructure, Generative AI, and Agentic AI.

title: Building a done-for-you website service as one React SPA: site, order flow, client portal and admin
description:
Written by the Take2 team. Disclosure: I'm a Take2 affiliate (Take2 Innovations Digital, a small web design shop).

Take2 Innovations Digital is a very small web design shop in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. We build websites for local businesses that don't have one yet, like diners, plumbers, salons, churches and lawn care crews. One person builds and one handles sales.

Before building anything for clients, we had to build the thing that sells and runs the service. That's this app: https://take2-innovations-digital.rork.app. This post covers what's in it, how it's put together, and what we'd do differently.

What we built

One app does four jobs:

  1. Marketing site. Home, Packages, Add-ons, Portfolio, Reviews, About, Contact and Legal pages.
  2. Order funnel. A multi-step order that ends in a signed agreement and a deposit.
  3. Client portal. After ordering, clients log in with a magic link to send content, track progress, request changes and pay the balance.
  4. Staff/admin area. Quotes, jobs, pricing overrides and stats.

The public pitch is simple: pick a package, tell us about your business, we build it, you approve it, and we keep it running every month. Setup is paid in two halves, half up front and half once the client is happy.

Stack

Frontend

  • Vite + React + TypeScript
  • Tailwind CSS with shadcn/ui (Radix primitives)
  • react-router-dom for routing
  • @tanstack/react-query for server state
  • react-hook-form + zod for the long order and quote forms
  • recharts for admin charts, jspdf for generating documents

Backend

  • A Cloudflare Worker with a Durable Object backed by SQLite, split into modules: billing, finance, jobs, portal, staff, store, stats and backup. Shared libs handle Stripe, email, push and crypto.
  • Stripe PaymentIntents for deposits and final payments, plus a /webhooks/stripe endpoint.
  • A small Supabase project that stores only analytics events (a site_events table and an export function).

The app is built and hosted on Rork, so the Worker runs on Rork's Cloudflare hosting.

API shape

Splitting routes by who's calling kept auth simple:

/public/{config, order, quote-request, contact, review, help}
/auth/{login, logout, magic, magic/verify}
/portal/*      # signed-in clients
/staff/*       # signed-in staff
/webhooks/stripe
/analytics/event
/stats/*

/public/config is the important one. It returns prices, feature flags and payment readiness, and the frontend renders from it. Defaults live in a pricing.ts file and an admin can override them without a deploy.

The order funnel

The order flow is a step machine:

Package → Your pages → About you → Your business → Web address → How we work → Sign & pay → Order placed → Client portal

Things that worked:

  • One zod schema per step. Each step validates on its own, so the user never gets a wall of errors at the end.
  • The agreement and deposit happen on one step. The client signs the terms and pays 50% together, which gives a clean record.
  • A parallel quote path. Not everyone wants to buy from a price list. Quote request → staff sends a quote → the client gets a quote link → quote checkout. It uses the same payment code with a different entry point.
  • Magic-link portal auth. Small business owners don't want another password. Email links fit the audience better.

Lessons learned

1. Run a funnel event on every step from day one

We log an analytics event per order step, which shows exactly where people stop. Our early numbers made it plain that most visitors look at packages and never reach the second step. Without per-step events we would only have known "nobody ordered."

2. A client-side SPA on a shared subdomain is close to invisible to search

The whole site is a single HTML shell rendered on the client. Every route has the same title and description, there's no sitemap.xml, no og:image and no LocalBusiness JSON-LD, and it sits on a platform subdomain. For a business that sells "get found on Google," that's the first thing we're fixing:

  • Prerender the marketing routes at build time
  • Give each route its own <title>, meta description and Open Graph tags
  • Add sitemap.xml and LocalBusiness structured data
  • Move to our own domain

3. Show samples before you have clients

A web shop with an empty portfolio is a hard sell. We put up sample designs for the kinds of businesses we serve, including a corner diner, a community church, lawn and landscaping, a local plumber, a hair salon, a barber shop, a roofer, auto repair, heating and air, a tire shop and a dry cleaner. Each one is labeled as a sample design. Labeling them keeps us honest, and visitors can still picture their own site.

4. Know your platform dependency

Building on a hosted platform got us from idea to a working site, portal and payments quickly. The trade-off is that the backend runs on someone else's hosting and is harder to move. Keep the data layer and Stripe logic in plain modules so you can migrate if you ever need to.

What's next

  • Prerendering plus per-page meta and a sitemap
  • A custom domain
  • Real client reviews to replace the empty Reviews page

If you're building a productized service, whether websites, design or bookkeeping, the pattern of a config-driven price list, a step-validated order flow, a magic-link portal and per-step analytics carries over well.

Sample work: https://take2-innovations-digital.rork.app/portfolio

Disclosure: written by the Take2 Innovations Digital team; we build websites for small businesses, and free quotes are available at https://take2-innovations-digital.rork.app.

title: Beyond 1,000 Rows: Building a TypeScript Data Grid That Actually Scales Across React, Vue, and Angular
description:
Originally published on tamiz.pro.

Most data grids start dying the moment you cross a thousand rows. The DOM chokes, the scroll janks, and your framework's reactivity system turns into a bottleneck. The fix isn't a library—it's an architecture. In this deep-dive, we'll build a framework-agnostic TypeScript data grid core that handles 100,000+ rows smoothly, then show how to plug it into React, Vue, and Angular without rewriting the logic.

  • 1. Why Data Grids Break Past 1,000 Rows
  • 2. Architecture: Framework-Agnostic Core
  • 3. Virtualization: The Key to Scale
  • 4. State Management and Change Detection
  • 5. Rendering Strategies for React, Vue, and Angular
  • 6. Implementing the Grid: A Complete Example
  • 7. Performance Tuning and Best Practices
  • 8. Conclusion
  • Frequently Asked Questions

1. Why Data Grids Break Past 1,000 Rows

A typical grid renders one <tr> per row. At 1,000 rows, that's 1,000 DOM nodes plus cells—already heavy but manageable. At 10,000 rows, you're pushing 100,000+ nodes, and the browser's layout engine spends more time recalculating styles than painting content. The problem compounds with reactive frameworks: every state change triggers a diff across the entire tree.

Three bottlenecks dominate:

  1. DOM size — The browser must create, style, and layout every node. Even if you render once, a 10,000-row table costs hundreds of milliseconds to paint.
  2. Framework reconciliation — React's virtual DOM, Vue's reactivity, and Angular's change detection all iterate over the full data set on updates.
  3. Scroll performance — Native scroll events fire at 60+ Hz. Without virtualization, every scroll event forces a full re-render.

The solution isn't to optimize the framework—it's to sidestep it. We'll build a core that manages data, selection, sorting, and virtualization in plain TypeScript. The framework layer becomes a thin adapter that only renders what's visible.

2. Architecture: Framework-Agnostic Core

Our design uses a core-plus-adapter pattern. The core is pure TypeScript, framework-agnostic, and testable. The adapter handles DOM mounting and framework-specific reactivity.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Framework Adapter              │
│  (React / Vue / Angular)                    │
│  - Subscribes to core events                │
│  - Renders visible rows only                │
│  - Handles user interactions                │
└──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                       │
                       │  events / commands
                       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 Grid Core                   │
│  - Data store (rows, columns)               │
│  - Selection & sorting state                │
│  - Virtualization math                      │
│  - Event emitter                            │
│  - Pure functions, no DOM                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The core exposes a simple API:

// core/types.ts
export interface GridColumn<T> {
  key: keyof T & string;
  header: string;
  width: number;
  sortable?: boolean;
  renderer?: (value: T[keyof T], row: T) => string;
}

export interface GridState<T> {
  rows: T[];
  columns: GridColumn<T>[];
  sortKey: keyof T | null;
  sortDirection: 'asc' | 'desc' | null;
  selectedRowIds: Set<string>;
  scrollTop: number;
  viewportHeight: number;
  rowHeight: number;
}

export interface GridEvent<T> {
  type: 'row-click' | 'sort' | 'selection-change' | 'scroll';
  payload?: T | keyof T | number;
}

The core is a class that maintains state and emits change events:

// core/GridCore.ts
import { GridColumn, GridEvent, GridState } from './types';

export class GridCore<T extends { id: string }> {
  private state: GridState<T>;
  private listeners: Array<(event: GridEvent<T>) => void> = [];

  constructor(rows: T[], columns: GridColumn<T>[], rowHeight = 40) {
    this.state = {
      rows,
      columns,
      sortKey: null,
      sortDirection: null,
      selectedRowIds: new Set(),
      scrollTop: 0,
      viewportHeight: 600,
      rowHeight,
    };
  }

  subscribe(listener: (event: GridEvent<T>) => void) {
    this.listeners.push(listener);
    return () => {
      this.listeners = this.listeners.filter((l) => l !== listener);
    };
  }

  private emit(event: GridEvent<T>) {
    this.listeners.forEach((l) => l(event));
  }

  setRows(rows: T[]) {
    this.state.rows = rows;
    this.emit({ type: 'selection-change' }); // generic refresh
  }

  sortBy(key: keyof T) {
    if (this.state.sortKey === key) {
      this.state.sortDirection = this.state.sortDirection === 'asc' ? 'desc' : 'asc';
    } else {
      this.state.sortKey = key;
      this.state.sortDirection = 'asc';
    }
    const dir = this.state.sortDirection === 'asc' ? 1 : -1;
    this.state.rows = [...this.state.rows].sort((a, b) => {
      if (a[key] < b[key]) return -1 * dir;
      if (a[key] > b[key]) return 1 * dir;
      return 0;
    });
    this.emit({ type: 'sort', payload: key });
  }

  selectRow(id: string) {
    if (this.state.selectedRowIds.has(id)) {
      this.state.selectedRowIds.delete(id);
    } else {
      this.state.selectedRowIds.add(id);
    }
    this.emit({ type: 'selection-change', payload: id });
  }

  getVisibleRows(scrollTop: number, viewportHeight: number): T[] {
    const { rows, rowHeight } = this.state;
    const startIndex = Math.floor(scrollTop / rowHeight);
    const endIndex = Math.min(
      rows.length,
      Math.ceil((scrollTop + viewportHeight) / rowHeight) + 1
    );
    return rows.slice(startIndex, endIndex);
  }

  getState() {
    return this.state;
  }
}

The core never touches the DOM. It only computes which rows are visible based on scrollTop and viewportHeight. That's the foundation for virtualization.

3. Virtualization: The Key to Scale

Virtualization means rendering only the rows that fit in the viewport, plus a small buffer. For a 100,000-row grid with a 40px row height and a 600px viewport, you render about 16 rows instead of 100,000.

3.1 The Math

Given scrollTop, viewportHeight, and rowHeight:

  • startIndex = floor(scrollTop / rowHeight)
  • endIndex = ceil((scrollTop + viewportHeight) / rowHeight)
  • Add a buffer of 2–5 rows above and below to avoid blank flashes during fast scrolling.

3.2 Overscan Buffer

A buffer of 3 rows is usually enough. For smooth scrolling, we render startIndex - 3 to endIndex + 3. This hides the moment when a row enters the viewport but hasn't been rendered yet.

3.3 Fixed vs. Variable Row Heights

Fixed heights are easy—the math above works. Variable heights require measuring each row after render and storing offsets. For simplicity, we'll assume fixed heights. If you need variable heights, maintain a Map<rowId, height> and compute cumulative offsets with a Fenwick tree or binary search.

4. State Management and Change Detection

The core emits events, but it doesn't know about frameworks. Each adapter subscribes and maps events to its own reactivity system. This keeps the core pure and makes it testable with plain Node.

4.1 Event-Driven Updates

Instead of frameworks polling the core, the core pushes changes. This is critical—if the framework has to check every row on every scroll, you're back to O(n) work.

4.2 Avoiding Full Re-renders

When the user scrolls, only the visible window changes. The adapter should:

  1. Compute the new visible rows via core.getVisibleRows().
  2. Update only the DOM nodes that changed, not the entire table.

In React, this means using useMemo and React.memo on row components. In Vue, use computed and v-memo. In Angular, use ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush and track by index.

5. Rendering Strategies for React, Vue, and Angular

Each framework has its own idiom for rendering a list of visible rows. The key is to never iterate over all rows in the template.

5.1 React 

// ReactAdapter.tsx
import React, { useMemo, useState, useEffect } from 'react';
import { GridCore } from './core/GridCore';

interface Props<T> {
  core: GridCore<T>;
  viewportHeight: number;
}

export function DataGrid<T extends { id: string }>({ core, viewportHeight }: Props<T>) {
  const [scrollTop, setScrollTop] = useState(0);

  const visibleRows = useMemo(
    () => core.getVisibleRows(scrollTop, viewportHeight),
    [core, scrollTop, viewportHeight]
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    const unsubscribe = core.subscribe((event) => {
      if (event.type === 'sort' || event.type === 'selection-change') {
        // Force re-render by updating a dummy state
        setScrollTop((prev) => prev);
      }
    });
    return unsubscribe;
  }, [core]);

  const handleScroll = (e: React.UIEvent<HTMLDivElement>) => {
    setScrollTop(e.currentTarget.scrollTop);
  };

  return (
    <div
      style={{ height: viewportHeight, overflowY: 'auto' }}
      onScroll={handleScroll}
    >
      <table>
        <thead>
          <tr>
            {core.getState().columns.map((col) => (
              <th key={col.key} style={{ width: col.width }}>
                {col.header}
              </th>
            ))}
          </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          {visibleRows.map((row) => (
            <Row
              key={row.id}
              row={row}
              columns={core.getState().columns}
              isSelected={core.getState().selectedRowIds.has(row.id)}
              onSelect={() => core.selectRow(row.id)}
            />
          ))}
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>
  );
}

const Row = React.memo(function Row<T extends { id: string }>({
  row,
  columns,
  isSelected,
  onSelect,
}: {
  row: T;
  columns: GridColumn<T>[];
  isSelected: boolean;
  onSelect: () => void;
}) {
  return (
    <tr
      onClick={onSelect}
      style={{ backgroundColor: isSelected ? '#e0f7fa' : 'transparent' }}
    >
      {columns.map((col) => (
        <td key={col.key}>{col.renderer ? col.renderer(row[col.key], row) : String(row[col.key])}</td>
      ))}
    </tr>
  );
});

5.2 Vue 

<!-- VueAdapter.vue -->
<template>
  <div ref="scrollContainer" class="grid" :style="{ height: viewportHeight + 'px' }">
    <table>
      <thead>
        <tr>
          <th v-for="col in columns" :key="col.key" :style="{ width: col.width + 'px' }">
            {{ col.header }}
          </th>
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr
          v-for="row in visibleRows"
          :key="row.id"
          :class="{ selected: isSelected(row.id) }"
          @click="core.selectRow(row.id)"
        >
          <td v-for="col in columns" :key="col.key">
            {{ col.renderer ? col.renderer(row[col.key], row) : row[col.key] }}
          </td>
        </tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>
</template>

<script setup lang="ts">
import { ref, computed, onMounted, onUnmounted } from 'vue';
import { GridCore } from './core/GridCore';

const props = defineProps<{
  core: GridCore<any>;
  viewportHeight: number;
}>();

const scrollTop = ref(0);
const scrollContainer = ref<HTMLElement | null>(null);

const columns = computed(() => props.core.getState().columns);
const visibleRows = computed(() =>
  props.core.getVisibleRows(scrollTop.value, props.viewportHeight)
);

const isSelected = (id: string) => props.core.getState().selectedRowIds.has(id);

const handleScroll = () => {
  if (scrollContainer.value) {
    scrollTop.value = scrollContainer.value.scrollTop;
  }
};

let unsubscribe: () => void;
onMounted(() => {
  unsubscribe = props.core.subscribe(() => {
    scrollTop.value = scrollTop.value; // trigger reactivity
  });
  scrollContainer.value?.addEventListener('scroll', handleScroll);
});

onUnmounted(() => {
  unsubscribe();
  scrollContainer.value?.removeEventListener('scroll', handleScroll);
});
</script>

5.3 Angular 

// angular-grid.component.ts
import { Component, Input, OnDestroy, OnInit, ChangeDetectionStrategy, ElementRef, ViewChild } from '@angular/core';
import { GridCore } from './core/GridCore';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-data-grid',
  template: `
    <div #scrollContainer class="grid" [style.height.px]="viewportHeight" (scroll)="onScroll()">
      <table>
        <thead>
          <tr>
            <th *ngFor="let col of columns" [style.width.px]="col.width">{{ col.header }}</th>
          </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr
            *ngFor="let row of visibleRows"
            [class.selected]="isSelected(row.id)"
            (click)="core.selectRow(row.id)"
          >
            <td *ngFor="let col of columns">
              {{ col.renderer ? col.renderer(row[col.key], row) : row[col.key] }}
            </td>
          </tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>
  `,
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
})
export class DataGridComponent<T extends { id: string }> implements OnInit, OnDestroy {
  @Input() core!: GridCore<T>;
  @Input() viewportHeight = 600;
  @ViewChild('scrollContainer') scrollContainer!: ElementRef<HTMLElement>;

  columns: GridColumn<T>[] = [];
  visibleRows: T[] = [];
  private unsubscribe: () => void = () => {};

  ngOnInit() {
    this.columns = this.core.getState().columns;
    this.updateVisibleRows();
    this.unsubscribe = this.core.subscribe(() => {
      this.updateVisibleRows();
    });
  }

  ngOnDestroy() {
    this.unsubscribe();
  }

  onScroll() {
    this.updateVisibleRows();
  }

  private updateVisibleRows() {
    const scrollTop = this.scrollContainer?.nativeElement.scrollTop ?? 0;
    this.visibleRows = this.core.getVisibleRows(scrollTop, this.viewportHeight);
  }

  isSelected(id: string) {
    return this.core.getState().selectedRowIds.has(id);
  }
}

6. Implementing the Grid: A Complete Example

Let's wire it all together with a concrete dataset. We'll generate 100,000 rows and render them in React (the same core works for Vue and Angular).

// main.tsx
import React from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { GridCore } from './core/GridCore';
import { DataGrid } from './ReactAdapter';

interface User {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  age: number;
}

const rows: User[] = Array.from({ length: 100_000 }, (_, i) => ({
  id: String(i),
  name: `User ${i}`,
  email: `user${i}@example.com`,
  age: Math.floor(Math.random() * 60) + 18,
}));

const columns = [
  { key: 'id', header: 'ID', width: 80, sortable: true },
  { key: 'name', header: 'Name', width: 200, sortable: true },
  { key: 'email', header: 'Email', width: 300 },
  { key: 'age', header: 'Age', width: 80, sortable: true },
] as const;

const core = new GridCore<User>(rows, columns, 40);

const App = () => (
  <div style={{ padding: '20px' }}>
    <h1>Scalable TypeScript Data Grid</h1>
    <button onClick={() => core.sortBy('age')}>Sort by Age</button>
    <DataGrid core={core} viewportHeight={600} />
  </div>
);

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(<App />);

This renders 100,000 rows in memory but only ~20 in the DOM. Sorting by age triggers a single core event, which re-renders only the visible window.

7. Performance Tuning and Best Practices

7.1 Use content-visibility: auto

CSS content-visibility: auto tells the browser to skip rendering off-screen content. Combined with virtualization, it reduces layout cost further.

.grid-row {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: 40px; /* matches row height */
}

7.2 Debounce Scroll Events

Scroll events fire too fast for React's setState to handle at 60fps. Use requestAnimationFrame to throttle:

let ticking = false;
const onScroll = (e: Event) => {
  if (!ticking) {
    requestAnimationFrame(() => {
      setScrollTop((e.target as HTMLElement).scrollTop);
      ticking = false;
    });
    ticking = true;
  }
};

7.3 Memoize Cell Renderers

Expensive cell renderers (e.g., formatting dates, computing badges) should be cached. Use a WeakMap keyed by row object to avoid recomputing on every scroll.

7.4 Avoid Recreating Column Arrays

Pass columns as a stable reference. If you define columns inline in the template, React will treat them as new on every render, breaking React.memo.

7.5 Use trackBy / key Correctly

Always provide a stable key (row.id) to help the framework identify which rows changed. Without it, frameworks will re-render all visible rows on every scroll.

7.6 Profile with DevTools

Use the Performance panel to check for layout thrash. If you see purple bars, you're reading layout properties (like offsetHeight) inside a scroll handler. Cache measurements instead.

8. Conclusion

A scalable data grid isn't about choosing the right framework—it's about separating concerns. Keep the data logic in a framework-agnostic TypeScript core, use virtualization to limit DOM nodes, and let each framework's adapter handle only the visible slice. With this architecture, 100,000 rows feel as smooth as 100.

If you want to see this pattern applied to real-world projects, check out Tamiz's Insights for more engineering deep-dives.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Why not just use a library like AG Grid or TanStack Table?

Libraries are great for generic needs, but they often bring their own rendering model and can be hard to customize. Building a core gives you full control over performance-critical paths and lets you integrate with any framework without fighting a library's abstractions. For very large datasets with complex interactions, a custom core is often worth the effort.

Q: How do I handle variable row heights?

Maintain a Map<rowId, height> and a prefix-sum array. On scroll, binary search for the start index using the cumulative offsets. After each row renders, measure its height and update the map. This is more complex but essential for grids with text wrapping or dynamic content.

Q: Does this work with server-side data?

Yes. The core only needs a slice of data. Replace getVisibleRows with an async fetch: when the scroll position crosses a threshold, request the next chunk from the server. The core's setRows method can append the new rows, and the adapter re-renders only the visible window.
