title: SIP: Security Immediate Plan for Java
description:
Building a secure software supply chain is often depicted as a monumental transformation of the existing practices. You need to redesign your CI/CD pipeline according to an established security framework such as SLSA, introduce provenance, implement zero trust principles, integrate security scanning tools, build a vulnerability management system, and do many more things. No wonder many teams postpone this task to better days with more time, larger security team, and a permission to rebuild the whole pipeline from scratch.
Indeed, a mature supply chain security program may take months to build, but the first meaningful improvements can be made much sooner and without tearing everything down. So where should a team start?
For Java teams, our answer is SIP: a Security Immediate Plan made of five controls that a technical leader can start implementing in hours rather than months. Each control strengthens the next step, from the code on a developer’s machine to the image released to production.

TL;DR — the SIP overview

  1. Isolate local AI coding agents.
  2. Freeze unvetted Java dependencies, build plugins, and annotation processors.
  3. Build the application in a hardened multi-stage container.
  4. Generate runtime and build-stage SBOMs and detailed provenance metadata.
  5. Scan every SBOM attached to the exact image digest and block findings under the runtime and build policies.

These five controls follow the Java software supply chain in order:

AI agent → Maven or Gradle dependencies → container build → attestations → vulnerability gate

The controls are intentionally small. Together, they give Java teams a practical starting point for securing both their application and the tools that build it.

Mohammad, one of the authors of this article, also created a portable SIP Agent Skill. You can tell a compatible AI coding agent to install it:

Install the SIP skill: https://github.com/ContainerSecurity-dev/sip-skill

The SIP Framework for Java

Here is the plan at a glance:

  1. Isolate local AI agents. Run coding agents in a sandboxed microVM with deny-by-default network access and host-managed secrets.
  2. Freeze unvetted build inputs. Pin Java dependencies and build plugins, reject snapshots and dynamic versions, and quarantine newly published artifacts for five days.
  3. Harden container builds. Compile in a JDK build stage and copy only the packaged application into a minimal, non-root JRE image.
  4. Generate SBOM and provenance attestations. Ask BuildKit to describe both the shipped runtime and the earlier Java build stages.
  5. Scan every attested inventory. Extract runtime and build-stage SBOMs from the immutable image digest, check their basic structure, and apply separate vulnerability policies.

The SIP Java companion repository contains a small Spring Boot application, the Dockerfiles below, and a script for scanning its SBOMs. We use Maven in the examples; Gradle teams can apply the same principles.

The workflow snippets illustrate the main steps. Full setup instructions, version pinning, and implementation details are in the companion repository.

1. Isolate Local AI Coding Agents

AI coding agents can read source code, execute build tools, install dependencies, edit CI workflows, and often even access credentials. Giving an agent unrestricted access to CI runner or a developer machine would mean that if an agent is compromised by a malicious prompt, the scope of its access will determine how much damage it can cause.

Therefore, a good security practice is to run an agent in an isolated execution environment with limited access to the rest of the system. Such an environment is called a sandbox. A sandbox does not prevent an agent from making a bad decision. Its goal is to reduce the blast radius if such a decision was made.

For Java projects, sandboxing may be especially relevant. Building a Java project could mean executing quite a lot of code like build scripts, plugins, code generators, etc. An AI Agent is an additional component that can decide when to execute that code. Plus, a Java project itself can integrate an AI agent using, for example, Spring AI or LangChain4j. If these in-built agents can execute commands, that will add to the issue we described.

Luckily, sandboxing is not a new technology, and there are a few ready solutions. For example, you can use Docker Sandboxes (sbx). Begin with a deny-by-default network policy:

sbx policy init deny-all

After that, allow only the destinations required for the task. For example, a Java project may need an AI provider, its source host, Maven Central, and the project’s approved artifact repository. This is how you can specify required destinations:

sbx policy allow network "api.openai.com,github.com,repo.maven.apache.org"

If your organization uses an internal Maven repository manager, allow that host instead of Maven Central. This ensures the build follows the same repository policy inside and outside the sandbox.

Store credentials through the sandbox rather than placing raw tokens in environment files that the agent can read:

sbx secret set github
sbx secret set artifact_repository

For Codex, OAuth can remain host-side:

sbx secret set openai --oauth
sbx run codex .

Note that hiding the credentials from an agent is only part of the deal. Even if an agent doesn’t see the credentials, it can still make authenticated requests using them. So apart from being hidden, credentials should also be short-lived and narrowly scoped.

2. Freeze Unvetted Java Build Inputs

Java builds execute more than the application’s dependencies. Maven plugins, Gradle plugins, annotation processors, compiler extensions, and test tooling can all run code during the build. A supply chain policy must therefore cover the entire build graph, not only the JAR files that ship with the application.

The sensible first step in implementing this policy is to gain visibility into the graph, pin the versions, and strengthen the trust paths. Apply these immediate rules to achieve that:

  • Pin dependency and plugin versions to limit unexpected changes. Avoid version ranges and selectors such as LATEST and RELEASE.
  • Reject SNAPSHOT dependencies in release builds: their contents can change without a new version number.
  • Commit and verify the Maven or Gradle wrapper, including its distribution checksum, so developers and CI use the same build tool.
  • Route downloads through an approved repository manager, including build plugins and annotation processors.
  • Quarantine new releases for five days to give the ecosystem time to spot problems. Allow reviewed exceptions for urgent security fixes.
  • Require checksums from a trusted source to detect altered downloads.

These controls reduce unexpected changes; they do not make every dependency safe or guarantee reproducible builds. Keep the sandbox from control one in place when running build code.

Maven has no built-in five-day release delay. Enforce that policy at your repository proxy, before artifacts reach the build. The same proxy should serve developer machines, CI, and container builds.

The artifact repositories must first be defined centrally by a responsible team. After that, they can be enforced in the build tool. For example, if you use Maven, configure a single approved mirror in the CI settings.xml:

<settings xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/SETTINGS/1.2.0"
          xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
          xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/SETTINGS/1.2.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/settings-1.2.0.xsd">
  <mirrors>
    <mirror>
      <id>approved-repository</id>
      <name>Approved and quarantined Java artifacts</name>
      <url>https://packages.example.com/maven</url>
      <mirrorOf>*</mirrorOf>
    </mirror>
  </mirrors>
</settings>

The mirror sends dependency and plugin requests to the approved repository; the repository enforces the quarantine. Use the same settings inside and outside Docker. The wrapper also downloads Maven itself, so route that download through the proxy with MVNW_REPOURL.

With those settings supplied by CI, run the familiar build command from the Maven project directory:

./mvnw --settings "$MAVEN_SETTINGS_FILE" --strict-checksums \
  --batch-mode --no-transfer-progress verify

The companion setup guide covers credentials, wrapper verification, and cache handling.

For Gradle, enable dependency locking, commit the lockfiles, enable dependency verification, and run with a trusted wrapper. The immediate rule remains the same:

Admit reviewed inputs before executing build-time code.

3. Harden the Java Container Build

The next step is to control what becomes part of the production image. Production images often include components not required by the running application: unnecessary OS packages, a full JDK with a compiler and development tools, build time dependencies. The bloat leads to increased attack surface and challenged vulnerability management. Besides, a package manager and other download utilities in a production image give an attacker a chance to install malicious packages.

Hardened images, a solution that has recently been gaining traction, aim to reduce these risks by providing a minimal base image with low-to-zero CVEs at the moment of release and provenance data. These images are continuously updated by the vendor to patch known CVEs. Migration to hardened images will help you drastically reduce the attack surface and get a more controlled runtime environment.

There are several offerings of hardened images. In the examples below, we will use Docker Hardened Images and BellSoft Hardened Images to illustrate the approach — both products are free to use with optional commercial support.

To minimize the Java production image and get the most out of hardened images it is recommended to use Docker multi-stage builds, where you compile the application with JDK at the first stage, and then transfer the JAR file to a JRE base image, leaving Maven, the compiler, and other build tools behind.

Docker Hardened Images (DHI) provide maintained, minimal images for application runtimes and build tools, together with SBOMs and build provenance. Separate development and runtime variants let you keep the tools needed for compilation out of production. In Docker’s Java pattern, the dhi.io/maven:...-dev image supplies Maven and a JDK, while the dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:... runtime contains only what is needed to run the application. That runtime has no package manager or shell and runs as a non-root user by default.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
ARG BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_STAGE=true
FROM dhi.io/maven:3-jdk25-alpine3.22-dev AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY --chmod=755 mvnw ./mvnw
COPY .mvn/ .mvn/
COPY pom.xml ./
COPY src/ src/
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=maven_settings,required=true \
    --mount=type=secret,id=maven_repository_url,env=MVNW_REPOURL,required=true \
    ./mvnw --settings /run/secrets/maven_settings --strict-checksums \
      --batch-mode --no-transfer-progress -Dmaven.repo.local=/build/repository verify

FROM dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:25-alpine3.22 AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /build/target/application.jar /app/application.jar
USER 10001:10001
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/application.jar"]

Adjust the JAR name to match the project. If the application is a Spring Boot executable JAR, consider extracting its layers so that application classes and third-party dependencies form separate container layers.

BellSoft Hardened Images (BHI) are built on Alpaquita Linux, BellSoft’s lightweight Linux distribution. Their Java images include Liberica JDK Lite, a compact OpenJDK distribution, with JDK and JRE options for building and running applications. BellSoft offers glibc and musl variants, plus non-root and distroless images; the distroless variants omit the shell and retain only essential runtime components. This gives Java teams a choice of small runtime images suited to their application’s requirements.

For Spring Boot, we can also separate the application’s classes from its dependencies. The following example combines layered extraction with BellSoft’s non-root JRE image.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
ARG BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_STAGE=true
FROM bellsoft/liberica-runtime-container:jdk-25-glibc AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY --chmod=755 mvnw ./mvnw
COPY .mvn/ .mvn/
COPY pom.xml ./
COPY src/ src/
# Both settings and the wrapper's repository override are mandatory.
# Keep downloaded artifacts in the stage filesystem for SBOM discovery.
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=maven_settings,required=true \
    --mount=type=secret,id=maven_repository_url,env=MVNW_REPOURL,required=true \
    ./mvnw --settings /run/secrets/maven_settings --strict-checksums \
      --batch-mode --no-transfer-progress -Dmaven.repo.local=/build/repository verify

FROM bellsoft/hardened-liberica-runtime-container:jre-25-glibc AS optimizer
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /build/target/application.jar application.jar
RUN ["java", "-Djarmode=tools", "-jar", "application.jar", "extract", "--layers", "--destination", "extracted"]

FROM bellsoft/hardened-liberica-runtime-container:jre-25-nonroot-glibc AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=optimizer /app/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=optimizer /app/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=optimizer /app/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=optimizer /app/extracted/application/ ./
USER 10001:10001
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/application.jar"]

The first stage compiles the project. The second extracts the JAR into layers. The final stage copies those layers into a non-root runtime and starts the generated application.jar. When only application code changes, Docker can reuse the dependency layers, reducing the amount of data transferred during an update.

Both Dockerfiles use the wrapper and repository settings from control two. Supply those settings as build secrets, and authenticate to the image registries as needed; the companion repository shows the commands. The BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_STAGE argument connects the build to our next control.

4. Generate SBOM and Provenance Attestations

A Software Bill of Materials, or SBOM, is an inventory of the components in an artifact. It helps answer a practical question: when a vulnerability is announced, where are we using the affected component?

Provenance records how the image was built and which inputs were used. Here we generate that record; signing and verifying it is a further step for establishing trust in the builder.

An SBOM created only by inspecting the final Java image can miss the JDK, Maven plugins, and other tooling used in an earlier build stage. BuildKit can generate the SBOM during the build, while those stages still exist.

After authenticating to the target registry, build and push a candidate identified by the Git commit:

- name: Build and attest Java candidate
  id: build
  uses: docker/build-push-action@<PINNED-SHA>
  with:
    context: examples/java
    file: examples/java/Dockerfile.bellsoft
    platforms: linux/amd64
    no-cache: true
    secrets: |
      "maven_settings=${{ secrets.MAVEN_SETTINGS }}"
      "maven_repository_url=${{ vars.APPROVED_MAVEN_REPOSITORY }}"
    tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
    sbom: true
    provenance: mode=max
    outputs: type=image,push=true,oci-mediatypes=true,oci-artifact=true

BuildKit stores the attestations alongside the image. sbom: true requests the inventory, and provenance: mode=max requests detailed build metadata. Because that metadata can include build-argument values, pass credentials through secrets, as shown above.

The action also returns an immutable digest:

${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}

Use that digest from this point onward. A tag can point to a different image later; the digest identifies the candidate you actually built.

Because the Dockerfile declares BUILDKIT_SBOM_SCAN_STAGE=true, BuildKit also scans the earlier Java build stage. This matters because a vulnerable or compromised Maven plugin, compiler, or JDK can influence the application even when it is absent from the runtime image.

There is one useful trap to understand: a BuildKit cache mount is outside the stage filesystem being scanned. If Maven stores its downloads in a cache mount, build-only dependencies can disappear from the inventory even though they influenced the build.

Our examples keep Maven downloads in the build-stage filesystem so the scanner can inspect them. The final image stays small because it receives only the packaged application. If you need cache mounts for performance, add a complementary dependency inventory; the companion guide explains the tradeoff.

5. Scan the Attested SBOM

Now turn the inventory into a release decision. Retrieve the SBOMs attached to the candidate’s digest and scan both the runtime and the earlier build stages. Scanning only the final image would miss the Maven plugins and other tools we set out to protect.

The companion gate script collects those inventories, checks that the required documents are present, and runs Trivy on each one. After installing a pinned Trivy version, call it from CI for the BellSoft example:

- name: Scan runtime and build inventories
  run: |
    python3 scripts/scan-attested-sboms.py \
      "ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}" \
      --platform linux/amd64 --min-build-sboms 2 \
      --require-build-name sbom-build --require-build-name sbom-optimizer \
      --runtime-severity CRITICAL --build-severity HIGH,CRITICAL

This example blocks fixable Critical vulnerabilities in the runtime and fixable High or Critical vulnerabilities in the build environment. A vulnerable build tool matters even when it is not shipped to users. Missing inventories or scanner errors also stop the release.

This is a starting policy: other findings still need review, and scanner coverage must match your packages and operating system. The companion repository documents the scanner limitations found in testing and how to adapt the gate to other Dockerfiles and platforms.

Before promotion, also start the candidate and check that the application responds. A clean scan is not a substitute for a working application.

Only after the gate and application checks pass should the candidate receive a release tag:

- name: Promote Java image
  run: |
    docker buildx imagetools create \
      --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest \
      ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}

This promotes the existing candidate with its attestations. It does not rebuild the application after the security check, so the release is the artifact you tested.

Putting It Together

The resulting release chain is:

Sandbox the coding agent
→ quarantine and verify Java build inputs
→ compile in a hardened JDK stage
→ run from a minimal non-root JRE image
→ attest the build and runtime inventory
→ scan runtime and build SBOMs attached to the immutable digest
→ promote only the artifact that passed.

Make each step visible in CI so a failure stops the release at the right point. The companion repository provides the implementation details, including pinning tools and protecting credentials.

Agent Prompt

If your coding client supports Agent Skills, install the SIP skill and give the agent this prompt inside the Java repository you want to secure:

$sip SIP it up! Adapt and implement controls ii through v for this Java project. Ask questions when in doubt.

Run the agent inside the sandbox from control one. Review every proposed dependency, Maven or Gradle plugin, Dockerfile change, and CI permission before merging it.

Conclusion

SIP is not a complete software supply chain security program. It is an immediate plan for reducing the most obvious risks while creating a trustworthy path from Java source code to a released container image.

For Java teams, that means looking beyond application JARs. The JDK, Maven or Gradle plugins, annotation processors, base images, build stages, attestations, and release tags are all part of the same chain.

Start with this connected path, test its failure cases, and extend it with verified provenance and ongoing vulnerability management.

title: Empowering AI Agents with agent-desktop
description:
A New Approach to the Problem

The agent-desktop repository addresses the challenge of enabling AI agents to effectively interact with desktop applications across different operating systems. By leveraging the OS accessibility tree, it allows agents to read and operate applications without pixel matching, which is often unreliable.

What is it and How it Works

agent-desktop is a CLI and C library developed for macOS, Windows, and Linux. It creates snapshots of the desktop environment, returning JSON representations of all elements an agent can interact with. The agent executes actions on these elements and verifies changes without requiring pixel recognition. Each CLI call operates in its own process, ensuring that headless calls do not interfere with the foreground application.

Key Features:

  • Cross-Platform Compatibility: Works on macOS, Windows, and Linux.
  • Snapshot Functionality: Returns a JSON object with references for every interactive element, allowing agents to perform actions and verify their results.
  • No Pixel Matching Required: The system uses the accessibility API, which is more reliable than pixel-based methods.
  • Privacy Considerations: Snapshots and outputs may contain sensitive data; users should manage this information carefully.

Key Capabilities & Developer Onboarding

Installation is straightforward via npm, Bun, Yarn, or pnpm:

npm install -g agent-desktop
agent-desktop version

For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, users can download the native archive from GitHub Releases and keep its helper beside the executable.

Here’s a quick start example showing how to interact with the Finder app on macOS:

agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i      # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8            # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i      # observe again to verify

The JSON response includes details about the application state, making it easier for developers to understand the environment.

Who Should Use It & Integration Scenarios

agent-desktop is ideal for developers building AI agents that need to automate desktop tasks across multiple operating systems. It is particularly useful for applications requiring interaction with GUI elements without direct user input. However, it may not be suitable for scenarios demanding real-time visual feedback or where pixel precision is critical.

Limitations & Trade-offs:

  • Platform-Specific Permissions: On macOS, accessibility permissions are required, which can add complexity to deployment.
  • Headless Operation Constraints: Although the system is headless by default, it requires a graphical session on Linux, which can limit usability in certain environments.
  • No Foreground Activation: Actions performed do not activate the foreground application, which may not align with all automation needs.

Community Pulse: What Developers Are Saying

Community discussions indicate a growing interest in the agent-desktop project, especially following the recent release of version v1.0.2 on October 30, 2026, which introduced various documentation improvements and clarified installation permissions. Users appreciate the simplicity of the API and the potential for integrating AI-driven workflows into desktop environments.

Our Read

Overall, agent-desktop presents a compelling solution for AI agent interactions with desktop applications, emphasizing cross-platform compatibility and privacy considerations. While it offers significant capabilities, potential users should be mindful of its limitations, particularly regarding permissions and headless operation constraints.

title: From Core Java to Spring Boot: When the Code Works, but the "Big Picture" is Still Loading
description:
Learning software engineering is an absolute ride. Some days you feel like your coding IQ is increasing exponentially; other days, you wish you were just born with all the skills already downloaded into your brain!

Lately, I’ve been making the transition from core Java OOP concepts into Spring Boot.

I get the concepts… but at the same time, I don’t quite get them yet. Funny, right?

💻 Where I’m At Right Now

I've been following along with structured literature, working through hands-on code examples line by line. Right now, I'm exploring Spring Context configurations, * lazy * initialization (*@lazy), *component stereotypes, and fetching beans dynamically via ApplicationContext.

🧠 The "Real-World Project" Gap

Even though the book examples run smoothly, I find myself pausing and asking:

"How does this actually map to a real, production-ready system?"

Because textbook exercises are isolated, it can be tricky to discern why a specific design choice is made until you’re building something substantial from scratch. I suspect the missing bridge is simply experience—I haven't built a massive end-to-end production application in Spring yet.

Despite the hurdles, the process has been genuinely fun. Watching how framework abstractions work after months of pure Java feels like discovering magic spells.

❓ To the Spring Devs out there: What was your turning point?

For anyone who has crossed this bridge before:

When did the "Spring Way" of thinking finally click for you? Was it during your first full project, or did a specific concept make it all fall into place?

What small starter project would you recommend for bridging the gap between textbook examples and real-world backend architecture?

If you're currently in the middle of learning Spring too, let me know how your journey is going in the comments below!

title: Password Reset Deliveries: 3 Receipt Template Controls for Email Domain Reputation
description:
Keep receipt templates under an explicit approval owner, and make sender-domain review part of releasing the receipt sent after payment settles. The deciding constraint is that receipt content, recipient selection, and sender identity have different owners, although their consequences can meet at the same domain reputation used to evaluate password reset mail.

TL;DR: Low email domain reputation can cause password reset messages to land in spam or be rejected. Providers consider domain reputation when evaluating spam; frequent invalid recipients and missing SPF, DKIM, or DMARC reduce trust. For an e-commerce receipt pipeline, adopt 3 controls: freeze an approved template revision, record its sender-domain review, and retain one auditable receipt intent per settlement. These are application safeguards, not an inbox-placement guarantee.

How does email domain reputation affect password reset deliveries?

The connection is the sender domain. If receipts and account recovery use the same domain, a reputation problem matters to both workflows, although settlement initiates one and an account holder initiates the other. Correct payment accounting does not establish successful receipt delivery. A legitimate reset request can still produce a message that the receiving system rejects or classifies as spam.

Protect the domain.

Frequent sending to invalid addresses lowers reputation and can lead to rejections; bulk password reset sending from a domain with poor reputation can also lead to blacklisting. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC contribute to trust, but publishing authentication records does not remove the need for regular monitoring and a clean recipient list. Nor does a domain verification result establish that the next message will reach an inbox. A template review therefore needs to identify the intended sender and audience alongside the visible receipt wording.

Consider the illustrative order order-284, with settlement settlement-284 and receipt revision receipt-r3. These are application identifiers. An editor changing the receipt's wording should not implicitly acquire permission to change the sender domain or broaden its recipients into a campaign audience, because those changes can affect delivery outside the receipt workflow. The proposed control is a separate approval decision for each such change.

That distinction matters most during retries: selecting the latest template can silently change the content associated with an already recorded settlement. Freeze the revision when creating the intent, then preserve the approval evidence that justified using it.

Decision record: bind template ownership to settlement evidence

The decision is to maintain an application-owned approval record even when a provider hosts the editable template. Record the immutable revision, sender domain, approval owner, and approved purpose; when payment settles, bind the receipt intent to that record. Hosting the template does not determine who has authority to approve it.

There are 3 invariants. A receipt requires settlement evidence; each settlement has one logical receipt intent; every dispatch decision identifies the approved revision and sender domain. An approval change creates a new revision rather than rewriting the historical meaning of a receipt. These are proposed application rules, not guarantees attributed to a mail provider.

The failure boundaries are equally explicit. Settlement establishes the financial event. The application records the receipt intent. The sender accepts a submission. The receiving system evaluates the message. Evidence from one boundary cannot prove success at the next, and an exactly-once mindset depends on keeping those states distinct in the audit trail rather than calling every accepted submission delivered.

A timeout is ambiguous.

Retrying an uncertain submission as a new business event can create another receipt, while marking it delivered can hide a missing message. Keep a stable intent identifier, use a verified provider idempotency contract where available, and reconcile uncertain outcomes before authorizing a fresh submission. Local deduplication alone cannot make a network side effect atomic with a database transaction. The policy must also specify who reviews suppression and rejection evidence before another attempt is permitted.

Compare services by the ownership contract you can enforce

Postmark, Amazon SES, and Twilio SendGrid are real alternatives for this evaluation. The useful comparison is the approval evidence the commerce team can preserve, rather than a claim that changing vendors bypasses domain reputation. The table specifies evaluation paths; it does not assert unverified account permissions, retention periods, or delivery rankings.

Candidate Template ownership evaluation Suitable boundary and trade-off
Postmark Start with its transactional email best practices and assess how receipt changes enter the team's approval process. A sensible evaluation for a transaction-focused workflow; published guidance does not itself prove your approval and audit requirements are met.
Amazon SES Review its template documentation against application-owned rendering and release controls. Consider it when the backend team wants to govern the rendering pipeline; require evidence that an earlier approved receipt remains reproducible after edits.
Twilio SendGrid Review its transactional template workflow against the handoff between content editors and backend maintainers. Consider it when that editorial handoff is central; confirm the available permissions and revision evidence before delegating approval authority.
Unified backend API One key, one wallet, one bill cover backend services rather than just email; the platform spans 295 routes across 20 modules. Fits an application-owned approval ledger when the team also operates surrounding backend capabilities. A single credential inventory and consolidated invoice reduce credential handoffs and billing reconciliation across that workflow; these advantages do not establish inbox placement or confer content approval authority.

Infrai offers a plain REST API, no SDK to install, one key, and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. Anything that can send an HTTP request can call it, so the receipt worker does not need a provider client library. Separately, the shared credential and consolidated invoice let the receipt team maintain one credential inventory and reconcile backend-service billing together. Public, self-describing discovery also lets a reviewer inspect the sending schema without a key, before approving the worker's integration contract.

The distinction between those last two benefits is practical. HTTP integration concerns how the receipt worker calls a service. One key and one bill concern operational ownership: a single API key spans 295 routes across 20 modules, while unified billing gives the team one invoice to reconcile for those backend services. In a receipt workflow that also uses surrounding capabilities, this reduces credential handoffs and separate invoice reconciliation; it does not replace the receipt approval ledger. For an email-only purchase, the broader platform benefit carries less weight. A template workflow that the actual approval owner can operate should dominate the choice.

Ask every candidate the same question: can an auditor reconstruct the approved content, its approver, the sender domain, and the evidence behind the dispatch decision? Where documentation leaves that unanswered, test the proposed workflow before adoption. An editable template is not sufficient evidence.

Compliance needs its own review. Domain authentication does not establish residency, consent, or the legality of a regional delivery arrangement; obtain affirmative evidence for the jurisdiction and provider combination the business requires. Procurement should also establish whether polling meets reconciliation needs, who owns email recovery codes, and whether SMTP relay, additional channels, scheduled-message cancellation, and tag-level accounting are requirements. For an SMS fallback, assign geographic abuse controls and country-level spending cutoffs explicitly. None follows automatically from template ownership.

Critical path: preserve the decision before sending

First inspect the sending contract. Public discovery requires no key and exposes request and response schemas; the read-only Go program below uses environment-based Bearer authentication to demonstrate the eventual integration boundary. Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented HTTPS API base ending in /v1, and INFRAI_API_KEY to your credential. The program retrieves the email sending schema, makes at most 3 attempts, and defers to an operator if a rate-limit delay exceeds one minute. It does not send mail or calculate reputation.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    base := strings.TrimRight(os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL"), "/")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    u, err := url.Parse(base)
    if err != nil || u.Scheme != "https" || u.Host == "" || key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set an HTTPS API base URL and API key")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, base+"/discovery/email.send", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 2<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 60 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("retry deferred: %s", value)
                }
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if until, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
                delay = time.Until(until)
            }
            if delay < 0 {
                delay = 0
            }
            if delay > time.Minute {
                return fmt.Errorf("retry deferred: %s", value)
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, data)
        }
        _, err = os.Stdout.Write(data)
        return err
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The following complete Go program models the approval boundary locally. It records one intent for a settled payment, recognizes a repeated settlement without replacing its frozen revision, and rejects a conflicting order identifier. Its identifiers, review flag, and data structures belong to the example application; the review flag represents an operator's approval, not a DNS-derived reputation score.

No email leaves.

package main

import "fmt"

type Settlement struct {
    ID      string
    OrderID string
    Settled bool
}

type Approval struct {
    Revision string
    Domain   string
    Owner    string
    Reviewed bool
}

type Intent struct {
    ID       string
    OrderID  string
    Revision string
    Domain   string
    Owner    string
}

type Ledger struct {
    Intents map[string]Intent
    Audit   []string
}

func (l *Ledger) Decide(s Settlement, a Approval) string {
    id := "receipt:" + s.ID
    if s.ID == "" || s.OrderID == "" {
        l.Audit = append(l.Audit, "blocked: missing settlement identity")
        return "blocked"
    }
    if previous, ok := l.Intents[id]; ok {
        if previous.OrderID != s.OrderID {
            l.Audit = append(l.Audit, id+": conflicting order")
            return "conflict"
        }
        l.Audit = append(l.Audit, id+": duplicate; retained "+previous.Revision)
        return "duplicate"
    }
    if !s.Settled || !a.Reviewed || a.Revision == "" ||
        a.Domain == "" || a.Owner == "" {
        l.Audit = append(l.Audit, id+": blocked by settlement or approval")
        return "blocked"
    }
    l.Intents[id] = Intent{
        ID: id, OrderID: s.OrderID, Revision: a.Revision,
        Domain: a.Domain, Owner: a.Owner,
    }
    l.Audit = append(l.Audit, id+": approved "+a.Revision+" by "+a.Owner)
    return "created"
}

func main() {
    l := Ledger{Intents: make(map[string]Intent)}
    s := Settlement{ID: "settlement-284", OrderID: "order-284", Settled: true}
    a := Approval{
        Revision: "receipt-r3", Domain: "receipts.example.com",
        Owner: "receipt-reviewer", Reviewed: true,
    }
    fmt.Println(l.Decide(s, a))
    a.Revision = "receipt-r4"
    fmt.Println(l.Decide(s, a))
    s.OrderID = "order-conflict"
    fmt.Println(l.Decide(s, a))
    for _, entry := range l.Audit {
        fmt.Println(entry)
    }
}

This is a sequential, in-memory demonstration. A production implementation needs a durable unique constraint on the receipt intent and a transaction that records the intent and its audit evidence together; otherwise two workers can both observe absence and create competing decisions. Preserve the actual approved content, or an immutable reference to it, as well as the revision identifier. An identifier pointing at mutable content cannot reproduce a historical receipt.

After that commit, a worker can submit the frozen intent under the chosen provider's documented contract. Keep submission attempts and subsequent delivery evidence separate from the approval record, and do not log reset tokens or unnecessary recipient data in the audit trail. Correctness includes the retention and access limits on that evidence.

Rejected option: let every retry render the current template

The rejected design lets the content editor update a template in place while each retry loads its current version. It removes the engineering work of retaining approved revisions, but it also allows one settlement's receipt to change during reconciliation, which defeats the decision record this workflow requires. A sender-domain change becomes particularly difficult to explain after the original content has been overwritten.

Mutable templates can still be appropriate for a disposable preview whose purpose is to show the latest draft. They are a poor default for reconstructing an issued receipt. Keep that preview convenience outside the settlement path, and evaluate account-recovery delivery using domain health and receiving-side evidence rather than template approval alone.

References

  • Postmark, Transactional Email Best Practices
  • Amazon SES, Sending personalized email using templates
  • Twilio SendGrid, Dynamic Templates
  • SPF specification
  • DKIM specification
  • DMARC specification

title: Savor: A Food Delivery Template for Restaurants and Local Fleets
description:
Delivery platforms take a big cut of every order, often between 15% and 30%. For a restaurant running on thin margins, that cut can be the whole profit. That's why so many restaurants, small chains and local delivery startups want their own ordering app, and why most of them give up when they see what it takes: a customer app, a kitchen screen, a courier app, an operations console, payments, maps and a server that ties it together.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Savor is all of that in one Java project. It's the third of this week's templates, after Skirmish and Parley, and it's a sibling of Wayline, the ride-hailing app from last week. Pick the food-delivery template in the Initializr, set your name and package, and you have a working delivery service. The source is under MIT-0, so the business you build on it is yours.

Restaurants near you.
Checkout.
Live tracking.

One app, four roles

Savor is a single app. The account's role decides the first screen: a customer sees restaurants, a merchant sees the order queue, a courier sees the delivery screen and an administrator sees the operations console. One build to publish, one code base to maintain.

Role What they can do
Customer Browse restaurants that deliver to their address, build a cart, pay by card or cash, tip, track the courier on a map and get refunds
Restaurant Accept or reject orders, mark them ready and see the queue update live
Courier Apply with documents, go online, accept offers, navigate to the pickup and the customer, and track earnings
Administrator Watch the dashboard and trends, review courier applications and manage accounts

The kitchen's queue.
A courier's offer.
The operations dashboard.

The hard parts are already handled

The screens are the visible part of a delivery service. The business rules underneath are where projects usually stall. Savor has them in place.

Money moves at the right time. The card is authorized for the total when the order is placed and captured when the food is delivered. A rejected or canceled order releases the hold, so customers are never charged for food they didn't get. From Payments.java:

/// Holds an order's total on the customer's card as the order is placed,
/// with no transaction open. Nothing is taken until the order arrives
/// ([#settle]); an order that never does lets the hold go ([#release]).
public String authorize(String orderId, String username, String methodId, long amountCents,
        String currency) throws IOException {
    if (CASH.equals(methodId)) {
        return CASH;
    }

With Stripe, cards are added on Stripe's own page, so card numbers never touch your app or your server. Other providers plug in through the PaymentProvider interface.

Orders and deliveries can't get confused. An order and its delivery are separate state machines that share an id. Every transition is a conditional update that names the states it can come from, so when a kitchen and a customer act at the same moment, only one of them wins.

Maps without an API key bill. Tracking uses OpenFreeMap vector tiles, OSRM routing and Photon place search. Updates arrive over a WebSocket as they happen, so the customer watches the courier move.

Everything Wayline learned, Savor reuses. Accounts, sign-in with phone verification, SMS and push providers, the live channel, the map, billing, the operations console, the database and hosting all come from Wayline. A delivery is, almost literally, a Wayline ride with a stop at the restaurant.

Make it yours

The guide covers the common ways to reshape Savor:

  • A single restaurant or a small chain. Turn off merchant sign-up and run Savor as your own branded ordering app. This is the case where avoiding platform commissions pays off fastest.
  • Pickup and scheduled orders, for when you don't want couriers at all, or not yet.
  • Your own couriers instead of a gig fleet.
  • Beyond food: groceries, pharmacy, flowers, laundry, anything that moves from a shop to a door. Point an AI agent at the project and describe the business. The model, the roles and the flow are already there.

The colors and corner radius are CSS variables in theme.css, the text is in five languages, and the SMS provider is a setting (savor.sms.provider takes Twilio, Vonage or MessageBird).

Try it

The development profile simulates kitchens and couriers, so you can place an order and watch it move through the whole flow with nothing installed. Use card 4242 4242 4242 4242 to pay, or 4000 0000 0000 0002 to see a decline. The Savor page has the overview, and the user's guide and implementor's guide go deeper.

Tomorrow the series moves from apps to the framework features they pushed into Codename One, starting with More of the Java API, and an Experiment With Unity Games.
